1. As you go DOWN a group (like from Sodium to Potassium), the atoms get an extra shell of electrons. They get bigger! So, Potassium (K) is bigger than Sodium (Na). Because K is bigger, its outermost electron is farther from the nucleus, making it easier to lose. So, K > Na in metallic character.
2. As you go ACROSS a period from left to right (like Na, Mg, Al), the atoms actually get smaller. Why? Because you are adding more positive protons to the nucleus, which pulls the electron shells in tighter. Sodium is bigger than Magnesium (Mg), which is bigger than Aluminum (Al). Because Na is the biggest of those three, it's the most generous. So, Na > Mg > Al.

Putting it all together, Potassium is the biggest and most generous, followed by Sodium, then Magnesium, and finally Aluminum. Therefore, the correct order is K > Na > Mg > Al. You've got this!

questions.Question: Q16. Match List - I with List - II
questions.Hint: Since the exact items weren't printed in the text, let's learn how to match the four blocks of the periodic table (s, p, d, f) to their famous family nicknames!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Sometimes, test papers get a little messy and cut off the actual lists! But don't worry, I know exactly the kind of matching question they love to ask here. They usually want you to match the different 'blocks' of the periodic table to their special names. Let's build it together!

Imagine List I has the blocks: A) s-block, B) p-block, C) d-block, D) f-block.
And List II has their identities: 1) Transition Elements, 2) Inner Transition Elements, 3) Alkali & Alkaline Earth Metals, 4) Representative Elements (Non-metals/Metalloids).

Let's break down the neighborhood of the Periodic Table:
- The s-block (A): These are the very first two columns on the left. They are extremely reactive metals that love to explode in water. We call them the Alkali and Alkaline Earth metals (matches with 3). 
- The p-block (B): This is the block on the far right side. It’s the most diverse neighborhood! It has metals, metalloids, non-metals, and the super-chill noble gases. Together with the s-block, they are called the 'Main Group' or 'Representative Elements' (matches with 4).
- The d-block (C): These are the sturdy metals in the middle, like Iron, Gold, and Copper. They transition the gap between the left and right sides of the table, so they are famous as the 'Transition Elements' (matches with 1).
- The f-block (D): These are the two long rows floating at the bottom of the map. They actually belong tucked inside the d-block, so we call them the 'Inner Transition Elements' (matches with 2).

Understanding these families makes navigating the periodic table feel like walking through a city where you know every neighborhood. The correct matching logic here would be A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2. Keep this map in your head, and you'll never get lost in chemistry!

questions.Question: Q17. Nd²⁺ = _______
questions.Hint: Remember the 'First In, First Out' rule for the 6s orbital! When forming positive ions, electrons are always removed from the outermost shell (highest 'n' value) first.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's figure out the secret code—the electron configuration—for the Neodymium ion, Nd²⁺. 

First, we need to know how many electrons a neutral Neodymium (Nd) atom has. Its atomic number is 60. Writing out 60 electrons would take forever, so we use a shortcut. We look at the closest Noble Gas that comes before it, which is Xenon (Xe) with 54 electrons. Xenon is like our 'save point' in a video game.

Now we have 6 more electrons to place (60 - 54 = 6). After Xenon, we are in the 6th period of the periodic table. The rules of energy levels (the Aufbau principle) tell us to fill the 6s orbital first. 
So, 2 electrons go into 6s: [Xe] 6s².
We still have 4 electrons left! Because Neodymium is in the lanthanide series (the f-block), these remaining 4 electrons dive deep into the 4f orbital. 
So, the neutral Nd atom is: [Xe] 4f⁴ 6s².

Now for the tricky part! The question asks for Nd²⁺. The '2+' means the atom has lost 2 electrons. But which ones does it lose? The ones in 4f or 6s?

Here is a golden rule to remember forever: Electrons are always removed from the outermost shell first. The outermost shell is the one with the highest number. Since 6 (from 6s) is bigger than 4 (from 4f), the 6s shell is on the 'outside' of the atom. Even though 4f fills up later, it is buried deeper inside the atom.

So, the atom hands over its two 6s electrons first. 
[Xe] 4f⁴ 6s² minus 2 electrons gives us [Xe] 4f⁴.

And there you have it! The Nd²⁺ ion has the configuration [Xe] 4f⁴. You've just mastered one of the most common traps in chemistry!

questions.Question: Q18. Which of the following elements have half-filled f-orbitals in their ground state? (Given: atomic number Sm=62; Eu=63; Tb=65; Gd=64, Pm=61) A. Sm B. Eu C. Tb D. Gd E. Pm
questions.Hint: An f-subshell can hold a maximum of 14 electrons. 'Half-filled' means it has exactly 7 electrons (f⁷). Subtract the Xenon core (54) and 2 for the 6s orbital, and see who has 7 left over!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic question about stability and symmetry! In the atomic world, symmetry means peace and quiet. An orbital is like a school bus. The 's' bus has 1 seat, the 'p' bus has 3 seats, the 'd' bus has 5 seats, and the giant 'f' bus has 7 seats. 

Since each seat can hold 2 electrons, the f-bus holds a maximum of 14 electrons. 
Now, electrons are a bit antisocial at first. They prefer to sit alone before they are forced to pair up. If exactly 7 electrons get on the f-bus, everyone gets their own seat. This perfect symmetry makes the atom incredibly stable! We call this a 'half-filled f-orbital' (4f⁷).

Let's test our five candidates to see who gets exactly 7 electrons in their 4f orbital. We start from the Xenon core (54 electrons) and remember that 2 electrons usually go into the 6s orbital first.

1. Samarium (Sm, 62): 62 - 54 (Xe) = 8 valence electrons. 2 go to 6s, leaving 6 for 4f. Configuration: [Xe] 4f⁶ 6s². Not half-filled.
2. Europium (Eu, 63): 63 - 54 = 9 valence electrons. 2 go to 6s, leaving 7 for 4f. Configuration: [Xe] 4f⁷ 6s². BINGO! Half-filled!
3. Gadolinium (Gd, 64): 64 - 54 = 10 valence electrons. You'd expect [Xe] 4f⁸ 6s². But wait! Having 8 electrons means one seat has a pair, ruining the beautiful symmetry of 7. So, one electron jumps into the slightly higher 5d orbital just to keep the 4f orbital perfectly half-filled! Configuration: [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s². BINGO! Half-filled!
4. Terbium (Tb, 65): 65 - 54 = 11 valence electrons. Configuration: [Xe] 4f⁹ 6s². Not half-filled.
5. Promethium (Pm, 61): 61 - 54 = 7 valence electrons. Configuration: [Xe] 4f⁵ 6s². Not half-filled.

So, Europium (Eu) and Gadolinium (Gd) are the special elements with perfectly half-filled f-orbitals. Therefore, the answer is B and D only. Isn't it amazing how atoms bend the rules just to feel comfortable?

questions.Chapter: The s and p Block Elements
questions.Question: Q19. Which one of the following elements will remain as liquid inside pure boiling water?
questions.Hint: Pure water boils at 100°C. You are looking for a metal that melts at a temperature lower than 100°C so that the hot water completely melts it into a liquid puddle!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
When we think of metals, we usually think of hard, solid materials like iron bars or copper wires. To melt them, you need massive furnaces that reach thousands of degrees! 

But not all metals are built the same. The question asks what would happen if we dropped a metal into pure boiling water. Pure water boils at exactly 100°C (at normal atmospheric pressure). So, the puzzle is asking: 'Which of these metals has a melting point lower than 100°C?'

Let's look at our options:
- Iron melts at around 1,538°C. Boiling water won't even tickle it.
- Copper melts at 1,085°C. Still way too hot!
- Tungsten has the highest melting point of all pure metals, a blistering 3,422°C (which is why it's used in lightbulb filaments!).

And then there's Gallium. Gallium is an incredible, peculiar metal in the p-block of the periodic table. Its atoms don't pack together perfectly like other metals; they form weird little pairs (dimers). Because of this clumsy structure, the bonds holding solid Gallium together are very weak. 

In fact, Gallium melts at just 29.76°C! Normal human body temperature is around 37°C. That means if you hold a piece of solid Gallium in the palm of your hand, your body heat alone is enough to melt it into a shiny, silvery puddle!

If Gallium melts in your hand at 37°C, it will absolutely be a liquid inside boiling water at 100°C. So, Gallium is your correct answer. Chemistry can be pretty magical!

questions.Question: Q20. The correct order of electronegativity for given elements is:
questions.Hint: Electronegativity increases as you move from left to right across the periodic table. The element closest to the top-right corner (ignoring noble gases) is the greediest of them all!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about 'Electronegativity.' That’s a big word, but it actually describes a very simple human emotion: Greed! 

Imagine two atoms sharing a pair of electrons in a chemical bond. They are supposed to share them 50/50, right? But atoms aren't always fair. Electronegativity is just a measurement of how strongly an atom pulls those shared electrons toward itself. The higher the electronegativity, the greedier the atom.

Now, how do we know who the greediest atoms are? We look at the periodic table! 
1. As you go from left to right across a period (like C, N, O, F), the nucleus gets more protons. More protons mean a stronger positive charge pulling on the negative electrons. 
2. Even though there are more electrons too, they are being added to the same outer shell (the same distance from the nucleus). So, the nucleus acts like an increasingly powerful magnet without the electrons getting any further away to escape it.

Let's line up Carbon (C), Nitrogen (N), Oxygen (O), and Fluorine (F). They are all in the second period, sitting right next to each other in that exact order.
Carbon has 6 protons. Nitrogen has 7. Oxygen has 8. Fluorine has 9.
Because Fluorine has the most protons pulling on that same 2nd shell, it pulls the hardest. Fluorine is actually the undisputed champion of electronegativity in the entire periodic table! It is the greediest element known to science.

Oxygen is second (8 protons), Nitrogen is third (7 protons), and Carbon is the least greedy of this bunch (6 protons). 

So, if we rank them from greediest to least greedy, the correct order is: Fluorine > Oxygen > Nitrogen > Carbon (F > O > N > C). Just remember: the closer you are to the top right of the periodic table, the greedier you are for electrons!

questions.Question: Q21. The correct order of metallic character is =
questions.Hint: Going down a group in the periodic table adds more electron shells. The bigger the atom, the weaker the nucleus holds the outermost electron, making it more 'metallic'!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Here we are looking at another great question about 'metallic character.' Remember our rule from earlier? A metal's job is to give away electrons. The easier it loses an electron, the more metallic it is!

This time, let's look at the elements from Group 1 (the Alkali Metals): Lithium (Li), Sodium (Na), Potassium (K), and Rubidium (Rb). They are all in the same vertical column. 

Imagine the atom as an onion. As you move down the group from top to bottom, the atom gets an entirely new layer (shell) of electrons. 
- Lithium has 2 layers.
- Sodium has 3 layers.
- Potassium has 4 layers.
- Rubidium has 5 layers.

Now, imagine the nucleus is a magnet right in the center of the onion. The outermost electron in Rubidium is sitting on the 5th layer, far, far away from the center. Not only is it far away, but all the inner layers of electrons act like a shield, blocking the magnetic pull of the nucleus. We actually call this the 'Shielding Effect' in chemistry!

Because Rubidium's outer electron is so far away and heavily shielded, Rubidium barely holds onto it. If another atom walks by and asks for an electron, Rubidium hands it over instantly! Lithium, on the other hand, is tiny. Its outer electron is very close to the nucleus, so Lithium holds on a bit tighter.

Therefore, as you go DOWN a group, the atoms get bigger, and their metallic character INCREASES. 

So, ranking them from most easily lost (most metallic) to least easily lost: Rubidium is greater than Potassium, which is greater than Sodium, which is greater than Lithium. 
The correct order is: Rb > K > Na > Li. 

Think: 'Bigger atom = better metal' when moving down a group!

questions.Question: Q22. For elements B, C, N, Li, Be, O and F, the correct order of first ionization enthalpy is
MCQ_Options: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F
Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F
F < O < N < C < B < Be < Li
Li < B < Be < C < N < O < F
questions.Hint: Remember the general rule: it gets harder to steal an electron as you move right across the periodic table. BUT watch out for elements with perfectly full (like Be) or exactly half-full (like N) electron subshells—they guard their electrons extra fiercely!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's tackle this concept together. Imagine atoms are like parents, and their electrons are their kids. 'Ionization Enthalpy' is simply the amount of energy you have to spend to 'kidnap' or steal one of those outer electrons away from the atom. 

As you read the periodic table from left to right (from Lithium towards Fluorine), the atoms get heavier. The nucleus at the center gets more and more positive protons. Because opposite charges attract, a nucleus with more protons acts like a stronger magnet, pulling those negative electrons closer and holding onto them tighter. So, as a general rule, it gets harder (takes more energy) to steal an electron as you go from left to right.

Following that basic rule, you'd expect the order to just match the atomic numbers: Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F. But chemistry is full of cool little twists! We have two rule-breakers here: Beryllium (Be) vs Boron (B), and Nitrogen (N) vs Oxygen (O).

Think about Beryllium. Its outer electrons are perfectly paired up in a cozy '2s' orbital room (2s2). It is perfectly balanced and very happy. Boron, on the other hand, has one lonely electron in a '2p' room (2s2 2p1). Boron is actually quite willing to let that one oddball electron go so it can be perfectly balanced like Beryllium. So, it is strangely EASIER to steal from Boron than Beryllium! This flips their order to B < Be.

Now, let's look at Nitrogen and Oxygen. Nitrogen has exactly 3 electrons in its '2p' subshell (2p3). Since the 2p subshell holds a maximum of 6, having exactly 3 means it's perfectly half-filled. In the atomic world, being perfectly half-filled is like sitting on a perfectly balanced tricycle—it feels incredibly stable! Oxygen has 4 electrons in its 2p subshell (2p4). One of those orbital 'seats' has to fit two electrons. Since electrons are both negative, they hate being next to each other and repel each other. This repulsion makes it much easier to pluck that extra electron away from Oxygen! So, it is easier to steal from Oxygen than Nitrogen. This flips their order to O < N.

When we put the whole puzzle back together with our two special flips, we get: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F. You just predicted quantum mechanical behavior!
questions.Answer: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F

questions.Concept: Standard Enthalpy of Formation and Lattice Energy
questions.Question: Q23. Identify the correct order of standard enthalpy of formation of sodium halides.
questions.Hint: Think about how closely the atoms can pack together. Smaller atoms like Fluorine can get much closer to Sodium than giant atoms like Iodine, creating a tighter bond and releasing a massive amount of energy!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let's talk about chemical matchmaking and energy! The 'standard enthalpy of formation' (we write it as $\Delta H_f)$ is just a fancy term for the amount of heat energy released or absorbed when a brand new compound is born from its raw ingredients.

Here, we are pairing up Sodium (Na), which is desperate to give away an electron, with the Halogen family (Fluorine, Chlorine, Bromine, Iodine), who are all desperate to grab an electron. When they meet, they form an ionic bond and lock together into a crystalline structure. This locking together releases a burst of energy, which means the enthalpy of formation is negative (energy is exiting the system).

Now, how much energy gets released? This is where size matters! Imagine holding two magnets. If you have two tiny, super-strong magnets and you let them snap together, they get incredibly close and hold on incredibly tight. It takes a ton of effort to pull them apart. But if you wrap one magnet in a big, fluffy blanket (like a giant atom) and try to stick it to the other, they can't get as close, so the magnetic pull is much weaker.

Sodium (Na^+) is a small positive ball. Now let's look at the negative guys. Fluoride (F^-) is incredibly tiny, while Iodide (I^-) is massive and bulky. When Sodium bonds with Fluorine, they get super close to each other. This creates a massive, powerful bond (high Lattice Energy), and they release a huge amount of heat energy as a result! When Sodium bonds with Iodine, the bulky Iodine keeps them further apart, making a weaker bond, so less energy is released.

Because the energy is being released, the values are negative. So NaF releases the MOST energy (let's say around -574 kJ/mol), making it the most negative number, while NaI releases the LEAST (around -288 kJ/mol). When we arrange these numbers algebraically from lowest to highest, -574 is smaller than -288. Therefore, the algebraic order is NaF < NaCl < NaBr < NaI. You successfully analyzed thermodynamic stability based just on the size of atoms!

questions.Question: Q24. Metals generally melt at very high temperature. Amongst the following, the metal with the highest melting point will be
questions.Hint: This metal is famous for being the little curly wire inside old-school glowing light bulbs because it can get incredibly hot without melting!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever looked at a classic, glowing, glass light bulb and wondered how the little metal wire inside gets so insanely hot and bright without just melting into a puddle? The answer is Tungsten!

But let's understand exactly WHY Tungsten is such an absolute beast when it comes to dealing with heat. To melt a metal, you have to pump in enough heat energy to make the atoms vibrate so violently that they break apart from their neighbors and start sloshing around as a liquid.

Metals stay solid because of something called 'metallic bonding'. Think of a metal like a giant, packed stadium of positive atoms surrounded by a 'sea' of fast-moving, negative electrons. The electrons act like the glue holding the positive atoms together. The more electrons an atom can throw into this shared 'sea', the stronger the glue becomes.

Transition metals (the big block in the middle of the periodic table) are special because they can use their inner 'd-orbital' electrons as glue, not just their outer ones! Tungsten (symbol W) hits the absolute sweet spot. It has exactly 5 electrons in its d-orbital, which means every single one of its 5 d-orbital 'rooms' has exactly one unpaired electron in it. These unpaired electrons act like tiny, super-strong grappling hooks that lock onto neighboring atoms.

Because Tungsten has the maximum number of these unpaired grappling hooks, its metallic bonds are stronger than almost any other element in the universe. It takes an outrageous temperature of over 3,400 degrees Celsius (over 6,100 degrees Fahrenheit!) to break those bonds. That's why Tungsten easily wins the heavy-weight championship of highest melting points!

questions.Question: Q25. Which of the following elements is considered as a metalloid?
questions.Hint: Look for the element that lives right on the 'zigzag staircase' boundary on the right side of the Periodic Table that separates the heavy metal lifters from the non-metal floaters.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the borderlands of the periodic table! The periodic table is basically a giant map of elements. On the far left and the middle, you have the Metals. Metals are shiny, conduct electricity well, and love to give away electrons. On the top right side, you have the Non-Metals (like Oxygen and Carbon). They are dull, don't conduct electricity, and love to steal electrons.

But what happens when you travel right across the border between the two? You meet the 'Metalloids'. These are the cool, shape-shifting elements of the universe. Depending on the situation, they can act a little bit like a metal, and a little bit like a non-metal! They might look shiny like a metal, but shatter easily like glass (a non-metal). Most importantly, they are 'semiconductors'—they only conduct electricity under certain conditions, which is why they are the absolute heart of all computers and smartphones!

If you look at the right side of the periodic table, there is an invisible zig-zag staircase line that divides the metals from the non-metals. The elements sitting directly on or under these stairs are the metalloids. The main squad of metalloids includes Boron (B), Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb), Tellurium (Te), and Polonium (Po).

Looking at our options, Lead (Pb) and Bismuth (Bi) are heavy metals living below the stairs. Phosphorus (P) is a classic non-metal living above and to the right of the stairs. But Arsenic (As) sits right on the staircase! Therefore, Arsenic is our shape-shifting metalloid.

questions.Question: Q26. The correct order of increasing ionic radii is
questions.Hint: When atoms have the exact same number of electrons (isoelectronic), the atom with the MOST protons in its nucleus will pull those electrons in the tightest, making it the SMALLEST in size!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Time for a microscopic game of tug-of-war! To understand how big an ion (a charged atom) is, you need to look at the battle happening inside it. 

In the center, you have the nucleus full of positive protons pulling inward. On the outside, you have a cloud of negative electrons pulling outward (and repelling each other). The size of the atom is completely decided by who is winning this tug-of-war.

Let's look closely at the elements in the correct answer: N^{3-}, O^{2-}, F^{-}, Na^{+}, Mg^{2+}, and Al^{3+}. 
At first glance, they look totally different. But let's count their electrons! 
Nitrogen normally has 7 electrons, but the '3-' means it gained 3. Total = 10 electrons.
Oxygen normally has 8, gained 2. Total = 10 electrons.
Fluorine normally has 9, gained 1. Total = 10 electrons.
Sodium normally has 11, but the '+' means it lost 1. Total = 10 electrons.
Magnesium (12) lost 2 = 10 electrons.
Aluminum (13) lost 3 = 10 electrons.

Wow! They ALL have exactly 10 electrons! In chemistry, we call this a family of 'isoelectronic' species ('iso' means same). Because the electron outward-pulling team is exactly the same strength (10 electrons) for all of them, the size of the ion is purely determined by the inward-pulling proton team in the nucleus.

Nitrogen only has 7 protons pulling on those 10 electrons. That's a very weak inward pull, so the electron cloud puffs out making it the biggest.
Aluminum has a whopping 13 protons pulling on those same 10 electrons! The 13 protons easily overpower the electrons and smash them into a tiny, tight ball, making it the smallest.

So, if we want to list them from smallest (increasing order) to largest, we start with the one with the most protons and go backwards: Al^{3+} (13 protons) < Mg^{2+} (12 protons) < Na^{+} (11 protons) < F^{-} (9 protons) < O^{2-} (8 protons) < N^{3-} (7 protons). It's all just a game of counting protons!

questions.Question:
Q27. Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. 
Assertion A: The first ionization enthalpy for oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen. Reason R: The four electrons in 2p orbitals of oxygen experience more electron-electron repulsion.
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.Hint: Think about seats on a bus! Nitrogen lets everyone have their own seat, but Oxygen forces two electrons to share one seat, and because they have the same negative charge, they really don't like being next to each other!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
You're going to love this one because it's a perfect logical puzzle. We have to decide if the Assertion (the claim) is true, if the Reason is true, and if they actually connect to each other.

Let's test Assertion A: 'The first ionization enthalpy for oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen.' 
Ionization enthalpy is the energy required to rip an outer electron away from an atom. Normally, as you move right on the periodic table, the nucleus gets stronger, so it should get harder to steal an electron. Since Oxygen is to the right of Nitrogen, you'd think Oxygen's ionization energy would be higher. But wait! There is a famous exception! Oxygen's ionization energy is actually LOWER than Nitrogen's. So Assertion A is absolutely TRUE.

But WHY does this exception exist? Let's check Reason R. It claims the '2p electrons in oxygen experience more electron repulsion.'
To picture this, imagine the '2p' subshell of an atom as a row of 3 empty seats on a bus. Nitrogen has exactly 3 outer electrons. According to chemistry rules (Hund's Rule), electrons like their personal space, so one electron sits in each of the three seats. Everyone is happy, peaceful, and balanced. It takes a LOT of energy to force one of these comfortable electrons off the bus.

Oxygen, however, has 4 outer electrons. The first 3 get their own seats, but that 4th electron has no choice but to squeeze into a seat that is already taken by the 1st electron. Now you have two electrons crammed into one orbital 'seat'. Since electrons are both negatively charged, they act like two negative magnets—they violently repel each other! Because they are already pushing each other away, it is surprisingly easy for an outside force to come along and rip that extra electron away. 

So, Reason R is also completely TRUE. The electron repulsion in Oxygen makes it easier to steal an electron, which perfectly explains why its ionization energy is mysteriously lower than Nitrogen's. Both statements are true, and the Reason perfectly explains the Assertion!
questions.Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.Question: Q28. The first ionization enthalpies of Be, B, N and O follow the order
questions.Hint: Look closely at who has full or exactly half-full orbital 'rooms'. Those atoms hold onto their electrons like a baby holding their favorite candy, flipping the normal left-to-right order!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's put your new superpower of spotting 'electron exceptions' to the test! This question combines everything we learned about Ionization Enthalpy (the energy cost to steal an electron).

The normal rule is simple: as you move to the right on the periodic table, the atom gets more protons, the inward magnetic pull gets stronger, and it becomes harder to steal an electron. The atomic numbers are Be(4), B(5), N(7), O(8). So the normal, boring order of 'hardest to steal from' should just be: Be < B < N < O.

But we know better! We have to check the orbitals (the rooms where electrons live) for perfectly filled or perfectly half-filled setups. 

Let's compare Beryllium (Be) and Boron (B) first. Beryllium has its outermost electrons packed neatly into a full '2s' orbital. It's a completely full house, very stable. Boron has that full '2s' house, plus one awkward, lonely electron sitting in a brand new '2p' room. Boron doesn't really care about that single electron, so it's easier to steal than Beryllium's tightly packed ones! So, the order flips: B is less than Be (B < Be).

Now let's compare Nitrogen (N) and Oxygen (O). Nitrogen has exactly 3 electrons in its '2p' orbital. Since the 2p orbital holds 6 total, having 3 means it's exactly half-full. In nature, half-full is incredibly stable and symmetric. Oxygen has 4 electrons in its 2p orbital, forcing two negative electrons to share one small orbital room. They hate this and repel each other, pushing each other toward the door. This makes it easier to steal an electron from Oxygen than from the ultra-stable Nitrogen. So, the order flips again: O is less than N (O < N).

Now, piece it all together! Boron is easier than Beryllium. Oxygen is easier than Nitrogen. And both B and Be are easier than O and N overall because they have fewer protons in their nucleus. 
The final, ultimate order is: B < Be < O < N. You just navigated through all the quantum traps to find the right answer!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Concept: Ionization Enthalpy and Electronic Configuration Stability
questions.Question: Q29. Outermost electronic configurations of four elements A, B, C, D are given below: (A) 3s² (B) 3s²3p¹ (C) 3s²3p³ (D) 3s²3p⁴. The correct order of first ionization enthalpy for them is:
questions.Hint: Think of fully-filled and half-filled electron shells as 'perfectly balanced and happy' rooms. It is much harder to steal an electron from a happy room!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let us dive into the fascinating world of Ionization Enthalpy. Imagine you are a tough negotiator trying to 'buy' or steal an electron from an atom. 'Ionization Enthalpy' is simply the price tag the atom puts on its outermost electron. The tighter the atom holds its electron, the higher the price!

Normally, as you move from left to right across a row (period) on the Periodic Table, atoms get smaller, the nucleus gets more positive, and the price tag (ionization energy) goes up. But chemistry is full of quirky personalities!

Let us look at our four suspects, who all live in the 3rd row (Period 3):
(A) 3s² (Magnesium): The 's' room is perfectly full with 2 electrons. It is very stable and happy. 
(B) 3s² 3p¹ (Aluminum): The 's' room is full, but there is one lonely electron sitting in the new 'p' room. Aluminum actually WANTS to get rid of this lonely electron so it can go back to being a perfectly stable 3s². So, its price drops! Therefore, stealing from (A) is harder than (B). So, A > B.

(C) 3s² 3p³ (Phosphorus): The 'p' room has 3 beds, and exactly 3 electrons are sleeping there (one in each bed). This is called a 'half-filled' state, and the universe LOVES symmetry. It is incredibly stable! 
(D) 3s² 3p⁴ (Sulfur): Here, we have 4 electrons in 3 beds. One bed has to be shared by two electrons. Electrons are both negatively charged, so they repel each other. They bicker and fight in that shared bed! Because of this tension, it is actually easier to kick out that 4th electron than to disturb the perfect harmony of (C). So, C > D.

Putting it all together from right to left (highest price to lowest price): The perfectly symmetrical (C) is the hardest, followed by (D), then the fully filled (A), and finally the easiest is the one with the lonely electron (B). 

Final Order: (C) > (D) > (A) > (B). You just outsmarted the Periodic Table!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q30. The correct decreasing order for metallic character is
questions.Hint: Metals are generous; they love giving away electrons! The larger the atom (further down and to the left of the periodic table), the looser it holds its electrons, making it more metallic.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Notice how the original question cut off before giving us the elements? No worries! I have created a classic set of elements (Potassium, Magnesium, Aluminum, and Boron) to teach you the exact secret behind this concept.

What does it mean to be 'metallic' in chemistry? In the human world, being generous means giving away your money or toys. In chemistry, 'metallic character' is all about how generously an atom gives away its electrons!

Here is the golden rule of the Periodic Table's geography:
1. As you go DOWN a group (column), atoms get fatter. The outermost electrons are so far away from the nucleus (the 'parent') that they easily wander off. So, metallic character INCREASES down a group.
2. As you go from LEFT to RIGHT across a period (row), the nucleus gets stronger and pulls the electrons in tighter. Atoms turn from generous givers (metals) into greedy takers (non-metals). So, metallic character DECREASES across a period.

Let us rank our elements based on this map:
- Potassium (K) is far to the left in Group 1, and down in Period 4. It is a huge, generous alkali metal. It is the most metallic!
- Magnesium (Mg) is slightly to the right (Group 2) and higher up (Period 3). It is still a great metal, but less generous than K.
- Aluminum (Al) is further to the right in Group 13. It is a metal, but holds onto its electrons a bit more tightly than Mg.
- Boron (B) is right above Aluminum. It is so small and tight with its electrons that it is not even considered a true metal anymore; it is a metalloid!

Therefore, the generosity (metallic character) from highest to lowest is: K > Mg > Al > B. Whenever you face a question like this, just picture the map: Bottom-Left is the Kingdom of Metals!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q31. The first ionization enthalpy of Na, Mg and Si, respectively, are: 496, 737 and 786 kJ mol⁻¹. The first ionization enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹) of Al is:
questions.Hint: Normally, ionization energy increases across a period (Na < Mg < Al < Si). But remember the 'happy room' rule! Magnesium (3s²) is more stable than Aluminum (3s² 3p¹).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a beautiful follow-up to our 'happy room' concept from Q29! We are given the actual real-life price tags (ionization enthalpies) for elements in the third row of the periodic table: Sodium (Na) is 496, Magnesium (Mg) is 737, and Silicon (Si) is 786. We need to find the missing price tag for Aluminum (Al).

If the world were perfectly simple, the price would go up steadily from left to right because the atoms are shrinking and the nucleus is getting stronger. You would expect the order to be Na < Mg < Al < Si. 
If that were true, Al's number would have to be somewhere exactly between 737 (Mg) and 786 (Si). 

But wait! Remember the quirky personalities of these atoms?
- Magnesium (Mg) ends in 3s². That is a perfectly filled, super stable room. It demands a very high price to give up an electron (737 kJ/mol).
- Aluminum (Al) ends in 3s² 3p¹. It has that one lonely, awkward electron in the 'p' room. Aluminum is secretly desperate to kick that single guy out so it can go back to being a perfect 3s². 

Because Aluminum WANTS to lose that electron, it puts a 'Discount' on its price tag. Its ionization energy drops LOWER than Magnesium's!

So the actual order of price tags is: Na < Al < Mg < Si. 
This means Aluminum's value must be strictly greater than Sodium (496) but less than Magnesium (737).

Look at our options:
- 760 is too high (greater than Mg).
- 480 is too low (less than Na).
- 800 is way too high.
- 577 sits perfectly in the sweet spot between 496 and 737! 

By simply understanding the psychology of the atom's electron rooms, you solved a complex numerical question without needing a calculator. Awesome, right?

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q32. Match List-I with List-II.
questions.Hint: Match the extreme properties: Who is the greediest atom? Who is the most generous? Who is completely unresponsive?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Uh oh, it looks like the original test paper accidentally erased the lists! But a true chemistry detective does not let that stop them. Let us create the ultimate Periodic Table matching game to learn exactly what this question tests!

Imagine List-I contains these superhero titles:
(A) Highest Electronegativity (The Greediest Atom)
(B) Highest Electron Affinity (The Atom that pays the most for an extra electron)
(C) Lowest Ionization Energy (The most Generous Atom)
(D) Completely Inert (The 'Do Not Disturb' Atom)

And List-II contains their secret identities:
(i) Chlorine
(ii) Fluorine
(iii) Helium
(iv) Cesium

Let us match them up!

(A) Highest Electronegativity belongs to Fluorine (ii). Electronegativity is how aggressively an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself in a bond. Fluorine is tiny and has a very strong nucleus. It is the absolute bully of the periodic table!

(B) Highest Electron Affinity belongs to Chlorine (i). Wait, why not Fluorine? Fluorine is so small that if you try to cram one more electron into its tiny outer shell, the other electrons crowd together and push back (repulsion). Chlorine is a bit bigger, so it comfortably accepts an extra electron and releases a massive amount of energy (joy) when it gets it.

(C) Lowest Ionization Energy goes to Cesium (iv). Cesium is a gigantic atom at the bottom-left of the table. Its outermost electron is so far from the nucleus that Cesium barely even notices if someone steals it. It has the lowest 'price tag'.

(D) Completely Inert belongs to Helium (iii). Helium is a noble gas with a perfectly full outer shell. It does not want to gain, lose, or share anything. It is completely happy in isolation.

So the perfect match is (A)-(ii), (B)-(i), (C)-(iv), (D)-(iii). By mastering these extremes, you can conquer any matching question they throw at you!

questions.Concept: Molecular Orbital Theory (Bond Order & Total Electrons)
questions.Question: Q33. AX is a covalent diatomic molecule, where A and X are second row elements of periodic table. Based on molecular orbital theory, the bond order of AX is 2.5. The total number of electrons in AX is .......... (Round off to the nearest integer).
questions.Hint: Remember the magic '14' rule of Molecular Orbital Theory! 14 total electrons equals a perfect Bond Order of 3.0. Every electron you add or subtract from 14 drops the bond order by 0.5.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us unlock one of the coolest cheat codes in chemistry: The Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) Magic Number!

The question asks for the total number of electrons in a molecule made of two atoms (AX), given that its 'Bond Order' is 2.5. 
What is Bond Order? It is simply the number of chemical bonds between the two atoms. A bond order of 1 means a single bond, 2 means a double bond, 3 means a triple bond. A bond order of 2.5 means it is a quirky molecule sitting halfway between a double and a triple bond!

Normally, to find this, you would have to draw a massive, complicated energy diagram. But here is the cheat code:
1. The magic number is 14. If a simple diatomic molecule has exactly 14 total electrons (like N$_2$, where Nitrogen has 7, so 7+7=14), it has a maximum Bond Order of 3.0.
2. For every step you take AWAY from 14, whether you go UP or DOWN, the bond order drops by exactly 0.5.

Let us map it out:
- 14 electrons = Bond Order 3.0
- 15 electrons = Bond Order 2.5
- 16 electrons = Bond Order 2.0 (like O$_2$, which has a double bond! 8+8=16)
- 13 electrons = Bond Order 2.5
- 12 electrons = Bond Order 2.0

The question tells us the bond order is 2.5. Looking at our magic map, the molecule must have either 13 or 15 electrons! 

Both are technically correct in chemistry (for example, the CN radical has 13 electrons, and the NO molecule has 15 electrons, and both have a bond order of 2.5!). However, Nitrogen Oxide (NO) is the most famous, stable, neutral diatomic molecule in this category, so 15 is the standard classic answer. If you typed either 13 or 15 on the actual test, you would get full marks! Is not that trick super fast?

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q34. Identify the elements X and Y using the ionisation energy values given below.
MCQ_Options: X = Alkali metal, Y = Alkaline earth metal
X = Alkaline earth metal, Y = Alkali metal
questions.Hint: Look for the massive 'jump' in energy! If the price skyrockets after removing 1 electron, it's an Alkali metal. If it skyrockets after removing 2, it's an Alkaline earth metal.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Oh no, the data table for this question vanished! But as your mentor, I will not leave you hanging. I am going to conjure up some hypothetical data to teach you how to 'read the fingerprint' of any element using Successive Ionization Energies.

Imagine we have this data table:
Element X: 
- 1st Ionization Energy: 500 kJ/mol
- 2nd Ionization Energy: 4,500 kJ/mol

Element Y:
- 1st Ionization Energy: 700 kJ/mol
- 2nd Ionization Energy: 1,400 kJ/mol
- 3rd Ionization Energy: 7,700 kJ/mol

Think of an atom like an onion. You can peel off the loose, outer layers (valence electrons) fairly easily. But once you reach the tight, deeply protected core (the noble gas inner shell), the atom fights back viciously, and the energy required to peel it skyrockets!

Let us analyze Element X:
The first electron costs 500. Easy! The second electron costs 4,500. WHOA! That is a massive 9x jump! What does this mean? It means Element X was perfectly happy to give away ONE electron, but trying to take a second one broke its core stability. Atoms that only want to give away 1 electron belong to Group 1: The Alkali Metals (like Sodium).

Let us analyze Element Y:
The first electron costs 700. The second costs 1,400 (a normal doubling, nothing crazy). But the third electron costs 7,700! A massive jump! This means Element Y was totally fine giving away TWO electrons, but the third one crossed the line. Atoms that want to give away exactly 2 electrons belong to Group 2: The Alkaline Earth Metals (like Magnesium).

So, by just looking at where the massive jump in numbers happens, you can pinpoint exactly what family the element belongs to! X is an Alkali metal, and Y is an Alkaline earth metal.
questions.Answer: X = Alkali metal, Y = Alkaline earth metal

questions.Question: Q35. Outermost electronic configuration of a group 13 element, E, is 4s², 4p¹. The electronic configuration of an element of p-block period-five placed diagonally to element, E is:
questions.Hint: Treat the Periodic Table like a chessboard! 'Diagonally' usually means moving one step down (to the next Period) and one step to the right (to the next Group).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic puzzle that turns the Periodic Table into a treasure map! Let us break it down step-by-step.

Step 1: Locate Element E.
The question tells us Element E is in Group 13, and its outermost shell is 4s² 4p¹. 
The big number '4' tells us that this element lives in the 4th Row (Period 4). 
So, Element E's address is: Period 4, Group 13. (Fun fact: This element is Gallium!).

Step 2: Follow the map's instructions.
The clue asks us to find the element placed 'diagonally' to Element E, and specifically mentions it is in Period 5. 
In the periodic table, moving diagonally means moving exactly like a pawn capturing in chess: one step DOWN, and one step to the RIGHT.
- One step DOWN from Period 4 puts us in Period 5.
- One step RIGHT from Group 13 puts us in Group 14.

Step 3: Write the configuration for the new location.
So, our mystery target element lives in Period 5, Group 14. (Fun fact: This is Tin!).
What is the outermost electronic configuration for ANY element in Group 14? Well, Group 13 has 3 valence electrons (s² p¹). Group 14 has 4 valence electrons, so they always end in s² p².
Since our target is in Period 5, the outermost shell number is 5.
Combine them: The configuration must be 5s² 5p².

It is that simple! You started at 4s² 4p¹, moved one row down (change the 4s to 5s), and one group right (add an electron to the p orbital, making it p²). Boom: 5s² 5p²!

questions.Question: Q36. The ionic radii of F⁻ and O²⁻ respectively are 1.33 Å and 1.4Å, while the covalent radius of N is 0.74Å. The correct statement for the ionic radius of N³⁻ from the following is:
MCQ_Options: It is between 1.33 Å and 1.4 Å
It is exactly equal to 0.74 Å
questions.Hint: Think about isoelectronic species! F⁻, O²⁻, and N³⁻ all have exactly 10 electrons. How does the number of protons in the nucleus affect the size of the ion when the electron count is the same?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's dive into an awesome concept called *isoelectronic species*. The word 'iso' means 'same', and 'electronic' refers to electrons. So, isoelectronic species are different atoms or ions that have the exact same number of electrons!

Let's look at the players in our question: Fluoride ($F^{-}$), Oxide ($O^{2-}$), and Nitride ($N^{3-}$).
- A neutral Fluorine atom has 9 electrons, but it gained 1 to become $F^{-}$. Total = 10 electrons.
- A neutral Oxygen atom has 8 electrons, but it gained 2 to become $O^{2-}$. Total = 10 electrons.
- A neutral Nitrogen atom has 7 electrons, but it gained 3 to become $N^{3-}$. Total = 10 electrons.

They all have exactly 10 electrons! So, why are their sizes different? This is where the protons come in. Protons are positively charged and live in the nucleus, pulling the negatively charged electrons inward.
- Fluorine has 9 protons pulling on 10 electrons.
- Oxygen has 8 protons pulling on 10 electrons.
- Nitrogen only has 7 protons pulling on 10 electrons.

**Analogy Time:** Imagine the nucleus is a team of teachers, and the electrons are a group of hyperactive kindergarteners running around.
In $F^{-}$, you have 9 teachers watching 10 kids. They keep the kids grouped pretty tightly.
In $O^{2-}$, you only have 8 teachers for those 10 kids. The kids spread out a bit more (radius = 1.4 $\mathring{A}$).
But in $N^{3-}$, you only have 7 teachers trying to control the same 10 kids! Because there are fewer teachers (protons) pulling on the kids (electrons), the kids spread out the furthest!

Therefore, the electron cloud of $N^{3-}$ expands the most, making its ionic radius significantly larger than that of $O^{2-}$. Since $O^{2-}$ is 1.4 $\mathring{A}$, the radius of $N^{3-}$ must be **bigger than 1.4 $\mathring{A}$**! (It's actually around 1.71 $\mathring{A}$).

questions.Question: Q37. Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A) Metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases on moving from left to right in a period. Reason (R) It is due to increase in ionisation enthalpy and decrease in electron gain enthalpy, when one moves from left to right in a period.
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.Hint: Metals love giving away electrons, while non-metals love taking them. Across a period, atoms shrink and grip their electrons tighter. Would they want to gain new electrons more or less?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello again! Let's tackle this puzzle by breaking down what makes a metal a metal, and what makes a non-metal a non-metal.

In chemistry, **metals** are like incredibly generous billionaires. They don't want to hold onto their outermost electrons; they love giving them away! **Non-metals**, on the other hand, are like super-greedy vacuum cleaners. They desperately want to pull in extra electrons to complete their collections (their outer shells).

When we move from left to right across a period in the periodic table (like going from Sodium to Chlorine), a few things happen:
1. The atoms get smaller because more protons are being added to the nucleus, pulling the electron shells closer and tighter.
2. Because the electrons are held so tightly, it becomes really, really hard to steal an electron away. In chemistry terms, the **Ionisation Enthalpy** (the energy required to remove an electron) *increases*.
3. Because the nucleus is so good at pulling electrons, these atoms actually *want* to gain new electrons. When they gain an electron, they release energy. This is called **Electron Gain Enthalpy**. As you move left to right, the atoms release more and more energy, meaning the Electron Gain Enthalpy becomes more negative (which we describe chemically as an increase in its magnitude).

Let's look at our statements:
**Assertion (A)** says metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases from left to right. This is **100% TRUE!** Elements turn from generous electron-givers to greedy electron-takers.
**Reason (R)** says this is due to an *increase* in ionisation enthalpy (which is true) and a *decrease* in electron gain enthalpy. This second part is **FALSE**! The electron gain enthalpy actually becomes *more negative* (its magnitude increases), meaning they want electrons *more*, not less.

Therefore, the Assertion is True, but the Reason contains a completely false statement!
questions.Answer: A is true but R is false

questions.Question: Q38. B has a smaller first ionization enthalpy than Be. Consider the following statements: (I) it is easier to remove 2p electron than 2s electron (II) 2p electron of B is more shielded from the nucleus by the inner core of electrons than the 2s electrons of Be (III) 2s electron has more penetration power than 2p electron (IV) atomic radius of B is more than Be (atomic number B=5, Be=4). The correct statements are:
questions.Hint: Write down the electron configurations for Beryllium ($1s^{2} 2s^{2}$) and Boron ($1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{1}$). Which subshell ($s$ or $p$) is closer to the nucleus and harder to pull an electron from?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic question because it tests whether you know *why* the periodic table rules have exceptions!

Normally, as you move from left to right across a period, atoms get smaller, the nuclear pull gets stronger, and it becomes harder to remove an electron. So, Ionization Enthalpy should increase. Based on this, Boron (B, atomic number 5) should have a higher ionization enthalpy than Beryllium (Be, atomic number 4). But it doesn't! Boron is actually easier to rob of an electron. Why?

Let's look at their electron configurations:
- Beryllium (Be): $1s^{2} 2s^{2}$
- Boron (B): $1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{1}$

**Analogy Time!** Think of the nucleus as a rock concert stage.
The $s$-orbitals are the VIP sections right up against the stage. They penetrate deep into the atom, very close to the nucleus.
The $p$-orbitals are the general admission sections slightly further back.

In Beryllium, you are trying to pull an electron out of the $2s$ VIP section. The nucleus has a tight grip on these electrons because they are so close. Plus, the $2s$ subshell is perfectly full, making it super stable!
In Boron, you are trying to remove the lone electron in the $2p$ general admission section. This electron is slightly further away from the nucleus and is also blocked (shielded) by the $1s$ and $2s$ electrons sitting in front of it.

Because the $2p$ electron of Boron is heavily shielded and sits in a less penetrating orbital than the $2s$ electron of Beryllium, it is much easier to pluck away! This makes statements (I), (II), and (III) completely correct!
Statement (IV) says Boron is larger than Beryllium. This is false! Boron has more protons (5 vs 4), which pulls the overall electron cloud tighter, making Boron smaller than Beryllium across the period.
So, our winning combo is (I), (II), and (III)!

questions.Question: Q39. The first and second ionisation enthalpies of a metal are 496 and 4560kJ mol⁻¹, respectively. How many moles of HCl and H₂SO₄, respectively, will be needed to react completely with 1 mole of the metal hydroxide?
MCQ_Options: 1 mole of HCl and 0.5 moles of H₂SO₄
2 moles of HCl and 1 mole of H₂SO₄
1 mole of HCl and 1 mole of H₂SO₄
0.5 moles of HCl and 1 mole of H₂SO₄
questions.Hint: Look at the massive jump between the first and second ionization enthalpies! This metal happily gives away exactly ONE electron, but refuses to give away a second. What does that make its valency?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Are you ready for some chemical detective work? Let's decode the clues hidden in these ionization enthalpy numbers!

**Ionization Enthalpy** is simply the 'price tag' or energy required to steal an electron from an atom.
For our mystery metal:
- Stealing the 1st electron costs 496 $kJ/mol$.
- Stealing the 2nd electron costs a whopping 4560 $kJ/mol$!

That is nearly a 10-fold jump in price! What does this massive jump tell us?
**Analogy Time:** Imagine you have a garage full of stuff. The first electron is like an old, rusty bicycle that you are happy to give away for a low price. But the second electron? That is your prized, brand-new sports car! You would demand an absurdly high price to even consider letting it go!

In chemical terms, this means the metal happily loses *one* electron to achieve a perfectly stable, happy noble gas configuration. Once it reaches that state, it refuses to lose another electron. This is the hallmark of Group 1 Alkali Metals, like Sodium (Na) or Potassium (K). They form ions with a +1 charge ($M^{+}$).

So, our metal forms a hydroxide with the formula $MOH$ (just like $NaOH$).
Now, let's look at the neutralisation reactions (Base + Acid $\rightarrow$ Salt + Water):
1. **With HCl:**
   $MOH + HCl \rightarrow MCl + H_{2}O$
   From the balanced equation, exactly 1 mole of HCl is needed to react completely with 1 mole of $MOH$.
2. **With $H_{2}SO_{4}$:**
   Sulfuric acid is diprotic (it has two $H^{+}$ ions to give).
   $2 MOH + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow M_{2}SO_{4} + 2 H_{2}O$
   It takes 2 moles of $MOH$ to react with 1 mole of $H_{2}SO_{4}$. Therefore, for just 1 mole of $MOH$, we only need half that amount, which is 0.5 moles of $H_{2}SO_{4}$.

So, the exact amounts needed are 1 mole of HCl and 0.5 moles of $H_{2}SO_{4}$. Mystery solved!
questions.Answer: 1 mole of HCl and 0.5 moles of H₂SO₄

questions.Question: Q40. The electron gain enthalpy (in kJ/mol) of fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine, respectively, are:
questions.Hint: Chlorine releases more energy than Fluorine when gaining an electron because Fluorine is so tiny that adding an extra electron causes major crowding and repulsion!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the Halogens (Group 17 of the periodic table): Fluorine (F), Chlorine (Cl), Bromine (Br), and Iodine (I). These elements are just one electron short of a perfect, full outer shell. Because of this, they are obsessed with gaining an electron!

When they successfully snatch an extra electron, they relax and release a bunch of energy. This released energy is called **Electron Gain Enthalpy**. Since energy is given off, the values are negative. The more they want the electron, the more energy they release (the more negative the number).

Normally, you'd expect Fluorine, the most fiercely electronegative element in the entire periodic table, to release the most energy. But chemistry loves plot twists! Fluorine releases less energy (-333 $kJ/mol$) than Chlorine (-349 $kJ/mol$). Why?

**Analogy Time:** Imagine Fluorine is a tiny, compact 2-seater sports car that already has 2 people crammed inside. When a 3rd person (the new electron) tries to squeeze in, the people already inside push back and complain. The space is too small, and there is intense 'inter-electronic repulsion'. Because of this pushing and shoving, Fluorine doesn't release as much energy as we'd expect.

On the other hand, Chlorine is like a spacious, comfortable minivan. It has a much larger atomic radius. When a new electron hops in, there is plenty of room! The existing electrons don't mind at all. So, Chlorine accepts the electron effortlessly and releases the maximum amount of energy (-349 $kJ/mol$).

As we move further down to Bromine and Iodine, the atoms get so incredibly large that the nucleus (the positively charged magnet) is too far away to pull strongly on a new electron. So, the energy released drops down to -325 $kJ/mol$ for Br and -296 $kJ/mol$ for I.

So the correct order of values for F, Cl, Br, and I is -333, -349, -325, and -296!

questions.Concept: IUPAC Nomenclature for Elements with Z > 100
questions.Question: Q41. The atomic number of Unnilunium is ________.
questions.Hint: In IUPAC naming, 'un' stands for 1, and 'nil' stands for 0. Break the word down chunk by chunk!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Did you know that you can name newly discovered chemical elements just by speaking a mix of Latin and Greek? It's true!

Whenever scientists smash atoms together in supercolliders to create brand-new, super-heavy elements, there is usually a long debate about what to name them permanently. To prevent arguments while the official name is being decided, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) created a super cool, logical naming system. It's essentially a secret code!

Here is the codebook for the numbers 0 through 9:
- 0 = nil
- 1 = un
- 2 = bi
- 3 = tri
- 4 = quad
- 5 = pent
- 6 = hex
- 7 = sept
- 8 = oct
- 9 = enn

To name an element, you just look at its atomic number, match the digits to the code words, string them together, and add '-ium' at the end!

Let's reverse-engineer the name given in our question: **Unnilunium**.
1. The first chunk is **'Un'**, which means the first digit is **1**.
2. The middle chunk is **'nil'**, which means the second digit is **0**.
3. The last chunk before the ending is **'un'**, which means the third digit is **1**.
4. The '-ium' ending just tells us it's a metal!

Put the digits together: 1 - 0 - 1.
The atomic number of Unnilunium is exactly **101**!

It's that simple! If you wanted to name element 118, you would say 'un' (1) + 'un' (1) + 'oct' (8) + 'ium' = Ununoctium. You are officially an expert at naming super-heavy elements!

questions.Question: Q42. The set that contains atomic numbers of only transition elements, is:
questions.Hint: Transition elements are found in the d-block (Groups 3 to 12). Remember that the very first transition metal is Scandium, which has an atomic number of 21!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the incredible geography of the periodic table!

The periodic table isn't just a random grid; it's a beautifully organized map.
- On the far left, you have the **s-block** (Groups 1 and 2). These are highly reactive metals.
- On the far right, you have the **p-block** (Groups 13 to 18). These are a mix of metals, metalloids, non-metals, and noble gases.
- But right in the center, acting as a massive bridge between the left and right, is the **d-block** (Groups 3 to 12).

The elements in this central d-block are known as the **Transition Elements**. They are the classic metals we use every day—like Iron, Copper, Gold, and Silver. They are called 'transition' elements because their properties smoothly transition from the extremely reactive metals on the left to the non-metals on the right.

The very first transition element you will encounter on the periodic table is Scandium (Sc), which has an atomic number of 21. From there, the d-block spans across periods 4, 5, 6, and 7.

Let's become detectives and investigate the given options to find the set where *every single number* belongs to a transition element!
- **Option A:** 21 (Scandium - Transition!), 25 (Manganese - Transition!), 42 (Molybdenum - Transition!), 72 (Hafnium - Transition!). Ding ding ding! We have a winner!
- **Let's check the others to be sure:**
  - Option C contains 9 (Fluorine) and 17 (Chlorine). These are halogens located way over in the p-block!
  - Option D contains 37 (Rubidium), which is an alkali metal in the s-block, and 50 (Tin) which is in the p-block.

**Analogy Time:** Think of the periodic table as a giant high school. The s-block and p-block are the classrooms where all the standard studying happens. The d-block is the massive gymnasium right in the middle of the school. The transition elements are the star athletes hanging out in the gym! Option A is the only group entirely made up of gym athletes!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Concept: Periodic Table Blocks and Groups (Actinides and Transactinides)
questions.Question: Q43. The elements with atomic numbers 101 and 104 belong to, respectively:
questions.Hint: Remember that the Actinide series is a special detached row at the bottom of the periodic table that runs from atomic number 89 to 103. Where does the table resume after 103?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine the periodic table as an enormous, meticulously organized hotel for elements. Most elements live in the main building (the s, p, and d blocks). However, to keep the building from getting ridiculously wide, the architects (chemists!) built a detached 'annex' at the very bottom, known as the f-block. 

This f-block has two rows: the Lanthanides (the top row) and the Actinides (the bottom row). The Actinide series is a group of heavy, radioactive elements that specifically occupy rooms numbered 89 (Actinium) all the way to 103 (Lawrencium). Because atomic number 101 (Mendelevium) falls perfectly between 89 and 103, it unequivocally belongs to the Actinides family!

But what happens when we reach element 104? The f-block annex is completely full! The 104th element (Rutherfordium) has to pack its bags and move back up into the main hotel building. Specifically, it resumes its place right after the f-block detour, landing squarely in the d-block. If you look at a standard periodic table, element 104 drops right into Group 4, directly underneath Hafnium (element 72). Therefore, element 101 is an Actinide, and element 104 belongs to Group 4.

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q44. The ionic radii of O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ are in the order:
questions.Hint: Count the number of electrons in each ion first. If they all have the exact same number of electrons, the one with the most protons will pull those electrons in the tightest!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play a microscopic game of tug-of-war! To understand how big an ion is, we need to look at the battle between the positively charged protons in the center (the nucleus) and the negatively charged electrons orbiting around them.

First, let's count the electrons for each ion. A neutral Oxygen (O) atom has 8 electrons, but O²⁻ gained 2, so it has 10. Fluorine (F) has 9, but F⁻ gained 1, giving it 10. Sodium (Na) has 11, but Na⁺ lost 1, leaving it with 10. Magnesium (Mg) has 12, but Mg²⁺ lost 2, leaving it with 10. Wow! They all have exactly 10 electrons. In chemistry, we call these 'isoelectronic' species ('iso' means equal).

Since the electron teams are exactly the same size, the winner of this tug-of-war depends entirely on the proton team in the nucleus. Oxygen only has 8 protons pulling on those 10 electrons. It's a weak pull, so the electrons drift further out, making O²⁻ the biggest, puffiest ion. Fluorine has 9 protons, pulling a bit tighter. Sodium has 11 protons, pulling even tighter. Finally, Magnesium has a massive team of 12 protons yanking on those 10 electrons! Because Mg²⁺ pulls the hardest, its electrons are drawn super close to the center, making it the smallest ion. 

Therefore, from largest to smallest, the order is: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺.

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Concept: Successive Ionization Enthalpies and Valence Electrons
questions.Question: Q45. The five successive ionization enthalpies of an element are 800, 2427, 3658, 25024 and 32824kJ mol⁻¹. The number of valence electrons in the element is:
questions.Hint: Look for the massive, sudden 'jump' in the energy required to remove an electron. That huge spike means you've finished removing the easily accessible outer electrons and are now trying to break into a highly stable inner core!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think of ionization energy as the 'price' you have to pay an atom to pluck away one of its electrons. Atoms have layers of electrons, just like an onion. The outer layers are called 'valence electrons.' Because they are far from the nucleus, they are relatively cheap and easy to steal. However, the inner layers are tightly guarded, highly stable, and incredibly expensive to break into.

Let's look at the price tags to steal this element's electrons, one by one:
1st electron: 800 kJ/mol (Okay, a bit of effort).
2nd electron: 2,427 kJ/mol (Harder, because the atom is now a positive ion and holds on tighter).
3rd electron: 3,658 kJ/mol (Even harder, but still a manageable, steady increase).

But wait... look what happens when we try to steal the 4th electron! The price skyrockets to a massive 25,024 kJ/mol! Why did the cost suddenly multiply by almost seven times? 

This massive jump is the atom's way of screaming 'NO!' It means the first three electrons were those easily accessible outer valence electrons. Once you took all three, the atom was left with a perfectly full, incredibly stable, deeply buried inner shell (like a noble gas configuration). Trying to rip an electron out of that perfect inner shell requires an astronomical amount of energy. 

Because the jump happens exactly after the 3rd electron is removed, we know there were only 3 outer electrons to begin with. This element is likely from Group 13, like Aluminum!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Concept: Periodicity of Oxide Nature (Acidic, Basic, Amphoteric)
questions.Question: Q46. Three elements X, Y and Z are in the 3rd period of the periodic table. The oxides of X, Y and Z, respectively, are basic, amphoteric and acidic. The correct order of the atomic numbers of X, Y and Z is:
questions.Hint: In the periodic table, metals are on the left and form basic oxides, while non-metals are on the right and form acidic oxides. Atomic numbers increase as you read the table from left to right!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's take a walk across the 3rd period of the periodic table, starting from the left side and moving right. As we walk, the atomic number increases step by step (from Sodium at 11, to Argon at 18). 

On the far left side, we find the strong, classic metals like Sodium (Na) and Magnesium (Mg). A fun rule in chemistry is that metals love to form 'basic' oxides (substances that act like bases when dissolved in water). Since element X forms a basic oxide, X must be a metal on the far left side of our period. This means X has the smallest atomic number of the three.

As we keep walking to the right, we hit the middle of the period. Here we find elements like Aluminum (Al). These middle-ground elements are a bit confused—they aren't purely metallic, but they aren't totally non-metallic either. Because of this identity crisis, they form 'amphoteric' oxides. 'Amphi' means 'both' (like amphibians living in water and land). Amphoteric oxides can act as both acids AND bases! Since element Y is amphoteric, it sits in the middle.

Finally, as we walk to the far right, we find pure non-metals like Sulfur (S) and Chlorine (Cl). Non-metals form 'acidic' oxides. Since element Z forms an acidic oxide, it must be on the right side, meaning it has the highest atomic number.

Reading from left to right (increasing atomic number), we go from Basic (X) to Amphoteric (Y) to Acidic (Z). Therefore, the atomic numbers must follow the order: X is smallest, then Y, then Z is largest. Written mathematically: X < Y < Z.

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q47. The correct order of the atomic radii of C, Cs, Al, and S is:
questions.Hint: Atoms get massively bigger as you go DOWN a group because you add whole new layers (shells) of electrons. They get slightly smaller as you go ACROSS a period (left to right) because more protons pull the same layer inward.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To solve this, we need to visualize the atomic 'onion'. Atoms are made of electron layers. As you travel down the periodic table, you add entirely new layers (shells) to the atom, making it drastically larger. 

Let's locate our elements:
- Carbon (C) is in Period 2. It has only 2 layers of electrons.
- Aluminum (Al) and Sulfur (S) are in Period 3. They have 3 layers of electrons.
- Cesium (Cs) is way down in Period 6. It has 6 massive layers of electrons!

Right away, Cesium is the undisputed heavyweight champion. With 6 layers, Cs is vastly larger than all the others. Conversely, Carbon is the tiniest because it only has 2 layers. So far, we know Cs is the biggest and C is the smallest.

But what about Aluminum and Sulfur? They both have 3 layers! How do we break the tie? To do this, we look at the horizontal trend (left to right). Aluminum is on the left side of Period 3, while Sulfur is on the right side. Sulfur has more protons in its nucleus than Aluminum. Imagine the protons as a magnet pulling on the electron layers. Because Sulfur has a stronger 'magnet' (more protons), it pulls its 3 layers inward tighter than Aluminum can. This stronger pull shrinks the atom! Therefore, Sulfur is smaller than Aluminum.

Putting it all together from largest to smallest: Cesium (6 layers) > Aluminum (3 layers, weaker pull) > Sulfur (3 layers, stronger pull) > Carbon (only 2 layers).

questions.Question: Q48. The 71st electron of an element X with an atomic number of 71 enters into the orbital:
questions.Hint: Follow the 'Aufbau' hotel filling rules! After the 6s orbital is full (56 electrons), the 4f orbital takes exactly 14 electrons (getting us to 70). Where must that single leftover 71st electron go?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the microscopic world of electron configuration, which is essentially the art of assigning hotel rooms to electrons! To find out where the 71st electron goes, we use the Aufbau Principle. This principle states that electrons are fundamentally lazy—they will always occupy the lowest energy 'rooms' (orbitals) available first before moving to higher floors.

Let's assign rooms to 71 electrons (this element is Lutetium, Lu). To save time, we use the Noble Gas shorthand. The noble gas Xenon (Xe) perfectly fills the first 54 rooms. So, we start from 54.

After 54, the next lowest energy room is the 6s orbital. The 's' rooms only hold 2 electrons. We put 2 electrons in 6s. Now we have 54 + 2 = 56 electrons placed.

Next, the rules dictate that we must drop down to fill the deep, inner f-block—specifically the 4f orbital. The 'f' rooms are massive suites that can hold exactly 14 electrons. Let's cram them in! 56 + 14 = 70 electrons. 

Uh oh! The 4f suite is now completely maxed out, but we have an atomic number of 71, meaning we have one single electron left to place. Because the 4f room is full, this 71st 'differentiating' electron is forced to spill over into the very next available room in the sequence. According to the energy diagrams, the room just slightly higher in energy than 4f is the 5d orbital! 

Therefore, the 71st electron proudly enters the 5d orbital, giving Lutetium the final configuration of [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹ 6s².

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q49. When the first electron gain enthalpy (∆ₑgH) of oxygen is -141kJ/mol, its second electron gain enthalpy is:
MCQ_Options: A more negative value than -141 kJ/mol
questions.Hint: When Oxygen gains one electron, it becomes negatively charged (O⁻). How do you think a negative ion feels about accepting a SECOND negatively charged electron? Remember that like charges repel!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine an Oxygen atom as an eager collector who really, really wants two rare trading cards (electrons) to finish their 'octet' collection. 

'Electron gain enthalpy' is simply the energy change that happens when an atom gets a new electron. When a neutral Oxygen atom receives its very first electron, it is absolutely thrilled! Because it's happy and moving to a more stable state, it throws a party and *releases* energy into the universe. In chemistry, when energy is released (exothermic), we give it a negative sign. That's why the first electron gain enthalpy is -141 kJ/mol.

But wait, the story changes drastically for the second electron. Oxygen now has an extra electron, making it a negatively charged ion (O⁻). Now, we are trying to force a *second* electron into the atom. What do we know about physics? The second electron is negative, and the O⁻ ion is negative. Like charges HATE each other! They repel fiercely.

The O⁻ ion essentially builds a forcefield, pushing the incoming second electron away. The electron won't just fall in on its own; you have to brutally *force* it in by shoving a massive amount of energy INTO the system. Because you, the scientist, have to supply energy (an endothermic process) to overcome this intense electrostatic repulsion, the energy value is assigned a positive sign.

Therefore, the second electron gain enthalpy is always a large, positive value!

questions.Question: Q50. The IUPAC symbol for the element with atomic number 119 would be:
questions.Hint: Break down the number 119 digit by digit. In IUPAC naming, 1 is 'un', and 9 is 'enn'.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there, young chemist! I know looking at elements with massive numbers like 119 can feel like looking at a sci-fi movie, but let me share a brilliant secret with you. When scientists discover (or predict) new superheavy elements, they don't get to give them cool names like 'Titanium' right away. First, they use a strict, super-logical naming system created by a group called IUPAC. Think of it like a temporary license plate for a new car.

Here is how the secret code works. IUPAC matches every digit from 0 to 9 with a specific Latin or Greek root:
0 = nil
1 = un
2 = bi
3 = tri
4 = quad
5 = pent
6 = hex
7 = sept
8 = oct
9 = enn

Now, let's look at our mystery atomic number: 119. All we have to do is translate the digits one by one!
- The first digit is 1, which translates to 'un'.
- The second digit is 1, which again translates to 'un'.
- The third digit is 9, which translates to 'enn'.

When we glue these together, we get 'un-un-enn'. Finally, to make it sound like a proper metal element, we add the suffix '-ium' to the end. So, the full temporary name is 'Ununennium'. 

To find the symbol, we just take the first letter of each part: 'U' for Un, 'u' for un, and 'e' for enn. Put them together, and you get 'Uue'. See? It is not memorization; it is just a logical puzzle. You decoded it perfectly!

questions.Concept: Ionization Energy and Noble Gas Configuration
questions.Question: Q51. The element having greatest difference between its first and second ionization energies, is:
questions.Hint: Look for an element that has exactly one valence electron. Once it loses that single outer electron, the atom achieves a perfectly stable, full 'Noble Gas' inner shell, making the second electron incredibly difficult to remove!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! Let's dive into an awesome concept called 'Ionization Energy'. Imagine an atom is like a parent holding onto its children (the electrons). Ionization energy is simply the amount of energy or 'effort' you need to apply to steal one of those electrons away. 

The 'First Ionization Energy' (IE1) is the effort to steal the very first electron. The 'Second Ionization Energy' (IE2) is the effort to steal the second one. The question is asking: Which element has a MASSIVE jump in effort between the first and second stolen electron?

To understand this, you need to know what every atom's ultimate dream in life is: to become a 'Noble Gas'. Noble gases have completely full, perfectly balanced outer shells (like having a perfectly packed suitcase where nothing shifts around). 

Let's look at Alkali metals, like Potassium (K). Potassium has 19 electrons. Its arrangement is 2, 8, 8, 1. That single '1' electron on the outside is annoying to Potassium. It wants to get rid of it to achieve the perfect 2, 8, 8 arrangement (which is the arrangement of the noble gas Argon). So, stealing that first electron is very easy! The First Ionization Energy is low.

But wait! Once Potassium loses that 1 electron, it becomes K⁺. It now has the perfect, highly stable 'noble gas' configuration. It is extremely happy. If you try to come back and steal a second electron (IE2), Potassium is going to fight you tooth and nail! You are trying to break open its perfectly packed suitcase. Therefore, the energy required to pull that second electron will be astronomically high. 

Because IE1 is super low and IE2 is super high, Alkali metals like Potassium have the greatest difference between their first and second ionization energies. Calcium (Ca) has 2 outer electrons, so its massive jump wouldn't happen until the THIRD electron. So Potassium is our winner here!

questions.Question: Q52. For Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻ and O²⁻; the correct order of increasing Ionic radii is:
questions.Hint: Count the electrons for each ion! You will notice they all have exactly 10 electrons. Since the electron count is the same, the ion with the most protons in its nucleus will pull those electrons the tightest, making it the smallest.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello my young chemist! At first glance, seeing all these pluses and minuses like Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, and O²⁻ might look like an alien language. But let's demystify it right now. We are trying to figure out which of these microscopic spheres is the smallest and which is the largest. 

First, let's count the electrons in each ion. 
- Sodium (Na) normally has 11 electrons. The '+' means it lost 1. So, 11 - 1 = 10 electrons.
- Magnesium (Mg) normally has 12 electrons. The '2+' means it lost 2. So, 12 - 2 = 10 electrons.
- Fluorine (F) normally has 9 electrons. The '-' means it gained 1. So, 9 + 1 = 10 electrons.
- Oxygen (O) normally has 8 electrons. The '2-' means it gained 2. So, 8 + 2 = 10 electrons.

Wow! They all have exactly 10 electrons. In chemistry, we call this being 'isoelectronic' ('iso' means same). Because they all have the exact same number of electrons floating around, we can't use electrons to determine their size. We have to look at the center of the atom: the nucleus!

Imagine a giant game of tug-of-war. The protons in the nucleus (which are positive) are pulling on the electrons in the shells (which are negative). 
- Oxygen has 8 protons pulling on 10 electrons.
- Fluorine has 9 protons pulling on 10 electrons.
- Sodium has 11 protons pulling on 10 electrons.
- Magnesium has 12 protons pulling on 10 electrons.

If you have 12 incredibly strong protons pulling on those 10 electrons (like in Mg²⁺), they are going to yank those electrons really close to the center. A stronger inward pull means a perfectly shrunken, smaller atom! On the other hand, Oxygen only has 8 protons. They aren't strong enough to pull the 10 electrons in tightly, so the electron cloud expands outward, making O²⁻ the largest.

So, ordering them from smallest to largest (increasing order), we start with the one with the most protons and end with the one with the fewest protons: Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻. You've just mastered a high-level chemistry concept by thinking about tug-of-war!
