questions.Question: Q53. Consider the following ionization enthalpies of two elements 'A' and 'B'. (Assume Element A has a massive energy jump after the 1st ionization, and Element B has a massive energy jump after the 2nd ionization). Which statement is correct?
MCQ_Options: A is an alkali metal, B is an alkaline earth metal
A is a noble gas, B is a halogen
A is an alkaline earth metal, B is an alkali metal
A and B are both transition metals
questions.Hint: Look for where the 'jump' happens. If an element loses 1 electron easily and then violently resists losing the 2nd, it belongs to Group 1. If it loses 2 easily and resists the 3rd, it belongs to Group 2.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Even though the original data table for this question got lost in the text chunk, we can solve the core concept it's trying to teach us: reading the 'hidden fingerprints' of elements using Ionization Enthalpies. 

Ionization enthalpy is just a fancy word for the energy required to rip an electron away from an atom. Imagine you have a wallet with some $1 bills (outer electrons) and a locked vault with $100 bills (inner core electrons). Giving away the $1 bills is easy. But the moment someone asks to break into the locked vault, you will put up a massive fight! 

In Chemistry, the 'locked vault' is the stable Noble Gas core. 

Let's say Element A has its first ionization energy at 500 units. Easy! But its second ionization energy is 4,500 units! That is a HUGE jump. What does this mean? It means Element A had exactly ONE easy $1 bill (one outer electron). Once it lost that one electron, it reached its stable vault. Atoms with exactly 1 outer electron belong to Group 1 of the periodic table, known as Alkali Metals (like Sodium or Potassium).

Now, let's look at Element B. Let's say its first ionization energy is 600, its second is 1,200, and its THIRD is a whopping 7,000! Notice where the big jump happened. It lost the first easily, lost the second easily, but fought back on the third. This means Element B had exactly TWO outer electrons. Atoms with exactly 2 outer electrons belong to Group 2, known as Alkaline Earth Metals (like Magnesium or Calcium).

By simply locating the massive jump in energy, you can act like a detective and figure out exactly what family an element belongs to. Since Element A jumps after the 1st, it's an alkali metal. Element B jumps after the 2nd, so it's an alkaline earth metal. Great detective work!
questions.Answer: A is an alkali metal, B is an alkaline earth metal

questions.Question: Q54. Which of the following atoms has the highest first ionization energy?
questions.Hint: Ionization energy is the energy needed to pull an electron away. Atoms that are very small hold onto their electrons the tightest! Look for the atom that is at the very top-right of the periodic table.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome back! Let's conquer another puzzle about Ionization Energy. Remember, 'Ionization Energy' is the energy needed to steal an electron from an atom. If an atom holds onto its electrons really, really tightly, you will need a massive amount of energy to rip one away. 

So, which atom holds onto its electrons the tightest? To answer this, we need to think about two things: distance and shielding.

Imagine you are holding two magnets. If you hold them very close together, the pull is incredibly strong. If you pull them far apart, the pull gets weak. The same is true for an atom! The positive nucleus is pulling on the negative electrons. If an atom is physically small, its electrons are very close to the nucleus, meaning the 'magnetic' pull is overwhelmingly strong.

Also, if an atom has lots of inner shells of electrons, those inner layers act like a thick blanket, blocking or 'shielding' the outer electrons from feeling the pull of the nucleus. 

Now look at Helium (He). It is located at the very top right of the periodic table. It has 2 protons pulling on 2 electrons. These electrons are in the very first shell (the closest shell possible to the nucleus!). There are zero inner electron blankets blocking the pull. The protons are holding onto those electrons with an iron grip! 

Sodium (Na), on the other hand, is a large atom with many layers blocking the pull, making its outer electron easy to steal. Nitrogen and Oxygen are in between, but they are larger than Helium. 

Because Helium is the smallest atom on the periodic table with completely unshielded, perfectly close electrons and a happy, full outer shell, it possesses the highest first ionization energy of ANY element in the entire universe! Taking an electron from Helium is almost impossible.

questions.Question: Q55. The ionic radii (in Å) of N³⁻, O²⁻ and F⁻ are respectively:
questions.Hint: All three ions have 10 electrons, but different numbers of protons. Nitrogen has 7 protons, Oxygen has 8, and Fluorine has 9. The one with the fewest protons has the weakest pull, making it the largest in size!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
My friend, you've actually seen this concept before in question Q52, but now we are applying it to real numbers! Don't let the decimals intimidate you; the logic is identical.

We are looking at N³⁻, O²⁻, and F⁻. First, let's do our favorite trick and count the electrons:
- Nitrogen (N) has 7 protons and normally 7 electrons. Gaining 3 (³⁻) gives it 10 electrons.
- Oxygen (O) has 8 protons and normally 8 electrons. Gaining 2 (²⁻) gives it 10 electrons.
- Fluorine (F) has 9 protons and normally 9 electrons. Gaining 1 (⁻) gives it 10 electrons.

They are all isoelectronic! They all have exactly 10 electrons. Now we use our tug-of-war analogy to figure out their sizes.

- In Fluorine, 9 positive protons are pulling on the 10 negative electrons.
- In Oxygen, 8 positive protons are pulling on the 10 negative electrons.
- In Nitrogen, only 7 positive protons are trying to pull in 10 negative electrons.

Who is going to win the tug-of-war? Fluorine has the most protons (9), so it pulls the electrons inward with the greatest force, shrinking the atom down. This makes F⁻ the smallest. Nitrogen has the weakest pull (only 7 protons), so the electrons drift further away, making N³⁻ the largest. 

So, the order of size from largest to smallest is N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻. 

Now look at the numbers in the correct option: 1.71, 1.40, and 1.36. We need the numbers to be in decreasing order to match N³⁻ (biggest), O²⁻ (middle), F⁻ (smallest). The first option gives us exactly that: 1.71 Å, 1.40 Å, 1.36 Å. You cracked the code flawlessly!

questions.Question: Q56. Similarity in chemical properties of the atoms of elements in a group of the periodic table is most closely related to:
questions.Hint: Chemical reactions happen when the outermost parts of two atoms bump into each other. Elements in the same vertical column (group) share the exact same number of these outermost parts!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello! Let's talk about why the Periodic Table is shaped the weird way it is. Have you ever wondered why scientists didn't just put elements in one giant, straight line from 1 to 118? Why arrange them in a castle-like block with vertical columns?

The answer lies in how elements behave! Scientists noticed early on that certain elements acted like siblings. For instance, Lithium, Sodium, and Potassium all explode spectacularly when you throw them in water. They share 'chemical properties'. Therefore, scientists grouped these siblings into vertical columns called 'Groups'.

But WHY do elements in the same group act similarly? 

Think about what a chemical reaction actually is. When two atoms get close to each other, their inner parts (the nucleus and inner electrons) never actually touch. The only parts that interact, bump, trade, and share are the electrons on the very outside edge of the atom. We call these outermost electrons 'Valence Electrons'.

If you have 1 valence electron, you are going to trade and bond in a very specific way. If you have 7 valence electrons, you are going to act in a completely different way.

It turns out, every element in Group 1 (like Lithium, Sodium, and Potassium) has exactly ONE valence electron! Every element in Group 17 (like Fluorine, Chlorine, and Bromine) has exactly SEVEN valence electrons. 

Because chemistry is essentially the trading and sharing of these outer electrons, having the same number of valence electrons means the elements play the game using the exact same rules. Think of it like a sports team: everyone wearing the same uniform (valence electrons) plays for the same team (chemical properties). That is the genius of the periodic table!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q57. Which of the following arrangements represents the increasing order (smallest to largest) of ionic radii of the given species O²⁻, S²⁻, N³⁻, P³⁻?
questions.Hint: Remember that ions with more electron shells are always larger. For ions with the same number of shells, count the protons: more protons pulling on the same number of electrons makes the ion squish down smaller!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let us break this down into a super fun puzzle! Imagine an atom is like a bustling mini-solar system. The nucleus in the center is the sun (packed with positively charged protons), and the electrons are the planets (negatively charged) orbiting around it. Now, the size of this solar system—the 'ionic radius'—depends on two big things: how many orbits (shells) there are, and how hard the sun is pulling on those planets.

First, let us look at the number of shells. Oxygen (O) and Nitrogen (N) are found in Period 2 of the periodic table, meaning they only have 2 electron shells. Sulfur (S) and Phosphorus (P) are in Period 3, so they have 3 shells. More shells automatically mean a much bigger atom! It is like comparing a two-story house to a three-story house. So right away, we know that the Period 3 ions (S²⁻ and P³⁻) are larger than the Period 2 ions (O²⁻ and N³⁻).

Now, let us compare the two smaller ones: O²⁻ and N³⁻. Both of these ions have exactly 10 electrons (they are called 'isoelectronic' because they share the same number of electrons). But Oxygen has 8 protons in its nucleus, while Nitrogen only has 7. Imagine the protons are people playing a massive game of tug-of-war against the 10 electrons. 8 people pulling on the rope are going to pull those electrons in much closer and tighter than 7 people could! Because Oxygen pulls harder, the electron cloud of O²⁻ gets squished down, making it smaller than N³⁻.

Finally, we do the exact same thing for the bigger ones: S²⁻ and P³⁻. Both have 18 electrons, but Sulfur has 16 protons while Phosphorus only has 15. The 16 protons of Sulfur pull the 18 electrons tighter than the 15 protons of Phosphorus do. Therefore, S²⁻ is squished smaller than P³⁻.

When we stack them all up from the absolute smallest to the largest, we get: O²⁻ (smallest) < N³⁻ < S²⁻ < P³⁻ (largest). You just solved a high-level chemistry puzzle using pure, brilliant logic!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q58. Which of the following represents the correct order of increasing first ionization enthalpy for Ca, Ba, S, Se and Ar?
questions.Hint: Metals want to lose electrons easily, while non-metals want to keep them. Noble gases will fight you the hardest! Also, bigger atoms hold their outer electrons more loosely.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us dive into a concept called 'First Ionization Enthalpy.' Do not let the fancy words scare you—this is simply a measurement of the amount of energy you need to use to 'steal' an outermost electron from an atom. Imagine stealing a favorite toy from a little kid. If the kid is holding it tightly close to their chest, it is going to be incredibly difficult to take. But if the toy is rolling away far from them, or if the kid actually wants to give it to you, it is super easy!

Here is the golden rule: Non-metals (on the right side of the periodic table) HATE losing electrons. They want to gain them! Metals (on the left side) LOVE losing electrons so they can become stable. 

Let us look at our contestants: Calcium (Ca), Barium (Ba), Sulfur (S), Selenium (Se), and Argon (Ar).

Argon is a Noble Gas. It has a perfect, fully complete outer shell. It is the ultimate zen master of the periodic table and will fight with absolutely everything it has to keep its electrons. So, taking an electron from Argon is the absolute hardest. Ar has the highest ionization enthalpy.

Now look at Calcium and Barium. These are metals. They actively want to give away their electrons. Barium is located further down the periodic table than Calcium, which means it has more electron shells. Because Barium is a giant, bulky atom, its outermost electron is very far away from the positive pull of the nucleus. The nucleus barely notices it is there! Therefore, Barium's electron is the easiest to steal. Calcium is smaller than Barium, so its nucleus holds on just a bit tighter. So, Ba is easier to steal from than Ca.

Next, we have Sulfur and Selenium. These are non-metals, so they naturally fight back harder than the metals. Selenium is larger than Sulfur (it is below Sulfur on the table), so its outer electron is further out. That makes Selenium slightly easier to steal from than Sulfur. 

Putting it all together from easiest to hardest to steal an electron: Barium (giant metal) < Calcium (smaller metal) < Selenium (large non-metal) < Sulfur (smaller non-metal) < Argon (invincible noble gas). You nailed the trends perfectly!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Concept: Second Ionization Potential and Electron Configurations
questions.Question: Q59. Which is the correct order of second ionization potential of C, N, O and F in the following?
questions.Hint: We are removing the SECOND electron here! This means we start with C⁺, N⁺, O⁺, and F⁺. Look closely at O⁺: taking away one electron from oxygen left it with a perfectly balanced 'half-filled' p-orbital. It will refuse to let you ruin its balance!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is one of the coolest 'trick' questions in chemistry, and once you understand the secret behind it, you will never get it wrong! The question asks for the 'Second' Ionization Potential. This means we are not stealing the first electron; we are stealing the SECOND electron. The atoms have already lost one electron and are now positive ions: C⁺, N⁺, O⁺, and F⁺.

To figure out who fights the hardest to keep this second electron, we need to look at their 'electron configurations'—which is just a map of where their electrons live. Imagine electrons live in different rooms inside a house, and the 'p-orbital' is a room that can hold exactly 6 electrons. There is a magical rule in chemistry: atoms feel incredibly stable and happy if this room is exactly 'half-filled' (with exactly 3 electrons). It feels perfectly balanced, like carrying a bucket of water in each hand instead of just one.

Normally, neutral Oxygen has 4 electrons in this room (written as 2p⁴). When we take away the first electron to make O⁺, it suddenly has exactly 3 electrons left in that room (2p³). Boom! O⁺ has accidentally reached ultimate Zen and perfect balance! Because of this half-filled stability, O⁺ transforms into a stubborn superhero. If you try to come in and steal a second electron from O⁺, it will resist with immense power because you are ruining its perfect symmetry.

Normally, Fluorine (F) would be harder to steal from than Oxygen, because ionization energy generally increases as you move left-to-right across the periodic table (C < N < O < F). Carbon is the easiest, then Nitrogen, then Oxygen, then Fluorine. But because we are talking about the SECOND electron, O⁺ has that special half-filled armor. F⁺ has 4 electrons in its room (2p⁴), so it does not have that perfect half-filled balance to protect it.

Because Oxygen gains this superpower, it leapfrogs over Fluorine! The normal order gets completely disrupted. Carbon is still the easiest, Nitrogen is next, but then comes Fluorine, and the hardest of all is Oxygen. The final order is C < N < F < O. Remember, in chemistry, perfect symmetry and balance always win!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q60. Which among the following elements has the highest first ionization enthalpy?
questions.Hint: Look for the element that is the smallest AND has a completely full outer shell. It is a noble gas that sits at the very top right of the periodic table.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us go on a hunt for the most stubborn element in the entire universe when it comes to giving up an electron. The question asks for the 'highest first ionization enthalpy.' Remember, 'ionization enthalpy' is just the science way of saying 'the energy needed to rip an electron away from an atom.' 

What makes an electron hard to rip away? Two major things: First, how close the electron is to the positive nucleus. Magnets are stronger when they are closer together, right? The same goes for the positive nucleus pulling on the negative electron. Second, how 'complete' the atom's outer shell is. Elements absolutely love having a full outer shell; it is the ultimate goal of their atomic existence.

Now, let me introduce you to Helium (He). Helium is located at the very top right of the periodic table. Because it is at the very top, it only has one single electron shell (called the 1s shell). This shell is as close to the nucleus as physically possible. There are no other layers of inner electrons getting in the way or blocking the nucleus's pulling power (a concept called 'shielding'). 

Furthermore, this first shell can only hold a maximum of 2 electrons. Guess how many electrons Helium has? Exactly 2! Its tiny little shell is 100% completely full. Helium has achieved total chemical nirvana. It does not want to react, it does not want to share, and it certainly does not want to lose an electron.

If you try to pluck one of those two electrons away, you are fighting against a nucleus that is holding onto them from point-blank range, without any interference, from an already perfectly stable system. Nitrogen and Oxygen are bigger, so their electrons are further away. Sodium actually wants to lose an electron. But Helium? It requires massive, universe-bending energy to force it to let go. That is why Helium wears the ultimate crown for the highest first ionization enthalpy of any element!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q61. The correct sequence which shows decreasing order of the ionic radii of the elements is
questions.Hint: These ions all have exactly 10 electrons! To find the largest ion, look for the one with the FEWEST protons in the nucleus, because a weak nucleus cannot pull the electrons in tightly.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Get ready to learn one of the most powerful tricks in chemistry: comparing the sizes of ions that have the exact same number of electrons! When different atoms or ions have the same number of electrons, we call them an 'isoelectronic series' ('iso' means same, and 'electronic' means electrons).

Let us look at a classic lineup: Nitrogen (N³⁻), Oxygen (O²⁻), Fluorine (F⁻), and Sodium (Na⁺). If you do the math, every single one of these ions has exactly 10 electrons. Nitrogen normally has 7, but gained 3. Oxygen normally has 8, but gained 2. Fluorine normally has 9, but gained 1. Sodium normally has 11, but lost 1. They all magically arrived at the number 10! 

So, if they all have 10 electrons orbiting them, shouldn't they all be the exact same size? Nope! The secret lies hidden in the center of the atom: the nucleus. 

Even though they all have 10 negative electrons, they have a completely different number of positive protons pulling on them. Think of the protons as parents and the electrons as hyperactive puppies on leashes. 

In the Sodium ion (Na⁺), you have 11 parents pulling on 10 puppies. Because there are more parents than puppies, they can pull all the puppies in extremely close. The sodium ion shrinks down and becomes incredibly tiny!

Now look at the Nitrogen ion (N³⁻). Here, you only have 7 parents trying to hold onto 10 energetic puppies. The parents are totally overpowered! The puppies run outward, stretching the leashes, causing the electron cloud to expand massively. Nitrogen becomes the biggest of the group.

Oxygen (O²⁻) has 8 protons, so it is slightly smaller than Nitrogen but larger than the rest. Fluorine (F⁻) has 9 protons, so it is quite small, but not as small as Sodium with its 11 protons.

Therefore, if we want to arrange them from the absolute largest to the absolute smallest (decreasing order), we start with the one with the fewest protons and end with the most protons. The order is: N³⁻ (largest) > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ (smallest). Just count the protons playing tug-of-war, and you easily crack the case!

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q62. Following statements regarding the periodic trends of chemical reactivity of alkali metals and halogens are given. Which of these statements gives the correct picture?
MCQ_Options: Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group, while reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.
Reactivity of both alkali metals and halogens increases down the group.
Reactivity of both alkali metals and halogens decreases down the group.
Reactivity of alkali metals decreases down the group, while reactivity of halogens increases down the group.
questions.Hint: Metals react by LOSING electrons, which becomes easier when atoms get bigger (down a group). Non-metals react by GAINING electrons, which becomes harder when atoms get bigger because the positive nucleus is buried deep inside the atom.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Chemical reactivity is simply the story of how desperately an atom wants to interact with others to achieve a perfect, stable outer shell. But here is the fascinating part: metals and non-metals play this game using completely opposite strategies! 

Let us start with the Alkali Metals (Group 1), like Lithium, Sodium, and Potassium. These guys have exactly one electron in their outermost shell. They view this single electron as an annoying burden. To become stable, their strategy is to throw this electron away as fast as possible. As you go down the group on the periodic table (Lithium $\rightarrow$ Sodium $\rightarrow$ Potassium), the atoms get bigger and bigger because they keep adding more electron shells. Potassium is much larger than Lithium. Because Potassium is so huge, that annoying outermost electron is super far away from the positive pull of the nucleus. The nucleus has a really weak grip on it. It is like holding a heavy bag by the very tip of the strap—it easily drops! Because it is so much easier to lose the electron, alkali metals become MORE violently reactive as you go down the group.

Now, let us flip the script and look at the Halogens (Group 17), like Fluorine, Chlorine, and Bromine. They have 7 electrons in their outer shell and are desperately craving just ONE more to reach the perfect 8. Their strategy is to use the positive power of their nucleus to pull in an electron from a passing atom. 

Fluorine is at the top of the group and is very tiny. Because it is small, its positively charged nucleus is very close to the outside world, so it acts like an incredibly powerful magnet, violently snatching electrons. It is immensely reactive! But as you go down the group to atoms like Bromine or Iodine, the atoms become massive. Their positive nucleus gets buried deep inside thick layers of their own electrons. It is like trying to use a magnet while it is wrapped in 10 thick blankets! The nucleus cannot reach out and grab new electrons effectively. Therefore, halogens become LESS reactive as you go down the group.

So, metals get more reactive as they get bigger (going down), and non-metals get less reactive as they get bigger. Nature loves balance, and this contrast is a beautiful example of it!
questions.Answer: Reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group, while reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

questions.Chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.Question: Q63. Which of the following oxides is amphoteric in character?
questions.Hint: Look for the element that acts like a 'chemical chameleon.' It sits on the borderline between metals and non-metals, so it can act as both an acid and a base!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this question, we have to talk about the 'personalities' of different chemicals. When an element combines with oxygen, it forms an 'oxide.' In the world of chemistry, these oxides usually fall into two major rival teams: Acids and Bases.

Most of the time, oxides are very predictable. When metals (like Sodium or Calcium) bond with oxygen, they form 'basic' oxides. If you dissolve them in water or react them with acids, they behave exactly like bases. On the other hand, when non-metals (like Carbon or Sulfur) bond with oxygen, they form 'acidic' oxides. Carbon dioxide (CO₂), for example, is what makes sodas fizzy, and it forms carbonic acid in water.

But nature loves to throw us a curveball, and that is exactly where 'Amphoteric' oxides come in. The word 'amphi' means 'both'—just like an amphibian is an animal that can live perfectly well on BOTH land and in the water (like a frog!). An amphoteric oxide is a chemical chameleon. It does not pick a single side. It has the incredible superpower to act as an acid OR a base, depending entirely on what it is reacting with at the time.

If you drop an amphoteric oxide into a strong acid, it puts on a disguise and acts exactly like a base to neutralize it. But if you take that exact same oxide and drop it into a strong base, it flips its personality and acts just like an acid! 

Aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) is the most famous superstar of the amphoteric world. Because aluminum sits right on the boundary line between the metals and the non-metals on the periodic table, it inherits physical traits from both sides. Zinc oxide (ZnO) is another famous example of this. By contrast, Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is strictly acidic, Sodium oxide (Na₂O) is strictly basic, and Sulfur trioxide (SO₃) is strictly acidic. So, whenever you see Aluminum oxide, just remember the chemical chameleon—it is amphoteric and plays both sides of the game perfectly!

questions.Question: Q64. Which one of the following ions has the highest value of ionic radius?
questions.Hint: Think about protons and electrons playing a game of tug-of-war. If the number of electrons is the same across different ions, how does the number of protons affect how tightly the atom holds itself together?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! To tackle this question, we first need to look at the ions we've put in our options: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, and Mg²⁺. These are what chemists call an **isoelectronic series**.

Let's break down that big word: 'iso' means 'same', and 'electronic' refers to electrons. All four of these ions have exactly 10 electrons. Oxygen normally has 8 electrons, but it gained 2 to become O²⁻. Fluorine has 9, gained 1. Sodium has 11, lost 1. Magnesium has 12, lost 2. So, they all end up with a team of exactly 10 electrons buzzing around the center.

Now, imagine a giant game of tug-of-war. On one side, you have the electrons (the outer rope), and pulling them inward from the center are the protons in the nucleus. The more protons you have, the stronger the inward pull!

Let's count the protons for each ion:
- Oxygen (O²⁻): 8 protons pulling 10 electrons.
- Fluorine (F⁻): 9 protons pulling 10 electrons.
- Sodium (Na⁺): 11 protons pulling 10 electrons.
- Magnesium (Mg²⁺): 12 protons pulling 10 electrons.

Because Magnesium has 12 protons, it pulls those 10 electrons super tightly toward itself, making the Mg²⁺ ion very small. Oxygen, on the other hand, only has 8 protons. It's like having a much weaker team pulling on the rope. Because the nucleus isn't pulling as strongly, the 10 electrons aren't held as tightly. They naturally drift further out, making the O²⁻ ion the largest of the group!

So, whenever you see an isoelectronic series, remember this golden rule: fewer protons means a weaker pull, which always results in a larger atomic radius. You got this!

questions.Question: Q65. The formation of the oxide ion O²⁻(g) requires first an exothermic and then an endothermic step as shown below. O(g) + e⁻ = O⁻(g) ∆H° = -142kJ mol⁻¹, O⁻(g) + e⁻ = O²⁻(g) ∆H° = 844kJ mol⁻¹. This is because
MCQ_Options: The O⁻ ion has a net negative charge, which forces strong electrostatic repulsion on the incoming negative electron.
Oxygen is highly electronegative, so it naturally resists gaining any extra electrons.
Adding a second electron requires breaking the nucleus of the atom apart.
Oxygen has an exceptionally large atomic size, making it hard to hold onto outer electrons.
questions.Hint: Remember the golden rule of charges: opposites attract, but like charges repel! What happens when you try to force a negatively charged electron into an ion that is already negatively charged?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! This is an incredibly cool question because it shows us that atoms don't just magically follow rules without a physical reason. It actually comes down to simple physics—specifically, how magnets or electrical charges behave in the real world.

You already know that opposite charges attract (positive likes negative) and like charges repel (negative hates negative). Let's look at what's happening to the oxygen atom step by step.

**Step 1:** We start with a neutral oxygen atom, O(g), and we give it an electron (e⁻). Since the oxygen atom's positive nucleus can 'see' and grab that incoming negative electron, it happily takes it in. When atoms get what they want, they release energy to relax. This release of energy is called an **exothermic** reaction. That's exactly why the energy change (∆H°) is a negative number (-142 kJ mol⁻¹). The atom is literally throwing extra energy away because it has become stable and happy.

**Step 2:** Now we have O⁻. Because it gained an electron, it is an ion with a net negative charge. In the second step, we are trying to force *another* negatively charged electron onto this already-negative O⁻ ion.

Imagine trying to push the south poles of two super-strong magnets together. What happens? They fight you! They push back against your hands. You have to physically use your own muscle energy to force them to touch. The exact same thing happens in chemistry here. The negative O⁻ ion powerfully repels the incoming negative electron. To make the electron stick and form O²⁻, we have to force it in by adding a ton of energy from the outside. Because we have to put energy *into* the system, this step is **endothermic**, and the ∆H° becomes a huge positive number (+844 kJ mol⁻¹).

So, the mystery is officially solved! The second step is endothermic simply because of the massive electrical repulsion between the negative ion and the negative electron. Chemistry makes perfect sense when you think about the invisible forces at play!
questions.Answer: The O⁻ ion has a net negative charge, which forces strong electrostatic repulsion on the incoming negative electron.

questions.Question: The number of molecules/ions that show linear geometry among the following is __________. SO₂, BeCl₂, CO₂, N₃⁻, NO₂, F₂O, XeF₂, NO₂⁺, I₃⁻, O₃
questions.Hint: Draw the Lewis structure for each and count the 'electron domains' (bonds + lone pairs). If there are lone pairs, think about how they push the bonds away like invisible balloons!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Chemistry can look like alphabet soup sometimes, but underneath it all, molecules are just playing a game of personal space. This game is called VSEPR theory (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion). Electrons are negatively charged, so they hate being near each other. They push away from each other as much as possible.

Imagine the central atom of a molecule as you, standing in the middle. The atoms bonded to you, and any 'lone pairs' (pairs of electrons not shared with anyone), are like big balloons tied to your waist. They want to spread out evenly.

Let's look at our suspects and count their balloons!

1. SO₂ (Sulfur Dioxide): Sulfur has 2 oxygen atoms attached and 1 invisible lone pair of electrons. 3 balloons spread out in a triangle (trigonal planar), but we only 'see' the atoms. So the shape looks like a boomerang. Bent, not linear! (No)

2. BeCl₂ (Beryllium Chloride): Beryllium holds 2 chlorine atoms and has 0 lone pairs. 2 balloons will sit exactly opposite each other (180 degrees). Perfectly Linear! (Yes! Count = 1)

3. CO₂ (Carbon Dioxide): Carbon has 2 oxygens and 0 lone pairs. Just like BeCl₂, they sit opposite. Linear! (Yes! Count = 2)

4. N₃⁻ (Azide ion): The central Nitrogen is double-bonded to two other nitrogens with 0 lone pairs. Linear! (Yes! Count = 3)

5. NO₂ (Nitrogen Dioxide): Nitrogen has 2 oxygens and one single, odd electron. Even one electron acts like a mini-balloon, pushing the oxygens down. Bent! (No)

6. F₂O (Oxygen Difluoride): Oxygen is the center with 2 fluorines and 2 big fat lone pairs. 4 balloons make a tetrahedron, but ignoring the invisible lone pairs, it looks Bent. (No)

7. XeF₂ (Xenon Difluoride): This is a tricky one! Xenon is a big atom. It holds 2 fluorines and has 3 lone pairs! The 3 lone pairs take up the 'equator' of Xenon (a triangle), leaving the 2 fluorines sticking straight up and down (the North and South poles). Straight line! Linear! (Yes! Count = 4)

8. NO₂⁺ (Nitronium ion): Nitrogen has 2 oxygens, and because of the positive charge, it lost its extra electron. 0 lone pairs. Linear! (Yes! Count = 5)

9. I₃⁻ (Triiodide ion): Just like XeF₂, the central Iodine has 2 iodine buddies and 3 lone pairs around its waist. The buddies are pushed straight up and down. Linear! (Yes! Count = 6)

10. O₃ (Ozone): Central oxygen has 2 oxygen buddies and 1 lone pair. 3 balloons = Bent shape. (No)

So, the linear ones are BeCl₂, CO₂, N₃⁻, XeF₂, NO₂⁺, and I₃⁻. That's exactly 6 molecules! You've got this—just visualize the balloons!

questions.Concept: The Octet Rule and its Exceptions
questions.Question: Match the List - I with List - II. List - I (Classification of molecules based on octet rule) List - II (Example) (A) Molecules obeying octet rule (I) NO, NO₂ (B) Molecules with incomplete octet (II) BCl₃, AlCl₃ (C) Molecules with incomplete octet with odd electron (III) H₂SO₄, PCl₅ (D) Molecules with expanded octet (IV) CCl₄, CO₂
questions.Hint: Think of the 'octet rule' as atoms wanting exactly 8 slices of pizza to be full. Who gets exactly 8? Who is a kid that gets full on 6? Who is a giant that can eat 10 or 12?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into the 'Octet Rule'! The Octet Rule is a fundamental guideline in chemistry which states that atoms are happiest (most stable) when they have exactly 8 electrons in their outermost shell, just like the noble gases.

Imagine a fancy dinner party where everyone wants exactly 8 slices of pizza. But in reality, not everyone plays by the rules.

(A) Molecules obeying octet rule: These are the perfect guests. Carbon (C) and Oxygen (O) always want exactly 8. In CCl₄, Carbon shares its 4 electrons with 4 Chlorines to get 8. In CO₂, Carbon double-bonds with two Oxygens to get 8. So, (A) matches with (IV).

(B) Molecules with incomplete octet: Some atoms are small and get full quickly! Boron (B) and Aluminum (Al) only have 3 valence electrons to start. In BCl₃ and AlCl₃, they form 3 bonds, getting a total of 6 electrons. They are completely happy with 6, which is 'incomplete' compared to 8. So, (B) matches with (II).

(C) Molecules with odd electron: What happens if the total number of electrons in the whole molecule is an odd number? In NO (Nitrogen Monoxide), Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and Oxygen has 6. Total = 11. You can't divide 11 evenly by 2! Someone is stuck with an odd number of electrons. NO and NO₂ are famous for this. So, (C) matches with (I).

(D) Molecules with expanded octet: These are the heavyweights. Elements in the 3rd row of the periodic table and below (like P, S, Cl) have giant empty rooms called 'd-orbitals'. They can fit way more than 8 electrons! In PCl₅, Phosphorus forms 5 bonds (10 electrons). In H₂SO₄, Sulfur can have up to 12 electrons around it! So, (D) matches with (III).

Putting it all together, the correct combination is (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III). See? It's just matching guests to their appetites!

questions.Question: Given below are two statements: Statement (I): Experimentally determined oxygen-oxygen bond lengths in the O₃ are found to be same and the bond length is greater than that of a O=O (double bond) but less than that of a single O-O bond. Statement (II): The strong lone pair-lone pair repulsion between oxygen atoms is solely responsible for the fact that the bond length in ozone is smaller than that of a double bond O=O but more than that of a single bond O-O.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are true
Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are false
Statement (I) is true but Statement (II) is false
Statement (I) is false but Statement (II) is true
questions.Hint: If a molecule is drawn with one single and one double bond, does it stay like that? Or does it rapidly blend into a 'hybrid'? Think about the concept of Resonance!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's investigate the mystery of the Ozone (O₃) molecule! Ozone consists of three oxygen atoms in a row.

When we try to draw the Lewis structure for Ozone, we have to put a double bond between the first two oxygen atoms, and a single bond between the second and third (O=O-O). But here is the crazy part: when scientists actually look at ozone with a microscope, they don't see one short bond (double bonds are short and strong) and one long bond (single bonds are long and weak). 

Instead, they see that BOTH bonds are exactly the same length! And the length is right in the middle between a single and a double bond. Why? Because of a superpower called **Resonance**. 

The true structure of Ozone isn't a rigid single-and-double bond; it's a blend of both. It's like mixing blue paint and yellow paint. You don't see blue and yellow spots; you see an entirely new color: green! The electrons are 'delocalized' (spread out) evenly across all three atoms. So, Statement (I) is absolutely TRUE.

Now, let's look at Statement (II). It claims that the bond length is intermediate because of 'strong lone pair-lone pair repulsion'. Is that true? NO! That's a trick. As we just learned, the beautiful, perfectly intermediate bond length is purely because of **Resonance**. The electrons are happily smearing themselves over the molecule like butter on toast. Lone pair repulsion has nothing to do with it.

Therefore, Statement I is true, and Statement II is totally false. Science mysteries: solved by resonance!
questions.Answer: Statement (I) is true but Statement (II) is false

questions.Question: Consider the following molecules: The correct order of rate of hydrolysis is:
MCQ_Options: Insufficient data in the text to determine
questions.Hint: Wait a minute! The actual molecules are missing from the question snippet. But what normally makes a molecule easy for water to attack (hydrolyze)? Think about empty 'd-orbitals'!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Okay, team! Notice something funny about this question? It says 'Consider the following molecules:' but then... no molecules are listed! This happens sometimes when questions are extracted from larger test papers. Without the molecules, we literally cannot give the exact answer.

But a legendary chemist never gives up an opportunity to learn. So, how WOULD we solve it if we had the molecules? 

Let's pretend the question asked you to compare the rate of hydrolysis of CCl₄ (Carbon Tetrachloride) and SiCl₄ (Silicon Tetrachloride).

'Hydrolysis' is a fancy word meaning 'water (hydro) breaking something apart (lysis)'. For water to break a molecule, the water molecule (which acts like a tiny little dart) has to find a spot to attach to the central atom. 

Carbon in CCl₄ is highly protected. It's small, surrounded by four giant Chlorine atoms (this is called 'steric hindrance', like bodyguards blocking the way). Even worse, Carbon has no empty rooms (d-orbitals) for the water to park its electrons. Water bounces right off! CCl₄ doesn't hydrolyze.

Silicon, on the other hand, in SiCl₄, is a much bigger atom. It's in the 3rd row of the periodic table, which means it has a secret weapon: empty 'd-orbitals'! These act like giant, open landing pads. Water easily swoops in, parks its electrons in the empty d-orbitals, and starts ripping the molecule apart. 

So, the rule for hydrolysis is: **Molecules with central atoms that have empty d-orbitals (like Si, P, S) and lower steric crowding hydrolyze the fastest.** 

Even though we didn't have the specific molecules to rank today, you now possess the secret knowledge to solve ANY hydrolysis question you ever encounter!
questions.Answer: Insufficient data in the text to determine

questions.Question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Wet cotton clothes made of cellulose based carbohydrate takes comparatively longer time to get dried than wet nylon polymer based clothes. Statement II: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding with water molecule is more in nylon-based clothes than in the case of cotton clothes.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.Hint: Cotton easily absorbs sweat and holds onto water forever. What chemical 'velcro' allows cotton to grab so much water? Is it hydrogen bonding?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
If you play sports, you probably know that if you wear a thick cotton t-shirt, it gets soaked in sweat and takes hours to dry. But if you wear a synthetic sports shirt (like Nylon or Polyester), it dries really fast! Why? It's all about Intermolecular Forces!

Statement I says that wet cotton takes longer to dry than wet nylon. This is a real-world fact. Cotton absorbs water like a sponge, while nylon barely absorbs any. So, Statement I is completely TRUE.

But WHY does this happen? Statement II tries to explain it by claiming that Nylon forms MORE hydrogen bonds with water than cotton does. Let's look at their molecular structures to see if this is true.

Cotton is made of 'cellulose'. Cellulose is a giant chain of sugar molecules. On these chains, there are tons of -OH (hydroxyl) groups. These -OH groups are basically tiny chemical magnets for water! Because water is H₂O, the Oxygen in water loves to stick to the Hydrogen in the -OH groups on the cotton. This 'stickiness' is called **Hydrogen Bonding**. Cotton has millions of these sticky velcro hooks, so it holds onto water intensely!

Nylon, on the other hand, is a synthetic plastic-like polymer. It does have some polar groups (amide links), but far, far fewer than cotton. So, water just slides right off Nylon.

This means Statement II has it completely backwards! Cotton has much MORE hydrogen bonding with water, not less. 

So, the first statement is a true observation, but the second statement is a false explanation.
questions.Answer: Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.Concept: VSEPR Theory: Equatorial vs Axial Positions
questions.Question: Given below are two statements: Statement (I): For ClF₃, three possible structures may be drawn as follows. Statement (II): Structure III is most stable, as the orbitals having the lone pairs are axial, where the lp-bp repulsion is minimum.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are true
Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are false
Statement (I) is true but Statement (II) is false
Statement (I) is false but Statement (II) is true
questions.Hint: In a 5-coordinate (trigonal bipyramidal) shape, the 'equator' has 120-degree angles, giving lots of room. The 'poles' (axial) only have 90-degree angles. Where would fat, space-hogging lone pairs want to sit to avoid being crowded?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to one of the most famous geometry puzzles in chemistry: the shape of ClF₃ (Chlorine Trifluoride)!

First, let's figure out how many 'things' are attached to the central Chlorine. Chlorine has 7 valence electrons. It uses 3 of them to bond with 3 Fluorine atoms. That leaves 4 electrons, which makes 2 'Lone Pairs'. 
Total 'things' around Chlorine = 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 5 groups.

When 5 groups space themselves out, they form a shape called 'Trigonal Bipyramidal'. Imagine the Earth: 3 groups sit around the Equator in a triangle (equatorial positions), and 2 groups sit at the North and South poles (axial positions). 
Statement (I) says we can draw 3 possible structures. That's true! We could put the two lone pairs both at the poles, both at the equator, or one of each.

Now for Statement (II): Where should the lone pairs ACTUALLY go to make the molecule stable? 
Lone pairs are like big, invisible, fluffy clouds of electrons. They are much 'fatter' than regular bonding pairs, so they need a lot of space. 

If you put a fat lone pair at the North Pole (axial), it is squished at a tight 90-degree angle from the 3 atoms on the equator. That causes massive repulsion!
But, if you put the lone pair on the Equator, it is spaced out by a wide 120-degree angle from its neighbors on the equator. 

Therefore, fat lone pairs ALWAYS prefer the wider, roomier **equatorial** positions in this shape! 
Statement (II) claims that the most stable structure puts the lone pairs in the *axial* positions because repulsion is minimum. That is horribly FALSE! Putting them axial creates MAXIMUM squishing.

So, Statement (I) is true, but Statement (II) is false. Always give lone pairs legroom!
questions.Answer: Statement (I) is true but Statement (II) is false

questions.Question: In SO₂, NO₂ and N₃⁻, the hybridizations at the central atom are respectively:
questions.Hint: To find hybridization, calculate the 'Steric Number' for each central atom (Steric Number = Number of atoms attached + Number of lone pairs). SN 2 = sp, SN 3 = sp², SN 4 = sp³.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's crack the code of Hybridization! Hybridization sounds complex, but it's just nature's way of mixing atomic orbitals (like mixing different flavors of dough) to make perfectly identical bonding arms.

To find the hybridization, we use a simple trick called the 'Steric Number'. 
Steric Number (SN) = (Number of atoms attached) + (Number of lone pairs on the central atom). 

If SN = 2, you mixed 1 's' and 1 'p' to make -> sp.
If SN = 3, you mixed 1 's' and 2 'p's to make -> sp².
If SN = 4, you mixed 1 's' and 3 'p's to make -> sp³.
Let's check our trio:

1. SO₂ (Sulfur Dioxide):
Sulfur is the center. It connects to 2 Oxygen atoms. Sulfur has 6 valence electrons; it uses 4 to make double bonds with the Oxygens, leaving 2 electrons (which is 1 lone pair).
Steric Number = 2 attached atoms + 1 lone pair = 3.
SN 3 means the hybridization is **sp²**.

2. NO₂ (Nitrogen Dioxide):
Nitrogen is the center. It connects to 2 Oxygen atoms. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. It uses 4 for bonding. It has 1 electron left over! A single odd electron still occupies an orbital and counts somewhat like a lone pair for geometry purposes.
Steric Number = 2 attached atoms + 1 odd electron domain = 3.
SN 3 means the hybridization is **sp²**.

3. N₃⁻ (Azide Ion):
Imagine a Nitrogen atom straight in the middle, double bonded to two other Nitrogens on the sides [N=N=N]⁻. The central Nitrogen uses all its available bonding capacity to form these two double bonds and has 0 lone pairs.
Steric Number = 2 attached atoms + 0 lone pairs = 2.
SN 2 means the hybridization is **sp**.

Putting them all in order, we get sp², sp², and sp. Boom! You just solved hybridization like a pro.

questions.Question: Q8. Number of compounds with one lone pair of electrons on central atom amongst following is O₃, H₂O, SF₄, ClF₃, NH₃, BrF₅, XeF₄ __
questions.Hint: Count the valence electrons of the central atom. Subtract the electrons used in bonding. The remaining electrons form pairs (lone pairs). Remember, oxygen in terminal positions usually forms double bonds or coordinate bonds!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! To solve this, let's play a game of 'Electron Banking.' Every atom in the periodic table has a specific number of 'valence electrons'—think of these as coins they can spend to make bonds. The central atom is the banker. Any coins left unspent after making bonds are kept in pairs, known as 'lone pairs.' Let's check the bank accounts of the central atoms in each of these molecules!

1. O₃ (Ozone): The central Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. It forms a double bond with one oxygen (spending 2 electrons) and a coordinate 'dative' bond with the other (spending 2 electrons without getting any back). That leaves 2 electrons, which is exactly ONE lone pair.

2. H₂O (Water): Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. It bonds with 2 Hydrogens (spending 2 electrons). It has 4 left over, which equals TWO lone pairs.

3. SF₄ (Sulfur Tetrafluoride): Sulfur is in Group 16, so it has 6 valence electrons. It makes 4 single bonds with Fluorine (spending 4). It has 2 left, which is ONE lone pair.

4. ClF₃ (Chlorine Trifluoride): Chlorine is in Group 17, giving it 7 valence electrons. It bonds with 3 Fluorines (spending 3). It has 4 left over, meaning TWO lone pairs.

5. NH₃ (Ammonia): Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. It bonds with 3 Hydrogens (spending 3). It has 2 left, meaning ONE lone pair.

6. BrF₅ (Bromine Pentafluoride): Bromine has 7 valence electrons. It bonds with 5 Fluorines (spending 5). It has 2 left, which makes ONE lone pair.

7. XeF₄ (Xenon Tetrafluoride): Xenon is a noble gas with 8 valence electrons! It bonds with 4 Fluorines (spending 4). It has 4 left, which means TWO lone pairs.

So, the molecules with exactly ONE lone pair are O₃, SF₄, NH₃, and BrF₅. That is a total of 4 molecules! You just successfully navigated the electron accounts of seven different molecules. Great job!

questions.Question: Q9. The total number of anti bonding molecular orbitals, formed from 2s and 2p atomic orbitals in a diatomic molecule is___
questions.Hint: When Atomic Orbitals mix together to form Molecular Orbitals, the total number of orbitals is conserved. Half of them become lower-energy bonding orbitals, and the other half become higher-energy anti-bonding orbitals.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have two rival teams of construction workers building a skyscraper. This skyscraper is our 'Diatomic Molecule' (a molecule made of two atoms, like N₂ or O₂). 

Each atom brings its own set of raw materials, called Atomic Orbitals. The question asks specifically about the 2s and 2p orbitals. For a single atom, how many orbitals are in the 2nd energy level? There is one '2s' orbital and three '2p' orbitals (px, py, and pz). That means one atom brings 1 + 3 = 4 atomic orbitals to the construction site.

Since this is a diatomic molecule, we have TWO atoms. If both atoms bring 4 orbitals each, the total number of raw atomic orbitals being mixed together is 4 + 4 = 8.

Now, here is the golden rule of Molecular Orbital Theory: Orbitals are never destroyed; they just transform! If you mix 8 atomic orbitals together, you must create exactly 8 Molecular Orbitals.

When these orbitals combine, they act like waves. Sometimes they add up perfectly to build strong floors (Bonding Orbitals), and sometimes they crash into each other and cancel out, creating unstable, empty spaces (Anti-bonding Orbitals). Nature loves balance, so the split is exactly 50/50.

Out of the 8 total Molecular Orbitals created, half of them will be Bonding Molecular Orbitals, and the other half will be Anti-bonding Molecular Orbitals. 

So, 8 divided by 2 gives us 4 Anti-bonding Molecular Orbitals. Specifically, these are the σ*(2s), σ*(2pz), π*(2px), and π*(2py) orbitals. (The little asterisk * symbol is the scientific way of labeling an orbital as 'anti-bonding'). You've just used high-level quantum mechanics using simple arithmetic!

questions.Question: Q10. Given below are two statements: Statement-I: Since fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen, the net dipole moment of NF₃ is greater than NH₃. Statement-II: In NH₃, the orbital dipole due to lone pair and the dipole moment of NH bonds are in opposite direction, but in NF₃ the orbital dipole due to lone pair and dipole moments of N-F bonds are in same direction.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are True
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are False
Statement-I is True but Statement-II is False
Statement-I is False but Statement-II is True
questions.Hint: Draw the structures of NH₃ and NF₃. Think of dipole moment as a 'tug-of-war' arrow pointing toward the more electronegative atom. Do the arrows add up or cancel each other out?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's uncover the truth behind these statements by treating dipole moments like an epic game of tug-of-war. A dipole moment happens when one atom is a 'bully' (more electronegative) and pulls the shared electrons towards itself. We represent this pull with an arrow pointing toward the bully.

First, let's look at Ammonia (NH₃). Nitrogen is more electronegative than Hydrogen. So, the three N-H bonds have arrows pointing UP from the Hydrogens towards the Nitrogen. Nitrogen also has a lone pair of electrons sitting on top of its head, and the arrow for a lone pair always points UP away from the atom. Since the bond arrows point UP and the lone pair arrow points UP, all the arrows add together to create a massive super-pull! This gives NH₃ a strong net dipole moment.

Now, let's look at NF₃. Fluorine is the ultimate bully of the periodic table; it is far more electronegative than Nitrogen. So, the three N-F bonds have arrows pointing DOWN, away from the Nitrogen and towards the Fluorines. However, the lone pair on Nitrogen still points UP. The downward pull of the Fluorines directly fights against the upward pull of the lone pair. Because they pull in opposite directions, they mostly cancel each other out! 

As a result, NH₃ actually has a much LARGER net dipole moment than NF₃. 

Let's evaluate the statements:
Statement-I says NF₃ has a greater dipole moment. As we just discovered, this is completely FALSE. NH₃ wins the tug-of-war.
Statement-II claims that in NH₃, the arrows are opposite, and in NF₃, they are the same. We just saw the exact reverse! In NH₃ they pull the same way, and in NF₃ they pull in opposite directions. So, Statement-II is also completely FALSE.

Both statements are trying to trick you, but knowing your electronegativity vectors keeps you safe!
questions.Answer: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are False

questions.Concept: Fajan's Rule (Covalent Character in Ionic Bonds)
questions.Question: Q11. Which of the following is least ionic? (Options created based on standard Fajan's Rule trends for this concept)
questions.Hint: According to Fajan's Rule, a bond becomes less ionic (and more covalent) when the positive ion (cation) has a very high charge and a very small size. Which of these metals has the highest positive charge?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the magical bridge between Ionic and Covalent bonds! When you first learn chemistry, you are told that bonds are either 'Ionic' (complete stealing of electrons) or 'Covalent' (friendly sharing of electrons). But the truth is, nothing is 100% black and white. 

Imagine a negative ion (like Chloride, Cl⁻) as a big, fluffy, squishy cloud of electrons. A positive ion (like a metal cation) acts like a vacuum cleaner trying to pull that fluffy cloud towards itself. This pulling effect is called 'polarization.' 

If the metal pulls hard enough, the fluffy electron cloud gets stretched into the space between the two atoms. When the electron cloud is in the middle, the atoms are technically sharing it. And what do we call sharing? Covalent bonding! Therefore, the harder the metal pulls, the more covalent (and the least ionic) the bond becomes.

This principle is known as Fajan's Rule. The rule states that a metal cation will pull harder if it has two things: a SMALL size and a HIGH positive charge. 

Let's look at our suspects:
1. Sodium (Na) in NaCl has a +1 charge.
2. Magnesium (Mg) in MgCl₂ has a +2 charge.
3. Aluminum (Al) in AlCl₃ has a +3 charge.
4. Silicon (Si) in SiCl₄ has a massive +4 charge!

Silicon has the highest positive charge (+4). Because of this huge positive charge, it acts like an incredibly powerful, tiny vacuum cleaner. It drastically distorts the electron clouds of the chlorine atoms, dragging the electrons into the middle to be shared. 

Because of this extreme sharing, SiCl₄ is highly covalent. And since being highly covalent is the exact opposite of being ionic, SiCl₄ is the 'least ionic' molecule in the list. You just outsmarted the black-and-white rules of bonding!

questions.Question: Q12. The number of molecules/ion/s having trigonal bipyramidal shape is ......... (Note: The original test text accidentally omitted the list of molecules, but we can still learn the concept!)
MCQ_Options: Cannot be determined without the list of molecules
questions.Hint: A Trigonal Bipyramidal shape happens when a central atom is surrounded by exactly 5 bonded atoms and 0 lone pairs. It looks like a fidget spinner with a stick poking through the top and bottom!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Oops! It looks like the examiner who wrote this test accidentally forgot to print the list of molecules for you to check! However, as a true student of chemistry, we don't need a list to master the concept. Let's talk about what 'Trigonal Bipyramidal' actually means so you'll be ready whenever you see it.

Molecules are three-dimensional, and their shape depends on how many electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) are gathered around the central atom. These electron groups hate each other because negative charges repel. They want to get as far away from each other as physically possible.

Imagine you are holding 5 balloons by their strings. If you tie them all together, how will they arrange themselves to have the maximum space? 

Three of the balloons will fan out flat like a fidget spinner, or a peace sign. This flat part is called the 'equator.' The angle between them is 120 degrees. The remaining two balloons will pop straight up and straight down, forming the 'axis.' The angle between the axis and the equator is 90 degrees. 

This exact shape is called Trigonal Bipyramidal (often abbreviated as TBP). 

To find out if a molecule has this shape, you calculate its 'Steric Number', which is the number of atoms bonded to the central atom PLUS the number of lone electron pairs. For a perfect Trigonal Bipyramidal shape, you need a Steric Number of 5, specifically consisting of 5 bonds and 0 lone pairs.

A classic, famous example of this is PCl₅ (Phosphorus Pentachloride). Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, and it uses all 5 to bond with 5 Chlorine atoms. Zero lone pairs left over! The 5 chlorine atoms space themselves out into that perfect 'fidget spinner with an axis' shape. 

If this question had provided a list, you would simply look for molecules with 5 bonds and 0 lone pairs on the central atom. Even without the list, you now hold the knowledge to defeat any TBP molecule that crosses your path!
questions.Answer: Cannot be determined without the list of molecules

questions.Question: Q13. What is the number of unpaired electron(s) in the highest occupied molecular orbital of the following species: N₂, N₂⁺, O₂, O₂⁺?
questions.Hint: Think of the Molecular Orbitals as a tall apartment building. Fill the rooms with electrons starting from the ground floor. The 'Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital' (HOMO) is the penthouse. Count the electrons living alone in the penthouse!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's take a tour of the 'Molecular Orbital Apartment Building.' When atoms join to form diatomic molecules like N₂ or O₂, their electrons move into a shared high-rise building called Molecular Orbitals. We fill these rooms from the ground floor up. The top-most floor that actually has electrons living in it is called the HOMO (Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital).

Let's check the residents for each species:

1. N₂ (Nitrogen gas): A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 electrons, so N₂ has 14 electrons. We fill the rooms from the bottom up. By the time we reach the 14th electron, we are filling the σ(2pz) orbital (the penthouse for N₂). Because orbitals hold exactly 2 electrons, the 13th and 14th electrons pair up nicely in this room. 
Unpaired electrons in the HOMO = 0.

2. N₂⁺ (Nitrogen ion): The little '⁺' means it lost an electron! It only has 13 electrons now. We go back to the σ(2pz) penthouse and take one away. Now, there is only 1 electron left sitting in that room all by itself.
Unpaired electrons in the HOMO = 1.

3. O₂ (Oxygen gas): An oxygen atom has 8 electrons, so O₂ has 16. Oxygen's apartment layout is slightly different. After filling the lower floors with 14 electrons, the 15th and 16th electrons move into the π*(2px) and π*(2py) anti-bonding penthouse suites. Because these two rooms are at the exact same height (energy level), Hund's Rule states that electrons prefer to have their own room before sharing. So, one goes into the px room, and one goes into the py room. They are both living alone!
Unpaired electrons in the HOMO = 2. (This is why liquid oxygen is magnetic!)

4. O₂⁺ (Oxygen ion): This has 15 electrons (one less than neutral O₂). We take one electron out of the penthouse. Now, only one room is occupied by a single electron.
Unpaired electrons in the HOMO = 1.

Putting our findings together in order: 0, 1, 2, 1. You've successfully mapped the quantum apartment building!

questions.Question: Q14. The number of given orbitals which have electron density along the axis is ________ pₓ, pᵧ, p_z, d_xy, d_yz, d_xz, d_z², d_x²-y²
questions.Hint: Look at the names (subscripts) of the orbitals. Orbitals with a single letter (like x, y, z) or a squared term (like x², y², z²) point directly ALONG the coordinate axes. Orbitals with mixed letters (like xy, yz) point diagonally BETWEEN the axes.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, let's picture balloons tied to the center of a 3D graphing plane—the kind with an x-axis (left/right), y-axis (up/down), and z-axis (forward/backward). Orbitals are basically 3D balloons where electrons like to hang out.

The question asks which of these balloons lie directly ON (along) the metal bars of the axes, rather than floating in the empty spaces between them.

First, let's look at the 'p' orbitals. They look like simple dumbbells (two balloons tied at the knot).
- pₓ points directly left and right along the x-axis.
- pᵧ points directly up and down along the y-axis.
- p_z points directly forward and backward along the z-axis.
All three of these live strictly on the axes! So that's 3 matches.

Next, let's look at the 'd' orbitals. These are more complex, usually looking like four-leaf clovers (four balloons tied together).
- d_xy, d_yz, and d_xz: The mixed letters are a secret code! It means these clover leaves sit flat in the plane between those two axes, pointing diagonally at 45-degree angles. They purposely avoid touching the axes. So, these 3 do NOT count.
- d_x²-y²: Whenever you see a squared term in the name, it means the balloons are speared directly on the axes. The four lobes of this orbital point perfectly along the x and y axes. So, this 1 counts!
- d_z²: This is the weirdest shape in chemistry. It looks like a dumbbell on the z-axis wearing a donut around its middle! Because its main dumbbell is skewered right on the z-axis, it definitely has electron density along the axis. So, this 1 counts!

Let's add up our winners: The 3 p-orbitals + the 2 special d-orbitals (d_x²-y² and d_z²) = 5 orbitals total that lie along the axes. You just navigated 3D quantum space like a pro!

questions.Question: Q15. Match List I with List II
questions.Hint: Look for the most obvious or unique pair first to eliminate wrong options immediately!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! You might notice that the text for this specific question didn't actually provide 'List I' and 'List II'. But don't worry! This is the perfect opportunity to learn a superpower for taking chemistry tests: How to conquer 'Match the Following' questions.

Imagine you are a detective trying to connect suspects (List I) to their fingerprints (List II). In chemistry, List I might be 'Molecules' (like water, methane, and ammonia) and List II might be their 'Shapes' (bent, tetrahedral, and pyramidal).

Here is the secret trick that top students use: You rarely have to solve all four matches! 

Step 1: Scan both lists. Find the ONE match you are 100% absolutely sure about. Let's say you know for a fact that water (H₂O) has a 'Bent' shape because of its two lone pairs. Let's pretend that is 'A' matching with 'ii'.

Step 2: Look at your multiple-choice options. You can immediately cross out any option that doesn't say 'A-ii'! Often, this simple trick eliminates two or even three wrong answers right away, saving you tons of time.

Step 3: If you still have two options left, find the point where they differ. If one says 'B-i' and the other says 'B-iv', you just need to figure out item B. Once you solve B, you win!

This kind of logic isn't just for chemistry; it works for biology, physics, and even history! It trains your brain to look for efficiency. So, while we don't have the exact chemicals to match here, always remember the 'Detective Method'—find your strongest clue, eliminate the impossible, and whatever remains must be the truth!

questions.Question: Q16. The number of species from the following which have square pyramidal structure is PF₅, BrF₄⁻, IF₅, BrF₅, XeOF₄, ICl₄⁻
questions.Hint: Count the valence electrons of the central atom, subtract the electrons used to make bonds, and find the number of 'lone pairs'. A square pyramidal shape is born when a molecule has exactly 5 bonds and 1 lone pair (6 total electron domains)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's think of atoms as people trying to sit around a central campfire (the central atom). Electrons hate each other because they are all negatively charged, so they want to sit as far apart as possible. This is the whole idea behind VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory!

When a central atom has 6 things attached to it (we call these 'electron domains'), they form an 'Octahedral' shape—like two pyramids stuck base-to-base. But what if one of those 6 things isn't an atom, but an invisible 'lone pair' of electrons? It still takes up space, but you can't 'see' it when looking at the final shape. If you erase one point of an octahedron, you are left with a flat square base and one point sticking up: A Square Pyramid!

So, our mission is to find the molecules with exactly 5 bonds and 1 lone pair. Let's check them all:

1. PF₅: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons. It uses all 5 to bond with Fluorine. 5 bonds + 0 lone pairs = Trigonal bipyramidal. (Nope!)

2. BrF₄⁻: Bromine has 7 valence electrons, plus 1 extra from the negative charge = 8. It uses 4 to bond with F. 8 - 4 = 4 left over (which makes 2 lone pairs). 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs = Square planar. (Nope!)

3. IF₅: Iodine has 7 valence electrons. It uses 5 to bond with F. 7 - 5 = 2 left over (1 lone pair). 5 bonds + 1 lone pair = Square pyramidal! (Yes! That's 1.)

4. BrF₅: Bromine has 7 valence electrons. It uses 5 to bond with F. 7 - 5 = 2 left over (1 lone pair). 5 bonds + 1 lone pair = Square pyramidal! (Yes! That's 2.)

5. XeOF₄: Xenon is a noble gas with 8 valence electrons. It uses 2 to double-bond with Oxygen, and 4 to single-bond with Fluorine. That's 6 electrons used. 8 - 6 = 2 left over (1 lone pair). It has 5 atoms attached + 1 lone pair = Square pyramidal! (Yes! That's 3.)

6. ICl₄⁻: Iodine has 7, plus 1 from the charge = 8. It uses 4 to bond with Cl. 8 - 4 = 4 left over (2 lone pairs). 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs = Square planar. (Nope!)

So, IF₅, BrF₅, and XeOF₄ are the three square pyramidal molecules!

questions.Chapter: Organic Chemistry - Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.Question: Q17. Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: Butan-1-ol has higher boiling point than ethoxyethane. Reason R: Extensive hydrogen bonding leads to stronger association of molecules.
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.Hint: Think about boiling as pulling sticky molecules apart. The 'stickier' the molecules are to each other, the more heat you need to boil them! Which molecule has an -OH group that can act like strong microscopic magnets?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine a giant game of 'Red Rover' or a group of friends holding hands tightly. To 'boil' a liquid and turn it into a gas, you have to pump in enough heat energy to break those friends apart so they can float away freely into the air.

Now, let's look at our two liquids: Butan-1-ol and Ethoxyethane. They actually have the exact same number of Carbon, Hydrogen, and Oxygen atoms (they are isomers with the formula C₄H₁₀O). But they are built differently!

Butan-1-ol is an alcohol. At the very end of its carbon chain, it has an oxygen atom attached directly to a hydrogen atom (-OH). Oxygen is what we call 'highly electronegative'—it's an electron bully! It pulls the shared electrons away from the hydrogen. This leaves the hydrogen slightly positive and the oxygen slightly negative. When two Butan-1-ol molecules get close, the positive hydrogen of one acts like a magnet and sticks tightly to the negative oxygen of the other. This super-strong connection is called 'Hydrogen Bonding'.

Ethoxyethane, on the other hand, is an ether. Its oxygen atom is trapped in the middle of the carbon chain (C-C-O-C-C). Because the oxygen isn't directly attached to a hydrogen, it can't form these super-strong hydrogen bonds with other ethoxyethane molecules. Its molecules just kind of weakly bump into each other.

Because Butan-1-ol's molecules are holding hands so tightly via hydrogen bonding, you have to crank up the stove (apply much more heat) to boil it. Therefore, Butan-1-ol definitely has a higher boiling point (Assertion A is true).

Why does it have a higher boiling point? Because hydrogen bonding causes the molecules to associate or stick together strongly (Reason R is true, and it explains A perfectly!).
questions.Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.Question: Q18. The pair from the following pairs having both compounds with net non-zero dipole moment is
questions.Hint: A 'dipole moment' measures if a molecule has a positive side and a negative side. If a molecule is perfectly symmetrical, all the microscopic pulls cancel out to zero! Look for the pair where BOTH molecules are asymmetrical (like being bent or lopsided).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play a microscopic game of Tug-of-War! 

In chemistry, atoms have different strengths when pulling on electrons. We call this strength 'electronegativity'. When a strong atom pulls electrons away from a weak atom, an invisible arrow of force is created. We call this a 'dipole'.

But here is the trick: if you have a perfectly symmetrical molecule, these tugs-of-war can cancel each other out completely! If three dogs are pulling a chew toy with exactly the same strength in a perfect triangle, the toy won't move. The net force is ZERO.

Let's test our options:

1. CH₄ and CCl₄: Both of these molecules are 'tetrahedral'—perfectly symmetrical 3D pyramids. The pulls in every direction cancel out exactly. Both have a dipole moment of ZERO. (Not our answer).

2. BF₃ and CO₂: BF₃ is a flat, perfect triangle (trigonal planar). The three fluorines cancel each other out. CO₂ is perfectly straight (O=C=O). The oxygens pull equally in exact opposite directions. Both have a dipole moment of ZERO. (Not our answer).

3. BeCl₂ and NH₃: BeCl₂ is a straight line, perfectly balanced. Dipole is zero. NH₃ (Ammonia) is like a little pyramid with a lone pair of electrons on top. It is NOT symmetrical, so it has a non-zero dipole. But we need BOTH to be non-zero! (Not our answer).

4. H₂O and SO₂: Water (H₂O) is shaped like a boomerang (it's 'bent' because of two invisible lone pairs on the oxygen). Because it's bent, the pulls don't cancel out! It has a strong non-zero dipole (which is why water is so good at dissolving things). SO₂ is also bent because of a lone pair on the sulfur atom! Because they are both bent and lopsided, neither can cancel out their forces. They BOTH have net non-zero dipole moments!

Whenever you see a central atom with lone pairs that mess up the perfect symmetry, you usually have a polar molecule (non-zero dipole)!

questions.Question: Q19. The sum of lone pairs present on the central atom of the interhalogen IF₅ and IF₇ is _______
questions.Hint: Look at the central Iodine (I) atom. Iodine starts with 7 valence electrons in its outermost shell. Subtract the number of electrons it uses to bond with the Fluorine atoms. Any leftover electrons sit together in pairs called 'lone pairs'!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine the central atom is a host at a party, and it only has a certain number of party hats (valence electrons) to give out to guests (the atoms bonding to it).

Our host for both of these molecules is Iodine (I). Iodine lives in Group 17 of the periodic table (the Halogens), which means it naturally has exactly 7 valence electrons in its outer shell. 

Let's look at the first party: IF₅ (Iodine pentafluoride).
Iodine has 5 Fluorine guests coming over. It needs to use 1 of its electrons to hold hands (bond) with each of the 5 Fluorines. 
Math time: 7 starting electrons - 5 used for bonding = 2 electrons left over.
Electrons hate being alone, so these 2 leftover electrons sit on the couch together as a pair. We call this ONE 'lone pair'. 
So, IF₅ has 1 lone pair on its central atom.

Now let's look at the second party: IF₇ (Iodine heptafluoride).
This time, Iodine has 7 Fluorine guests! It has to use all 7 of its valence electrons to bond with them. 
Math time: 7 starting electrons - 7 used for bonding = 0 electrons left over.
There are no electrons left to sit on the couch. 
So, IF₇ has 0 lone pairs on its central atom.

The question asks for the SUM of the lone pairs on the central atoms of both molecules.
Sum = 1 (from IF₅) + 0 (from IF₇) = 1.

See? By just counting what you start with and subtracting what you use, chemistry becomes just like simple math!

questions.Question: Q20. The bond order and magnetic property of acetylide ion are same as that of
questions.Hint: Species that have the exact same total number of electrons (called isoelectronic species) usually fill up their molecular orbitals the exact same way. Count the total electrons in the acetylide ion (C₂²⁻) and find the option that matches!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever heard the phrase 'twins separated at birth'? In chemistry, we have a similar concept called 'isoelectronic species'. These are molecules or ions that might be made of totally different atoms, but they possess the exact same total number of electrons. Because they have the same number of electrons, they organize those electrons in identical patterns (Molecular Orbitals), making them behave like twins!

First, let's figure out what the 'acetylide ion' is. It's written as C₂²⁻. 
Let's count its electrons: 
A single Carbon (C) atom has 6 electrons.
So, two Carbon atoms = 6 + 6 = 12 electrons.
But wait, it has a '2-' charge! That means it stole 2 extra electrons from somewhere.
Total electrons for C₂²⁻ = 12 + 2 = 14 electrons.

Now, we just need to look at our options and find its 'twin'—the molecule that also has exactly 14 electrons!

1. O₂: Oxygen has 8 electrons. Two oxygens = 8 + 8 = 16 electrons. (Not twins).
2. N₂: Nitrogen has 7 electrons. Two nitrogens = 7 + 7 = 14 electrons. (BINGO! We found the twin!)
3. O₂⁻: 16 electrons + 1 extra = 17 electrons. (Nope).
4. F₂: Fluorine has 9 electrons. Two fluorines = 9 + 9 = 18 electrons. (Nope).

Because C₂²⁻ and N₂ both have 14 electrons, their Molecular Orbital diagrams look exactly the same. Nitrogen has a famous triple bond (Bond Order = 3), and all of its electrons are paired up (which makes it 'diamagnetic'—meaning it is slightly repelled by magnets). 

Therefore, the acetylide ion also has a bond order of 3 and is diamagnetic. By simply counting electrons, you unlocked the secret identity of the molecule!

questions.Question: Q21. ClF₅ at room temperature is a:
questions.Hint: Physical states (solid, liquid, gas) depend on molecular weight and intermolecular forces. Lighter molecules with weaker forces tend to fly around as gases! ClF₅ boils at around -13 degrees Celsius.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think about the elements on the periodic table like heavy weights. The heavier the atoms in a molecule are, the stronger their 'van der Waals forces' (the sticky forces that hold molecules together). 

For example, Iodine is a very heavy, massive atom. Because of this, pure Iodine is a solid at room temperature. Bromine is a bit lighter, so it's a liquid. Chlorine and Fluorine are the lightest halogens, so they are gases!

When you mix halogens together, you get 'interhalogen compounds'. ClF₅ (Chlorine pentafluoride) is made of relatively light atoms. Because it's light and roughly symmetrical around the central chlorine, the forces holding the different ClF₅ molecules together aren't incredibly strong.

Because these forces are weak, it doesn't take much heat at all to make the molecules break apart and float into the air. In fact, ClF₅ boils at a freezing -13 $^\circ$C (about 9 $^\circ$F)!

Room temperature is usually around 25 $^\circ$C. So, by the time your room has warmed up to normal temperatures, the ClF₅ has already absorbed more than enough heat to boil. Therefore, sitting on a desk at room temperature, it exists entirely as a gas.

Also, unlike the heavier halogens that have beautiful deep colors (like purple iodine or reddish-brown bromine), the combinations of light halogens like Cl and F don't absorb visible light in the same way. Thus, it appears completely colourless. 

So, if you ever had a jar of ClF₅ at room temperature, it would just look like an empty jar filled with invisible air (a colourless gas) — though you definitely wouldn't want to open it, as it is highly reactive!

questions.Question: Q22. Given below are two statements: Statement I: SO₂ and H₂O both possess V-shaped structure. Statement II: The bond angle of SO₂ less than that of H₂O
MCQ_Options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
questions.Hint: Think about the starting geometric shape! SO₂ starts from a 120-degree triangle, while H₂O starts from a 109.5-degree 3D tetrahedron. How do the lone pairs squeeze those angles?
