Because of this, it refuses to share its electrons in a big 'metallic sea' like Aluminum does. Instead, Boron forms incredibly strong covalent bonds. But it doesn't just form simple, small molecules. Boron atoms link together to form a complex 12-atom structure (like a 20-sided dice!). Then, these dice link up to other dice in every direction, creating a colossal, unbreakable 3D network.

Imagine trying to destroy a massive fortress built entirely out of Lego bricks, where every single brick is glued to the bricks around it with industrial superglue! In chemistry, this giant fortress is called a 'covalent lattice', and the energy holding it all together is the 'lattice energy'. 

Statement I says Boron is extremely hard due to this high lattice energy. This is absolutely true! Because you have to break millions of strong superglue bonds just to scratch it, Boron is one of the hardest elements in the universe (second only to diamond).

Statement II says Boron has the highest melting and boiling points in its group. Because of that same glued-together Lego fortress, trying to melt Boron means you have to pump in huge amounts of heat to rip the atoms apart. It melts at over 2000 degrees Celsius! Meanwhile, Gallium melts in your hand. So, Statement II is also completely correct. Both statements are spot on!
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.Concept: Preparation of Alkaline Earth Metal Halides
questions.Question: Q19. Better method for preparation of BeF₂, among the following is
MCQ_Options: Reacting Be metal directly with F₂ gas
questions.Hint: Beryllium loves to trap water and is very tricky to isolate directly. What if we use a special, dry chemical 'package' that naturally breaks down when heated, leaving only pure BeF₂ behind?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Beryllium (Be) is the top element in Group 2 (the Alkaline Earth Metals), and it is famously stubborn! Let's say you want to make pure Beryllium Fluoride (BeF₂). Your first thought might be to just take some Beryllium Oxide (BeO) and throw Hydrofluoric acid (HF) on it. Makes sense, right?

Well, Beryllium has a secret obsession: it LOVES water. It has a super high 'hydration energy'. So, when you do that reaction, the Beryllium wraps itself in water molecules. You don't get pure BeF₂, you get a wet, hydrated version. 'No problem,' you think, 'I'll just heat it up in an oven to bake the water away!' But here's the frustrating part: when you heat wet BeF₂, it destroys itself! It undergoes a reaction called hydrolysis and turns right back into Beryllium Oxide and HF gas. You're back where you started! It's like trying to bake a wet cake, but instead of drying out, the cake turns back into flour and eggs.

To outsmart stubborn Beryllium, chemists invented a brilliant ninja technique. They use a completely dry, special complex compound called Ammonium tetrafluoroberyllate. Its formula is (NH₄)₂BeF₄. 

Think of this compound as a special delivery box. Inside the box is your precious BeF₂ molecule, perfectly dry, packed safely with some Ammonium Fluoride (NH₄F) packing peanuts. When you take this dry box and heat it up (this is called 'thermal decomposition'), the packing peanuts (NH₄F) turn into a harmless gas and float out the chimney. What is left behind? A beautiful, perfectly dry, pure pile of BeF₂! It is the cleanest, most efficient way to prepare this compound, bypassing the water trap entirely.

questions.Question: Q20. For a good quality cement, the ratio of silica to alumina is found to be
questions.Hint: Think of Silica as the strong 'backbone' of the cement and Alumina as the 'quick-drying' agent. We need a lot more backbone than quick-dry material, but not too much!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about something you see every single day but probably never think about: Cement! Cement is absolutely magical. You take a gray powder, mix it with water, and over a few hours, it turns into solid, artificial rock! But how does it work without crumbling into dust?

Creating high-quality Portland cement is a lot like baking the world's most perfect chocolate chip cookie. If you put too much sugar, it burns; too much flour, it's dry. For cement, engineers mix limestone (calcium) with clay. The two superstar active ingredients that come out of this mix are Silica (SiO₂, which is basically purified sand) and Alumina (Al₂O₃, found in clay).

Let's imagine these two ingredients as a superhero construction team. 
Silica is the 'Tank'. It provides the ultimate, long-lasting strength that keeps the concrete from breaking under the weight of skyscrapers. But Silica acts very slowly.
Alumina is the 'Speedster'. It reacts with water almost instantly, helping the cement set and harden quickly so you don't have to wait weeks to build your house.

Now, imagine if your team is almost entirely made of Speedsters (too much Alumina). The cement would flash-freeze into solid rock before the construction workers could even pour it! Plus, it would be brittle and crack easily. 
On the flip side, if your team is all Tanks (too much Silica), the cement would be super strong eventually, but it would take months to harden!

Through decades of chemistry optimization, scientists found the 'Goldilocks' magic ratio. For the highest quality cement, the ratio of Silica to Alumina should be between 2.5 and 4. This means having about 2.5 to 4 times as much strength-building Silica as quick-setting Alumina. This perfect balance ensures the cement sets exactly when you need it to, and cures strong enough to build cities!

questions.Concept: Stability and Steric Hindrance of Nitrogen Halides
questions.Question: Q21. The most stable trihalide of nitrogen is:
questions.Hint: Nitrogen is extremely tiny. If it tries to hold onto three giant atoms, the giant atoms will bump into each other and the whole molecule will explode! Which halogen atom is small enough to fit safely?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore the crazy, explosive world of Nitrogen compounds! Nitrogen is the lightweight champion of Group 15 on the periodic table. It is a very small atom. Now, to make a 'trihalide', we need to attach three halogen atoms (Fluorine, Chlorine, Bromine, or Iodine) to one single Nitrogen atom.

Let's visualize this using a car analogy. Imagine the tiny Nitrogen atom is a very small, two-seater sports car. You are trying to pack three passengers (the halogen atoms) into this tiny car. 

First, let's try Fluorine. Fluorine atoms are incredibly small—like little kids. Three kids fit perfectly into the tiny sports car. They don't bump elbows, they are perfectly comfortable, and they share electrons happily. Because both Nitrogen and Fluorine are small, their chemical 'handshake' (orbital overlap) is super strong. This makes NF₃ an incredibly happy, stable gas.

Now, imagine trying to fit three massive, 300-pound professional wrestlers into that exact same tiny sports car. These wrestlers represent the much larger atoms: Chlorine, Bromine, and especially the giant Iodine. What happens? They are completely crushed! They elbow each other in the face, the car doors are bursting at the seams, and everyone is incredibly angry. 

In chemistry, we call this extreme crowding 'steric hindrance'. Because the large Chlorine, Bromine, or Iodine atoms are repelling each other violently around the tiny Nitrogen atom, the bonds are stretched and incredibly weak. 

Because of this, NCl₃ is an unstable, oily liquid that can explode. And NI₃? It is notoriously one of the most sensitive contact explosives in the world! It is so unstable that even a mosquito landing on it, or touching it with a feather, will cause a massive purple explosion! 

So, because of perfect sizing and lack of crowding, the tiny NF₃ is the only truly stable nitrogen trihalide.

questions.Question: The number of bridged oxygen atoms present in compound B formed from the following reactions is Pb(NO₃)₂ $\rightarrow$ A + PbO + O₂, A $\rightarrow$ B
questions.Hint: First, figure out what brown gas 'A' is produced when Lead Nitrate is heated. Then think about what happens to this gas when it cools down (it partners up with a clone of itself to form 'B').
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's solve this chemical mystery step-by-step like a detective. 

**Step 1: Identifying Gas A**
When we heat lead nitrate, Pb(NO₃)₂, it breaks down (decomposes). Imagine it shattering from the heat to form lead oxide (PbO), oxygen gas (O₂), and a brownish, nasty-smelling gas. That brown gas is Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂). So, our compound A is **NO₂**.
Here is the reaction: 
2Pb(NO₃)₂ $\xrightarrow{\Delta} 2$PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂

**Step 2: Identifying Compound B**
Now, let's look at NO₂. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. In NO₂, it makes bonds with two oxygen atoms, leaving one single, lonely, unpaired electron sitting on the nitrogen atom. In chemistry, unpaired electrons make atoms super restless and eager to find a partner! So, when the temperature drops, two NO₂ molecules run into each other, and their lonely electrons hold hands to form a bond. This is called 'dimerization'. 
2NO₂ $\rightleftharpoons$ N₂O₄
So, Compound B is **N₂O₄**.

**Step 3: Finding the Bridged Oxygens**
What does 'bridged' mean? A bridged atom is like a bridge over a river$\u2014$it connects two big pieces together. In our case, an oxygen bridge would look like Nitrogen-Oxygen-Nitrogen (N-O-N). But let's draw N₂O₄! When the two NO₂ molecules pair up, they connect directly Nitrogen-to-Nitrogen. The shape is O₂N-NO₂. 
Since the two nitrogens hold hands directly, the oxygen atoms are just stuck on the outside like sidekicks. They don't bridge the gap between the nitrogens at all! 

Therefore, the number of bridged oxygen atoms is a big, round **0**.

questions.Question: Choose the correct stability order of group 13 elements in their +1 oxidation state.
questions.Hint: Remember the 'Inert Pair Effect'! As atoms get heavier down the group, their innermost outer-shell electrons get too lazy to participate in bonding.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about a super cool chemistry phenomenon called the **Inert Pair Effect**! 

Group 13 on the periodic table includes Boron (B), Aluminum (Al), Gallium (Ga), Indium (In), and Thallium (Tl). Because they are in Group 13, their outermost shell has 3 electrons: 2 in the 's' room (ns²) and 1 in the 'p' room (np¹). Usually, atoms want to use all 3 electrons to bond, giving them a +3 oxidation state.

But as you go down the group to the heavier elements like Indium and Thallium, the atom gets huge. Inside these massive atoms are 'd' and 'f' orbitals. Think of these orbitals like really bad curtains$\u2014$they do a terrible job of blocking (shielding) the positive pull of the nucleus from the outer electrons.

Because the nucleus is pulling so hard through these bad curtains, the 2 electrons sitting in the 's' room get pulled really close to the nucleus and become extremely lazy. They refuse to get out of bed and bond! This is the Inert Pair Effect. 

Since the 2 's' electrons are lazy, only the 1 'p' electron goes out to work and form bonds. This results in a +1 oxidation state. 
Because the 'bad curtain' effect gets stronger as atoms get heavier, the heaviest guy (Thallium, Tl) is the most perfectly happy forming a +1 charge. Aluminum (Al) is super light and doesn't have this problem, so its +1 state is very unstable.

Therefore, the stability of the +1 state increases as you go down the group: **Al < Ga < In < Tl**.

questions.Question: Gallium is less toxic and has a very high boiling point, so it is used in high temperature thermometers. Which of the following statements best explains why Gallium is chosen for high-temperature thermometers over Mercury?
MCQ_Options: Gallium has a remarkably wide liquid range, melting near room temperature and boiling around 2400 $\circ$ C.
Gallium does not conduct heat well, protecting the thermometer glass.
Gallium boils at a lower temperature than mercury, making it safer.
Gallium turns into a gas at room temperature to measure pressure.
questions.Hint: A thermometer needs a liquid to expand and show the temperature. Think about what states of matter you absolutely need if you are trying to measure extremely high temperatures without the thermometer exploding!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered what's inside a thermometer? Usually, it's a silver liquid called Mercury. Mercury is cool, but it boils and turns into a gas at about 356 $\circ$ C. 

Imagine trying to measure the temperature of a glowing hot pizza oven at 800 $\circ$ C with a mercury thermometer. The mercury would boil, turn into a massive cloud of gas, and explode the glass tube! Plus, mercury vapor is super toxic. Yikes!

Enter our superhero metal: **Gallium**. Gallium is a very magical element. If you put a solid block of Gallium in the palm of your hand, your body heat alone (around 37 $\circ$ C) is enough to melt it into a liquid! Its melting point is super low (about 30 $\circ$ C). 

But the crazy part? Once it is a liquid, you can heat it up to a mind-boggling 2400 $\circ$ C before it finally boils into a gas! This means Gallium stays in a liquid state across a massive range of temperatures (from a warm summer day all the way up to temperatures that would melt rocks).

Because it stays perfectly liquid at super high temperatures and won't turn into a high-pressure exploding gas, and because it isn't dangerously toxic like mercury, it is the absolute perfect choice for high-temperature thermometers. It literally has one of the widest 'liquid ranges' of any element known to humanity!
questions.Answer: Gallium has a remarkably wide liquid range, melting near room temperature and boiling around 2400 \circ C.

questions.Question: The geometry around boron in the product 'B' formed from the following reaction is: BF₃ + NaH $\rightarrow$ A + NaF, A + NMe₃ $\rightarrow$ B
questions.Hint: When BF₃ reacts with NaH, it forms a famous 'electron-deficient' boron gas (Diborane). When this gas reacts with NMe₃, the Nitrogen shares its extra lone pair of electrons with the hungry Boron atom. Count the total bonds Boron has at the end!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let's break this down into a cool story about sharing pizza! 

**Reaction 1: Making Compound A**
First, Boron Trifluoride (BF₃) reacts with Sodium Hydride (NaH). The hydrogens swap out the fluorines to make Boron Hydride. But BH₃ is super unstable because Boron only has 6 electrons in its outer shell (it wants 8 for a full 'pizza' octet). So, two BH₃ molecules merge together to form **Diborane (B₂H₆)**. This is compound A.
2BF₃ + 6NaH $\xrightarrow{450K}$ B₂H₆ + 6NaF

**Reaction 2: Making Compound B**
Now, we take our Diborane (B₂H₆) and introduce it to Trimethylamine (NMe₃). 
Think of NMe₃ as a really generous friend. The Nitrogen atom in the middle has a 'lone pair' of electrons. That's like having two extra slices of pizza that it's holding in its hands.
Diborane splits back into two BH₃ pieces, and the Boron says, 'Hey, I only have 6 electrons, I am starving!' Nitrogen swoops in and says, 'Don't worry, you can share my two extra electrons.' 
Nitrogen points its lone pair straight at Boron, forming a coordinate bond (also called an adduct).
B₂H₆ + 2NMe₃ $\rightarrow 2$$[BH₃ \leftarrow NMe₃]$
Compound B is **BH₃ $\cdot$ NMe₃**.

**Finding the Geometry:**
Let's look at the Boron atom in this new molecule. It is connected to 3 Hydrogen atoms normally, and it has 1 new bond connecting it to the Nitrogen. 
Total connections (electron domains) = 4.
When an atom has 4 bonding pairs around it, they want to spread out as far away from each other as physically possible in 3D space to avoid crowdedness (electron repulsion). The shape that allows 4 things to be as far apart as possible is a pyramid-like structure called a **Tetrahedron** (sp³ hybridization). 
So, the geometry around Boron is Tetrahedral!

questions.Concept: Properties of Elements based on Periodic Position
questions.Question: The metal that has very low melting point and its periodic position is closer to a metalloid is
questions.Hint: This metal has a famously low melting point of about 30 $\circ$ C (it literally melts in the palm of your hand) and its atomic number is 31, sitting right next to Germanium (a classic metalloid).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine holding a solid piece of metal in your hand, and just the warmth of your skin causes it to melt into a shiny, silvery puddle, just like an ice cube! 

Out of all the metals in the options, **Gallium (Ga)** is famous for this party trick. It has a surprisingly low melting point of roughly 29.8 $\circ$ C (about 86 $\circ$ F). Since normal human body temperature is around 37 $\circ$ C, the heat from your hand easily turns solid Gallium into liquid Gallium.

Now let's verify its position on the periodic table to make sure it fits the second clue: 'closer to a metalloid'.
Gallium is in Group 13. Its atomic number is 31.
If we look at its next-door neighbor on the periodic table, atomic number 32, we find Germanium (Ge).
What is Germanium? It's a classic metalloid! (A metalloid is an element that acts like a mashup of a metal and a non-metal, like Silicon or Germanium).

Aluminium melts at a really high temperature (660 $\circ$ C), and while Indium and Thallium have relatively low melting points for metals, they are much further down the periodic table and aren't as famously close to the 'staircase' of metalloids as Gallium is. 
So, Gallium is the absolute perfect match for both clues!

questions.Question:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. 
Assertion A: Boric acid is a weak acid. 
Reason R: Boric acid is not able to release H\+ ion on its own. It receives OH\- ion from water and releases H\+ ion.
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.Hint: Does Boric Acid actually have its own H\+ ready to fire out like a pitcher throwing a baseball, or does it 'steal' an OH\- from water and leave the water's H\+ behind to make the solution acidic?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's uncover the sneaky behavior of Boric Acid!

Normally, when you think of an acid (like Hydrochloric Acid, HCl), you think of a molecule that has a Hydrogen atom locked and loaded, ready to fire off as an H\+ ion into the water. We call these 'Bronsted acids'. Because they give away H\+ so easily, they are usually strong acids.

But **Boric Acid (H₃BO₃ or B(OH)₃)** is a chemical rule-bender! 
If you look at Boric acid, the central Boron atom is bonded to 3 OH groups. Boron only has 6 electrons in its outer shell. It desperately wants 8 to be happy (an octet). Boron says, 'I am not giving anything away; I am hungry for electrons!'

So, when Boric acid is tossed into water (H₂O, or H-OH), it doesn't give away an H\+. Instead, it acts like a thief! It spots an oxygen atom in the water molecule that has extra electrons and steals the entire OH\- piece! 

Reaction:
B(OH)₃ + H₂O $\rightleftharpoons$ B(OH)₄\- + H\+

By kidnapping the OH\- from water, it forces the water molecule to leave its poor H\+ ion behind. It's this abandoned, floating H\+ ion that makes the water acidic! 
Because Boric acid accepts electron pairs, it's called a **Lewis Acid**. And because it doesn't directly release its own H\+ ions and relies on this sneaky, reversible stealing process, it generates very few H\+ ions. That's exactly why it is a very **weak acid**.

So, Assertion A is completely true (it's a weak acid), and Reason R is completely true AND it perfectly explains *why* the assertion is true!
questions.Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.Question: Q29. Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Boron is unable to form BF₆³⁻. Reason (R): Size of B is very small.
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.Hint: Does Boron have empty d-orbitals to hold extra electrons? Look at its row on the periodic table!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's think of electron orbitals as pockets in a backpack. Every atom wants to carry 'electron pairs' (which form bonds) in its pockets. Boron is an element located in the 2nd row (n=2 period) of the periodic table. Because it's only in the second row, it only has access to the 2s and 2p subshells. Mathematically, that means Boron has exactly 1 s-orbital and 3 p-orbitals. That is a total of just 4 'pockets' available to hold electron pairs. 

Because of this strict physical limit, Boron can only form a maximum of 4 bonds. It can easily form BF₄⁻ by using all 4 pockets. However, to form BF₆³⁻, Boron would need to bond with 6 Fluorine atoms. That requires 6 pockets! Elements in the 3rd row, like Aluminum, have access to an extra set of pockets called the 'd-orbitals' (3d), so Aluminum CAN form AlF₆³⁻. Boron simply doesn't have d-orbitals.

Now, let's look at the logic of the Assertion and Reason. The Assertion says Boron can't form BF₆³⁻. This is absolutely TRUE! The Reason says the size of Boron is very small. This statement is also factually TRUE—Boron is indeed the smallest atom in its group. But here is the critical thinking part: does Boron's small size EXPLAIN why it can't form 6 bonds? No! The real, scientific cause is the complete absence of d-orbitals. While being small and lacking d-orbitals often happen together (since n=2 atoms are small), the true chemical explanation for the covalency limit is orbital availability. Therefore, both statements are true facts, but the Reason is not the correct explanation for the Assertion.
questions.Answer: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.Question: Q30. When borax is heated with CoO on a platinum loop, blue coloured bead formed is largely due to
questions.Hint: When borax is heated, it melts into a glassy mixture containing boric anhydride (B₂O₃). How might this interact with a basic metal oxide like CoO?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are a detective chemist 150 years ago, and you are trying to identify a mystery rock. You would use a brilliant and beautiful technique called the 'Borax Bead Test'! Here is how the magic works. 

Borax is a naturally occurring mineral powder with the formula Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O. When you scoop a little bit of this powder onto a tiny platinum wire loop and heat it fiercely in a burner flame, something awesome happens. First, it puffs up and bubbles as the water inside it boils away. Then, it melts down into a beautiful, completely clear, glass-like drop called a 'bead'. Chemically, this hot liquid glass is a mixture of Sodium Metaborate (NaBO₂) and Boric Anhydride (B₂O₃).

Now for the detective work. If you touch this hot, clear glass bead to a speck of an unknown metal powder—in this case, Cobalt(II) Oxide (CoO)—and stick it back into the flame, a chemical reaction happens right inside the liquid glass. The B₂O₃ acts like an acidic oxide and reacts beautifully with the basic CoO. They merge together to form a brand new chemical complex: Cobalt(II) metaborate, which has the chemical formula Co(BO₂)₂.

The most magical part of this reaction? This new metaborate compound acts like a vibrant dye. It instantly turns the clear glass bead into a stunning, deep sapphire blue! As a chemist, the moment you see that specific blue color, you know immediately: 'Aha! There is cobalt in this sample!'

questions.Concept: Chemical Properties of Water (Water Gas reaction)
questions.Question: Q31. Water does not produce CO on reacting with
questions.Hint: Carbon monoxide (CO) forms when water (steam) is forced to give its oxygen up to a carbon-containing fuel. Which option already has plenty of oxygen and absolutely refuses to take any more?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine a fierce tug-of-war over oxygen atoms. Industrially, chemists love to create a highly useful mixture of Carbon Monoxide (CO) and Hydrogen gas (H₂). This mixture is called 'Syngas' (Synthesis Gas), and it is made through a process called steam reforming.

Here is how it works: you take a carbon-based fuel, heat it up to incredibly hot temperatures, and blast it with steam (vaporized H₂O). At these extreme temperatures, carbon-based fuels act very greedy for oxygen. If you use pure Carbon (coal), it rips the oxygen right off the water: C + H₂O $\rightarrow$ CO + H₂. If you use Methane (CH₄), the same thing happens: CH₄ + H₂O $\rightarrow$ CO + 3H₂. Even Propane (C₃H₈) will tear the water molecules apart to steal the oxygen and form CO.

But what happens if we try this trick with Carbon Dioxide (CO₂)? Think of CO₂ as a carbon atom that has already eaten a massive, Thanksgiving-sized meal of oxygen. It already has two oxygen atoms securely attached to it (O=C=O). It is completely 'full' and fully oxidized! If you blast CO₂ with steam, the carbon atom isn't 'hungry' for oxygen anymore. It simply refuses to react with water to form Carbon Monoxide. (In fact, forming CO from CO₂ would mean losing oxygen, which water cannot force it to do in this setting). Because CO₂ is already fully oxidized, it is the odd one out and does not react with water to yield CO.

questions.Question: Q32. Al₂O₃ was leached with alkali to get X. The solution of X on passing of gas Y, forms Z. X, Y and Z respectively are:
MCQ_Options: X = Na[Al(OH)₄], Y = CO₂, Z = Al₂O₃·xH₂O
X = NaAlO₂, Y = SO₂, Z = Al(OH)₃
X = Al(OH)₃, Y = CO₂, Z = Al₂O₃
X = Na[Al(OH)₄], Y = O₂, Z = Al₂O₃·xH₂O
questions.Hint: Think about how we extract pure aluminum from a dirty rock. Aluminum oxide dissolves in strong bases, but we can precipitate it back out by bubbling a common, slightly acidic gas (found in our breath) into the water!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you dig up a heavy reddish rock from the earth called Bauxite. You know there is shiny, valuable Aluminum trapped inside it, but it is tightly mixed with useless dirt, rust (iron oxides), and sand. How do you get just the pure aluminum out? You can't just pick it apart with tweezers! Instead, we use a brilliant chemical trick called the 'Bayer Process'.

Step 1 is called 'Leaching'. Aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) is a special substance called an 'amphoteric' oxide. This is a fancy way of saying it acts like a chemical chameleon—it can react with both acids and bases! The dirt and rust in the rock mostly cannot do this. So, we dump the crushed rock into a vat of hot, highly concentrated base: Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH). The Al₂O₃ happily reacts and dissolves entirely into the liquid, forming a complex molecule called Sodium Aluminate, which we write as Na[Al(OH)₄]. This dissolved molecule is our 'X'. The useless dirt stays solid and gets filtered out. Now we have a completely clear liquid holding all our precious aluminum!

Step 2 is getting the aluminum back out as a solid. How do we undo what we just did? We need to carefully neutralize the strong base. We do this by blowing bubbles of Carbon Dioxide gas (CO₂)—our 'Y'—into the liquid. When CO₂ dissolves in water, it forms carbonic acid, a very gentle weak acid. As the pH of the liquid slowly drops, the dissolved aluminum complex becomes unstable and crashes out of the water as a pure, snowy-white solid powder. This powder is Hydrated Alumina, written as Al₂O₃·xH₂O (our 'Z'). Later on, this pure powder is heated to become the aluminum metal we use for airplanes and foil!
questions.Answer: X = Na[Al(OH)₄], Y = CO₂, Z = Al₂O₃·xH₂O

questions.Question: Q33. The incorrect statement regarding the structure of C₆₀ is
MCQ_Options: It contains 12 six-membered rings and 20 five-membered rings.
All carbon atoms are sp² hybridized.
It has a soccer-ball like structure.
Each carbon atom forms three sigma bonds and one pi bond.
questions.Hint: Think of a real, physical soccer ball! Do classic soccer balls have more hexagons (six-sided patches) or pentagons (five-sided patches)?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Carbon is an amazing element. For centuries, people thought pure carbon only came in two main forms: super-soft, slippery Graphite (like pencil lead) and ultra-hard, sparkly Diamond. But in 1985, scientists vaporized carbon with lasers and discovered a brand-new form that completely blew their minds. They discovered a molecule made of exactly 60 carbon atoms curved into a perfectly symmetrical, hollow sphere. 

Because it looked exactly like the geodesic dome buildings designed by a famous architect named Buckminster Fuller, they named this molecule 'Buckminsterfullerene', or 'Buckyballs' for short! 

The geometry of a Buckyball is literally identical to a classic black-and-white soccer ball. If you want to build a completely closed, round dome out of flat shapes, mathematical rules dictate that you must use a combination of hexagons (6-sided rings) and pentagons (5-sided rings). If you ever get the chance to hold a classic soccer ball, count the patches! You will find that there are always exactly 20 hexagons (usually the white patches) and 12 pentagons (the black patches). 

This makes the first option mathematically backwards! It claims there are 12 six-membered rings and 20 five-membered rings, which is upside down and physically could never close into a sphere. Therefore, this is the incorrect statement.

By the way, the other statements are totally true! The molecule DOES look like a soccer ball. Every single carbon atom is sp² hybridized, meaning it bonds to exactly 3 other carbon atoms (forming 3 strong sigma bonds). Because carbon has 4 outer electrons, the 1 leftover electron from each atom forms a network of pi bonds (double bonds) that smear around the whole ball, making it incredibly stable.
questions.Answer: It contains 12 six-membered rings and 20 five-membered rings.

questions.Question: Q34. Given below are the statements about diborane (a) Diborane is prepared by the oxidation of NaBH₄ with I₂ (b) Each boron atom is in sp² hybridized state (c) Diborane has one bridged 3 centre-2-electron bond (d) Diborane is a planar molecule
questions.Hint: Diborane (B₂H₆) is famous for breaking the rules and having weird 3D 'banana bonds'! Knowing its true 3D shape will help you cross out most of these statements instantly.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Diborane (B₂H₆) is one of the coolest, most rule-breaking molecules in all of chemistry. Usually, a chemical bond consists of 2 electrons shared tightly between 2 atoms (a 2-center-2-electron bond). But Boron is an element that is famously 'electron deficient'—it’s like a group of friends trying to buy pizza but they never have quite enough money to pay for normal slices.

In Diborane, there are two central Boron atoms and six Hydrogen atoms. But altogether, they only have 12 valence electrons to share! If you try to draw standard stick bonds between all of them, you literally run out of electrons. To survive, they do something amazing: they form 'Banana Bonds'! Two of the hydrogen atoms act as bridges directly between the two borons. In these bridges, 3 atoms (B - H - B) share only 2 electrons. This is called a '3-center-2-electron' bond. Because the bond physically curves through space to connect all three atoms, it looks like a banana! 

Now let's check our statements:
(c) says it has ONE banana bond. This is FALSE. It actually has TWO bridging hydrogens, so it has TWO 3-center-2-electron bonds.
(d) says it's a planar (flat) molecule. This is FALSE. The bridging hydrogens stick up above and push down below the plane. It is very much 3D!
(b) says the Boron is sp² hybridized. FALSE again! Because the Boron is surrounded by 4 bonds (two normal bonds to terminal hydrogens, and two banana bonds), it adopts a tetrahedral-like geometry and is sp³ hybridized.

This leaves only statement (a). This is completely TRUE! In the lab, we prepare Diborane by reacting Sodium Borohydride (NaBH₄) with Iodine (I₂). The chemical equation is: 2NaBH₄ + I₂ $\rightarrow$ B₂H₆ + 2NaI + H₂. Here, the Iodine steals electrons (acting as an oxidizing agent) from the hydride ions, forcing the boron pieces to stitch together into Diborane!

questions.Question: Q35. In which one of the following molecules strongest back donation of an electron pair from halide to boron is expected?
questions.Hint: For atoms to easily share an electron pair backwards to each other (back-bonding), their electron clouds (orbitals) need to be very similar in size so they overlap perfectly. Which halogen is closest in size to tiny Boron?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine two people standing next to each other. One person is holding a basket full of apples (representing a lone pair of electrons), and the other person has a completely empty basket (representing an empty electron orbital). If both people are the exact same height and stand close together, it is incredibly easy for the first person to just reach over and share some apples into the empty basket. In chemistry, this awesome sharing process is called 'back-bonding'!

In our molecules, Boron is the guy with the empty basket. Boron only has 6 valence electrons in its outer shell in these molecules, so it desperately wants 2 more to complete its octet rule. The Halogens (Fluorine, Chlorine, Bromine, Iodine) are standing right next to Boron, and they have tons of extra electron pairs.

Because Boron and Fluorine are both located in the 2nd row of the periodic table, their outermost electron orbitals (the 2p orbitals) are exactly the same size. They match up perfectly! So, Fluorine beautifully and easily shares its electrons backward into Boron's empty pocket. We call this '2p$\pi - 2p\pi$ back-donation', and it makes the BF₃ molecule incredibly stable and strong.

Now, look at the other options: Chlorine is in the 3rd row, Bromine is in the 4th, and Iodine is way down in the 5th row. As you go down the periodic table, the atoms get absolutely massive! Iodine's outer orbitals (5p) are giant, bloated, and completely mismatched with Boron's tiny 2p orbital. It's like a towering 8-foot giant trying to carefully pass an apple into the tiny basket of a toddler—the distance is awkward, the overlap is terrible, and the sharing (back-bonding) barely happens at all. 

Therefore, because their sizes match perfectly, BF₃ experiences the absolute strongest back donation!

questions.Question: Q36. The reaction of H₃N₃B₃Cl₃(A) with LiBH₄ in tetrahydrofuran gives inorganic benzene (B). Further, the reaction of (A) with (C) leads to H₃N₃B₃(Me)₃. Compounds (B) and (C) respectively, are:
questions.Hint: Think about what molecule is famously nicknamed 'inorganic benzene'. Then, figure out what reagent acts as a powerful source of methyl (Me) groups to replace halogens.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's uncover the identity of these mystery molecules! Have you ever heard of Benzene? Benzene is a famous organic molecule made of a flat hexagon of six carbon atoms. 'Inorganic benzene' is a fascinating copycat! It's a hexagon ring too, but instead of carbon, it alternates between Boron and Nitrogen atoms, giving it the chemical formula B$_3$N$_3$H$_6$. We call this specific molecule 'Borazine'. It looks, smells, and behaves somewhat like benzene, hence the awesome nickname! Now, let's look at the first reaction. You start with B,B,B-trichloroborazine (Compound A). This is a borazine ring where the three hydrogen atoms attached to the boron atoms have been replaced by chlorine atoms. When you react this with LiBH$_4$, which is a 'reducing agent', it acts like a giant hydrogen delivery truck. It literally drives up to the molecule, strips away those heavy chlorine atoms, and forces hydrogen atoms in their place. This returns the molecule back to normal Borazine (Compound B). So, B is definitely Borazine! Next, the problem asks what happens if we react our starting molecule (A) with a mysterious Compound (C) to get H$_3$N$_3$B$_3$(Me)$_3$. Notice exactly what changed here! The chlorines are gone again, but this time, methyl groups (Me, which is -CH$_3$) have taken their place on the boron atoms. In organic chemistry, to force a carbon group (like methyl) onto another atom, we need a special reagent that makes the carbon act negatively (a nucleophile). Grignard reagents are absolutely legendary for doing exactly this! A Grignard reagent like Methylmagnesium bromide (MeMgBr) acts as a powerful, aggressive source of methyl groups. It swaps out the chlorines and attaches the methyls directly to the boron. Therefore, Compound C must be a strong methylating agent like MeMgBr.

questions.Question: Q37. The relative stability of +1 oxidation state of group 13 elements follows the order:
questions.Hint: Remember the 'Inert Pair Effect'! As atoms get extremely massive and heavy down the group, their innermost valence s-electrons become super lazy and refuse to bond.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Imagine you have exactly three cookies to share with your friends. In chemistry terms, Group 13 elements (which include Boron, Aluminium, Gallium, Indium, and Thallium) have exactly three valence electrons to share (two are in the inner 's' subshell and one is in the outer 'p' subshell). When an element shares all three of these electrons, it reaches a +3 oxidation state. For lighter elements near the top of the periodic table, like Aluminium, sharing all three is extremely easy and natural! They love to form +3 states. But as you travel down the column on the periodic table, the atoms get much heavier and significantly larger. By the time you reach Thallium (Tl) at the very bottom, the nucleus is massive—packed with a huge number of positively charged protons. Because of a quirky phenomenon where inner electrons (specifically d and f orbitals) do a terrible job of acting as a shield against this strong positive pull, the nucleus pulls the two 's' electrons incredibly close and holds them super tight. These two electrons essentially become 'lazy' and outright refuse to leave their home to participate in chemical bonding. Chemists call this the 'Inert Pair Effect'. Because the two 's' electrons are stuck (inert), Thallium only has the 1 single 'p' electron left over to share with other atoms. Therefore, it strongly prefers forming a +1 oxidation state! As you move step-by-step down the group from Aluminium to Thallium, this inward pull gets stronger and stronger. So, the stability of the +1 state naturally increases as the atoms get heavier: Al < Ga < In < Tl.

questions.Question: Q38. The electronegativity of aluminium is similar to:
questions.Hint: Look diagonally up and to the left on the periodic table! Elements situated diagonally across from each other often share surprising chemical similarities.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Did you know the periodic table has a secret, hidden pattern called a 'diagonal relationship'? To understand this awesome trick, let's talk about electronegativity. Electronegativity is simply a measure of how strongly an atom pulls on electrons in a chemical bond. Imagine it like a microscopic game of tug-of-war for electrons. As you move from left to right across a row (period) on the periodic table, atoms get physically smaller and pack more protons in their center, so they pull on electrons much harder. Their electronegativity increases. However, as you move straight down a column (group), atoms add entirely new electron shells. They get much bulkier, and the nucleus is now further away from the outside, so their pull on outer electrons gets dramatically weaker. Their electronegativity decreases. Now, what happens if you go diagonally down and to the right? You are doing both at the exact same time! Moving right makes the pull stronger, but moving down makes the pull weaker. These two opposite effects end up perfectly canceling each other out! Because of this beautiful trick of physics, elements situated diagonally from each other often have almost the exact same properties. If you look at Beryllium (Be) in Group 2, and look diagonally down and to the right, you land perfectly on Aluminium (Al) in Group 13. Because of this specific diagonal relationship, they have almost identical electronegativity values (they both measure around 1.5 on the Pauling scale!).

questions.Question: Q39. Aluminium is usually found in +3 oxidation state. In contrast, thallium exists in +1 and +3 oxidation states. This is due to:
questions.Hint: As atoms get extremely massive, their deepest valence electrons get pulled incredibly close to the nucleus and become 'too lazy' to participate in bonding.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: This is a classic chemistry mystery that can be perfectly solved by understanding something called the 'Inert Pair Effect'. Group 13 elements, which include both Aluminium (Al) near the top and Thallium (Tl) at the very bottom, all have exactly 3 valence electrons in their outermost shell (two live in the 's' orbital and one lives in the 'p' orbital). For Aluminium, which is relatively light and small, it eagerly shares all three of these electrons when forming bonds with other atoms. Therefore, we almost always see Aluminium hanging out in the +3 oxidation state. However, Thallium is located way down at the very bottom of Group 13. It is a massive atom with an extremely heavy, highly charged nucleus. In heavy atoms like Thallium, the inner 'd' and 'f' electrons do a really poor job of acting like a protective shield against the nucleus's intense positive charge. As a result of this weak shielding, the positively charged nucleus pulls incredibly hard on the two electrons sitting in the 's' orbital. It holds onto them so tightly that they refuse to leave the atom to participate in chemical bonding at all! We literally call these two lazy electrons an 'inert pair' because they just sit there doing nothing. Because those two electrons are stuck tightly to the nucleus, Thallium can only use its 1 remaining 'p' electron to form bonds. This is exactly why Thallium frequently and happily exists in the +1 oxidation state, while its lighter cousin Aluminium does not.

questions.Question: Q40. The element that does NOT show catenation is:
questions.Hint: Catenation is the ability to form long chains with atoms of the same element. Think about which atom is so incredibly large that its bonds with itself are too weak to hold a chain together.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: 'Catenation' is one of the coolest and most important concepts in all of chemistry! It is a fancy word that describes an element's special ability to hold hands with atoms of the exact same element to form incredibly long chains, branches, or rings. Carbon is the absolute, undisputed king of catenation. It can link Carbon-to-Carbon millions of times to create DNA, proteins, plastics, and practically every living thing around us! As we move down Group 14 on the periodic table (which lists Carbon, Silicon, Germanium, Tin, and finally Lead), the atoms naturally get larger and larger because they are adding more electron shells. Silicon and Germanium can still form chains, although their chains are much shorter and significantly less stable than Carbon's amazing chains. But Lead (Pb) is at the very, very bottom of the group. Lead atoms are genuinely gigantic! Imagine two people wearing giant, inflatable sumo wrestler suits trying to hold hands; they can barely reach each other, and their grip is terrible. In the exact same way, when two huge Lead atoms try to bond with each other, the physical distance between their nuclei is very long, making the Pb-Pb bond incredibly weak. Because the bond energy holding them together is so low, any chain they try to form just breaks apart immediately. Therefore, Lead is practically unable to link up with itself and does not show catenation.

questions.Question: Q41. The chloride that CANNOT get hydrolysed is:
questions.Hint: For water to attack (hydrolyse) a molecule, the central atom needs an empty room (empty d-orbital) for water's oxygen to park its unshared electrons.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's break down what 'hydrolysis' actually means in a simple way. 'Hydro' means water, and 'lysis' means to break or split. So, we are essentially trying to use water molecules as tiny weapons to attack and break down these chloride compounds. For a water molecule to successfully attack, the oxygen atom in the water (which has two pairs of unshared, extra electrons) needs a safe place to park those electrons on the central atom of the target molecule. Think of the central atom as a hotel, and water's electrons as guests looking for an empty room to stay in. Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), and Tin (Sn) are larger atoms found in the 3rd period of the periodic table or lower. This is a crucial detail because it means they all have empty 'd-orbitals'. These empty d-orbitals act exactly like vacant rooms in our hotel! Water can easily park its extra electrons in those empty rooms, attach itself firmly to the atom, and start the chemical process of tearing the molecule apart. However, Carbon (in CCl$_4$) is a very small atom from the 2nd period. It only has 's' and 'p' orbitals, and all of them are completely full of its own electrons. Carbon has absolutely zero empty d-orbitals. So, when water confidently knocks on the door of CCl$_4$ to attack, Carbon basically replies, 'Sorry, we are fully booked! No empty rooms!' Because water has literally nowhere to attach its electrons, the reaction cannot even start. Therefore, CCl$_4$ is safe and cannot get hydrolysed.

questions.Question: Q42. Correct statements among 'A' to 'D' regarding silicones are: (A) They are polymers with hydrophobic character. (B) They are biocompatible. (C) In general, they have high thermal stability and low dielectric strength. (D) Usually, they are resistant to oxidation and used as greases.
questions.Hint: Think about silicone spatulas in your kitchen or waterproof sealants! They love high heat, repel water, and are safe around living tissue. But what about electricity? They are actually great insulators.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Silicones are incredibly fascinating and versatile materials that you probably use every day! Unlike natural organic polymers (like rubber or plastic) that are built entirely out of long chains of carbon atoms, silicones are synthetic polymers built on a strong, alternating backbone of Silicon and Oxygen atoms (-Si-O-Si-O-). Attached to the silicon atoms on the outside of this strong backbone are organic groups, typically methyl groups (-CH$_3$). Let's look at the given statements to see what is scientifically true about them. Statement A says they are hydrophobic. This is completely true! The organic groups pointing outward act like thousands of tiny umbrellas that hate water, making silicone an excellent waterproof sealant (think of the flexible caulk used to seal the edges of your bathtub). Statement B says they are biocompatible. This is also completely true! Because they are remarkably stable and unreactive, the human body's immune system usually ignores them entirely, which is why they are widely used in medical implants, pacemakers, and soft contact lenses. Statement C says they have high thermal stability and low dielectric strength. This is actually a trick—it's half false! While it is completely true they have high thermal stability (you can put silicone baking mats in a 400-degree oven without them melting), they actually possess HIGH dielectric strength. This simply means they are brilliant electrical insulators and stubbornly prevent electricity from flowing through them. Statement D says they are resistant to oxidation and used as greases. This is true! The incredibly strong Si-O bonds are very tough for oxygen to attack, so they don't break down or degrade easily over time, making silicone grease an excellent, long-lasting lubricant for machines. Therefore, only statements A, B, and D are factually correct.

questions.Question: The correct statements among I to III regarding group 13 element oxides are: (I) Boron trioxide is acidic. (II) Oxides of aluminium and gallium are amphoteric. (III) Oxides of indium and thallium are basic.
questions.Hint: Remember the periodic trend! As you travel down any group from the top to the bottom, the elements change from non-metals to metals. How does that change the 'personality' of their oxides?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let us dive into a really fascinating pattern that happens on the periodic table. Imagine a family tree where the members change their personality completely from the oldest to the youngest. The Group 13 family is exactly like this! At the very top, we have Boron. Boron is a non-metal. In chemistry, non-metals love to form acidic oxides. For example, carbon makes CO2, which gives soda water its bite! So, Boron forms Boron trioxide (B2O3), which is strictly acidic. Statement I is absolutely correct!

As we take a step down the family, we meet Aluminium and Gallium. These guys are somewhere in the middle. They are 'metalloids' or weak metals, so they have a bit of an identity crisis. They play both sides! The word for this in chemistry is 'amphoteric' (derived from the Greek 'amphi', meaning 'both', just like an amphibian lives in both water and land). This means their oxides can react like an acid OR a base depending on who they are talking to. Statement II is right on the money!

Finally, as we reach the bottom of the group, we meet Indium and Thallium. These are massive, true metals. True metals like to give away their electrons, and in water, this creates a basic environment (like rust or magnesium). So, their oxides are totally basic. Statement III is also completely true! 

Because all three statements correctly track this awesome top-to-bottom personality change from acidic to amphoteric to basic, all of them are right!

questions.Question: Diborane (B₂H₆) reacts independently with O₂ and H₂O to produce, respectively;
questions.Hint: Diborane is extremely reactive. It violently burns in oxygen to form an oxide. When thrown in water, it rips the water apart to grab the -OH groups, forming an acid often used in eye drops!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us talk about Diborane (B2H6). This is a wildly fascinating and super-reactive gas! Imagine Boron as a kid who really, really wants electrons to feel full and happy, but just does not have quite enough. When it bonds with hydrogen, it forms weird, strained 'banana bonds' which are notoriously unstable. 

When Diborane sees Oxygen gas (O2), it is like a starving kid seeing an endless buffet! It combusts (burns) violently and releases a massive amount of heat. Oxygen is much better at sharing electrons and stabilizing Boron than Hydrogen is. So, Boron kicks Hydrogen to the curb and forms a super strong bond with oxygen, creating Boron trioxide (B2O3). The leftover hydrogens pair up with some oxygen to make water vapor. 

But the question also asks what happens when Diborane reacts directly with liquid Water (H2O). Water is packed with oxygen atoms too! When Diborane hits water, the reaction is vigorous. Boron eagerly grabs the hydroxide part (-OH) of the water molecules. Since Boron likes forming three bonds, it grabs three -OH groups to become Boric Acid, which is written as B(OH)3 or H3BO3. The hydrogen atoms from the Diborane and the remaining hydrogens from the water team up and bubble violently away as Hydrogen gas (H2).

So, to summarize: reacting with O2 gives you Boron trioxide (B2O3), while reacting with H2O gives you Boric Acid (H3BO3). Boron is basically an oxygen-magnet!

questions.Question: The basic structural unit of feldspar, zeolites, mica, and asbestos is:
questions.Hint: Think of Silicon as Carbon's bigger cousin. Just like Carbon, Silicon loves making exactly 4 bonds. It sits right in the center of a 3D pyramid made entirely of oxygen atoms!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, let us zoom all the way down to the atomic level of the Earth's crust. Introduce yourself to Silicon! Silicon sits right under Carbon in the periodic table. Just like Carbon loves to form 4 bonds, Silicon absolutely loves to do the exact same thing. However, Silicon is a bit bigger and has a massive crush on Oxygen. 

Imagine a Silicon atom as a tiny, positively charged core. Because opposites attract, it wants to surround itself with negatively charged Oxygen atoms. Since it wants 4 bonds, exactly 4 Oxygen atoms arrange themselves around the Silicon. If you connect the centers of these 4 Oxygen atoms with imaginary lines, you get a beautiful 3D pyramid with a triangular base. In geometry, this shape is called a 'tetrahedron.' 

The formula for this single, tiny pyramid is SiO4. But wait, what about the charge? Silicon brings a +4 charge to the table, and the 4 Oxygen atoms bring a -2 charge each (totaling -8). Combine them: +4 and -8 leaves us with an overall charge of -4! So, the formula is SiO4(4-). 

These individual SiO4(4-) tetrahedrons are the universal building blocks—the fundamental Lego pieces—for almost all rocks, sand, and clay on Earth! Whether you are looking at Feldspar in hard rocks, Zeolites used in water filters, the shiny flaky layers of Mica, or stringy Asbestos fibers, they are ALL built by clicking these SiO4(4-) Lego blocks together in different patterns (like chains, sheets, or massive 3D webs). The basic unit always remains exactly the same!

questions.Chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.Question: The C-C bond length is maximum in:
questions.Hint: Remember this rule: single bonds are longer and more relaxed than double or triple bonds. Which of these molecules contains ONLY pure single bonds between its carbon atoms?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question wants to test how well we understand the way atoms hold onto each other! Let us imagine chemical bonds like holding hands with a friend. 

If two Carbon atoms share one pair of electrons, it is a 'single bond.' It is relaxed, and the atoms can stay a comfortable, long distance apart. If they share two pairs of electrons (a 'double bond'), they have to pull in much closer, like holding both hands with someone. If they share three pairs (a 'triple bond'), they are basically bear-hugging incredibly tight, pulling their centers as close as physically possible! Therefore, single bonds are the longest, and triple bonds are the shortest.

Now, let us inspect our options. Ethyne has a carbon-carbon triple bond. Very short and tight! Ethene has a carbon-carbon double bond. A bit longer, but still pretty tight. That leaves us with Diamond and Graphite, which are both forms of pure solid carbon.

Graphite is made of flat sheets of carbon. Inside these sheets, the carbons form a cool mix of single and partial double bonds. Thanks to a neat trick called 'resonance', electrons smear around, giving the bonds a partial double-bond character. Because of this, the atoms are pulled in a bit tight (around 141.5 picometers).

Diamond, however, is a massive 3D jungle gym where EVERY single carbon is attached to 4 others using pure, 100% single bonds! Because they are pure single bonds, they are the most relaxed and therefore have the 'maximum' possible length (about 154 picometers). So, Diamond wins the length contest!

questions.Question: The correct order of catenation is:
questions.Hint: Catenation is the superpower to form long chains. The smaller the atom, the stronger the bond it forms with itself! Who is the smallest element in Group 14?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
First, let us figure out what 'catenation' actually means. It is a fancy chemistry word derived from the Latin word 'catena', which simply means 'chain.' So, catenation is an element's superpower to bind with other atoms of itself to form incredibly long chains, branches, and rings.

Carbon is the absolute, undefeated champion of catenation in the entire universe. That is exactly why we have an entire subject called Organic Chemistry and why DNA and life can even exist! But why is Carbon the best? It all comes down to size and bond strength. Carbon atoms are very small. When two Carbon atoms bond, their centers are super close together. This allows their electron clouds to overlap deeply and form a super-strong, tight grip. Because the C-C bond is so incredibly strong, you can build massive, stable chains without them breaking apart.

Now, what happens as we go down Carbon's family (Group 14) in the periodic table? The order is Carbon (C), Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Tin (Sn), and Lead (Pb). As you move down the list, the atoms gain more and more electron shells, meaning they get bigger and bigger! Imagine two giant sumo wrestlers trying to hold hands—their big bellies keep them apart, so their grip is very weak. 

Because Silicon is bigger than Carbon, the Si-Si bond is much weaker. Germanium and Tin are even bigger, so their bonds are even weaker (in fact, their abilities to chain are roughly similar, hence the $\approx$ symbol). Finally, Lead (Pb) is so massive that a Pb-Pb bond is incredibly weak, meaning it basically does not form chains at all. Therefore, the ability to build chains perfectly matches the size trend from top to bottom: C is much greater than Si, then Ge, then Sn, and Pb is last.

questions.Question: When metal 'M' is treated with NaOH, a white gelatinous precipitate 'X' is obtained, which is soluble in excess of NaOH. Compound 'X' when heated strongly gives an oxide which is used in chromatography as an adsorbent. The metal 'M' is:
questions.Hint: Look for the ultimate clue: what oxide is famously used as a stationary powder in chromatography alongside silica gel? Also, this metal plays both sides—it reacts with bases (NaOH) too, meaning it's amphoteric!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question feels exactly like a detective mystery! Let us decode the clues one by one to find out the identity of metal 'M'.

Clue 1: We have a metal 'M' that reacts with sodium hydroxide (NaOH, which is a very strong base) to form a white, jelly-like (gelatinous) solid precipitate 'X'.
Clue 2: If you keep adding MORE NaOH to the beaker, this solid magically dissolves!
Clue 3: When you heat 'X', it turns into an oxide that is famous for being used as an 'adsorbent' in chromatography.

Let us start with Clues 1 and 2. Usually, metals ignore bases; they prefer reacting with acids! A metal that reacts with bases (and acids too!) is called 'amphoteric'. The two most famous amphoteric metals you will ever study are Aluminium (Al) and Zinc (Zn). When Aluminium reacts with a bit of NaOH, it forms Aluminium Hydroxide, Al(OH)3. This happens to be a beautiful white, jelly-like precipitate! So 'X' is Al(OH)3. When you dump a ton of extra NaOH into the mix, the Aluminium acts like an acid toward the strong base, forming complex ions ([Al(OH)4]-) that dissolve perfectly into the water.

Now for the nail in the coffin, Clue 3: Heating Al(OH)3 acts like a drying process. It drives off the water and leaves behind pure Aluminium Oxide, Al2O3, which is also known as Alumina. If you ever study a fun technique called Thin Layer Chromatography (which forensic scientists use to separate colors and chemicals), you will learn that the white powder painted on the plates to 'catch' or adsorb the chemicals is almost always Silica gel or Alumina! Zinc's oxide is not famous for this specific job at all. So, the mystery metal 'M' is undoubtedly Aluminium!

questions.Question: A group 13 element 'X' reacts with chlorine gas to produce a compound XCl₃. XCl₃ is electron deficient and easily reacts with NH₃ to form Cl₃X$\leftarrowNH$₃ adduct, however, XCl₃ does not dimerize. X is:
questions.Hint: Aluminium chloride (AlCl3) famously joins up with a twin to form Al2Cl6 (a dimer). Which element in group 13 is just too tiny to squeeze four giant chlorine atoms around itself?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a classic chemistry puzzle about the Group 13 elements. Let us break it down logically!

Group 13 consists of Boron (B), Aluminium (Al), Gallium (Ga), Indium (In), and Thallium (Tl). The puzzle tells us that our mystery element 'X' reacts with chlorine to make a molecule with the formula XCl3. Because 'X' is in Group 13, it has exactly 3 electrons in its outermost shell to share. By sharing them with 3 Chlorines, the central atom 'X' ends up with 6 electrons total in its outer shell.

But wait a minute! The famous 'Octet Rule' says atoms want 8 electrons to feel completely stable and happy. Because 'X' only has 6, it is 'electron-deficient'. It acts like a hungry vacuum looking for a pair of electrons. Ammonia (NH3) happens to have a lone pair of extra electrons just sitting on its Nitrogen atom. So, the hungry XCl3 happily accepts those electrons from NH3 to form a bond (which we call an 'adduct'), making everyone happy. This behavior is actually true for BOTH Boron and Aluminium! So how do we choose the right answer?

The ultimate clue is the last sentence: 'XCl3 does NOT dimerize.' Dimerize simply means two identical molecules join hands to form a twin (a dimer). Aluminium Chloride (AlCl3) famously DOES dimerize. Two AlCl3 molecules stick together to share Chlorines, forming Al2Cl6. Why? Because Aluminium is physically large enough to comfortably fit 4 massive Chlorine atoms around itself.

Boron, however, is incredibly tiny! It is the smallest element at the very top of Group 13. If two BCl3 molecules tried to stick together, the giant Chlorine atoms would aggressively bump into each other and push each other apart. In chemistry, this physical crowding is called 'steric hindrance'. It is like trying to fit 4 giant beach balls around a tiny marble—it just will not work! Since BCl3 is too tiny to dimerize, our mystery element 'X' must be Boron!

questions.Question: In graphite and diamond, the percentage of p-characters of the hybrid orbitals in hybridisation are respectively:
questions.Hint: Think about how many neighbors each carbon atom has in graphite versus diamond. This will help you find their hybridization (sp² vs sp³), and from there, you can calculate the 'p' percentage!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about what 'hybridization' even means! Imagine you have different colors of paint. You have one bucket of red paint (let's call it the 's' orbital) and three buckets of blue paint (let's call them the 'p' orbitals). When atoms form bonds, they like to mix these paints together to create identical, uniform orbitals to share electrons.

In Graphite, each carbon atom holds hands (forms bonds) with 3 other carbon atoms. To do this, it mixes one 's' bucket and two 'p' buckets. This creates three mixed buckets called "sp²" orbitals. Since 2 out of the 3 total buckets used were 'p' (blue paint), the percentage of 'p' character is 2 divided by 3. If you do the math, 2/3 equals 0.6667, or 66.67%! That's the p-character for graphite.

Now, let's look at Diamond. Diamond is super strong because every single carbon atom holds hands with 4 other carbon atoms in a sturdy 3D pyramid shape. To do this, it needs to mix one 's' bucket with all three 'p' buckets. This creates four mixed buckets called "sp³" orbitals. Here, 3 out of the 4 total buckets used were 'p' (blue paint). The percentage of 'p' character is 3 divided by 4, which is exactly 0.75, or 75%!

So, graphite's hybrid orbitals have 66.67% p-character, and diamond's hybrid orbitals have 75% p-character. Thinking about how many neighbors an atom has helps you figure out the paint-mixing ratio instantly!

questions.Question: Identify the reaction which does not liberate hydrogen:
questions.Hint: Remember the reactivity series! Metals below hydrogen (like Copper) cannot displace hydrogen from acids. Additionally, nitric acid is a strong oxidizing agent that acts like a bully, changing the rules of the reaction.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever seen the 'Reactivity Series' of metals? It's basically a ranking of how tough or active metals are. Metals high up on the list (like Sodium, Zinc, and Aluminum) are strong and active. Hydrogen is also on this list, usually somewhere in the middle. Metals that are above Hydrogen are stronger, and they can 'kick out' or displace hydrogen from acids and water, releasing bubbly Hydrogen gas ($H_2$). 

Let's look at our options. Zinc ($Zn$) reacting with dilute $HCl$ is a classic. Zinc is stronger than Hydrogen, so it kicks Hydrogen out: $Zn + 2HCl \rightarrow ZnCl_2 + H_2$. Boom, hydrogen gas is liberated! 

Sodium ($Na$) is extremely reactive. If you drop it in water, it aggressively kicks Hydrogen out of the water molecules, making $NaOH$ and $H_2$ gas (sometimes even catching fire!). 

Aluminum ($Al$) is special—it's 'amphoteric,' meaning it can react with both acids and bases. If you put it in a strong base like aqueous $NaOH$, it dissolves and liberates $H_2$ gas.

But Copper ($Cu$) is below Hydrogen in the reactivity series. It's too weak to kick Hydrogen out of an acid! Even worse, concentrated Nitric Acid ($HNO_3$) is what we call a 'strong oxidizing agent.' It's like a bully. Even if the reaction tries to form a little bit of Hydrogen gas, the $HNO_3$ instantly attacks that Hydrogen and oxidizes it into Water ($H_2O$), while giving off toxic brown Nitrogen Dioxide ($NO_2$) gas instead. So, no hydrogen gas is liberated here!

questions.Concept: Electrical Conductivity and Hybridization of Allotropes
questions.Question: Assertion: Among the carbon allotropes, diamond is an insulator, whereas, graphite is a good conductor of electricity. Reason: Hybridization of carbon in diamond and graphite are sp³ and sp², respectively.
MCQ_Options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
questions.Hint: Electricity needs moving charges (like free electrons) to flow. Think about whether the sp³ or sp² hybridization leaves any unbound, free electrons behind!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine electricity as a stream of flowing water, but instead of water droplets, it's a continuous flow of tiny, negatively charged particles called 'electrons.' For any material to conduct electricity, it must have loose, free-roaming electrons that can travel around easily. 

Carbon naturally has 4 electrons in its outermost shell that it uses to make bonds. In Diamond, carbon uses $\text{sp}^3$ hybridization. This means every single carbon atom forms 4 super-tight bonds with 4 other carbon atoms. All 4 of its outer electrons are locked up in these strong bonds. Because there are zero free electrons, electricity cannot flow through it at all. That makes diamond an excellent insulator!

Graphite, the stuff in your pencil, is entirely different. It uses $\text{sp}^2$ hybridization. This means each carbon atom only bonds with 3 other carbon atoms. Wait a minute—if carbon has 4 outer electrons and only forms 3 bonds, what happens to the 4th electron? That 4th electron is left unbound! It sits in an unhybridized p-orbital. Because graphite is arranged in flat sheets, these leftover 4th electrons can form a giant invisible highway between the sheets, freely zipping around from atom to atom. Since there are free-roaming electrons, graphite is a wonderful conductor of electricity!

So, the Assertion is totally correct (diamond = insulator, graphite = conductor), and the Reason perfectly explains *why* it happens (it all comes down to $\text{sp}^3$ vs $\text{sp}^2$ hybridization locking up or freeing those electrons).
questions.Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are correct, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.

questions.Question: In the following sets of reactants which two sets best exhibit the amphoteric characters of Al₂O₃·xH₂O? Set 1: Al₂O₃·xH₂O(s) and OH⁻(aq), Set 2: Al₂O₃·xH₂O(s) and H₂O(l), Set 3: Al₂O₃·xH₂O(s) and H⁺(aq), Set 4: Al₂O₃·xH₂O(s) and NH₃(aq)
questions.Hint: 'Amphi' means 'both' (like an amphibian that lives in water and on land). An amphoteric substance can act as both an acid and a base. Therefore, it should be able to react with a strong acid AND a strong base!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
In chemistry, the word 'amphoteric' is like being a chameleon. A chameleon changes its color to match its environment, right? An amphoteric substance changes its chemical behavior depending on what it is mixed with. Specifically, an amphoteric substance can act like a base when it is near an acid, and it can act like an acid when it is near a base!

Aluminum oxide ($Al_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O$) is a famous chemical chameleon. To prove to the world that it is truly amphoteric, we need to test it against a strong acid and a strong base to see if it dissolves and reacts with both. 

Let's look at the sets provided. Set 1 uses $OH^-$, which is the hydroxide ion. This is the universal sign of a strong base (like sodium hydroxide). Set 3 uses $H^+$, which is the hydrogen ion. This is the universal sign of a strong acid (like hydrochloric acid). 

If you put $Al_2O_3$ in water (Set 2), nothing really happens because water is neutral; it doesn't force the chameleon to change. If you put it in $NH_3$ (Set 4), which is ammonia, it's too weak of a base to make the solid aluminum oxide fully dissolve. 

But when you mix it with strong $OH^-$ (Set 1), the aluminum oxide acts like an acid and dissolves to form a soluble aluminate complex $[Al(OH)_4]^-$. When you mix it with strong $H^+$ (Set 3), it acts like a base and dissolves to form free aluminum ions $Al^{3+}$. Thus, reacting it with a strong base (Set 1) and a strong acid (Set 3) are the absolute best tests to prove its amazing amphoteric superpower!

questions.Question: Example of a three-dimensional silicate is:
questions.Hint: Think of a structure where every single oxygen atom is shared between silicon atoms in all directions, making a giant continuous 3D network. This mineral is super hard and makes up beach sand!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Silicates are minerals that make up over 90% of the Earth's crust! You can think of them as the building blocks of rocks. The fundamental, tiny Lego block of all silicates is the $(SiO_4)^{4-}$ tetrahedron. Imagine a tiny silicon atom in the center surrounded by four oxygen atoms forming a 3D pyramid (a tetrahedron). 

Depending on how these tiny Lego blocks share their corner oxygen atoms with each other, they create different shapes. If they don't share any corners, they are single, isolated blocks (orthosilicates). If they share two corners, they link up to form long, 1D chains (like Pyroxenes). If they share three corners, they link up to form flat, 2D sheets (like Mica, which you can physically peel apart into super-thin layers!).

But what if every single oxygen atom (all four corners) of the tetrahedron is shared with another silicon atom? The Lego blocks link up in every single direction—up, down, left, right, forwards, and backwards! This creates a massive, strong, continuous 3-Dimensional network. 

Quartz is the perfect example of this 3D network silicate. Because all the oxygen atoms are locked tightly into this giant 3D jungle gym, Quartz is a very hard, durable crystal (it's what makes up most sand and beautiful clear rock crystals!). Zeolites and Feldspars are also 3D silicates. So, if you ever see a tough, unpeelable rock crystal like Quartz, you are looking at a 3D silicate network!

questions.Concept: General Properties and Atomic Radii Trends
questions.Question: Identify the incorrect statement:
MCQ_Options: Atomic radius of Gallium is larger than that of Aluminum.
PbO\_2 is a stronger oxidizing agent than SnO\_2.
Carbon shows a maximum covalency of 4.
questions.Hint: Think about the 'd-block contraction' (or poor shielding effect) that happens right after the transition metals! It makes a certain Group 13 atom unexpectedly small.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play 'spot the lie' with these chemistry statements! We are looking for the incorrect one. 

Statement B: $PbO_2$ is a stronger oxidizing agent than $SnO_2$. This is actually true! Lead ($Pb$) is at the very bottom of the carbon family, and it desperately wants to be in a +2 oxidation state instead of +4 due to something called the 'Inert Pair Effect'. So $PbO_2$ (where Pb is forced to be +4) aggressively steals electrons from other things to become +2. Stealing electrons makes it a great oxidizing agent!

Statement C: Carbon shows a maximum covalency of 4. True! Carbon only has 4 valence electrons and only 4 orbitals (one 2s and three 2p) available in its outer shell. It physically cannot form more than 4 bonds.

Statement D: Diamond is a covalent solid. True! Diamond is a giant 3D network of carbon atoms held together entirely by strong covalent bonds. 

Statement A: Atomic radius of Gallium is larger than that of Aluminum. THIS IS THE LIE! Normally, as you go down a group on the periodic table (from Boron to Aluminum to Gallium), the atoms get bigger because they get brand new rings (shells) of electrons. So, logically, Gallium *should* be bigger than Aluminum. However, right before you get to Gallium on the periodic table, you have to pass through a whole row of transition metals. These transition metals put electrons into 'd' orbitals. 'd' orbitals have a very weird, spread-out shape and are absolutely terrible at shielding the outer electrons from the positive pull of the nucleus. Because of this poor shielding (called the 'd-block contraction'), the nucleus pulls Gallium's outer electrons inward super tightly! As a result, Gallium shrinks and is actually unexpectedly *smaller* than Aluminum!
questions.Answer: Atomic radius of Gallium is larger than that of Aluminum.

questions.Question: In view of the signs of $\Delta_r G^\circ$ for the following reactions: PbO\_2 + Pb $\rightarrow 2$PbO, $\Delta_r G^\circ$ < 0, SnO\_2 + Sn $\rightarrow 2$SnO, $\Delta_r G^\circ$ > 0. Which oxidation states are more characteristics for lead and tin?
questions.Hint: A negative Gibbs free energy ($\Delta_r G^\circ$ < 0) means a reaction wants to happen naturally. Notice what happens to the oxidation states of Lead (Pb) vs Tin (Sn) in the reactions that occur naturally!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
In chemistry, $\Delta_r G^\circ$ stands for the 'Standard Gibbs Free Energy Change.' It sounds like scary math, but it's really just a way to measure if a reaction wants to happen all on its own. Imagine a ball resting on a hill. If the ball rolls down the hill, it happens automatically. We call this a negative Gibbs Free Energy ($\Delta_r G^\circ < 0$). If you want the ball to roll UP the hill, it won't happen naturally; you have to push it hard. That's a positive Gibbs Free Energy ($\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$).

Look at the first reaction for Lead (Pb): $PbO_2 + Pb \rightarrow 2PbO$. We are told $\Delta_r G^\circ < 0$. This means the reaction rolls down the hill automatically! In $PbO_2$, Lead has a +4 charge (oxidation state). In the product $PbO$, it has a +2 charge. Because this happens naturally, Lead is shouting, 'I prefer to be in the +2 state!' 

Now look at Tin (Sn): $SnO_2 + Sn \rightarrow 2SnO$. We are told $\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$. This is rolling a ball up a hill. It will NOT happen naturally. Tin in $SnO_2$ has a +4 charge, and it absolutely refuses to turn into $SnO$ (+2 charge). Tin is saying, 'I prefer to stay in the +4 state!'

Why does this happen? It's due to a cool phenomenon called the 'Inert Pair Effect.' As atoms get really heavy (like Lead, which is at the bottom of the periodic table), their innermost 's' electrons get pulled super close to the heavy nucleus and refuse to bond (they become lazy, or 'inert'). Since Lead holds tightly onto those 2 's' electrons, it only uses its 2 'p' electrons to bond, resulting in a +2 state. Tin is much lighter, so it happily shares all 4 of its outer electrons, strongly preferring the +4 state.

questions.Question: Q57. Which one of the following is the correct statement?
MCQ_Options: Boric acid is a strong Arrhenius acid.
Beryllium exhibits a maximum coordination number of 6.
Chlorides of both beryllium and aluminium have bridged chloride structures in solid phase.
questions.Hint: Think about the special 'diagonal relationship' on the periodic table between Group 2 and Group 13.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's solve this mystery by looking at how elements behave. Have you ever noticed how sometimes two people from completely different families act exactly like twins? In chemistry, we have something very similar called the 'Diagonal Relationship'. 

Normally, elements in the same vertical column (group) share similar personalities. But sometimes, the first element of a group feels a strong connection to the second element of the neighboring group diagonally to its right! This happens because their atomic sizes and the pull of their nucleus (charge-to-size ratio) are almost perfectly matched. A classic example is Beryllium (Be) in Group 2 and Aluminium (Al) in Group 13. 

Let's look at the options to see why Option C is the perfect match! 

Option A claims Boric acid is a strong Arrhenius acid. An Arrhenius acid is something that freely gives away its own H+ ions in water (like HCl). But Boric acid (B(OH)3) is actually a sneaky 'Lewis acid'. It doesn't give away its own protons; instead, it steals an OH- from water and forces the water to give up an H+. So, it's not an Arrhenius acid at all!

Option B says Beryllium can have a coordination number of 6. Coordination number is just the number of 'hands' an atom can use to hold onto other atoms. Beryllium is tiny! It only has s and p orbitals (which can hold a max of 8 electrons, or 4 bonds). It literally doesn't have the space (no d-orbitals) to hold 6 things. So, its maximum is 4.

Option D says Diborane (B2H6) is a Lewis base. A Lewis base is a rich chemical that donates extra electrons. But Boron only has 3 valence electrons! Diborane is actually desperately short on electrons (electron-deficient), making it a Lewis acid (electron acceptor), not a base.

Finally, Option C! Because of their diagonal twin-like relationship, both Beryllium and Aluminium struggle with being electron-deficient when they bond with chlorine (forming BeCl2 and AlCl3). To survive, they both form fascinating 'bridged' structures in their solid states, where they share chlorine atoms with their neighbors to feel full and stable. They form polymeric chains or dimers using these bridges. This statement is 100% correct!
questions.Answer: Chlorides of both beryllium and aluminium have bridged chloride structures in solid phase.

questions.Question: Q58. The stability of dihalides of Si, Ge, Sn and Pb increases steadily in the sequence
questions.Hint: Remember the 'Inert Pair Effect' as you travel down a heavy group in the periodic table. The heaviest elements get 'lazy' with their inner s-orbital electrons!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are packing for a winter vacation. You put your favorite heavy jacket deep at the bottom of the suitcase, and some light t-shirts right on top. When you quickly need to grab clothes, you are only going to take the t-shirts on top because digging to the bottom is too much work. The heavy jacket is just 'inert' or stubbornly stuck there. Chemistry works just like this!
