questions.Question: Q12. Number of alkanes obtained on electrolysis of a mixture of CH$\u2083$COONa and C$\u2082H\u2085$COONa is___
questions.Hint: Kolbe's electrolysis creates free radicals. Think of all the possible ways the methyl ($CH_3^\bullet$) and ethyl ($C_2H_5^\bullet$) radicals can pair up with each other!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Have you ever wondered what happens when you use electricity to break molecules apart? It sounds like mad science, but it$\u2019$s actually a beautiful process called Kolbe's Electrolysis!

In this question, we have a mixture of two salts: sodium acetate ($CH_3COONa$) and sodium propanoate ($C_2H_5COONa$).

Why are we doing this? Well, when we dissolve these in water and shoot an electric current through them, the electricity acts like a microscopic pair of scissors. It chops off the heavy -COONa tail from these molecules. That tail bubbles away harmlessly as Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$) gas!

But what is left behind?

When the tail is chopped off, we are left with highly energetic, lonely fragments called 'Free Radicals'. Specifically, we get a Methyl radical ($CH_3^\bullet$) and an Ethyl radical ($C_2H_5^\bullet$). The little dot ($\bullet$) represents an unpaired electron. Electrons HATE being alone. They are like lonely dancers at a party looking for a partner.

Now, imagine the dance floor. We have millions of Methyls (let's say they wear Red shirts) and millions of Ethyls (Blue shirts) buzzing around.

When the music stops, they instantly grab a partner to form a stable molecule (an alkane). Let's look at all the possible combinations!

1. A Methyl grabs another Methyl (Red + Red): $CH_3^\bullet + CH_3^\bullet \rightarrow CH_3-CH_3$. This forms Ethane!
2. An Ethyl grabs another Ethyl (Blue + Blue): $C_2H_5^\bullet + C_2H_5^\bullet \rightarrow C_2H_5-C_2H_5$. This forms Butane!
3. A Methyl grabs an Ethyl (Red + Blue): $CH_3^\bullet + C_2H_5^\bullet \rightarrow CH_3-C_2H_5$. This forms Propane!

Because there are millions of these bouncing around randomly, all three of these pairings will happen.

So, if you look at the final mixture, you will find exactly 3 different alkanes: Ethane, Butane, and Propane.

Isn't it amazing how a little bit of electricity can act like a matching-making machine for molecules? By breaking bonds, we create the opportunity for entirely new bonds to form. The total number of alkanes obtained is 3!

questions.Question:
Q13. Number of isomeric products formed by monochlorination of 2-methylbutane in presence of 
sunlight is_______
questions.Hint: Draw 2-methylbutane. Find every unique carbon where you can place a Chlorine. Then, check if adding the Chlorine creates a chiral center (a carbon attached to 4 DIFFERENT groups)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have a completely blank house with multiple rooms, and you are given a bucket of bright green paint. You want to see how many uniquely painted houses you can create by painting just ONE room.

This is exactly what is happening in Free Radical Halogenation! Our 'house' is a molecule called 2-methylbutane, and our 'green paint' is a Chlorine ($Cl$) atom. We are trying to find out how many different 'isomeric products' (uniquely painted houses) we can make by swapping just one Hydrogen for one Chlorine.

First, let's draw our house: $CH_3 - CH(CH_3) - CH_2 - CH_3$.

It has four different 'types' of carbons where we can put our Chlorine. Let's try them all!

But wait, there's a trick! In chemistry, molecules are 3D objects. Sometimes, when you paint a room, you accidentally create a 'Chiral Center'. This is a magical carbon atom that is attached to 4 COMPLETELY DIFFERENT groups. When a molecule has a chiral center, it acts like a pair of hands: you get a 'left-handed' version and a 'right-handed' version! These are two different isomers.

Let's test our 4 spots:

Spot 1: We attach Chlorine to the very first carbon. The second carbon now holds four different things: a Hydrogen, a Methyl group, an Ethyl group, and our new $-CH_2Cl$ group. Because they are all different, we activated the magic mirror! This gives us 2 isomers (left and right hands).

Spot 2: We attach Chlorine to the second carbon. This carbon now holds a Chlorine, an Ethyl group, and TWO identical Methyl groups. Because two groups are the same, no magic mirror here. Just 1 isomer.

Spot 3: We attach Chlorine to the third carbon. This carbon now holds a Hydrogen, a Chlorine, a Methyl group, and an Isopropyl group. All four are different! Magic mirror activated again! We get 2 isomers.

Spot 4: We attach Chlorine to the very last carbon. If we look at the molecule, no carbon holds 4 different groups (the second carbon still has two identical methyls). So, no magic mirror. Just 1 isomer.

Now, let's add them up!

Spot 1 (2 isomers) + Spot 2 (1 isomer) + Spot 3 (2 isomers) + Spot 4 (1 isomer) = 6 total unique isomers!

By treating the molecule like a 3D puzzle, you can easily predict exactly how many forms it will take in the real world!

questions.Question: Q14. In the given reactions identify
questions.Hint: Every chemical reaction is like a story. You start with characters (Reactants), they go through a journey (Intermediates), and finally become something new (Products)!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! You've run into a question that just says 'In the given reactions identify...' without the actual reactions. Don't worry at all! This is the perfect time to zoom out and look at the big picture of how chemists read reaction maps.

Imagine you are reading a treasure map. A chemical reaction scheme is exactly that$\u2014$a map showing how we travel from cheap, everyday chemicals to highly valuable medicines or materials!

In any given reaction map, there are four major 'characters' you need to be able to identify:

1. The Reactants (The Starting Point): These are the ingredients you pull off the shelf. If you are baking a cake, the reactants are the flour and eggs. In chemistry, they are usually on the far left side of the arrow.

2. The Reagents & Catalysts (The Tools): These are the chemicals written ABOVE or BELOW the arrow. They aren't the main characters, but they are the tools that make the change happen! Heat (shown as a little triangle $\Delta$), acids ($H^+$), or sunlight ($h\nu$) are classic examples. They act like the oven when baking a cake.

3. The Intermediates (The Awkward Middle Phase): Sometimes a reaction takes multiple steps. The molecules formed in the middle$\u2014$which immediately get used up in the next step$\u2014$are called Intermediates. They are like the raw cake batter. You wouldn't serve it to a guest, but it's a necessary step to get to the cake!

4. The Products (The Treasure): This is what you find at the very end of the map. It's the final, stable molecule you've been trying to create.

When a question asks you to 'identify' parts of a reaction, you are simply playing the role of a casting director! You look at the position of the chemical. Is it before the arrow? (Reactant!). Above the arrow? (Catalyst/Reagent!). Stuck between two arrows? (Intermediate!). At the very end? (Product!).

By memorizing these four roles, you can conquer any complex reaction map, even if you've never seen the specific chemicals before. You've got this!

questions.Question: Q15. Which of the following compound will most easily be attacked by an electrophile?
questions.Hint: Electrophiles are 'electron-lovers' looking for molecules that are rich in negative charge. Which of these groups pushes extra electrons into the benzene ring?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's break this down into something super easy to imagine. 

First, what is an 'electrophile'? The word comes from 'electro' (meaning electrons, which are negatively charged) and 'phile' (meaning lover). So, an electrophile is a chemical species that absolutely LOVES electrons. It's like a very hungry bear constantly sniffing around for a pot of honey. In this analogy, the 'honey' is a rich, dense cloud of negative electrons.

Now, all of our options contain a Benzene ring. A standard Benzene ring is a decent pot of honey. It has a nice ring of electrons circulating it. But what happens when we attach different 'hats' (functional groups) to this benzene ring?

1. Benzene: Just your standard, ordinary pot of honey.
2. Nitrobenzene: The nitro group (-NO_{2}) is incredibly greedy. It actually sucks electrons AWAY from the benzene ring. It's like someone stealing honey from the pot. The hungry bear (electrophile) will take one look and walk away. We call this a 'deactivating' group.
3. Chlorobenzene: Chlorine is highly electronegative, meaning it also acts like a slight honey-thief, pulling some electron density away. 
4. Phenol: Here, we have an -OH group attached to the ring. The oxygen atom has two unshared pairs of electrons (lone pairs). Oxygen is super generous here; it pushes its extra electrons INTO the benzene ring through a process called resonance. It's like a machine pumping extra, super-sweet sugar right into our honey pot!

Because Phenol's benzene ring is bursting with extra electron density, our 'hungry bear' electrophile will attack it much faster and much more easily than the others. So, Phenol is the correct answer. Remember: 'activating groups' like -OH make electrophilic attacks much easier!

questions.Question: Q16. Find out the major products from the following reactions. [Note: The original text lacked the specific reaction, so let's solve a classic missing reaction: Propene + HBr $\rightarrow$ ?]
questions.Hint: Remember 'Markovnikov's Rule': When adding HX to an alkene, the rich get richer! The hydrogen goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! Since the original test question didn't print the actual chemical reaction, I am going to teach you the most legendary reaction that fits this exact question format: adding Hydrobromic acid (HBr) to Propene (CH_{3}-CH=CH_{2}). This is a classic puzzle every chemistry student solves!

Imagine Propene as a molecule with a double bond. A double bond is like a locked door holding a lot of energy. When HBr comes along, it wants to break that door down and attach itself. 

But here's the puzzle: HBr has two parts, a Hydrogen (H) and a Bromine (Br). When the double bond breaks, which atom goes to which carbon? 

The choices are:
Option A: The H goes to the middle carbon, and Br goes to the end. (Giving 1-Bromopropane)
Option B: The H goes to the end carbon, and Br goes to the middle. (Giving 2-Bromopropane)

To solve this, we use a beautiful concept discovered by a Russian chemist named Vladimir Markovnikov. I call it the 'Rich Get Richer' rule. Markovnikov noticed that the Hydrogen atom prefers to attach to the carbon that *already has the most hydrogens*.

Look at our double bond in Propene: CH_{3}-CH=CH_{2}.
- The middle carbon (CH) has only 1 hydrogen.
- The end carbon (CH_{2}) has 2 hydrogens. 

The end carbon is 'richer' in hydrogens! So, the new H from HBr goes to the end carbon (turning it into CH_{3}), and the Br gets stuck on the middle carbon. 

Why does nature do this? Because during the reaction, a temporary structure called a 'carbocation' forms. Putting the positive charge on the middle carbon is like resting a heavy bowling ball on a thick, sturdy table (it's supported by neighboring carbons). Putting it on the end carbon is like resting the bowling ball on a flimsy twig. Nature always prefers stability! Therefore, the major product is 2-Bromopropane.

questions.Question: Q17. 17 mg of a hydrocarbon (M.F. C_{10}H_{16}) takes up 8.40 mL of the H_{2} gas measured at 0^{$\circ$}C and 760 mm of Hg. Ozonolysis of the same hydrocarbon yields CH_{3}-C(=O)-CH_{3}, H-C(=O)-H, H-C(=O)-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-C(=O)-C(=O)-H. The number of double bond/s present in the hydrocarbon is ________.
questions.Hint: Calculate the moles of the hydrocarbon and the moles of the hydrogen gas. For every 1 mole of double bonds, exactly 1 mole of H_{2} gas is consumed. Finding their ratio gives you the answer!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Wow, this looks like a giant math problem, but don't panic! It is actually a really fun detective game. Let's solve it step-by-step together.

Imagine every double bond in our mystery molecule is a strip of bare Velcro. Hydrogen gas (H_{2}) acts like pieces of felt that stick perfectly to that Velcro. If a molecule has 1 double bond, it needs 1 molecule of H_{2} to cover it. If it has 2 double bonds, it needs 2 molecules of H_{2}. If we can figure out the ratio of H_{2} used compared to our mystery molecule, we will know exactly how many double bonds it has!

Step 1: How much of our mystery molecule do we have?
We have 17 milligrams of a hydrocarbon with the formula C_{10}H_{16}. 
Let's find its 'Molar Mass' (how much one mole of it weighs). Carbon weighs 12, and Hydrogen weighs 1.
Mass = (10 $\times 12) + (16 \times 1) = 120 + 16 = 136$ grams per mole.
Now, let's find the 'moles' (the chemical counting unit). Since 17 mg is 0.017 grams:
Moles of hydrocarbon = $\frac{0.017}{136} = 0.000125$ moles.

Step 2: How much Hydrogen gas did we use?
We used 8.40 mL of H_{2} gas at standard conditions (0^{$\circ$}C and 760 mm Hg, which is 1 atm). A cool rule in chemistry is that 1 mole of ANY ideal gas at these conditions takes up exactly 22,400 mL of space.
Moles of H_{2} = $\frac{8.40}{22400} = 0.000375$ moles.

Step 3: The Magic Ratio!
Let's compare the two: $\frac{0.000375 \text{ moles of } H_{2}}{0.000125 \text{ moles of hydrocarbon}} = 3$.

This means it took exactly 3 times as much Hydrogen to satisfy the molecule. Therefore, the molecule must have exactly 3 double bonds (3 strips of Velcro)!

The second part of the question talks about 'Ozonolysis'. Ozone (O_{3}) acts like molecular scissors that snip double bonds. When it snips the molecule into fragments, we get 3 pieces, which perfectly confirms that 3 cuts were made. But the math already gave us the exact answer effortlessly! The number of double bonds is 3.

questions.Question: Q18. The major products 'A' and 'B', respectively, are [Note: To make this a fantastic learning moment, let's assume the classic sequential reaction: Alcohol + PBr_{3} $\rightarrow$ A, followed by A + KCN $\rightarrow$ B]
questions.Hint: Reagents like PBr_{3} are designed to replace an OH group with a Halogen. After that, KCN acts as a nucleophile to swap the Halogen for a Cyanide group.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello! The original text missed printing the specific chemical diagram, so I am going to teach you the most fundamental 'A to B' reaction sequence in all of organic chemistry. Think of organic chemistry like playing with Lego pieces, where we slowly pop off one block and snap another one on.

Let's imagine we start with a simple molecule called an Alcohol (an Alkyl chain attached to an -OH block). 

Reaction 1: Making Product A
We treat the alcohol with a chemical called PBr_{3} (Phosphorus tribromide). Think of PBr_{3} as a specialized mechanic. Its only job is to unbolt the -OH 'block' from our molecule and snap a Bromine (Br) 'block' in its place. 
So, Alcohol + PBr_{3} $\rightarrow$ Alkyl Bromide. 
Product A is an Alkyl Bromide! 

Reaction 2: Making Product B
Now we take Product A (our new Alkyl Bromide) and mix it with KCN (Potassium Cyanide). Inside KCN, the Cyanide part (CN^{-}) is negatively charged and super aggressive. We call this a 'Nucleophile' (nucleus lover). The Cyanide zooms in, kicks the Bromine off the molecule, and takes its place. This 'kicking off' process is called a Substitution reaction. 
So, Alkyl Bromide + KCN $\rightarrow$ Alkyl Cyanide (also known as a Nitrile). 
Product B is a Nitrile!

Chemists love sequences like this because they allow us to build massive, complicated medicines step-by-step. First, you swap a poor connection (-OH) for a good leaving piece (-Br), and then you use that piece to attach a brand new carbon chain (-CN). It's architectural brilliance! So, A is an Alkyl Bromide, and B is a Nitrile.

questions.Question: Q19. But-2-yne is reacted separately with one mole of Hydrogen as shown below: B $\leftarrow$ Na, liq NH_{3}; CH_{3}-C$\equiv C$-CH_{3} $\rightarrow$ Pd/C $\rightarrow$ A. Identify the incorrect statements from the options given below: A. A is more soluble than B. B. The boiling point & melting point of A are higher and lower than B respectively. C. A is more polar than B because dipole moment of A is zero. D. Br_{2} adds easily to B than A.
questions.Hint: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/C) creates 'cis' alkenes (both groups on the same side, creating a polar molecule), while Na in liquid ammonia creates 'trans' alkenes (groups on opposite sides, perfectly balanced, zero polarity).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into the shape-shifting world of Alkynes! 

We start with But-2-yne. Think of this molecule as a straight, rigid stick because of its triple bond: CH_{3}-C$\equiv C$-CH_{3}. We want to turn that triple bond into a double bond by adding Hydrogen (H_{2}). But here is where chemistry gets super cool: we have two different machines (catalysts) to do this, and they build completely different shapes!

Machine 1: Pd/C (Lindlar's Catalyst). 
Imagine Lindlar's catalyst as a flat metal floor. The alkyne lands on the floor, and the catalyst slaps two Hydrogen atoms onto the molecule from the *exact same side*. The result is a 'U-shaped' molecule. We call this 'Cis'. So, Product A is Cis-but-2-ene. It looks like a little boat.

Machine 2: Sodium in liquid Ammonia (Na/NH_{3}).
This machine is chaotic. It adds one Hydrogen, forces the molecule to twist to avoid crowding, and then adds the second Hydrogen on the *completely opposite side*. The result is a 'Z-shape'. We call this 'Trans'. So, Product B is Trans-but-2-ene. It looks like a perfectly balanced seesaw.

Now, let's look at the statements to find the lie:
Product A (Cis/boat shape) is lopsided. All its heavy CH_{3} groups push their electrons in the same direction. This creates a 'polarity' (a tiny magnetic-like field). It has a net dipole moment.
Product B (Trans/seesaw shape) is perfectly balanced. The forces cancel each other out entirely! Its dipole moment is exactly ZERO.

Look at Statement C: 'A is more polar than B because dipole moment of A is zero.'
Wait a minute! That's backwards! A has a dipole moment. It is B that has a dipole moment of zero. Statement C is trying to trick us by mixing up the facts. Since it contains a completely false scientific claim, Statement C is the incorrect statement!

questions.Question: Q20. Molar mass of the hydrocarbon (X) which on ozonolysis consumes one mole of O_{3} per mole of (X) and gives one mole each of ethanol and propanone is _______ g mol^{-1} (Molar mass of C:12g mol^{-1}, H:1g mol^{-1})
questions.Hint: There's a typo in the classic question text: ozonolysis produces 'ethanal' (an aldehyde), not 'ethanol' (an alcohol). To find the original hydrocarbon, take Ethanal and Propanone, face their Oxygen atoms towards each other, erase the Oxygens, and draw a double bond between the carbons!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the ultimate molecular jigsaw puzzle! 

Ozonolysis is a reaction where Ozone (O_{3}) acts like a brutal pair of scissors. It finds a double bond in a molecule, snips it completely in half, and slaps an Oxygen atom (=O) onto the fresh cuts to cap them off.

Usually, questions ask: 'If I cut this molecule, what pieces do I get?' But this question is much cooler. It gives us the broken pieces and asks: 'What did the original molecule look like before I destroyed it?'

First, a tiny correction. The question text says 'ethanol', but ozonolysis only produces carbonyls (molecules with C=O bonds), like aldehydes and ketones. Ethanol is an alcohol. The test-makers definitely meant 'ethanal' (acetaldehyde). So, let's look at our two broken pieces:

Piece 1: Ethanal: CH_{3}-CH=O
Piece 2: Propanone (Acetone): O=C(CH_{3})_{2}

To put the molecule back together, we just reverse the scissor-cut! 
1. Point the two oxygen atoms so they look directly at each other.
CH_{3}-CH=O     +     O=C(CH_{3})_{2}

2. Erase the oxygen atoms completely!
CH_{3}-CH      and       C(CH_{3})_{2}

3. Smash the two broken carbon ends together and stitch them up with a double bond.
CH_{3}-CH=C(CH_{3})_{2}

Boom! We just reverse-engineered the mystery molecule! Its name is 2-methylbut-2-ene.

Finally, the question asks for its molar mass. Let's count the atoms. 
We have 5 Carbons in total. (C_{5})
We have 10 Hydrogens in total. (H_{10})
Formula: C_{5}H_{10}.

Mass of Carbon = 5 $\times 12 = 60$.
Mass of Hydrogen = 10 $\times 1 = 10$.
Total Molar Mass = 60 + 10 = 70 g/mol. 

You solved a complex reverse-engineering chemistry problem and didn't even break a sweat!

questions.Question: Q21. Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: [Missing text in original - Let's assume: Cyclohexanone] can be subjected to Wolff-Kishner reduction to give [Cyclohexane]. Reason R: Wolff-Kishner reduction is used to convert [carbonyl compounds into hydrocarbons].
MCQ_Options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.Hint: Wolff-Kishner reduction uses Hydrazine (NH_{2}NH_{2}) and a strong base (like KOH) to totally erase a double-bonded oxygen (=O) and replace it with two hydrogen atoms (H_{2}).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello! The original test had some blanks, but I can see exactly what they were trying to test you on. This is about a very famous chemical demolition crew known as the 'Wolff-Kishner Reduction'. 

Imagine you have a molecule called a Ketone. A ketone has a carbon atom that is double-bonded to an oxygen atom (C=O). Think of this C=O group like a tall chimney sticking out of the roof of a molecular house. 

Sometimes, chemists want to completely destroy that chimney and just make a flat roof. How do we erase that oxygen atom? We call in the Wolff-Kishner demolition crew! 

The crew consists of two chemicals: Hydrazine (NH_{2}NH_{2}) and a strong base like KOH, mixed with a lot of heat. When they attack the ketone, they completely rip the Oxygen atom off the molecule and release it. To make sure the carbon atom doesn't fall apart, they staple two Hydrogen atoms in its place. 

So, the C=O group (carbonyl) is transformed directly into a CH_{2} group (methylene). It turns a molecule with oxygen into a pure hydrocarbon!

Let's look at our Assertion (A): It claims a molecule with a ketone (like Cyclohexanone) can be subjected to Wolff-Kishner to become a pure hydrocarbon ring (Cyclohexane). This is 100% TRUE.

Let's look at the Reason (R): It claims Wolff-Kishner reduction is used to convert carbonyl compounds into hydrocarbons. This is exactly what we just learned! The reason flawlessly explains why the assertion works. Therefore, both statements are correct, and R perfectly explains A.
questions.Answer: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.Question: In the following reaction 'X' is CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₃ $\rightarrow$ X (major product)
questions.Hint: Count the carbon atoms! A 6-carbon straight chain likes to fold into a perfect hexagon and lose hydrogen when heated with special metal oxide catalysts.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's decode this chemical puzzle together. First, let's look at the molecule we are starting with: CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₃. If we count the carbon atoms, there is 1 on the left, 4 in the middle, and 1 on the right. That makes exactly 6 carbon atoms connected in a straight line. In chemistry, a 6-carbon straight-chain alkane is called 'n-hexane' (the 'n' stands for 'normal', meaning a straight line). 

Now, the text of this question is actually missing the 'reagents' (the chemicals or conditions written above the arrow), which happens sometimes in test papers! But in the context of competitive exams like JEE, when you see n-hexane undergoing a major transformation, it is almost always pointing to a famous reaction called 'Aromatization'. 

Imagine n-hexane as a lazy snake lying completely straight. If we heat it to a very high temperature (around 773 K) and use a special catalyst like Chromium oxide (Cr₂O₃) or Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) placed on top of Aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), the snake wakes up! The high heat and the catalyst act like a chemical personal trainer. First, they force the snake to bite its own tail, turning that straight 6-carbon chain into a ring called cyclohexane. But it doesn't stop there! The catalyst then forcefully strips away 6 hydrogen atoms from this ring. 

Why does it do this? Because by losing those hydrogens, the ring forms three alternating double bonds. It transforms into 'Benzene' (C₆H₆). Benzene is extremely stable due to a magical property called 'aromaticity'—which is basically a perfect ring of shared electrons. So, the straight chain folds up and locks itself into the most stable shape possible. Therefore, the major product 'X' is Benzene!

questions.Question: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The presence of weaker $\pi$-bonds make alkenes less stable than alkanes. Statement II: The strength of the double bond is greater than that of carbon-carbon single bond.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.Hint: Think of a single bond as a solid stone bridge, and a double bond as that same stone bridge PLUS a wooden rope bridge above it. Does the wooden bridge make the whole crossing stronger? Yes! Does it also give invaders an easy target to attack? Also yes!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic question because it tests whether you know the difference between 'physical strength' and 'chemical stability'. Let's break it down using a cool analogy. 

Imagine two carbon atoms are holding hands. In an alkane, they share one pair of electrons. This is a single 'sigma' ($\sigma)$ bond. It's like a direct, incredibly strong handshake. In an alkene, the carbons have a double bond. They still have that strong sigma handshake, but they also share a 'pi' ($\pi)$ bond. A pi bond is formed by electron clouds overlapping above and below the handshake. It's like they are high-fiving while shaking hands! 

Let's look at Statement II first. Is a double bond (handshake + high-five) stronger than just a single bond (handshake)? Yes, absolutely! It takes more energy to break a double bond completely apart than to break a single bond. So, Statement II is physically true. The total bond dissociation energy of C=C is greater than C-C.

Now, let's look at Statement I. It says alkenes are 'less stable' because of the weaker pi-bond. Here, 'stable' means 'chemically lazy' or unreactive. Remember that pi-bond 'high-five' floating above and below the atoms? It's heavily exposed! If an energetic chemical (a reactant) floats by, it can easily see and grab those exposed pi-electrons. It takes much less energy to break *just* the pi-bond than to break a sigma bond. Because that pi-bond is so easy to attack and break open to form new connections, alkenes are highly reactive. In chemistry, being highly reactive means you are chemically 'less stable'. Alkanes, which only have the tough, protected sigma bonds, are very unreactive (stable). Therefore, Statement I is also completely correct! Both statements are true and beautifully highlight the difference between total physical bond strength and chemical reactivity.
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.Question: Halogenation of which one of the following will yield m-substituted product with respect to methyl group as a major product?
questions.Hint: Look for a molecule where a very strong 'bossy' group (like an -OH) forces the incoming halogen to a spot right next to it, which coincidentally happens to be exactly 3 steps away (meta) from the methyl group!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the world of Benzene seating arrangements! Imagine a benzene ring is a circular VIP table with 6 seats (numbered 1 to 6). When a new guest (a halogen atom) wants to sit down, the people already sitting at the table get to tell the guest where to sit. These people are called 'directing groups'. 

There are two main types of bosses: 'ortho/para' directors (who send guests to seats right next to them, or directly across the table) and 'meta' directors (who send guests to the seats in between). A methyl group (-CH₃) is a mild ortho/para director. It gently tells incoming halogens to go to the ortho (position 2 or 6) or para (position 4) spots. 

The question asks: in which molecule will the halogen end up sitting 'meta' (at a 1,3-relationship) to the methyl group? If methyl is an ortho/para director, it would never naturally send a halogen to its own meta position! This means there MUST be another group at the table, a 'super boss', who completely overrules the methyl group and forces the halogen into a seat that just happens to be meta to the methyl. 

Let's look at our winning option: p-Cresol (also known as 4-methylphenol). In this molecule, an -OH (hydroxyl) group sits at seat 1, and the methyl group sits straight across at seat 4. The -OH group is a SUPER ortho/para director. It is much, much stronger than the methyl group because it pushes its own lone pair of electrons straight into the ring! 

The -OH group takes command. It tells the incoming halogen, 'You must sit ortho to ME!' The ortho seats to the -OH group are seats 2 and 6. So, the halogen sits at position 2 or 6. 

Now, let's check the distance between the new halogen (at seat 2) and the methyl group (at seat 4). From 2 to 4 is exactly a 1,3 relationship! In chemistry, a 1,3 relationship is called 'meta'. So, because the super-bossy -OH group forced the halogen to sit next to itself, the halogen ended up perfectly meta to the methyl group! This is a brilliant chemical trick.

questions.Question: What will be the major product of following sequence of reactions? n-Bu$\equiv \rightarrow$ (i) n-BuLi, n-C_5H_{11}Cl (ii) Lindlar cat, H_2
questions.Hint: First, the two carbon chains snap together like Lego bricks to make an 11-carbon internal alkyne. Then, Lindlar's catalyst acts like two gentle hands that attach hydrogen atoms from the exact same side, creating a 'cis' bend in the chain!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a wonderful two-step chemical construction project! Let's build our molecule step-by-step just like putting together Lego blocks.

**Step 1: Building a bigger carbon chain.**
We start with 'n-Bu$\equiv$', which represents a terminal alkyne called 1-hexyne. It has a 4-carbon chain (n-Butyl) attached to a carbon-carbon triple bond ending in a hydrogen: (n-Bu-C$\equivC$-H). That hydrogen at the end of the triple bond is quite special—it's slightly acidic! 
When we add 'n-BuLi' (n-Butyllithium), we are adding a very strong base. The base steals that acidic hydrogen away, leaving behind a negatively charged alkyne (an acetylide ion). Now, our alkyne is a super-charged nucleophile looking to attack something. We then feed it 'n-C₅H₁₁Cl' (1-chloropentane, a 5-carbon chain with a chlorine attached). Our negatively charged alkyne attacks the carbon holding the chlorine, and kicks the chlorine out! Snap! We just joined a 6-carbon piece (including the triple bond) to a 5-carbon piece. 6 + 5 = 11 carbons. We now have a long chain with a triple bond buried inside it: an internal alkyne called undec-5-yne.

**Step 2: The magical Lindlar's Catalyst.**
Now we have our big triple bond, and we want to add Hydrogen (H₂) to it. Usually, adding hydrogen to a triple bond will break it all the way down to a single bond (an alkane). But we are using 'Lindlar's catalyst'. This is a special, 'poisoned' catalyst. Imagine a racecar driver who drank a bit too much sleepy tea. The catalyst is slow and stops working halfway through! It only allows one molecule of H₂ to add, turning the triple bond into a double bond (an alkene). 
But here is the coolest part: because of the flat, solid surface of the Lindlar catalyst metal, both hydrogen atoms must attach to the carbon chain from the exact same side! In chemistry, when two groups attach to the same side of a double bond, it creates a 'cis' geometry. The chain bends beautifully into a U-shape. 
Therefore, our 11-carbon triple bond (undec-5-yne) gets gently reduced to a double bond with a 'cis' shape, resulting in 'cis-undec-5-ene'.

questions.Question: In Friedel-Crafts alkylation of aniline, one gets
MCQ_Options: No Friedel-Crafts product (forms a Lewis acid-base complex instead)
questions.Hint: Friedel-Crafts reactions require a catalyst like AlCl₃, which is desperately hungry for electrons. Aniline has a nitrogen atom holding a juicy, exposed pair of electrons. What do you think the hungry catalyst will attack first?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a classic trap question in organic chemistry, and it's super interesting because it shows us what happens when a chemical reaction gets 'distracted'! 

To understand this, we need to know the players in a Friedel-Crafts alkylation. Normally, you have a benzene ring, an alkyl halide (like CH₃Cl), and a catalyst like Aluminum Chloride (AlCl₃). AlCl₃ is what we call a 'Lewis Acid'. It has an empty orbital and is desperately hungry for electrons. Its job is to pull the chlorine off the CH₃Cl, creating a positively charged CH₃⁺ ion that can then attack the benzene ring. 

But here, our benzene ring is 'Aniline'. Aniline is a benzene ring attached to an -NH₂ (amino) group. The nitrogen atom in that -NH₂ group has a 'lone pair' of electrons just sitting there, exposed and highly concentrated. Aniline is technically a 'Lewis Base'. 

So, what happens when we mix our hungry Lewis Acid (AlCl₃) with our Lewis Base (Aniline)? Before the AlCl₃ even gets a chance to look at the alkyl halide and start the intended reaction, it sees that juicy lone pair of electrons on Aniline's nitrogen and attacks it immediately! 

They lock together, forming a strong complex (an acid-base salt). Because the nitrogen just had its electrons stolen by the aluminum, the nitrogen atom gets a strong positive charge. 

Here is the fatal blow: a positive charge right next to a benzene ring acts like an incredibly powerful vacuum cleaner. It violently sucks electron density out of the benzene ring. For a benzene ring to undergo alkylation, it needs to be rich in electrons. Because the nitrogen vacuum cleaner has sucked the ring dry of electrons (we call this being 'strongly deactivated'), the ring completely shuts down. The intended Friedel-Crafts reaction fails entirely, and you get no Friedel-Crafts product! Instead, you are just left with that stuck acid-base complex.
questions.Answer: No Friedel-Crafts product (forms a Lewis acid-base complex instead)

questions.Question: In the presence of sunlight, benzene reacts with Cl_2 to give product, X. The number of hydrogens in X is _________.
questions.Hint: Normal reactions with benzene 'substitute' one hydrogen for a halogen. But sunlight creates crazy 'free radicals' that don't follow the rules! They forcefully break all the double bonds and 'add' to the ring without kicking anyone out.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's talk about how sunlight can make chemicals go completely wild. 

Normally, Benzene (C₆H₆) acts like a very proud, aristocratic molecule. It loves its stable ring of alternating double bonds (its aromaticity). If you try to react it with Chlorine (Cl₂) in the dark with a catalyst, benzene behaves politely. It undergoes 'substitution': it politely asks one of its 6 hydrogen atoms to leave, and a chlorine atom takes its seat. The formula would just be C₆H₅Cl, and the ring stays intact. 

But the problem says 'in the presence of sunlight'. Sunlight contains ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which carries a lot of energy! When UV light hits a Cl₂ molecule, it acts like a tiny karate chop, splitting the molecule right down the middle into two Chlorine 'free radicals'. Free radicals are highly energetic, super aggressive atoms with unpaired electrons. 

These aggressive chlorine radicals don't care about benzene's polite rules. They swarm the benzene ring and forcefully attack all three of the double bonds! When you break a double bond, two new attachment spots open up. Since benzene has three double bonds, breaking them all opens up 6 new attachment spots. 

So, 6 chlorine atoms attach themselves all the way around the ring. This is an 'addition' reaction, not a substitution. Because the chlorines just added themselves to the newly opened spots, absolutely none of the original 6 hydrogen atoms were kicked out! 

They are still right there, attached to their carbon atoms. The new molecule has 6 carbons, 6 hydrogens, and 6 chlorines. Its formula is C₆H₆Cl₆ (commonly known as Benzene Hexachloride, BHC, or Gammexane). 

The question simply asks: what is the number of hydrogens in this new product X? Because we merely added atoms and didn't substitute any, the answer remains exactly 6!

questions.Question: In the following reaction The \% yield for reaction I is 60\% and that of reaction II is 50\%. The overall yield of the complete reaction is _______\%. [nearest integer]
questions.Hint: If you bake 100 cookies, but only 60% survive without burning in the oven, and then you try to frost them but mess up 50% of the frosting, what percentage of your original 100 cookies are perfectly baked AND frosted?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's talk about the math of chemistry, specifically 'percentage yield'. 

Imagine you are making a super cool, custom-built skateboard. The process has two steps. Step one is cutting the wooden board. Step two is painting it perfectly. 

Now, let's say in step one, you try to cut 100 boards, but the saw is a bit tricky, and you only successfully cut 60 perfect boards. Your 'yield' for step one is 60%. 

Now you move to step two with those 60 boards. Step two is painting, but the spray paint nozzle keeps jamming, and you only manage to perfectly paint 50% of the boards you started step two with. You don't get 50% of the original 100 boards; you only get 50% of the 60 boards you managed to cut! 

What is half (50%) of 60? It is 30. So, out of the 100 boards you originally planned to make, you only end up with 30 perfectly cut and painted skateboards. Your overall yield is 30%! 

This is exactly how chemical reactions work when they happen in a sequence. We call these 'sequential reactions'. The product of Reaction I becomes the starting material (reactant) for Reaction II. 

The problem states Reaction I has a 60% yield. This means if we expected 100 molecules, we only got 60 (or as a fraction, 0.60). Reaction II has a 50% yield. This means it only successfully converts 50% (or 0.50) of those remaining molecules into the final product. 

Mathematically, to find the total success rate, we just multiply the fractions or decimals together. 

Overall Yield = (Yield of Step 1) $\times$ (Yield of Step 2)
Overall Yield = 0.60 $\times 0.50$ 

What is 0.60 times 0.50? It is 0.30! To convert this decimal back into a percentage, we simply multiply by 100, which gives us exactly 30%. It's a simple multiplication trick, but remembering that you take a 'percentage of a percentage' is the ultimate key to solving these real-world chemistry math problems!

questions.Question: Q30. In bromination of Propyne, with Bromine, 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane is obtained in 27% yield. The amount of 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane obtained from 1g of Bromine in this reaction is _______ x10⁻¹g. (Nearest integer) (Molar Mass: Bromine = 80g/mol)
questions.Hint: First, write the balanced equation to see how many moles of Bromine gas (Br₂) react with one mole of propyne. Then calculate the theoretical product mass from 1g of Br₂, and don't forget to multiply by the 27% yield! Also, remember Bromine gas is Br₂, so its molecular mass is 160 g/mol.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's break down this awesome chemistry puzzle together. 

Imagine you are building a chemical Lego set. Our starting piece is **Propyne**. Propyne is an alkyne, meaning it has a carbon-carbon *triple bond*. Think of a triple bond as a strong connection holding two extra 'parking spaces' (we call them pi bonds) that can be opened up for new atoms to attach.

Now, we are adding **Bromine**. In nature, Bromine atoms hate being alone, so they pair up to form bromine gas, $Br_2$. Since the problem tells us the atomic mass of a single Bromine atom is $80\text{ g/mol}$, the molecular mass of a $Br_2$ molecule is $80 + 80 = 160\text{ g/mol}$.

When Propyne ($CH_3-C\equiv CH$) meets Bromine ($Br_2$), the triple bond opens its parking spaces. Since it's a triple bond, it actually has *two* pi bonds to open up! Therefore, one molecule of propyne can comfortably park *two* molecules of $Br_2$. 

The balanced chemical equation is:
$C_3H_4 + 2Br_2 \rightarrow C_3H_4Br_4$ (which is 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane).

Let's do some quick math on the weights. 
We need 2 moles of $Br_2$, which weighs $2 \times 160\text{ g} = 320\text{ g}$.
The product, $C_3H_4Br_4$, has a molar mass of: 
(3 Carbons $\times 12$) + (4 Hydrogens $\times 1$) + (4 Bromines $\times 80$) = $36 + 4 + 320 = 360\text{ g/mol}$.

This tells us the perfect 'recipe': **320 grams of Bromine will perfectly create 360 grams of our product.**

But wait, the problem says we only started with **1 gram** of Bromine! 
If 320g of Bromine makes 360g of product, then 1g of Bromine should make: 
$\frac{360}{320} \times 1\text{ g} = 1.125\text{ g}$ of product. 
This $1.125\text{ g}$ is our 'Theoretical Yield'—the amount we would get if the universe were absolutely perfect.

However, in real chemistry, things are messy. Some chemicals spill, some evaporate, or they just get lazy. This reaction only has a **27% yield**. It's like baking a batch of 10 cookies, but you drop a few on the floor and only get to eat 2.7 of them!

So, we take our perfect yield and multiply it by $27\%$ ($0.27$):
$1.125\text{ g} \times 0.27 = 0.30375\text{ g}$.

Finally, the question asks us to format our answer as `_______ $\times 10^{-1}\text{ g}$`.
Let's slide that decimal point over by one spot to the right to see it clearly:
$0.30375\text{ g} = 3.0375 \times 10^{-1}\text{ g}$.

The question asks for the 'nearest integer' (the closest whole number). The closest whole number to $3.0375$ is **3**! 

You did it! You successfully navigated stoichiometry, limiting reactants, and percentage yield!

questions.Concept: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) and Directing Effects
questions.Question: Q31. The correct sequence of reagents used in the preparation of 4-bromo-2-nitroethyl benzene from benzene is
MCQ_Options: (i) CH₃CH₂Cl, anhyd. AlCl₃ (ii) Br₂, FeBr₃ (iii) Conc. HNO₃, Conc. H₂SO₄
(i) Br₂, FeBr₃ (ii) Conc. HNO₃, Conc. H₂SO₄ (iii) CH₃CH₂Cl, anhyd. AlCl₃
(i) Conc. HNO₃, Conc. H₂SO₄ (ii) Br₂, FeBr₃ (iii) CH₃CH₂Cl, anhyd. AlCl₃
(i) CH₃CH₂Cl, anhyd. AlCl₃ (ii) Conc. HNO₃, Conc. H₂SO₄ (iii) Br₂, FeBr₃
questions.Hint: Think of the benzene ring as a dinner table! The first guest who sits down decides where the next guests sit. Alkyl groups (like ethyl) are friendly and direct new guests to Ortho/Para seats. Nitro groups are grumpy and direct to Meta. Also, Friedel-Crafts alkylation refuses to work if the ring has a grumpy, deactivating Nitro group on it!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the strategic game of Chemistry Chess! 

We are starting with a plain **Benzene** ring—a beautiful, perfectly symmetric hexagon of six carbon atoms. Our goal is to attach three specific 'guests' to this table:
1. An Ethyl group ($CH_3CH_2-$)
2. A Bromo group ($-Br$) at position 4 (Para to Ethyl)
3. A Nitro group ($-NO_2$) at position 2 (Ortho to Ethyl)

In Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS), the order in which we add groups is *everything*, because the first group attached becomes the 'host' and dictates where all future guests are allowed to sit. 

Let's look at the personalities of our potential guests:
- **Ethyl group**: A friendly, 'Activating' group. It invites new guests to sit right next to it (**Ortho**, position 2) or directly across the table (**Para**, position 4).
- **Bromo group**: A slightly grumpy but rule-following 'Deactivating' group. Despite being a bit negative, it still invites guests to **Ortho** and **Para** seats.
- **Nitro group**: A very grumpy, highly 'Deactivating' group. It hates crowds and forces new guests to sit one seat away from the Ortho position (**Meta**, position 3).

If we put the **Nitro group** on first (using $HNO_3/H_2SO_4$), the ring becomes so miserable and deactivated that our next reaction, Friedel-Crafts Alkylation (adding the Ethyl group), will flat-out refuse to work! So, Nitro *cannot* be first.

Let's try putting the **Ethyl group** on first! We do this using **$CH_3CH_2Cl$ and anhydrous $AlCl_3$**. 
Great! Now we have Ethylbenzene. The friendly Ethyl group is hosting the party, and it will direct the next guest to Ortho (2) or Para (4).

Next, we need to decide: do we add Bromine or Nitro second?
If we add Nitro second, it will go to Ortho and Para positions, creating a messy mix. Then adding Bromine would be a nightmare because both groups will fight over where Bromine should sit.

Let's add **Bromine** second (using **$Br_2, FeBr_3$**). Because the Ethyl group is a bit bulky, it prefers the new Bromine guest to sit far away, directly across the table at the **Para** position (position 4). Perfect! Now we have **p-bromoethylbenzene**.

Finally, we add the **Nitro group** (using **Conc. $HNO_3$, Conc. $H_2SO_4$**). Now we have a battle of the hosts! 
- The Ethyl group wants Nitro to go Ortho to it (position 2 or 6).
- The Bromo group wants Nitro to go Ortho to *it* (position 3 or 5).
Who wins? The Ethyl group is an 'Activating' group (it pumps electron wealth into the ring), while Bromo is 'Deactivating' (it pulls wealth away). In chemistry, the wealthier, activating group *always* wins the directing battle! 

Therefore, the Ethyl group takes charge and places the Nitro group at position 2 (Ortho to Ethyl). 

Boom! We have exactly what we wanted: **4-bromo-2-nitroethylbenzene**. 

The winning sequence is:
(i) $CH_3CH_2Cl$, anhyd. $AlCl_3$ 
(ii) $Br_2, FeBr_3$ 
(iii) Conc. $HNO_3$, Conc. $H_2SO_4$
questions.Answer: (i) CH₃CH₂Cl, anhyd. AlCl₃ (ii) Br₂, FeBr₃ (iii) Conc. HNO₃, Conc. H₂SO₄

questions.Question: Q33. Given below are two statements. Statement-I: 2-methylbutane on oxidation with KMnO₄ gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol. Statement-II: n-alkanes can be easily oxidised to corresponding alcohols with KMnO₄.
MCQ_Options: Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are true.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are false.
Statement-I is false but Statement-II is true.
questions.Hint: Alkanes are known as 'paraffins', which means they have very little affinity or reactivity. They act like heavily armored knights! However, a carbon attached to three other carbons (a tertiary carbon) is a weak spot in the armor that strong oxidizers like KMnO₄ absolutely love to attack.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into the fascinating world of Alkanes and their resistance to change! 

In chemistry, Alkanes (chains of carbons with only single bonds, surrounded by hydrogens) are historically called **'paraffins'**. The word comes from Latin: *parum* meaning 'little' and *affinis* meaning 'affinity'. They are the introverts of the chemical world—they really don't like reacting with anyone! You can pour powerful acids, bases, or strong oxidizing agents like Potassium Permanganate ($KMnO_4$) on regular straight-chain alkanes (n-alkanes), and they will just shrug it off like heavy armor deflecting a wooden sword. 

Because of this heavy armor, **Statement-II is absolutely False.** Normal straight-chain alkanes (n-alkanes) CANNOT be easily oxidized to alcohols with $KMnO_4$. 

But wait... what about Statement-I? Let's look at **2-methylbutane**. 
If you draw 2-methylbutane, you'll see a four-carbon chain, with a single methyl ($CH_3$) group branching off the second carbon. 
Let's zoom in on that second carbon atom. It is holding hands with **three** other carbon atoms! In chemistry, we call a carbon that is attached to three other carbons a **Tertiary (3°) Carbon**. 

Because this Tertiary carbon is so busy holding onto three other big carbon groups, the single Hydrogen atom attached to it is held rather loosely. This Tertiary Carbon-Hydrogen bond is the ultimate 'Achilles' Heel' of the alkane molecule! 

While $KMnO_4$ bounces harmlessly off primary and secondary carbons, the moment it spots that weak Tertiary C-H bond, it strikes! $KMnO_4$ smoothly inserts an Oxygen atom right between the Carbon and Hydrogen, converting the $C-H$ bond into a $C-OH$ (alcohol) group.

So, 2-methylbutane reacts with $KMnO_4$ to become **2-methylbutan-2-ol** (where the $OH$ is on the 2nd carbon). 

Because this chemical trick works perfectly, **Statement-I is True!**

To summarize: Straight-chain alkanes are tough as nails and ignore oxidizers. Branched alkanes with a Tertiary hydrogen have a weak spot and turn into alcohols!

Therefore, the correct answer is: Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false.
questions.Answer: Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false.

questions.Question: Q36. Which one of the following compounds is not aromatic?
questions.Hint: To be aromatic, a molecule needs a 'magic number' of pi-electrons (2, 6, 10, 14...). This is called Hückel's Rule ($4n+2$). Count the dancing electrons!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! To tackle this, let's talk about a super exclusive VIP club in chemistry called the 'Aromatic Club.' Molecules in this club are incredibly stable and relaxed. But to get in, a molecule must follow three strict rules set by a chemist named Erich Hückel.

Rule 1: The molecule must be cyclic (a continuous ring, like a necklace).
Rule 2: It must be totally flat (planar), and every atom in the ring must have a 'p-orbital' (an empty or occupied parking space for electrons) so the electrons can run laps around the whole ring without stopping.
Rule 3: It must have a 'magic number' of running electrons (called pi-electrons). The formula is $4n+2$, where $n$ is any whole number (0, 1, 2...). If we plug in numbers, the magic numbers are 2, 6, 10, 14, and so on.

Now, let's look at our suspects!
Benzene has 6 pi-electrons (3 double bonds $\times$ 2 electrons). 6 is a magic number! It's in the club.
Pyrrole has 4 electrons from double bonds, plus a lone pair (2 electrons) on the Nitrogen that jumps in to help. Total = 6. Welcome to the club!
Cyclopentadienyl anion has 4 electrons from double bonds and 2 from the negative charge. Total = 6. It's in!
But what about Cyclooctatetraene? It has 4 alternating double bonds. 4 $\times$ 2 = 8 pi-electrons. Uh oh! 8 is NOT a magic number (it fits the anti-aromatic formula $4n$). Because having 8 electrons actually makes it super unstable and 'frustrated,' the molecule decides to bend itself out of shape into a tub (like a boat) just so it breaks Rule 2 and avoids being anti-aromatic. Therefore, it is definitely NOT aromatic!

questions.Question: Q37. Which one of the following compounds is aromatic in nature?
questions.Hint: Look for a molecule where either a negative charge (lone pair) or a positive charge (empty parking space) perfectly completes the ring and creates a magic number of electrons (2, 6, 10...).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome back to the Aromatic VIP club! Let's use the exact same rules we just learned: 1. Cyclic, 2. Flat with a continuous path, 3. Magic number of electrons ($4n+2$, meaning 2, 6, 10...). 

Let's test the options:
1. Cyclopentadiene: This molecule has a ring of 5 carbons. Two double bonds give it 4 pi-electrons. But there is a huge roadblock! One of the carbons has no double bond and is completely saturated ($sp^3$ hybridized). Think of it like a broken bridge. The electrons can't do full laps. Not aromatic.

2. Cycloheptatriene: Ring of 7 carbons, 3 double bonds (6 electrons). It has the magic number! But wait! Just like the first one, it has one $sp^3$ carbon acting like a wall. The electrons can't go all the way around. Not aromatic.

3. Cyclopropenyl cation: A 3-carbon ring with one double bond (2 electrons). 2 IS a magic number ($4(0)+2=2$). The positive charge means there's an empty p-orbital, acting as a bridge so electrons can do full laps. This IS actually aromatic! Wait, let me check the other option.

4. Cyclopentadienyl anion: We start with Cyclopentadiene (the one with the broken bridge). If we remove an $H^+$ from that roadblock carbon, it leaves its 2 electrons behind, creating a negative charge! Now that carbon has a p-orbital with 2 electrons. The bridge is fixed! Plus, 4 electrons (from the double bonds) + 2 electrons (from the negative charge) = 6 electrons! Magic number! It perfectly satisfies all conditions.

Both Cyclopropenyl cation and Cyclopentadienyl anion are classic examples of aromatic ions! Usually, in JEE, Cyclopentadienyl anion is the absolute favorite answer for this specific question because of how dramatically it gains stability by losing a proton. Let's select it as our star answer!

questions.Concept: Stability of Dienes and Heat of Combustion
questions.Question: Q38. The correct order of heat of combustion for following alkadienes is:
questions.Hint: Heat of combustion is like a 'frustration meter.' The more unstable and cramped a molecule is, the more energy it furiously releases when you burn it! Highly stable molecules release the least heat.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have three different springs. One is coiled incredibly tight and is shaking (unstable), one is just somewhat tight, and the last one is completely relaxed. If you let them go, which one releases the most explosive energy? The tightest one, right? 

In chemistry, 'Heat of Combustion' measures exactly this! When we burn a molecule, it releases energy. If the molecule was already super unstable (high energy), it will release a LOT of heat. If it was stable and relaxed (low energy), it releases less heat. So, Heat of Combustion is INVERSELY proportional to stability.

Let's look at our three isomers of pentadiene ($C_5H_8$):
1. 1,3-pentadiene (Conjugated Diene): The double bonds are separated by exactly one single bond (double-single-double). This allows the electrons to spread out over the whole system (delocalization). Spreading out electrons makes the molecule super relaxed and highly stable. Since it's the most stable, it releases the LEAST heat.

2. 1,4-pentadiene (Isolated Diene): The double bonds are separated by multiple single bonds. The electrons can't communicate with each other. It's just 'okay' in terms of stability. It will release a medium amount of heat.

3. 1,2-pentadiene (Cumulated Diene): The double bonds are directly attached to the SAME carbon atom (double-double). The electron clouds violently repel each other because they are crammed into the same space. This molecule is furious and highly unstable! Therefore, it releases the MOST heat when burned.

So, the order of heat released from greatest to least is: Cumulated (1,2-pentadiene) > Isolated (1,4-pentadiene) > Conjugated (1,3-pentadiene).

questions.Concept: Stereochemistry and Reaction Mechanisms (SN2 vs SN1)
questions.Question: Q39. Which of the following reactions will not produce a racemic product?
MCQ_Options: Free radical chlorination of butane at C-2
questions.Hint: A 'racemic' product means you get a 50/50 mix of left-handed and right-handed molecules. Look for a reaction mechanism that attacks strictly from ONE side, preventing a mixture!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's unravel this stereochemistry puzzle! First, what is a 'racemic' product? 
Imagine you are putting on gloves blindly, and you end up with exactly 50 left-handed gloves and 50 right-handed gloves. In chemistry, some molecules have 'handedness' (chirality). A racemic mixture is a perfect 50/50 mix of left-handed and right-handed versions of a molecule.

How do we get a 50/50 mix? Usually, it happens when the reaction goes through a 'flat' intermediate. Imagine a completely flat piece of paper on a desk. If a tennis ball (another chemical) falls onto it, it has an equal 50% chance of hitting the top side, and a 50% chance of hitting the bottom side. 
- When we add HCN to 2-butanone, the 2-butanone is flat. 50/50 mix! (Racemic)
- SN1 reactions form a carbocation, which is totally flat. 50/50 mix! (Racemic)
- Free radical reactions form a flat radical intermediate. 50/50 mix! (Racemic)

But what about the SN2 reaction? 'SN2' stands for Substitution Nucleophilic Bimolecular. I like to call it the 'Sneak Attack' or the 'Umbrella Flip'. In SN2, there is no flat intermediate. Instead, the incoming molecule (like $OH^-$) sneaks up directly from the BACK of the molecule to push the old piece (like $Br^-$) out the front. 
Because the $OH^-$ HAS to attack from the back, the molecule pops inside out like an umbrella in a windstorm! This means if you start with a 100% left-handed molecule, the SN2 sneak attack forces it to become a 100% right-handed molecule. You get ONE specific product, not a 50/50 mix. Therefore, the SN2 reaction will NOT produce a racemic product!

questions.Concept: Sequential Reactions: Hydration of Alkynes, Grignard Addition, Dehydration
questions.Question: Q40. The major product (Y) in the following reactions is: CH₃-CH(CH₃)-C≡CH $\rightarrow$ [H₂O, HgSO₄, H₂SO₄] $\rightarrow$ X $\rightarrow$ [(i)C₂H₅MgBr, H₂O (ii)Conc. H₂SO₄/∆] $\rightarrow$ Y
questions.Hint: Take it step-by-step! Step 1 turns the triple bond into a ketone. Step 2 uses Grignard to turn the ketone into an alcohol. Step 3 removes water to create a double bond. Remember Zaitsev's rule: the most highly substituted double bond wins!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a classic 3-step organic chemistry jigsaw puzzle! Don't let the long string of letters intimidate you; we will solve it one step at a time.

**Step 1: The Kucherov Reaction ($H_2O, HgSO_4, H_2SO_4$)**
We start with 3-methyl-1-butyne: $CH_3-CH(CH_3)-C \equiv CH$. The reagents basically force WATER ($H-OH$) to add across the triple bond. Following Markovnikov's Rule ('the rich get richer'), the hydrogen goes to the carbon on the end (which already has a hydrogen), and the OH goes to the inner carbon. This forms an enol, which instantly magically transforms (tautomerizes) into a ketone! 
So, intermediate X is: $CH_3-CH(CH_3)-C(=O)-CH_3$ (which is 3-methyl-2-butanone).

**Step 2: Grignard Magic ($C_2H_5MgBr, H_2O$)**
Grignard reagents are amazing carbon-chain builders. $C_2H_5MgBr$ acts like a negatively charged ethyl group ($CH_3CH_2^-$) looking for a positive target. It attacks the partially positive carbon of the ketone we just made! After we add water to finish the step, the ketone's '=O' becomes an '-OH' alcohol.
Now we have: $CH_3-CH(CH_3)-C(OH)(CH_2CH_3)-CH_3$. We just built a tertiary alcohol!

**Step 3: Dehydration (Conc. $H_2SO_4 / \Delta$)**
Concentrated sulfuric acid and heat (the $\Delta$ symbol means heat) act as a sponge. They brutally rip water ($H_2O$) out of the molecule. We remove the -OH from the center carbon, and we must steal a Hydrogen from one of the neighboring carbons to form a new double bond. 
But which neighbor do we steal the hydrogen from? 
According to Zaitsev's Rule, molecules want to be as stable as possible. A double bond is most stable when it is hugged by as many carbon groups as possible. 
If we take H from the left (the $CH$ group), the double bond is surrounded by 4 carbon groups (tetrasubstituted).
If we take H from the bottom (the $CH_2$ group), it's only surrounded by 3 groups.
If we take H from the right (the $CH_3$ group), it's only surrounded by 2 groups.
Nature chooses the most stable path! So, we remove the H from the left $CH$ group. 
The final molecule Y is $CH_3-C(CH_3)=C(CH_2CH_3)(CH_3)$, which we name 2,3-dimethyl-2-pentene!

questions.Question: Q41. Consider the following reactions: I. Friedel-Crafts alkylation of nitrobenzene. II. Nitration of benzene. III. Friedel-Crafts alkylation of toluene. Which of these reactions is NOT possible?
questions.Hint: Friedel-Crafts reactions require a super 'electron-rich' benzene ring to work. If the ring has a group that strongly sucks electrons away (deactivating group), the reaction is totally dead!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, let's picture the Benzene ring as a massive, glowing dance floor of electrons. For an Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) reaction to happen, an electrophile (a positively charged molecule that LOVES electrons) jumps onto the dance floor.

Now, different chemical groups attached to the benzene ring can either be 'VIP Promoters' or 'Strict Bouncers'.
- VIP Promoters (like Methyl, $-CH_3$) pump MORE electrons onto the dance floor. They make the ring super attractive. We call them 'Activating Groups.'
- Strict Bouncers (like Nitro, $-NO_2$) ruthlessly suck electrons AWAY from the dance floor. They leave the ring totally empty and dark. We call them 'Strongly Deactivating Groups.'

Let's evaluate the reactions:
Reaction II (Nitration of benzene): Normal benzene has a decent dance floor. Nitration works perfectly fine.
Reaction III (Friedel-Crafts of toluene): Toluene is benzene with a methyl group. The methyl group pumps electrons! The Friedel-Crafts electrophile sees this amazing dance floor and jumps right in. This reaction works great!
Reaction I (Friedel-Crafts of nitrobenzene): Uh oh. Nitrobenzene has the massive $-NO_2$ bouncer group. It drains all the electrons. Furthermore, the Friedel-Crafts electrophile (like an alkyl cation) is super sluggish and lazy. When it sees an empty, dark, deactivated benzene ring, it just refuses to react. 

Because the Nitro group is strongly deactivating, Friedel-Crafts reactions NEVER happen on nitrobenzene! Therefore, Reaction I is the only one that is impossible.

questions.Question: Q42. The increasing order of the boiling point of the major products A, B and C of the following reactions will be: (Let A = Butane, B = 2-Bromobutane, C = 2-Butanol)
questions.Hint: Boiling means pulling molecules apart from each other. Think about what forces hold molecules together. Hydrogen bonding is like super-strong Velcro, while Van der Waals forces are like weak static cling!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into the fascinating world of boiling points! What does it actually mean to 'boil' a liquid? It means you heat it up so much that the molecules violently vibrate and tear away from their friends to float into the air as a gas. 
So, the stronger the molecules hold onto each other (Intermolecular Forces), the more heat (temperature) you need to rip them apart!

Let's analyze our three molecules to see how sticky they are to each other:
1. Product A (Butane): This is just carbon and hydrogen. They share electrons incredibly equally, meaning the molecule has no poles (non-polar). The only thing holding butane molecules together is a super weak, temporary force called 'Van der Waals forces.' It's basically weak static cling. It takes very little heat to pull them apart, so it has a VERY LOW boiling point.

2. Product B (2-Bromobutane): Bromine is greedy for electrons (electronegative). It pulls the electrons toward itself, creating a permanent negative pole, leaving the carbon slightly positive. This makes the molecule a 'dipole'. Dipoles act like little magnets, where the positive end of one sticks to the negative end of another. Magnets are stronger than static cling! So it has a MEDIUM boiling point.

3. Product C (2-Butanol): This molecule has an '-OH' group. When Hydrogen is directly attached to Oxygen, Nitrogen, or Fluorine, it creates an extreme dipole called 'Hydrogen Bonding'. Hydrogen bonding isn't just a magnet; it's like chemical super-Velcro! It takes a massive amount of energy (heat) to pull Hydrogen-bonded molecules apart. So, it has the HIGHEST boiling point.

Therefore, the order of boiling point from lowest to highest is: Butane (A) < 2-Bromobutane (B) < 2-Butanol (C).

questions.Chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.Question: Q43. Among the following compounds, geometrical isomerism is exhibited by: [Note: Options were added based on standard JEE formats] A) 1-Butene, B) 2-Butene, C) 2-Methylpropene, D) Propene.
questions.Hint: Look for a carbon-carbon double bond where EACH of the two carbon atoms is attached to two completely DIFFERENT atoms or groups.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's talk about 'Geometrical Isomerism.' Imagine you and a friend are standing face-to-face, holding both of each other's hands tightly. Because you are holding both hands (this is like a chemical 'double bond'), neither of you can twist your body around without letting go. You are locked in place! In chemistry, carbon atoms double-bonded to each other are similarly locked; they cannot rotate. 

Now, imagine you are holding a red apple in your left hand and a green apple in your right hand. Your friend is doing the same. Because you can't twist, there are two permanent ways you could be standing: either your red apples are on the SAME side (Cis), or they are on OPPOSITE sides (Trans). This is Geometrical Isomerism! 

But what if you were holding a red apple in BOTH hands? Then, even if your friend flipped their apples, the overall picture looks exactly the same, because your side is perfectly symmetrical. 

This gives us our golden rule: For a molecule to show geometrical isomerism, it must have a double bond, AND both carbon atoms in that double bond must be holding two DIFFERENT things.

Let's test our options:
1) Propene (CH\_3-CH=CH\_2): The carbon on the far right is holding two identical Hydrogen atoms. No geometrical isomerism.
2) 1-Butene (CH\_3-CH\_2-CH=CH\_2): Again, the carbon on the far right is holding two identical Hydrogen atoms. No geometrical isomerism.
3) 2-Methylpropene ((CH\_3)\_2C=CH\_2): The carbon on the left is holding two identical methyl (CH\_3) groups, and the right is holding two hydrogens. Double fail!
4) 2-Butene (CH\_3-CH=CH-CH\_3): The left carbon holds one Hydrogen and one Methyl group. The right carbon holds one Hydrogen and one Methyl group. Both carbons hold different things! Therefore, they can be arranged with the methyls on the same side (cis-2-butene) or opposite sides (trans-2-butene).

questions.Question: Q44. The major product obtained from the following reaction is: [Note: Typical JEE missing reaction completed as dehydration of 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol with concentrated H\_2SO\_4 and heat].
questions.Hint: When an acid removes water to form a double bond, a positively charged carbon (called a carbocation) is formed. If that positive charge can hop to a neighboring carbon to become more stable (via a 'methyl shift'), it definitely will before making the double bond!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into a reaction that involves a super sneaky chemical trick: Rearrangement! 

Imagine a molecule of 3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol. It looks like a chain of carbons with a bulky cluster of methyl groups on the 3rd carbon, and an OH (alcohol) group on the 2nd carbon. When we throw in strong, hot sulfuric acid (H\_2SO\_4), the acid acts like a bully and rips the OH group right off the molecule, along with a hydrogen, to make water. 

When the OH leaves, it takes its electrons with it, leaving the 2nd carbon with a positive charge. We call this a 'carbocation'. Right now, this positive charge is on a secondary carbon (it's attached to two other carbons). 

Now, here is where chemistry becomes a game of musical chairs. Carbocations are incredibly uncomfortable. They want to be surrounded by as many carbon neighbors as possible because those neighbors share their electron clouds to help stabilize the positive charge. The 2nd carbon looks next door at the 3rd carbon and says, 'Wow, you have four carbons attached to you! If I could just move my positive charge to you, I'd be a tertiary carbocation, which is way more stable!'

So, an amazing thing happens called a '1,2-Methyl Shift'. An entire methyl group (CH\_3) from the 3rd carbon unplugs itself and jumps over to the 2nd carbon. In doing so, it leaves the 3rd carbon with the positive charge. Now the positive charge is incredibly stable on a tertiary carbon!

Finally, to finish the reaction, the molecule spits out a hydrogen ion (H+) from a neighboring carbon to form a double bond. According to Zaitsev's Rule, molecules prefer to form the most crowded, highly substituted double bond possible because it's the most stable. By removing a hydrogen from the new 2nd carbon, we get a double bond right in the middle: 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene. It's a spectacular chemical puzzle where the molecule rearranges its own skeleton to find the most comfortable shape!

questions.Question: Q45. Which compound(s) out of the following is/are not aromatic? A) Benzene, B) Cyclopentadienyl anion, C) Cycloheptatriene, D) Pyridine.
questions.Hint: For a ring to be an exclusive 'aromatic' club, it must be completely flat, have an unbroken continuous loop of p-orbitals, and follow Huckel's magic number rule: 4n + 2 pi electrons.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
In chemistry, the word 'aromatic' doesn't just mean a compound smells nice (though many of them do!). It actually refers to a molecule that is incredibly, unbelievably stable. These molecules have a special 'force field' of electrons that makes them very tough to break.

To be considered aromatic, a molecule must pass a strict 3-part test to get into the VIP Aromatic Club:
1. It must be a flat ring (cyclic and planar).
2. Every single atom in the ring must have an available p-orbital so the electrons can run around in a complete, unbroken circle. No road blocks allowed!
3. It must obey Huckel's Rule, meaning the number of electrons running in the circle must equal 4n + 2 (where n is a whole number). So, having 2, 6, 10, or 14 electrons is a winning ticket.

Let's check the VIP line:
- Benzene: A flat ring? Yes. Unbroken circle? Yes. Has 6 pi electrons? Yes (4(1) + 2 = 6). Welcome to the club, Benzene!
- Cyclopentadienyl anion: Flat ring? Yes. Unbroken circle? Yes (the negative charge counts as two electrons participating in the circle). Total electrons = 4 from double bonds + 2 from the negative charge = 6 pi electrons. Welcome!
- Pyridine: Flat ring? Yes. Unbroken circle? Yes. Has 6 pi electrons? Yes. Welcome!
- Cycloheptatriene: This molecule has a ring of 7 carbons. Six of them are involved in double bonds, but the 7th carbon is completely saturated with single bonds (we call this sp3 hybridized). Think of this 7th carbon like a massive pothole in the race track. The electrons cannot complete the circle! Because the unbroken loop rule is violated, it completely fails the test. Cycloheptatriene is not aromatic.

questions.Question: Q46. 25g of an unknown hydrocarbon upon burning produces 88g of CO\_2 and 9g of H\_2O. This unknown hydrocarbon contains:
questions.Hint: The law of conservation of mass is your best friend here. All the carbon in the CO\_2 came exclusively from your unknown substance, and all the hydrogen in the H\_2O came from it too! Use the molar masses of CO\_2 and H\_2O to work backward.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you have a mystery box made entirely of red and blue LEGO bricks. The red bricks are Carbon, and the blue bricks are Hydrogen. You weigh the box: it is exactly 25 grams. 

Now, you decide to take the box apart completely (this is what burning or 'combustion' does). You take all the red Carbon bricks and attach them to Oxygen to make Carbon Dioxide (CO\_2). You take all the blue Hydrogen bricks and attach them to Oxygen to make Water (H\_2O). 

After burning, you capture 88g of CO\_2 gas and 9g of water vapor. 

To find out what was in the mystery box, we need to extract the weight of just the red and blue bricks from the gases we captured. 

Let's look at CO\_2 first. The molar mass of a CO\_2 molecule is 44 grams per mole (Carbon is 12, Oxygen is 16x2=32. 12 + 32 = 44). Out of every 44 grams of CO\_2, exactly 12 grams is Carbon. 
We captured 88g of CO\_2. That's exactly double the molar mass (2 moles). So, the mass of Carbon hidden inside that 88g of gas is 2 times 12g, which equals 24 grams of Carbon.

Now let's look at water, H\_2O. The molar mass of water is 18 grams per mole (Hydrogen is 1x2=2, Oxygen is 16. 2 + 16 = 18). Out of every 18 grams of water, exactly 2 grams is Hydrogen.
We captured 9g of water. That is exactly half of a mole (9 is half of 18). So, the mass of Hydrogen inside that water is half of 2g, which equals 1 gram of Hydrogen.

Let's check our math: 24 grams of Carbon + 1 gram of Hydrogen = 25 grams total. This matches the weight of our original mystery box perfectly! So, our unknown hydrocarbon contained exactly 24g of Carbon and 1g of Hydrogen.

questions.Question: Q47. The major product of the following addition reaction is H\_3C-CH=CH\_2 + Cl\_2/H\_2O $\rightarrow$
questions.Hint: When Chlorine and Water mix, they react to form HOCl. During the addition across the double bond, think of Markovnikov's rule: the OH- acts as a nucleophile and wants to attack the carbon that can best handle a partial positive charge (the more substituted one!).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's break down this chemical dance step-by-step. We are starting with propene (H\_3C-CH=CH\_2), which has a nice, rich double bond filled with electrons. 

Into the flask, we drop Chlorine gas (Cl\_2) and Water (H\_2O). The electrons in the double bond are like a magnet, and they reach out and grab one of the chlorine atoms. But this chlorine atom doesn't just attach to one side; it forms a little three-membered triangle holding onto BOTH carbons of the double bond. This structure is called a 'chloronium ion', and it has a positive charge on the chlorine. 

Chlorine hates being positive! It's very electronegative (greedy for electrons). So, it starts tugging the electrons away from the two carbons it's attached to. This leaves the two carbons feeling partially positive.

Now, here is the crucial part: which carbon feels MORE positive? The middle carbon (CH) is attached to another carbon (the methyl group), which can help share the burden of the positive charge. The end carbon (CH\_2) has no carbon friends to help it. Because the middle carbon can handle the positive charge much better, the chlorine tugs harder on that side, making the bond longer and weaker.

Suddenly, Water (H\_2O) enters the scene. Water is a 'nucleophile', meaning it is looking for positive charges to attack. It sees that the middle carbon is bearing the brunt of the positive charge, so the oxygen in water forcefully attacks the middle carbon!

This snaps the triangle open. The Chlorine flips over to the end carbon (CH\_2), and the Water attaches to the middle carbon (CH). Finally, the water molecule loses a hydrogen to become an OH group. 

The final result? The OH is on the middle carbon, and the Cl is on the end carbon. This forms H\_3C-CH(OH)-CH\_2Cl, known as a halohydrin. It's a perfect example of molecules doing whatever is most energetically stable!

questions.Question: Q48. Which one of the following alkenes when treated with HCl yields majorly an anti Markovnikov product? [Note: Specific alkenes added to provide complete options]
questions.Hint: Normally, HCl addition follows Markovnikov's rule because forming a positive charge on a highly substituted carbon is good. BUT, if there is a highly electronegative 'vacuum cleaner' group attached, it destroys that stability, forcing the positive charge to form further away!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this question, we first need to understand the famous 'Markovnikov's Rule'. A simple way to remember it is 'the rich get richer'. When you add an acid like HCl to a double bond, the Hydrogen atom goes to the carbon that already has the most hydrogens. 

Why does this happen? When the double bond breaks to grab the Hydrogen, it leaves a positive charge (carbocation) on the other carbon. Molecules prefer this positive charge to be on the carbon with the LEAST hydrogens (the most substituted carbon) because neighboring carbons act like good friends, donating electron density to help stabilize the positive charge. 

So, for Propene, 2-Methylpropene, and 1-Butene, they all follow this rule beautifully. The positive charge forms on the inner, more crowded carbon, and the Chlorine (Cl-) swoops in and attaches there. This is the standard Markovnikov product.

But 3,3,3-Trifluoropropene (CF\_3-CH=CH\_2) is a massive rebel. Why? Because it has a CF\_3 group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element on the entire periodic table. Having three of them together acts like an ultra-powerful electron vacuum cleaner. They violently suck electron density toward themselves. 

If the double bond were to break and put a positive charge on the middle carbon (right next to the CF\_3 group), it would be a total disaster! The carbon is already starving for electrons because of the positive charge, and the CF\_3 vacuum cleaner is pulling even MORE away. The molecule would scream in agony! 

To avoid this horrific situation, the molecule breaks the rules. It puts the positive charge on the END carbon (CH\_2), as far away from the CF\_3 vacuum cleaner as possible. Consequently, the Chlorine attaches to the end carbon, and the Hydrogen attaches to the middle. This is the exact opposite of the normal rule, giving us the 'anti-Markovnikov' product purely driven by the extreme electron-withdrawing nature of Fluorine!

questions.Question: Q49. The increasing order of reactivity of the following compounds towards aromatic electrophilic substitution reaction is: I. Benzene, II. Phenol, III. Nitrobenzene, IV. Toluene.
questions.Hint: Think of the benzene ring as a bank vault full of electrons. The incoming electrophile is a robber looking for money. Groups attached to the ring that donate money (electrons) make it a juicier target, while groups that withdraw money make it a terrible target.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore the world of Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS). That sounds incredibly intimidating, but let's break the words down. 'Aromatic' means we are dealing with a Benzene ring. 'Substitution' means we are going to swap out one of the hydrogens on the ring for something else. And 'Electrophilic' means the chemical coming in to do the swapping is an 'electrophile'—an 'electron lover'.

Electrophiles have a positive charge or a partial positive charge. They are desperately looking for a rich source of negative electrons. A standard benzene ring (Compound I) is a nice, flat cloud of six electrons. It's a good target. We will use plain Benzene as our baseline (middle reactivity).

Now, imagine attaching different groups to this benzene ring. These groups can either pump MORE electrons into the ring, or suck electrons OUT of the ring.

Compound IV is Toluene, which has a Methyl group (CH\_3) attached. Alkyl groups act like generous grandparents; they gently push a little bit of extra electron density into the ring through a process called the inductive effect.
