Now, what exactly are these new pollutants? The sun bakes the exhaust into molecules like Ozone (O3) and PAN (Peroxyacetyl nitrate). These specific molecules are incredibly greedy in the chemical world$\u2014$they aggressively want to steal electrons from other molecules. In chemistry, electron-stealers are called 'oxidizing agents'. Because it is packed full of these greedy, electron-stealing chemicals, photochemical smog is classified as an 'oxidizing smog'. It is definitely NOT a reducing smog (which gives away electrons). Therefore, the only perfectly accurate statement is that it contains high concentrations of oxidizing agents like ozone and PAN. If you ever walk outside in a big city on a hot summer day and your eyes start stinging, you can blame the ozone and PAN in the photochemical smog!
questions.Answer: It contains high concentrations of oxidizing agents like ozone and PAN.

questions.Question: Q18. The mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol is an example of
questions.Hint: Think back to when you were younger, scraped your knee, and your mom or dad applied a distinct-smelling brownish-yellow liquid from the first-aid kit to stop the wound from getting infected.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about what happens when you are riding your bicycle, take a sharp turn too fast, and scrape your knee on the pavement. Ouch! When you break your skin, bad bacteria from the dirt can sneak into the wound and cause a painful, nasty infection. To stop this from happening, we immediately reach into our first-aid kit for a chemical defender! 

In chemistry and medicine, we have different tools for fighting germs. If you want to kill germs on a non-living surface (like a bathroom floor or a dirty toilet), you use a strong, harsh chemical called a 'Disinfectant'. But you would NEVER pour toilet cleaner on your scraped knee! It would burn your skin and destroy your living tissues. Instead, for living human skin, we use a much gentler, perfectly balanced chemical called an 'Antiseptic'. Antiseptics kill the bad microbes but are safe enough not to harm your own living cells. 

One of the most famous and widely used antiseptics in the entire world is Dettol. If you grab a bottle of liquid Dettol and read the incredibly tiny ingredient print on the back label, you will discover a cool chemistry secret! Dettol is actually a specific mixture of two chemical compounds: 'chloroxylenol' and 'terpineol'. Chloroxylenol is the tough guy; it's the active ingredient that punches holes in the bacteria's cell walls and kills them. Terpineol, which is naturally found in pine tree oil, helps the mixture dissolve properly and gives Dettol that classic, fresh, clean smell we all instantly recognize. So, whenever you see a mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol, you instantly know you are looking at the chemical recipe for a skin-saving Antiseptic!

questions.Question: Q19. The photochemical smog does not generally contain:
questions.Hint: Which of these chemicals is famous for destroying the protective ozone layer way, way up high in the Earth's stratosphere, rather than forming smog down here at ground level where we breathe?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To figure out what does NOT belong in photochemical smog, we first need to completely master what DOES belong in it. As we learned earlier, photochemical smog is the brownish, irritating haze you often see hanging over big, sunny, busy cities with lots of traffic. It is cooked up when the sun bakes car exhaust. 

The standard recipe for this toxic city soup includes unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides (the raw ingredients from cars). Once the sunlight bakes them, it produces 'secondary pollutants'. The major secondary pollutants are Ozone (O3), PAN (Peroxyacetyl nitrate), Acrolein, and Formaldehyde. These are the troublemakers that make your eyes water and your lungs cough on a smoggy day. So, Ozone, PAN, and Acrolein are definitely present in photochemical smog.

But wait, notice the odd one out? Let's talk about Chlorofluorocarbons, or 'CFCs'. Decades ago, CFCs were heavily used inside refrigerators, air conditioners, and aerosol spray cans (like hairspray). When these CFC gases leak out into the air, they don't stick around the ground level to form smog. Instead, they are very lightweight and stable, so they float way, way, way up high into the Earth's upper atmosphere, called the stratosphere. Once they get up there, intense space radiation breaks them apart, and they start acting like little pac-men, gobbling up and destroying the Earth's protective Ozone Layer! 

So, while CFCs are terrible for the environment because they cause 'Ozone Depletion' in outer space, they play absolutely zero role in creating 'Photochemical Smog' down here in our cities. Therefore, photochemical smog does NOT contain CFCs. You've just mastered the difference between a ground-level pollutant and a high-altitude pollutant!

questions.Concept: Matching Environmental Terms with their Causes/Effects
questions.Question:
Q20. Match List I with List II. [Note: The original text chunk omitted the specific lists. To help you master this concept, here is a highly relevant environmental chemistry matching puzzle!]
List I: 
A) Tropospheric Ozone 
B) Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) 
C) Sulphur Dioxide (SO2) 
D) Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) 

List II: 
i) Acid rain 
ii) Photochemical smog 
iii) Ozone layer depletion 
iv) Water pollution
questions.Hint: Take it one step at a time! Where do CFCs go? (Up to the ozone layer!). What does burning coal (which makes SO2) cause when it rains?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
In chemistry, we often have to play detective and connect specific chemicals to the real-world environmental problems they cause. Since the original problem asked us to match two lists but forgot to provide them, let's solve this ultimate environmental chemistry matching puzzle I've built for you!

Let's break down the matches one by one:
1. Tropospheric Ozone (A): The 'troposphere' is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, right here at ground level where we live and breathe. While ozone high up in the sky protects us from the sun, ozone down here on the ground is toxic! As we learned earlier, ground-level ozone is heavily produced by sunlight baking car exhaust. Therefore, Tropospheric Ozone is the major culprit behind Photochemical Smog! (A matches with ii).

2. Chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs (B): Remember the old refrigerators and hairsprays? These chemicals float high up into the stratosphere and rip apart the Earth's protective sunscreen layer. Therefore, CFCs are responsible for Ozone Layer Depletion! (B matches with iii).

3. Sulphur Dioxide or SO2 (C): When massive factories burn cheap coal, they release tons of sulphur dioxide gas into the sky. This gas floats up, mixes with rain clouds, and literally turns the water into mild sulphuric acid! When this falls back to earth, it can dissolve marble statues and kill trees. Therefore, SO2 is the main cause of Acid Rain! (C matches with i).

4. Biochemical Oxygen Demand or BOD (D): We already know this one! BOD measures how much oxygen an army of bacteria needs to eat all the organic waste dumped into a river. The higher the BOD, the dirtier the river. Therefore, BOD is directly tied to Water Pollution! (D matches with iv).

Putting it all together flawlessly, we get A-ii, B-iii, C-i, D-iv! You just reviewed four massive environmental concepts in a single question. Great job!

questions.Concept: Water Pollution, DO, BOD, and Eutrophication
questions.Question: Q21. Given below are two statements: Statement I: In polluted water values of both dissolved oxygen and BOD are very low. Statement II: Eutrophication results in decrease in the amount of dissolved oxygen.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
questions.Hint: If there is a ton of pollution, bacteria will work overtime to eat it. Will their DEMAND for oxygen (BOD) be low or high? And if plant life explodes on a lake (Eutrophication) and then dies, what happens to the oxygen when bacteria eat the dead plants?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive deep into the fascinating underwater ecosystem to understand exactly what happens when water gets polluted! Imagine a perfectly pristine, crystal-clear pond filled with happy fish. The fish are happy because the water is packed with 'Dissolved Oxygen' (DO), allowing them to breathe easily. 

Now, let's look at Statement I. Imagine someone accidentally dumps a massive truckload of sewage (organic waste) into our beautiful pond. It instantly becomes heavily polluted water. A massive army of bacteria arrives to feast on this waste. Because they are working so hard and multiplying so fast, their *demand* for oxygen absolutely skyrockets! This means the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) becomes extremely HIGH, not low. At the exact same time, because the bacteria are aggressively consuming all the oxygen to digest the food, the actual amount of Dissolved Oxygen (DO) left in the water drops tremendously. So, Statement I is completely false because it incorrectly claims that *both* DO and BOD are very low. In reality, in polluted water, DO is low but BOD is VERY high!

Now, let's look at Statement II and the word 'Eutrophication'. Imagine a rainstorm washes a ton of chemical fertilizer from a nearby farm straight into a lake. The fertilizer acts like super-food for aquatic plants and algae. The algae grow incredibly fast, covering the entire surface of the lake in a thick, green blanket (an algal bloom). But eventually, these billions of algae plants die. What happens next? You guessed it! The bacteria army returns to eat the dead algae. The bacteria consume massive amounts of oxygen during this cleanup process, sucking nearly all the Dissolved Oxygen out of the water. Without oxygen, the fish and other aquatic life sadly suffocate and die. So, Eutrophication definitely results in a severe decrease in the amount of dissolved oxygen. Statement II is 100% correct! 

Therefore, Statement I is totally wrong, and Statement II is right on the money.
questions.Answer: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

questions.Question: Which among the following pairs has only herbicides?
questions.Hint: Think about chemicals used specifically to kill unwanted weeds and plants, rather than insects.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Start by defining what pesticides are broadly. Imagine you have a beautiful garden, but there are pests trying to ruin it. You generally have two types of pests: insects eating your leaves, and weeds stealing the water and nutrients from the soil. 'Pesticide' is an umbrella term for any chemical that kills pests. Under this giant umbrella, we have 'insecticides' (killers of insects) and 'herbicides' (killers of herbs, weeds, and unwanted plants).

The question asks for a pair containing ONLY herbicides. Let's look at the chemicals we often see in chemistry. DDT, Aldrin, Dieldrin, and BHC are all famous (and rather infamous!) insecticides. They were used heavily in the mid-20th century to kill mosquitoes and crop-eating bugs, but they are highly toxic and persist in the environment for years. So, any option containing these bug-killers is out.

On the other hand, sodium chlorate ($NaClO_3$) and sodium arsenite ($Na_3AsO_3$) are chemicals used strictly to clear out unwanted vegetation. If you apply them to a field, they will chemically attack and kill the weeds. Therefore, they belong to the category of classical inorganic herbicides. It is super important in environmental chemistry to know which chemical belongs to which category, because spraying an insecticide on a weed won't help your garden at all! To answer correctly, simply remember that chlorates and arsenites are traditional plant-killers.

questions.Question: Given below are two statements. Statement I: The pH of rain water is normally ~5.6. Statement II: If the pH of rain water drops below 5.6, it is called acid rain.
MCQ_Options: Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.Hint: Does natural rain have a completely neutral pH of 7, or does it dissolve gases from the atmosphere making it slightly acidic even before pollution?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
When you think of pure water, you probably think of a completely neutral pH of exactly 7.0. But the rain falling from the sky is actually a little bit acidic naturally! Why is that?

Imagine millions of raindrops falling through the Earth's atmosphere. The air isn't empty; it's filled with naturally occurring gases, including Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$). As the water drops fall, the $CO_2$ dissolves into the water, just like how carbon dioxide gas is pushed into water to make your bubbly soda. This reaction creates a very mild, weak acid called carbonic acid ($H_2CO_3$). Because of this naturally occurring carbonic acid, normal, perfectly clean rain has a pH of about 5.6. So, Statement I is absolutely true!

Now, what happens when humans build factories and drive millions of cars? We release nasty pollutants into the air, specifically sulfur dioxide ($SO_2$) and nitrogen oxides ($NO_x$). These harmful gases also dissolve in the falling raindrops, but unlike $CO_2$, they form incredibly strong, dangerous acids: sulfuric acid ($H_2SO_4$) and nitric acid ($HNO_3$). These strong acids completely overpower the raindrop and drag the pH way down, below 5.6. When the pH drops below this 5.6 threshold, the rain becomes highly corrosive and dangerous to plants, aquatic life, and even marble buildings (like the Taj Mahal!). Scientists officially call this specific phenomenon 'acid rain.' Therefore, Statement II is also completely true. Since both are scientifically accurate facts about our atmosphere, both statements are true.
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true

questions.Question: Given below are two statements. Statement I: The value of the parameter "Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)" is important for survival of aquatic life. Statement II: The optimum value of BOD is 6.5 ppm.
MCQ_Options: Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.Hint: High BOD means bacteria are using up all the oxygen in the water to eat garbage. If clean water has a BOD of less than 5 ppm, is 6.5 ppm a good 'optimum' value?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine the oxygen dissolved in a beautiful, clear lake is like a massive pizza buffet, and the fish are the VIP guests at the party. Fish absolutely need this dissolved oxygen to breathe and survive. But suddenly, raw sewage or dead plant matter (organic waste) is illegally dumped into the lake. This waste attracts millions of microscopic bacteria who crash the party to eat the garbage. However, to break down all this waste, the bacteria need to breathe too, and they aggressively start consuming the oxygen (eating all the pizza!).

'Biochemical Oxygen Demand' or BOD is a measure of exactly this: how much oxygen do the bacteria 'demand' to break down the organic waste in the water? If the BOD is very high, it means there is a ton of garbage, and the bacteria will suck all the oxygen out of the water, suffocating the poor fish. Therefore, Statement I is true: checking the BOD is incredibly crucial for the survival of aquatic life. We must make sure the fish have enough oxygen left!

Now, let's look at the numbers. Pure, clean water has a BOD of less than 5 ppm (parts per million). It means very little oxygen is being demanded by bacteria because there's barely any waste to eat. Highly polluted water has a BOD of 17 ppm or more. Statement II claims the 'optimum' (ideal) value is 6.5 ppm. Wait a minute! If the BOD is 6.5 ppm, the water is already starting to get significantly polluted. You want the BOD to be as close to zero as possible, and definitely under 5 ppm! So, 6.5 ppm is not an optimum or healthy value at all. Therefore, Statement II is entirely false.
questions.Answer: Statement I is true, Statement II is false

questions.Concept: Crystal Field Theory / Valence Bond Theory
questions.Question: The hybridisation and magnetic nature of [Mn(CN)₆]⁴⁻ and [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻, respectively are
questions.Hint: Find the oxidation state of the central metal ion first. Count the remaining d-electrons. Then consider the effect of Cyanide ($CN^-$) being a 'strong field' ligand that forces electrons to pair up.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question might look like an intimidating alphabet soup, but it's actually an amazing puzzle about how atoms build tiny molecular apartments! Let's break it down using Crystal Field Theory, step by step.

Step 1: Identify the metals and their charges. We have Manganese (Mn) and Iron (Fe). The cyanide ligand ($CN^-$) has a -1 charge. In $[Mn(CN)_6]^{4-}$, six cyanides give a -6 charge, but the overall molecule's charge is -4. So, Manganese must be balancing it out with a +2 oxidation state ($Mn^{2+}$). In $[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}$, six cyanides give -6, but the total is -3. So, Iron is in a +3 oxidation state ($Fe^{3+}$).

Step 2: Count the d-electrons. A neutral Manganese atom has the outer electron configuration of $3d^5 4s^2$. When it becomes $Mn^{2+}$, it loses the two 4s electrons first, leaving exactly 5 electrons in the 3d orbitals ($3d^5$). A neutral Iron atom is $3d^6 4s^2$. When it becomes $Fe^{3+}$, it loses two from 4s and one from 3d, leaving—you guessed it—exactly 5 electrons in the 3d orbitals ($3d^5$)! They are identical twins in this specific scenario!

Step 3: Meet the ligand. Cyanide ($CN^-$) is what chemists call a 'strong field ligand.' Imagine cyanide is a very strict, bossy dorm warden. Normally, electrons want to spread out into their own separate orbital rooms to avoid repelling each other. But the strict warden forces them to squish together into the lower energy rooms (called $t_{2g}$). The 5 electrons pair up as much as possible: two pairs and one lone electron.

Because there is still one unpaired electron wandering around in both molecules, both act like tiny magnets. We call this 'Paramagnetic.' Also, because the electrons were forced to pack tightly into the inner 3d orbitals, two empty 3d rooms are left wide open. The metal uses these inner 3d rooms to bond with the incoming cyanides, creating a $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation. In conclusion, they both have the exact same hybridisation ($d^2sp^3$) and the exact same magnetic nature (paramagnetic)!

questions.Question: The gas released during anaerobic degradation of vegetation may lead to:
questions.Hint: When dead plants break down in places completely without oxygen (like underwater or inside a cow's stomach), what flammable gas is produced that acts like a blanket over the Earth?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about what happens when living things die and break down. If a tree falls in a forest and breaks down in the open air, bacteria use the abundant oxygen in the air to decompose it, usually releasing Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$). This is called 'aerobic' (with oxygen) degradation.

But what if autumn leaves fall deep to the bottom of a swamp, or a cow eats grass and digests it deep inside its stomach? In these places, there is absolutely no oxygen available. This is called 'anaerobic' (without air) degradation. The special bacteria that live in these dark, oxygen-free zones have a totally different way of eating and digesting. When they break down the vegetation, they don't produce $CO_2$. Instead, they 'burp' out a completely different gas: Methane ($CH_4$). Methane is actually commonly known as marsh gas because of this exact swampy process!

Now, why do we care about methane? Methane is an incredibly potent Greenhouse Gas. Imagine the Earth is wearing a jacket to stay warm. Greenhouse gases act like the fluffy stuffing inside the jacket—they trap the heat from the sun so it doesn't escape back out into freezing outer space. While we definitely need some greenhouse gases to keep the Earth from freezing into an ice ball, releasing massive amounts of extra Methane traps way too much heat. This creates a thick, heavy thermal blanket around our planet, leading directly to Global Warming. So, the anaerobic breakdown of vegetation releases methane, which cranks up the thermostat of our entire planet!

questions.Question: Reducing smog is a mixture of
MCQ_Options: Ozone, oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons
questions.Hint: Reducing smog is also famously called 'Classical smog' or 'London smog'. It happens in cold, damp weather when people burn lots of coal that contains a specific yellow element!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
You have probably heard the word 'Smog' on the news before. It's a clever mashup of two simple words: Smoke + Fog. But did you know there are actually two totally different chemical recipes for smog?

The first type is called 'Photochemical Smog', which is famous in sunny, warm cities heavily reliant on cars, like Los Angeles. It forms when sunlight bakes car exhaust, creating toxic ozone. Because ozone loves to steal electrons from other molecules (a process called oxidation), this is known as oxidizing smog.

But this question is specifically asking about 'Reducing Smog,' which is also known in history as 'Classical Smog' or 'London Smog.' To understand it, travel back in your imagination to a cold, damp, completely foggy winter day in 19th-century London. Millions of people are burning cheap coal in their home fireplaces to stay warm. This coal naturally contains a lot of sulfur. When the coal burns, it releases thick black smoke, and the sulfur chemically burns to create a choking, invisible gas called Sulfur Dioxide ($SO_2$).

When this thick black smoke and sulfur dioxide gas get trapped directly inside the heavy, wet winter fog, it creates Classical Smog. Chemically, Sulfur Dioxide ($SO_2$) acts as a 'reducing agent'—which means it absolutely loves to give away its electrons to other molecules, acting as the exact opposite of the sunny Los Angeles smog! Therefore, reducing smog is simply a mixture of smoke, fog, and sulphur dioxide. It's a chilly, coal-burning disaster that we fortunately see much less of today!

questions.Question: The green house gas/es is (are) (A) carbon dioxide (B) oxygen (C) water vapour (D) methane
questions.Hint: A greenhouse gas must be able to trap heat. Look for complex molecules that have 3 or more atoms (or are unsymmetrical) so they can vibrate and absorb heat. Is the oxygen we breathe every day a greenhouse gas?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To perfectly answer this question, we have to understand how the 'Greenhouse Effect' actually works on a tiny, microscopic molecular level. Imagine the Earth is wrapped in an invisible blanket of atmospheric gases. When the sun shines, it warms the Earth's surface. The Earth then tries to radiate that warmth back out into cold space in the form of infrared energy (heat).

Now, imagine you are a gas molecule floating high up in the sky. If you are a simple, perfectly symmetric molecule made of only two identical atoms tightly bound together—like Oxygen ($O_2$) or Nitrogen ($N_2$)—you are stiff and rigid. When the heat tries to hit you, it just passes right through you because you are too stiff to bend or wiggle to absorb that heat energy.

But, if you are a larger molecule made of three or more atoms—like Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$, 3 atoms), Water Vapour ($H_2O$, 3 atoms), or Methane ($CH_4$, 5 atoms)—you are floppy and flexible! You act exactly like a tiny molecular spring. When the infrared heat hits you, you start to vibrate, wiggle, bend, and dance! By doing this energetic dance, you physically absorb the heat and trap it directly in the atmosphere, warming up the whole planet.

This is exactly why Carbon dioxide (A), Water vapour (C), and Methane (D) are officially classified as greenhouse gases. They have the right shape and flexibility to catch the heat. Oxygen (B) is just too stiff and simple to catch the heat, so it is definitely not a greenhouse gas. Thus, A, C, and D are the correct choices!

questions.Question: Q29. Given below are two statements: Statement I: Non-biodegradable wastes are generated by the thermal power plants. Statement II: Bio-degradable detergents leads to eutrophication.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
questions.Hint: Think about what is left over when we burn coal for electricity. Also, remember that even 'natural' or degradable soaps often contain nutrients that algae love to eat!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's break down this environmental chemistry puzzle together. 

Imagine a giant thermal power plant. How does it make electricity? It burns massive amounts of coal to heat water into steam, which spins giant turbines. But just like a campfire leaves behind ash when the wood burns away, burning coal leaves behind something called 'fly ash' and bottom ash. Can a bacteria eat this ash and decompose it? Nope! It's just inorganic burnt minerals. This makes it strictly 'non-biodegradable' (nature can't break it down). So, Statement I is completely true!

Now, let's look at Statement II. You might be thinking, 'Wait, if a detergent is bio-degradable, isn't that a good thing?' Well, yes, it means bacteria can break it down, which is better than toxic chemicals. However, many biodegradable detergents contain chemical compounds called 'phosphates', which act as water softeners. When these phosphates wash down the drain and reach lakes, they act like a super-steroid fertilizer for algae. 

The algae eat the phosphates, go crazy, and multiply rapidly, covering the entire surface of the lake like a thick green carpet. This is called an 'algal bloom'. This green blanket blocks out sunlight, so underwater plants die. Then, bacteria multiply to eat the dead plants, breathing in all the dissolved oxygen in the water. Without oxygen, the fish suffocate and the lake essentially dies. This tragic chain reaction—too many nutrients causing plant overgrowth and oxygen loss—is called 'Eutrophication'. Therefore, even bio-degradable detergents can cause terrible eutrophication. So, Statement II is also true!

Both statements describe exactly how human activities, even seemingly harmless ones, impact our natural world.
questions.Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.Question: Q30. Arrange the following metal complex/compounds in the increasing order of spin only magnetic moment. Presume all the three, high spin system. (Atomic numbers Ce = 58, Gd = 64 and Eu = 63.) A. (NH₄)₂[Ce(NO₃)₆] B. Gd(NO₃)₃ and C. Eu(NO₃)₃
questions.Hint: First, find the oxidation state (charge) of the metal in each compound. Then, figure out how many unpaired (lonely) electrons are left in the f-orbitals. More unpaired electrons = higher magnetic moment!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! Don't let these big chemical formulas intimidate you. We are going to solve this like detectives. 

In chemistry, atoms act like tiny magnets. But why? It's all because of 'unpaired electrons'. Think of electrons as tiny tops spinning on a table. If two electrons share a room (an orbital), they spin in opposite directions, and their magnetic forces cancel each other out perfectly. But if an electron is all alone in its room (unpaired), its magnetic force is unopposed! So, the rule is simple: The more lonely, unpaired electrons an atom has, the stronger its magnetic moment.

Let's check our suspects:

1. Suspect A: (NH₄)₂[Ce(NO₃)₆]
Let's find the charge of Cerium (Ce). The whole molecule is neutral. We have 2 Ammonium ions (NH₄⁺), which give a +2 charge. We have 6 Nitrate ions (NO₃⁻), which give a -6 charge. To balance this to zero: (+2) + Ce + (-6) = 0. So, Ce must be +4. 
Cerium's normal atomic number is 58. Its electron arrangement is [Xe] 4f¹ 5d¹ 6s². When it becomes +4, it loses 4 electrons (both 6s, the 5d, and the 4f). What's left? Absolutely zero electrons in the outer shell. Zero unpaired electrons means zero magnetism! 

2. Suspect B: Gd(NO₃)₃
Nitrate is -1, and there are 3 of them, so Gadolinium (Gd) is +3. 
Gd's atomic number is 64. Normal setup: [Xe] 4f⁷ 5d¹ 6s². Losing 3 electrons (the two 6s and the one 5d) leaves us with [Xe] 4f⁷. The f-subshell has exactly 7 rooms, and we have 7 electrons. That means 1 electron per room. That's 7 unpaired electrons! This is the maximum magnetism you can get!

3. Suspect C: Eu(NO₃)₃
Europium (Eu) is also +3 here. 
Eu's atomic number is 63. Normal setup: [Xe] 4f⁷ 6s². Losing 3 electrons (the two 6s and one from the 4f) leaves us with [Xe] 4f⁶. That gives us 6 unpaired electrons.

Let's rank them by unpaired electrons: A (0) < C (6) < B (7). Therefore, the magnetic moment perfectly follows this order: A < C < B. You're basically just counting the lonely electrons!

questions.Question: Q31. Match List - I with List - II:
MCQ_Options: Data is missing to answer the question
questions.Hint: Notice anything strange about this question? There are no lists! In exams, knowing when a question is faulty is just as important as knowing the science.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Sometimes the most valuable lesson in chemistry (and in life) is realizing when you don't have all the pieces to the puzzle. 

If you look closely at this question, it says 'Match List - I with List - II:', but then... the text just stops! There is no List I, and there is no List II. 

Why am I pointing this out to a 14-year-old science enthusiast? Because when you are taking big, scary, high-pressure exams (like the JEE), sometimes the test itself has a typo or a printing error. Many students panic when this happens. They think, 'Oh no, I must be missing something!' and waste 10 minutes staring at a broken question. 

The secret skill of top students is confidence. If you read a question and the data is literally missing, trust yourself! Skip it immediately and move on to the next question. Your time is your most precious resource in an exam.

Now, if we were to guess what this question *wanted* to ask, since it's surrounded by Environmental Chemistry questions, it was likely going to ask you to match Pollutants to their Effects. For example, it might have asked you to match 'Chlorofluorocarbons' to 'Ozone Depletion', or 'Sulfur Dioxide' to 'Acid Rain'. Whenever you study Environmental Chemistry, try making your own matching lists of pollutants and what they do. It's a fantastic way to memorize them!
questions.Answer: Data is missing to answer the question

questions.Question: Q32. Which one of the following gases is reported to retard photosynthesis?
questions.Hint: Plants need healthy green leaves to absorb sunlight. Which of these gases is a nasty, reddish-brown toxic smog component that damages plant leaves like a bad sunburn?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore how air pollution messes with nature! 

You already know that plants are amazing chemical factories. They take sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water, and magically turn them into food (sugar) and the oxygen we breathe. This process is called photosynthesis. The plant's leaves are like solar panels capturing the sunlight. 

Now, imagine what would happen if someone sprayed a toxic, acidic mist all over those solar panels. They wouldn't be able to absorb light properly, right? That is exactly what Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) does.

NO₂ is a nasty, reddish-brown gas that comes from car exhausts and factories burning fossil fuels. When this gas builds up in the air, it is highly toxic to living tissues. When plants are exposed to high concentrations of NO₂, it actually damages the plant cells. The leaves can become spotted, yellow, or even die off (a condition called necrosis or chlorosis). 

Because the 'solar panels' (leaves) are damaged by the NO₂ gas, the plant's ability to create food drops drastically. In scientific terms, it 'retards' (slows down) the rate of photosynthesis. 

What about the other options? Carbon Monoxide (CO) is dangerous to humans because it suffocates our blood, but plants don't care much about it. CFCs destroy the ozone layer way up in the sky. Methane is a greenhouse gas that traps heat. Only Nitrogen dioxide directly attacks the plant's food-making machinery!

questions.Question: Q33. In stratosphere most of the ozone formation is assisted by
questions.Hint: What invisible, high-energy rays from the sun cause sunburns on your skin? These same intense rays have enough power to split oxygen molecules in the sky!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's take a journey 30 kilometers straight up into the sky! This layer of our atmosphere is called the Stratosphere, and it contains our planet's superhero shield: the Ozone Layer.

But how does ozone (O₃) actually get made up there? 

Well, most of the oxygen we breathe is O₂—two oxygen atoms holding hands tightly. They are very happy and stable this way. If visible light (the light we can see) or infrared light (heat) hits them, nothing happens. It's too weak to break their bond. 

But the sun also blasts out Ultraviolet (UV) radiation. UV radiation is basically invisible light on steroids. It has so much energy that when a high-energy UV ray crashes into an O₂ molecule, it acts like a pair of super-sharp molecular scissors. It violently snaps the bond between the two oxygen atoms! 

The chemical equation looks like this: 
$\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{UV light}} \text{O}^{\bullet} + \text{O}^{\bullet}$

Now you have two lonely, highly active single oxygen atoms. These single atoms are desperate for a partner. So, they fly around and bump into unbroken, happy O₂ molecules. They stick to them, turning a duo into a trio!

$\text{O}_2 + \text{O}^{\bullet} \rightarrow \text{O}_3$ (Ozone!)

And just like that, ozone is born! So, without the super-strong energy of Ultraviolet (UV) radiation to act as the initial scissors, the oxygen duos would never break apart, and we would have no ozone layer to protect us.

questions.Question: Q34. The gas 'A' is having very low reactivity reaches to stratosphere. It is non-toxic and non-flammable but dissociated by UV-radiations in stratosphere. The intermediates formed initially from the gas 'A' are
questions.Hint: Gas 'A' is a CFC (Chlorofluorocarbon), used in old refrigerators. When UV light hits it, the weakest bond snaps. Which atom is easier to break off: Fluorine (small and grips tightly) or Chlorine (larger and grips loosely)?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is the story of how a seemingly 'perfect' human invention accidentally punched a hole in our sky.

Decades ago, scientists invented gases called Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). They were miracle chemicals! They were completely non-toxic (you could breathe them), non-flammable (they wouldn't catch fire), and incredibly stable (low reactivity). We used them in millions of refrigerators and air conditioners. This is our 'Gas A'.

Because Gas A is so tough and stable, when it leaks out of a fridge, it doesn't break down in the lower atmosphere. It just floats higher and higher, surviving for years, until it finally reaches the stratosphere (where the ozone layer lives).

Down on Earth, nothing could break CFCs. But the stratosphere is a warzone of intense, high-energy Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun. When UV light hits a CFC molecule (like CF₂Cl₂), the immense energy forces the molecule to crack open. 

But which piece breaks off? A CFC is made of Carbon, Fluorine, and Chlorine. The Carbon-Fluorine bond is incredibly short and strong—they hold hands very tightly. But the Carbon-Chlorine bond is longer and weaker. 

So, the UV light acts like a karate chop right on the weakest link, snapping the C-Cl bond! 

$\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{UV}} \text{CF}_2\text{Cl}^{\bullet} + \text{Cl}^{\bullet}$

This releases a single, highly energetic Chlorine atom called a 'Chlorine free radical' ($\text{Cl}^{\bullet})$. Free radicals are like chemical ninjas—they are insanely reactive. A single Chlorine free radical will go on a rampage, tearing apart 100,000 ozone molecules before it finally settles down. This is exactly how the ozone hole was created!

questions.Question: Q35. BOD values (in ppm) for clean water (A) and polluted water (B) are expected respectively
questions.Hint: BOD stands for 'Biochemical Oxygen Demand'. Think of it as a 'room service bill' for bacteria. Do bacteria order more oxygen in a clean, empty river, or a dirty river filled with sewage they can eat?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into water testing! To figure out if a river or lake is clean, scientists measure something called BOD: Biochemical Oxygen Demand. 

What does that mean? Let me give you a fun analogy. 

Imagine bacteria in a lake are guests at a hotel, and oxygen is their food. If the water is crystal clear and pristine (clean water), there isn't much garbage, dead leaves, or sewage in it. Because there is no food, very few bacteria live there. Therefore, the bacteria's 'demand' for oxygen is extremely low. 

Scientifically, clean, pure water has a very low BOD value, usually less than 5 ppm (parts per million). It means the bacteria are only asking for a tiny bit of oxygen.

Now, imagine someone dumps a truckload of sewage or organic waste into the river (polluted water). Suddenly, it's an all-you-can-eat buffet for the bacteria! Millions of bacteria arrive for the feast. As they eat all that waste, they breathe in massive amounts of dissolved oxygen. Their 'demand' for oxygen skyrockets. 

Highly polluted water has a BOD value that is much higher, typically greater than 17 ppm. Because the bacteria are greedily taking all the oxygen to digest the waste, there is no oxygen left for the poor fish, and they suffocate.

So, the golden rule is: Low BOD = Clean water (less than 5 ppm). High BOD = Dirty, polluted water (greater than 17 ppm). This matches our first option perfectly!

questions.Question: Among the gases, (a)-(e) the gases that cause greenhouse effect are: (1) CO₂ (2) H₂O (3) CFCs (4) O₂ (5) O₃
questions.Hint: Think about whether symmetrical diatomic molecules like Nitrogen or Oxygen can absorb infrared radiation.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Imagine it is a freezing winter night and you pull a big, cozy blanket over yourself. How exactly does it keep you warm? The blanket doesn't magically create heat; it just traps the body heat you are already giving off so it doesn't escape into the cold room. Our Earth operates in a very similar way! It has a giant, invisible blanket made of gases called the atmosphere. The sun sends us bright light, which warms the Earth. Then, the Earth tries to cool off by shining invisible heat rays (called Infrared or IR radiation) back out into deep space. 

But wait! Some gases in the atmosphere catch those heat rays and send them bouncing right back down to the ground. This trapping of heat is called the 'Greenhouse Effect,' and the gases that do it are 'Greenhouse Gases.' Without them, Earth would be an icy wasteland. Now, which ones are they? Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is the famous one we breathe out and cars produce. Water vapor (H₂O) is actually the biggest natural greenhouse gas, forming clouds and trapping a massive amount of heat. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which come from old air conditioners, are super strong synthetic heat-trappers. Ozone (O₃) also acts as a greenhouse gas when it's hovering lower to the ground. 

But what about Oxygen (O₂)? Oxygen is a very neat, perfectly symmetrical molecule made of two identical atoms pulling on each other equally. Because it is completely balanced (it has no 'dipole moment' when it vibrates), it simply ignores the infrared heat rays. The heat passes right through it like a ghost! Thus, O₂ is NOT a greenhouse gas. Therefore, the gases that cause the greenhouse effect are CO₂, H₂O, CFCs, and O₃. Choosing the option that excludes Oxygen gives us our perfect answer!

questions.Question: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) is the amount of oxygen required (in ppm):
MCQ_Options: by bacteria to break down organic matter in a certain volume of a sample of water.
by aquatic animals to survive in a polluted water body.
to chemically oxidize all organic and inorganic impurities in water.
by aquatic plants to perform photosynthesis during the night.
questions.Hint: Focus on the word 'Biochemical'. It relates to living organisms (bio) performing a chemical breakdown of waste.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine a bustling underwater city inside a river, filled with millions of tiny, invisible bacteria. These bacteria act as the ultimate 'clean-up crew' of the water. Whenever dead leaves, animal waste, or human sewage (we call all of this 'organic matter') falls into the water, these bacteria enthusiastically get to work eating and breaking it down. But just like you and me, bacteria need to breathe oxygen while they do hard physical work! 

Biochemical Oxygen Demand, or BOD for short, is exactly what it sounds like. It is the 'demand' or amount of 'oxygen' that these 'biochemical' creatures (the bacteria) need to completely break down the organic waste in a certain amount of water over a specific period (usually 5 days). 

Why is this so important for scientists to measure? Well, if a factory dumps a massive amount of raw sewage into a beautiful, clear lake, the bacteria get an all-you-can-eat buffet. They multiply rapidly and eat like crazy, breathing in almost ALL the dissolved oxygen in the water. If the bacteria greedily use up all the oxygen, there is none left for the poor fish, crabs, and plants! The fish eventually suffocate, and the lake essentially dies. 

Therefore, scientists measure BOD to see exactly how polluted a body of water is. A low BOD (like 1 to 2 ppm, which stands for parts per million) means the water is beautifully clean and fresh, with very little trash for the bacteria to eat. A high BOD (like 10 to 20 ppm or higher) means the water is heavily polluted with organic waste, and the oxygen is being drained dangerously fast. So, BOD measures the exact amount of oxygen required by bacteria to break down organic matter!
questions.Answer: by bacteria to break down organic matter in a certain volume of a sample of water.

questions.Question: Thermal power plants can lead to:
questions.Hint: Thermal power plants burn fossil fuels like coal, which releases massive amounts of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides into the air.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered exactly where the electricity to charge your smartphone or run your television comes from? A huge portion of it comes from gigantic factories called 'Thermal Power Plants.' These massive plants generate electricity by burning mountains of coal to boil water, creating steam that spins giant turbines. It sounds great, but there is a major environmental catch. 

Coal isn't just pure, clean carbon. It is a rock pulled from deep underground, and it has lots of nasty impurities packed inside it, predominantly sulfur and nitrogen. When you throw coal into a blazing furnace, you don't just get heat; you also accidentally 'burn' those impurities. The sulfur reacts with oxygen to turn into Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂), and the nitrogen turns into various Nitrogen Oxides (usually written as NO_x). 

These gases float out of the massive smokestacks and travel high up into the clouds. Up there in the sky, they meet water droplets (H₂O) and atmospheric oxygen. A slow but powerful chemical reaction happens, transforming the sulfur dioxide gas into Sulfuric Acid (H₂SO₄) and the nitrogen oxides into Nitric Acid (HNO₃). Do those names sound slightly scary? They should—they are incredibly strong acids! 

When the clouds finally burst and it rains, these liquid acids mix with the raindrops and fall directly back to Earth. This phenomenon is known as 'Acid Rain.' Acid rain is devastating for the environment. It burns and strips the leaves off trees, turns beautiful fresh-water lakes incredibly toxic so fish can no longer survive, and even slowly eats away at solid stone statues and historical monuments, like the beautiful white marble of the Taj Mahal! Therefore, the pollution from thermal power plants directly leads to acid rain.

questions.Question: The statement that is not true about ozone is:
MCQ_Options: It is a beneficial gas in the troposphere.
It protects us from harmful UV radiation in the stratosphere.
It is a pale blue gas with a strong, pungent smell.
questions.Hint: Remember the golden rule of atmospheric ozone: 'Good up high, bad nearby.'
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the incredible molecule called Ozone (O₃). Ozone is fascinating because it has a classic 'Jekyll and Hyde' personality—it can be a life-saving superhero or a toxic villain, depending entirely on *where* it is located! 

Imagine our Earth is wrapped in layers of air. The bottom layer, where we live, build houses, breathe, and fly kites, is called the Troposphere. The next layer up, way above the rain clouds and commercial airplanes, is called the Stratosphere. 

Up in the stratosphere, ozone is our ultimate superhero. It forms a dense, invisible shield around the Earth that actively absorbs deadly Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. Without this shield, the sun's harsh rays would cause severe sunburns, skin cancer, and destroy plant life. We desperately need it up there! This makes the statement 'It protects us from harmful UV radiation in the stratosphere' absolutely true. 

However, down here in the troposphere, ozone is a nasty villain. It is not naturally supposed to be near the ground in high concentrations. Down here, it forms artificially when exhaust fumes from millions of cars mix with bright sunlight in a process called photochemical smog. When humans or animals breathe in ozone gas, it severely irritates our lungs, triggers coughing and asthma attacks, and even damages the leaves of crops. The scientific phrase to remember this is: 'Good up high, bad nearby.'

Therefore, the statement 'It is a beneficial gas in the troposphere' is completely FALSE! In the troposphere, it is a highly toxic pollutant. (As a fun fact, the other options are true: it is rapidly destroyed by CFCs from old aerosols, and it actually is a pale blue gas with a sharp, electrical smell—like the crisp smell in the air right after a heavy lightning storm!).
questions.Answer: It is a beneficial gas in the troposphere.

questions.Question: The presence of soluble fluoride ion upto 1ppm concentration in drinking water, is:
MCQ_Options: Harmful and causes mottling of teeth.
Harmful and causes severe bone damages.
questions.Hint: At very low concentrations (around 1 ppm), fluoride acts as a medicine for your tooth enamel. It only becomes dangerous at higher levels.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why your toothpaste tube usually proudly advertises 'Fluoride Toothpaste' on the front? The fluoride ion is a super interesting chemical because it perfectly operates on the 'Goldilocks Principle'—the amount you consume needs to be *just right*. 

Our teeth are covered in a hard, protective outer shell called enamel. Enamel is mostly made of a natural mineral called hydroxyapatite. When you have a tiny, controlled bit of soluble fluoride in your daily drinking water (specifically around 1 part per million, or 1 ppm), something amazing happens on a microscopic level. The fluoride ions literally swap places with parts of your tooth enamel, converting the standard hydroxyapatite into a new, upgraded material called *fluorapatite*. 

Why is this an upgrade? Fluorapatite is much tougher, physically harder, and vastly more resistant to the nasty acids that cavity-causing bacteria produce in your mouth. So, at a low dose of 1 ppm, fluoride is your best friend—it safely and effectively acts like an invisible shield, preventing tooth decay and cavities! 

But if the concentration gets too high, things go very wrong. At around 2 ppm or more, it causes a condition called 'mottling,' which means your teeth develop ugly, permanent brown patches. And if the concentration gets insanely high (above 10 ppm), it actually stops helping your teeth and starts attacking your bones, making them painfully stiff and deformed in a horrible disease called skeletal fluorosis. 

The question specifically asks about the presence of fluoride *up to 1 ppm*. Because this is the perfect 'Goldilocks' zone, it is absolutely safe and incredibly beneficial. This is exactly why many cities around the world purposefully add just 1 ppm of fluoride to their public tap water to protect everyone's smiles!

questions.Question: The upper stratosphere consisting of the ozone layer protects us from the sun's radiation that falls in the wavelength region
questions.Hint: Visible light is roughly 400-700 nm. The dangerous UV radiation the ozone layer absorbs has shorter wavelengths (higher energy) than visible light.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever noticed that if you stay out in the bright summer sun too long without sunscreen, your skin turns fiery red and painful? That burn doesn't come from the bright visible sunlight that helps you see; it comes from invisible, highly energetic rays called Ultraviolet (UV) radiation. 

The Sun is like a giant cosmic radio tower, blasting out energy waves in all shapes and sizes, which scientists measure in 'wavelengths.' Visible light, which lets our eyes see all the beautiful colors of the rainbow, has a wavelength between 400 and 700 nanometers (nm). 

But UV rays are different. They have *shorter* wavelengths than visible light. In the rules of physics, a shorter wavelength means the wave carries *higher energy*. That extreme high energy is exactly what makes UV rays dangerous—they can literally smash into your skin cells like tiny bullets, breaking chemical bonds and damaging your DNA, leading to skin cancer! 

The most dangerous types of UV rays are categorized as UV-B and UV-C, and their wavelengths fall right into the 200 to 315 nm range. If these specific high-energy rays hit the ground at full force, life on Earth's surface would practically be cooked! 

But thankfully, we have an invisible superhero floating high up in the sky: the Ozone Layer in the upper stratosphere. The ozone molecules (O₃) are specifically tuned by nature to absorb energy right in that sweet spot of 200 - 315 nm. When the deadly UV radiation hits an ozone molecule, the ozone absorbs the blast of energy and safely breaks apart into standard oxygen gas (O₂) and a free oxygen atom (O), instead of letting the radiation pass through to the ground. It sacrifices itself to shield the Earth! Therefore, the ozone layer perfectly blocks the sun's harmful radiation in the 200 - 315 nanometer wavelength region.

questions.Question: The compound that is NOT a common component of photochemical smog is:
questions.Hint: Photochemical smog is formed near the ground from car exhaust. Think about which of these compounds comes from refrigerators and floats to the upper atmosphere instead.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever looked at a skyline of a heavily populated city on a hot, sunny summer day and noticed a thick, hazy, yellowish-brown fog hanging in the air? That ugly, irritating haze is called 'Photochemical Smog.' 

Let's break down the name to understand it better: 'Photo' means light, and 'chemical' means reactions. So, it's a type of smog created when chemicals bake and react in the bright sunlight! But where do the chemicals come from? When millions of cars are stuck in traffic burning gasoline, their tailpipes spit out unburnt fuel vapors (called hydrocarbons) and nitrogen oxides (NO_x). 

When the sun's intense UV rays hit these specific exhaust gases hovering over the city, it acts like turning on a giant chemical blender. The gases undergo complex chain reactions and form a highly toxic soup of brand new, irritating compounds. The main, notorious ingredients of this spicy smog soup are Ozone (O₃), Acrolein (which is what makes your eyes intensely water and burn on a smoggy day), Formaldehyde, and a terribly nasty chemical called Peroxyacetyl Nitrate (we just call it PAN for short). All of these exist right down here on the ground, making us cough. 

But what about Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)? CFCs are completely different types of chemicals. They are artificial gases that used to be heavily used in old refrigerators, air conditioners, and aerosol spray cans. Down here on the ground, CFCs are super stable and incredibly 'lazy'—they do not participate in the chaotic, sunny reactions of city smog at all! Instead, because they don't react with anything near the ground, they slowly and quietly float all the way up into the stratosphere, where they eventually cause massive damage by attacking the ozone layer. 

Since CFCs have absolutely zero to do with the sunny, exhaust-filled smog of the lower atmosphere, they are definitely NOT a component of photochemical smog!

questions.Question: Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), an eye irritant, is produced by:
questions.Hint: Think about the type of smog that occurs in warm, sunny, and dry climates where heavy traffic and car exhaust are common. It requires sunlight to form!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Have you ever walked through a really busy city on a hot, sunny day, and suddenly your eyes started stinging and watering? That burning sensation is often caused by a sneaky chemical called PAN, which stands for Peroxyacetyl Nitrate. But here is the wild part: cars and factories do not actually release PAN into the air. So, where does it come from? 

PAN is what chemists call a 'secondary pollutant'. Imagine you are baking a cake. You do not just pull a fully baked cake out of a bag of flour; you have to mix ingredients together and put them in an oven. The atmosphere does the exact same thing! 

When cars run, their engines get super hot and release two main 'ingredients' into the air: Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) and Unburnt Hydrocarbons (which are just tiny, vaporized bits of fuel). When these ingredients float up into the sky, the bright, warm sunlight acts exactly like an oven. The UV rays from the sun cook these chemicals, causing them to react with each other and with oxygen. 

First, the sunlight breaks down the Nitrogen Oxides, which leads to the creation of Ozone ($O_3$) down near the ground where we breathe. Then, this Ozone reacts with those unburnt bits of fuel (hydrocarbons). The final result of this sunny atmospheric baking session? A nasty mix of chemicals including our eye-stinging friend, PAN! Because this whole process requires 'photons' (light particles from the sun) to trigger the chemical reactions, the resulting pollution cloud is called 'Photochemical Smog'. It literally translates to 'smog made by light and chemicals'. So, the next time your eyes water on a smoggy summer day, you know exactly which 'bakery' made it!

questions.Question: The higher concentration of which gas in air can cause stiffness of flower buds?
questions.Hint: This gas is famously produced when we burn sulfur-containing fossil fuels like coal, and it smells sharply like a freshly struck match. Plants absolutely hate it!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are a beautiful little flower bud, just getting ready to bloom. You need fresh, clean air to grow properly. But suddenly, the air fills up with a sharp, choking gas that smells exactly like burnt matches. How would you react? You'd probably tense up! 

In the plant world, this happens for real, and the culprit is a gas called Sulfur Dioxide ($SO_2$). We humans release a massive amount of $SO_2$ into the air mostly by burning coal in power plants and roasting sulfur-containing metal ores. While it makes humans cough and wheeze, plants are actually much, much more sensitive to $SO_2$ than we are. 

When a plant breathes in $SO_2$ through the tiny pores on its leaves (called stomata), the gas mixes with the moisture inside the plant. Sulfur dioxide plus water creates a weak acid called sulfurous acid. This acid is toxic to the delicate inner workings of the plant. It disrupts their ability to make food (chlorophyll) and messes up their cellular structure. 

Because of this chemical stress, the tissues in the flower buds lose their natural flexibility. They become incredibly stiff and rigid, almost as if the plant is paralyzed. Because they become so stiff, these buds end up falling off the plant before they even have a chance to open up into flowers. It is a sad side effect of air pollution, but understanding it helps environmental chemists design better scrubbers for factory smokestacks to trap the $SO_2$ before it can hurt the flowers!

questions.Question: Water samples with BOD values of 4ppm and 18ppm, respectively, are:
questions.Hint: BOD stands for 'Biochemical Oxygen Demand'. Think of it as the 'appetite' of bacteria. If the appetite is very high, it means there is a ton of garbage (organic waste) for them to eat!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us talk about the 'appetite' of rivers and lakes! Yes, bodies of water have an appetite, but not for pizza or burgers—they are hungry for oxygen. We measure this hunger using a brilliant concept called BOD, which stands for Biochemical Oxygen Demand.

Here is how it works. When leaves, animal waste, or sewage fall into a river, tiny microscopic bacteria rush in to eat it. But to break down (oxidize) this organic waste, the bacteria need to breathe oxygen, just like we do! The more waste there is in the water, the more bacteria show up to the feast, and the more oxygen they suck out of the water. 

Therefore, BOD is simply a measurement of how much oxygen the bacteria demand to clean up the water. 

If you have a pristine, sparkling mountain stream, there is barely any waste in it. The bacteria don't need much oxygen at all. By definition, clean water has a BOD value of less than 5 ppm (parts per million). It's like having a very clean bedroom—it only takes 5 minutes of energy to tidy up.

But what if a sewer pipe leaks into a lake? The water becomes filled with waste. The bacteria multiply like crazy and demand a massive amount of oxygen. Highly polluted water has a BOD value of 17 ppm or higher. It's like a bedroom that looks like a tornado hit it—it takes a huge amount of energy to clean!

So, looking at our two water samples: The first one has a BOD of 4 ppm, which is under 5, meaning it's wonderfully clean. The second sample has a BOD of 18 ppm, which is over 17, meaning it is highly polluted. So the answer is 'Clean and highly polluted'. Easy, right?

questions.Question: The concentration of dissolved oxygen (DO) in cold water can go up to:
questions.Hint: Think about a bottle of soda. Does it stay fizzier (keep its dissolved gas) when it is freezing cold in the fridge, or when it is sitting hot in the sun?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how fish breathe underwater? They don't have scuba gear, and they certainly cannot break apart the $H_2O$ water molecules to get oxygen. Instead, they rely on 'Dissolved Oxygen' (abbreviated as DO). These are free oxygen gas molecules from the air that have mixed and dissolved perfectly into the liquid water.

But here is a super cool rule of chemistry: gases dissolve much better in cold liquids than in hot liquids. Think about a bottle of soda. The 'fizz' is just dissolved carbon dioxide gas. If you leave a soda out in the hot sun, it goes flat really fast. Why? Because the heat gives the gas molecules extra kinetic energy. They start jumping around frantically and eventually escape into the air. But if you keep the soda in a cold fridge, the gas molecules are sluggish, lack energy, and stay happily trapped in the liquid.

Oxygen in water behaves the exact same way! In warm water, oxygen molecules easily escape into the atmosphere. But in freezing cold water, the oxygen stays trapped. 

Even in the best, coldest conditions, water isn't great at holding oxygen. The absolute maximum amount of dissolved oxygen cold water can hold is about 10 ppm (parts per million). To put that in perspective, out of 1 million molecules of water, only 10 of them will be oxygen gas! It sounds tiny, but it is just enough for fish to survive. If the water warms up or gets polluted and the DO drops below 6 ppm, fish start struggling to breathe and can die. So, the magic upper limit for dissolved oxygen in cold water is roughly 10 ppm.

questions.Question: A water sample has ppm level concentration of the following metals: Fe = 0.2; Mn = 5.0; Cu = 3.0; Zn = 5.0. The metal that makes the water sample unsuitable for drinking is:
questions.Hint: Our bodies are actually pretty okay with small amounts of zinc, copper, and iron. But there is one metal on this list whose strict safety limit is extremely low—just 0.05 ppm! Which one is exceeding its limit by 100 times?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Drinking water isn't just pure $H_2O$. It actually contains microscopic amounts of dissolved metals! Believe it or not, your body actually *needs* some of these metals to survive. Iron helps your blood carry oxygen, zinc boosts your immune system, and copper helps form red blood cells. 

But in chemistry and biology, there is a golden rule: 'The dose makes the poison.' Think of it like adding salt to a bowl of soup. A tiny pinch makes it delicious and healthy. But if you accidentally dump the entire salt shaker into your bowl, the soup becomes toxic and impossible to eat. 

To keep us safe, scientists at health organizations (like the WHO or the Bureau of Indian Standards) have set strict upper limits for how much of each metal is allowed in our drinking water. Let us look at the report card for this specific water sample:

1. Iron (Fe): The allowed limit is 0.2 ppm. Our sample has 0.2 ppm. It's right on the edge, but safe!
2. Copper (Cu): The allowed limit is 3.0 ppm. Our sample has exactly 3.0 ppm. Safe!
3. Zinc (Zn): The allowed limit is 5.0 ppm. Our sample has exactly 5.0 ppm. Safe!
4. Manganese (Mn): The allowed limit for Manganese is incredibly tiny—only 0.05 ppm! But our water sample has 5.0 ppm of Manganese. 

If you do the math, 5.0 is exactly 100 times larger than the allowed limit of 0.05! Drinking water with that much manganese can cause serious neurological damage over time. Because manganese has massively failed its safety test, it is the one metal that makes this entire water sample completely unsuitable and dangerous for drinking.

questions.Question: The pH of rain water, is approximately:
questions.Hint: Normal, unpolluted rain isn't perfectly neutral! It is actually slightly acidic because it naturally mixes with carbon dioxide in the atmosphere to make a very weak acid.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Pop quiz: What do you think the pH of totally pure, unpolluted rain is? If you guessed 7.0 (which is the pH of perfectly neutral pure water), you are thinking exactly like a scientist! But surprisingly, you would be slightly wrong. 

The true pH of normal, clean rainwater is actually around 5.6. Let us become atmospheric detectives to figure out why normal rain is slightly acidic.

As a raindrop falls from the clouds, it travels miles and miles through Earth's atmosphere. Our atmosphere is full of naturally occurring Carbon Dioxide gas ($CO_2$). As the raindrop plummets, some of this $CO_2$ dissolves into the water. 

When water ($H_2O$) and Carbon Dioxide ($CO_2$) mix, they chemically react to form something called Carbonic Acid ($H_2CO_3$). This is the exact same weak acid that gives soda and sparkling water its sharp, fizzy taste! 

Because this carbonic acid releases a few positively charged Hydrogen ions ($H^+$) into the raindrop, the pH drops from a neutral 7.0 down to about 5.6. This is totally natural and completely harmless to us and the environment. 

However, you might have heard of the scary term 'Acid Rain'. Acid rain happens when human pollution (like Sulfur Dioxide and Nitrogen Oxides) gets into the air and creates strong acids like Sulfuric Acid and Nitric Acid. If the pH of rain drops *below* 5.6, then we officially call it Acid Rain, and that is when it starts damaging statues, trees, and lakes. But for regular, healthy rain, 5.6 is the magic number!

questions.Question: The correct set of species responsible for the photochemical smog is:
MCQ_Options: NO, NO$_{2}$, O$_{3}$, and unburnt hydrocarbons
questions.Hint: Photochemical smog is born from car exhausts baking in the bright sunlight. What specific nitrogen gases and fuel remnants come from car engines to start this sunny chemical chain reaction?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let us become chemical chefs and write down the exact recipe for Photochemical Smog! 'Photochemical' sounds like a big, intimidating word, but 'photo' simply means light, and 'chemical' means... well, chemicals! So, photochemical smog is just air pollution created by chemicals reacting in the presence of bright sunlight.

Here is how the recipe unfolds step-by-step in the sky above a busy city:

Step 1: The Heat. Inside a car engine, it gets incredibly hot. It is so hot that the normally peaceful Nitrogen ($N_2$) and Oxygen ($O_2$) in the air are forced to combine, creating Nitric Oxide ($NO$). The car exhaust burps this $NO$ out into the street.

Step 2: The Oxidation. Once in the open air, the $NO$ quickly grabs more oxygen to become Nitrogen Dioxide ($NO_2$). This gas has an ugly yellowish-brown color, which is why smog looks so dirty.

Step 3: The Sunlight. Here comes the 'photo' part! Bright UV rays from the sun crash into the $NO_2$ molecules, acting like a hammer that shatters them apart into $NO$ and a highly active, lone Oxygen atom ($O$).

Step 4: The Ozone. That lone Oxygen atom is lonely and aggressive. It immediately attacks regular oxygen molecules ($O_2$) in the air to form Ozone ($O_3$). Ozone is great high up in the atmosphere, but down here on the ground, it is toxic to breathe!

Step 5: The Final Mix. Finally, the Ozone ($O_3$) and the Nitrogen gases ($NO$, $NO_2$) react with 'unburnt hydrocarbons'—which are tiny, vaporized droplets of gasoline that escaped the car engine without burning. Together, they form horrible chemicals like PAN and formaldehyde that make our eyes burn and our lungs ache.

So, looking at our ingredients list, the core species responsible for this whole messy chain reaction are $NO$, $NO_2$, $O_3$, and unburnt hydrocarbons!
questions.Answer: NO, NO$_{2}$, O$_{3}$, and unburnt hydrocarbons

questions.Question: Q50. The regions of the atmosphere, where clouds are formed and where we live, respectively, are:
questions.Hint: Think about the layer of the Earth's atmosphere that touches the ground and contains almost all of the planet's water vapor.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the Earth's atmosphere, which is basically the invisible ocean of air we live at the bottom of! Imagine the atmosphere as an onion with different layers wrapped around the planet. The very first layer, starting right from the ground where you are sitting right now and going up to about 10 kilometers (or 6 miles) high, is called the 'Troposphere'. The word 'tropos' comes from an old Greek word meaning 'change' or 'turning'. This is a perfect name because this layer is constantly moving, mixing, and changing—which is exactly what we call 'weather'!

Because gravity pulls most of the air molecules and water vapor down towards the Earth's surface, almost 99% of all the water vapor in the entire atmosphere is trapped right here in the troposphere. Since clouds are just giant floating collections of tiny water droplets or ice crystals, they can only form where there is water vapor. Therefore, all the fluffy clouds, rainstorms, and snowstorms happen in this exact same layer.

So, to answer the question: where do we live? We live on the ground, inside the troposphere. Where do clouds form? Up in the sky, but still inside that very same troposphere! Even though airplanes sometimes fly at the very top of it to avoid storms, we are all sharing this first layer of our atmospheric onion.

questions.Question: Q51. Excessive release of CO₂ into the atmosphere results in:
questions.Hint: Carbon dioxide acts like a thick blanket around the Earth, trapping the heat that tries to escape into space.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever stepped inside a car that has been parked in the hot sun with its windows rolled up? You probably noticed it feels like an oven inside! This happens because the clear glass windows let the sunlight in, but they trap the heat and stop it from escaping back out into the air. This exact same process happens to our entire planet, and it is called the 'Greenhouse Effect'.

In our atmosphere, Carbon dioxide (CO₂) acts exactly like the glass windows of that hot car. When sunlight hits the Earth, the Earth absorbs it and warms up. The Earth then tries to radiate this heat back out into deep space as invisible infrared energy. However, carbon dioxide molecules are perfectly shaped to absorb this infrared heat, trapping it in the atmosphere.

A normal amount of CO₂ is actually a good thing—it keeps our planet warm enough for liquid water and life. But here is the problem: humans have been burning a massive amount of fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas, which releases an 'excessive' (way too much) amount of CO₂ into the air. By adding more CO₂, we are basically rolling up the Earth's windows and adding extra heavy blankets. This traps way too much heat, causing the overall temperature of the Earth to rise. This planetary heating is what we call 'Global Warming', which leads to melting ice caps, rising sea levels, and extreme weather.

questions.Question: Q52. The layer of atmosphere between 10km to 50km above the sea level is called as:
questions.Hint: This layer sits right above our weather layer and contains the protective ozone shield.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's take a journey upward into the sky! As we learned earlier, the first layer of the atmosphere—where we live and where all the crazy weather happens—is the troposphere, which goes from the ground up to about 10 kilometers. But what happens if we keep flying higher, breaking past the clouds, from 10 kilometers all the way up to 50 kilometers above sea level? You have just entered the 'Stratosphere'!

The word 'strata' means layers. Unlike the troposphere, which is super windy and chaotic, the stratosphere is very calm, stable, and horizontally layered. The heavy, cold air sits safely at the bottom, and the warmer air sits at the top. Because it is so wonderfully calm and completely lacks messy weather or thunderstorms, commercial airline pilots love to fly jet planes in the lower part of the stratosphere to give passengers a smooth, bump-free ride!

But the stratosphere has a much more important job for us living down on Earth: it is the home of the 'Ozone Layer'. Ozone is a special type of oxygen molecule made of three oxygen atoms (O₃). This layer acts like the Earth's giant pair of sunglasses or a planetary sunscreen. It happily absorbs almost all of the sun's dangerous ultraviolet (UV) radiation before it can reach the ground and give us sunburns. So, when you hear about the layer sitting strictly between 10km and 50km high, remember the calm, storm-free Stratosphere and its highly protective ozone shield.

questions.Question: Q53. Assertion: Ozone is destroyed by CFCs in the upper stratosphere. Reason: Ozone holes increase the amount of UV radiation reaching the earth.
MCQ_Options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct
questions.Hint: Does UV radiation reaching the earth chemically explain WHY Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) break down ozone molecules?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a classic 'Assertion and Reason' question, which asks us to play detective. We have two statements, and we need to figure out if they are individually true, and if the second one explains the first. Let's look at the Assertion (the main claim): 'Ozone is destroyed by CFCs in the upper stratosphere.' CFCs stand for Chlorofluorocarbons. These are human-made chemicals that used to be in old refrigerators, air conditioners, and hairspray cans. When they leak and float up to the stratosphere, the sun's harsh UV rays break them apart, releasing hungry Chlorine atoms. Think of Chlorine like Pac-Man—a single chlorine atom can chomp and destroy up to 100,000 ozone (O₃) molecules! So, the Assertion is absolutely True.

Now let's look at the Reason: 'Ozone holes increase the amount of UV radiation reaching the earth.' As we know, ozone acts like Earth's sunscreen. If Pac-Man (Chlorine) eats the ozone, it creates a 'hole' or a dangerously thin patch in our sunscreen. Without that protection, dangerous UV light from the sun easily sneaks through and hits the Earth. So, the Reason is also absolutely True!

But here is the trick: Does the Reason *explain* the Assertion? Let's test it by putting the word 'because' between them. 'Ozone is destroyed by CFCs BECAUSE ozone holes increase UV radiation.' Does that make sense? No! The destruction of ozone CAUSES the UV radiation to increase, not the other way around. The reason CFCs destroy ozone is due to their chemical reaction with O₃, not because of the UV light hitting the Earth's surface. Therefore, both statements are true facts, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation for the Assertion.
questions.Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion

questions.Question: Q54. The recommended concentration of fluoride ion in drinking water is up to 1ppm as fluoride ion is required to make teeth enamel harder by converting [3Ca₃(PO₄)₂·Ca(OH)₂] to:
questions.Hint: Fluoride replaces the hydroxide (OH) group in your tooth enamel to form a much stronger compound. Look for the option where OH is swapped with F.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Did you know that chemistry is the reason you don't get cavities every single time you eat candy? Let's talk about your teeth! The hard, white outer layer of your teeth is called enamel. Enamel is actually a crystal made of calcium and phosphate, and its chemical name is Hydroxyapatite. The formula for this tooth crystal looks pretty scary: $[3Ca₃(PO₄)₂\cdot Ca(OH)₂]$. Notice that little 'OH' at the end? That stands for a hydroxide ion.

When you eat sugary foods, the bacteria in your mouth feast on the sugar and poop out acid. This acid attacks the weak 'OH' part of your tooth enamel, dissolving it and causing painful holes known as cavities!

This is where Fluoride comes to the rescue! Fluoride is an ion (a negatively charged fluorine atom, F⁻) that we intentionally put in toothpaste and drinking water (up to 1 part per million, which is super tiny but effective). When the fluoride washes over your teeth, it does a sneaky chemical swap. It kicks out the weak 'OH' group and replaces it with itself, turning the enamel into a brand new crystal called Fluorapatite: $[3Ca₃(PO₄)₂\cdot CaF₂]$.

Why does this matter? Fluorine is a smaller, tougher, and much more stubborn atom than the OH group. Once it locks into your tooth structure, it makes the enamel significantly harder and much more resistant to the acid produced by mouth bacteria. By simply swapping one tiny piece of the molecule, fluoride literally acts like an armor upgrade for your teeth!

questions.Question: Q55. Biochemical oxygen demand(BOD) value can be a measure of water pollution caused by the organic matter. Which of the following statements is correct?
MCQ_Options: Clean water has a BOD value of less than 5 ppm
Highly polluted water has a BOD value of less than 5 ppm
Clean water has a BOD value of greater than 17 ppm
BOD is a measure of inorganic pollutants only
questions.Hint: If there is no garbage in the water, bacteria won't need to breathe much oxygen. Therefore, clean water should have a very low 'demand' for oxygen.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's imagine a beautiful, crystal-clear pond. If someone dumps a lot of organic garbage into it—like dead leaves, raw sewage, or leftover food—what happens? Bacteria in the water will get super excited and start eating all that organic matter. But just like humans, bacteria need to breathe oxygen to digest their food. As they feast on the garbage, they constantly breathe in the dissolved oxygen from the water.

If there is a massive amount of garbage, the bacteria will multiply and demand a huge amount of oxygen. They will literally suck the water dry of oxygen, leaving none for the fish, causing the fish to suffocate! This demand for oxygen by bacteria is called Biochemical Oxygen Demand, or BOD.

BOD is basically a 'pollution thermometer' for water. If the water is totally clean and pure, there is no organic garbage for the bacteria to eat, so they don't demand much oxygen at all. Clean drinking water has a very low BOD value, usually less than 5 ppm (parts per million). On the other hand, if a river is heavily polluted with sewage, the bacteria are having a massive feast and stealing all the oxygen. Highly polluted water will have a very high BOD value, sometimes greater than 17 ppm!

Looking at our options, we want the statement that perfectly matches this concept. Since low BOD means low pollution (because bacteria aren't consuming the oxygen), the completely correct statement is that clean water has a BOD value of less than 5 ppm. High BOD always points to high organic pollution!
questions.Answer: Clean water has a BOD value of less than 5 ppm

questions.Question: Q56. Which of the following is a set of green house gases?
questions.Hint: Greenhouse gases are molecules that have three or more atoms (or are unsymmetrical), which allows them to vibrate and trap infrared heat.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand greenhouse gases, you have to imagine the Earth trying to stay warm in the freezing cold vacuum of space. The sun sends us heat, but if the Earth didn't have a way to hold onto it, we would freeze into a giant ice ball every single night! Thankfully, certain gases in our atmosphere act like heavy winter blankets, trapping the heat so it doesn't escape back into space. These are brilliantly called 'Greenhouse Gases.'

Why do some gases act like blankets while others do not? It all comes down to the shape of the molecules! The air we naturally breathe is mostly Nitrogen (N₂) and Oxygen (O₂). These molecules are made of two identical atoms bonded together in a straight, rigid line. Because they are so symmetric and tight, they cannot absorb the invisible infrared heat that the Earth radiates. The heat just passes right through them like they aren't even there.

However, molecules with three or more atoms—or atoms of different types—are much more wobbly and flexible. Carbon dioxide (CO₂), Methane (CH₄), Nitrous Oxide (N₂O, laughing gas), Ozone (O₃), and human-made Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) have shapes that perfectly catch and absorb infrared heat waves. When the heat hits them, they start vibrating, dancing, and trapping that wonderful warmth inside the atmosphere.
