2$. NaCl (Table Salt): As soon as salt hits water, it splits into two ions: Na+ and Cl-. 1 salt molecule gives 2 particles! So, i = 2.$
3$. K2SO4: This breaks into two K+ ions and one SO4(2-) ion. That's 2 + 1 = 3 particles! So, i = 3.$
4$. Al2(SO4)3: This is the heavyweight champion! It splits into TWO Al(3+) ions and THREE SO4(2-) ions. That's 2 + 3 = 5 pieces! So, i = 5.$

Because$ Al2(SO4)3 produces the maximum number of particles in the water (it brings a squad of 5 to the party), it will get in the way of the water molecules the most. Therefore, it will cause the LARGEST freezing point depression. Water will have to get super, super cold to freeze through all those obstacles!

questions.Question: Q38. Of the following four aqueous solutions, total number of those solutions whose freezing point is lower than that of 0.10M C2H5 OH is ............... . (Integer answer) (i) 0.10M Ba3(PO4)2 (ii) 0.10M Na2SO4 (iii) 0.10M KCl (iv) 0.10M Li3PO4
questions.Hint: Ethanol (C2H5OH) doesn't split into ions in water. Check the other compounds to see if they split into multiple pieces. More pieces mean a greater drop in the freezing point!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let's play a game of 'Who can freeze the water last?'$

We$ have a standard solution to beat: 0.10M of Ethanol (C2H5OH). Ethanol is an organic molecule, meaning it does NOT break apart into charged ions when it dissolves in water. If you put 1 ethanol molecule in water, it stays as 1 particle. So, its Van't Hoff factor (i) is 1. The effective concentration of particles in the water is simply 0.10 M $	imes 1 = 0.10$ M.$

Now$, let's look at the challengers. Remember, the more particles dissolved in the water, the more they disrupt the water's ability to lock into ice. More particles = more depression (lowering) of the freezing point. So, a 'lower freezing point' just means we need a solution with MORE dissolved particles!$

Let$'s break down the challengers:$

($i) Ba3(PO4)2: When this hits water, it splits into three Barium ions (Ba2+) and two Phosphate ions (PO4 3-). Total pieces = 3 + 2 = 5! Effective concentration = 0.10 $	imes 5 = 0.50$ M.$

($ii) Na2SO4: Splits into two Sodium ions (Na+) and one Sulfate ion (SO4 2-). Total pieces = 2 + 1 = 3! Effective concentration = 0.10 $	imes 3 = 0.30$ M.$

($iii) KCl: Splits into one Potassium ion (K+) and one Chloride ion (Cl-). Total pieces = 1 + 1 = 2! Effective concentration = 0.10 $	imes 2 = 0.20$ M.$

($iv) Li3PO4: Splits into three Lithium ions (Li+) and one Phosphate ion (PO4 3-). Total pieces = 3 + 1 = 4! Effective concentration = 0.10 $	imes 4 = 0.40$ M.$

Look$ at those effective concentrations! Ethanol is sitting at 0.10 M, while our challengers are at 0.50 M, 0.30 M, 0.20 M, and 0.40 M. Because ALL four of these ionic compounds break apart into multiple pieces, they all produce a higher concentration of particles than ethanol.$

Therefore$, ALL 4 solutions will cause a larger freezing point depression, meaning they will all have a LOWER freezing point than ethanol. The total number is 4!

questions.Question: Q39. If 80g of copper sulphate CuSO4.5H2O. is dissolved in deionised water to make 5L of solution. The concentration of the copper sulphate solution is x × 10−3 mol L−1. The value of x is ......... . [Atomic masses Cu = 63.54u, S = 32u, O = 16u, H = 1u ]
questions.Hint: Don't forget to include the 5 water molecules (5H2O) when calculating the molar mass of the beautiful blue copper sulphate crystals!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think of Molarity like making the perfect glass of chocolate milk. 'Molarity' is simply asking: 'How many scoops of chocolate powder (moles) did you mix into your total jug of milk (liters of solution)?'$

Let$'s figure out our 'scoops' first.$
We$ have 80g of bright blue copper sulphate crystals. The chemical formula is CuSO4 $\u00$b7 5H2O. $
Wait$, what is that dot doing there? That dot means there are 5 water molecules physically trapped inside the solid crystal structure for every 1 unit of CuSO4! These are called 'waters of crystallization'. When you weigh out 80g of this powder, you are weighing those trapped water molecules too, so we MUST include them in our molar mass calculation!$

Let$'s calculate the mass of 1 mole (Molar Mass) of CuSO4 $\u00$b7 5H2O:$
Copper$ (Cu): 63.54$
Sulphur$ (S): 32$
Oxygen$ (O) in sulphate: 4 $	imes 16 = 64
Water$ (H2O): H is 1, O is 16, so water is (2$	imes1 + 16) = 18$. Since there are 5 waters: 5 $	imes 18 = 90.

Total$ Molar Mass = 63.54 + 32 + 64 + 90 = 249.54 g/mol.$

Now$, how many 'moles' (scoops) is 80g?$
Moles$ = Given Mass / Molar Mass$
Moles = 80 / 249.54 = 0.32059$ moles.$

Now$ for the concentration (Molarity). We dissolve this into a massive 5 Liter jug.$
Molarity$ (mol/L) = Moles / Volume in Liters$
Molarity = 0.32059$ moles / 5 L = 0.064118 mol/L.$

But$ the question wants the answer in a very specific format: 'x $	imes 10^{-3}$'. Let's convert our decimal to that format by shifting the decimal point 3 places to the right:$
0.064118 = 64.118 	imes 10^{-3}$ mol/L.$

The$ question asks for the value of x as an integer (usually rounded to the nearest whole number in such formats). Rounding 64.118 gives us 64.$

So$, x = 64! You've just calculated the exact chemical concentration of a huge vat of blue solution!

questions.Question: Q40. Two open beakers one containing a solvent and the other containing a mixture of that solvent with a non volatile solute are together sealed in a container. Over time:
MCQ_Options: (A) volume of solvent decreases and solution increases
(B) volume of solvent increases and solution decreases
questions.Hint: Pure solvent evaporates faster than the solution. Since they share the same air space in a sealed container, water vapour will travel through the air from the high-evaporating beaker and condense into the low-evaporating beaker!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a fantastic thought experiment! Imagine placing two open cups inside a giant, sealed glass box. $
Cup$ A has pure water (solvent). $
Cup$ B has water mixed with lots of sugar (solution with a non-volatile solute).$

What$ happens at the surface of the water?$
In$ Cup A, the surface is 100% pure water molecules. They are jumping into the air rapidly, turning into water vapour. This creates a high 'Vapour Pressure'.$
In$ Cup B, the sugar molecules are bulky and block the surface. Because there are fewer water molecules at the surface, fewer of them can jump into the air. This creates a low 'Vapour Pressure'.$

Now$, the sealed box starts filling up with water vapour in the air. The vapour bounces around everywhere, and eventually, the air says, 'Whoa, there's too much water vapour here! We need to push some back into the liquid.' This is called condensation.$

Here$ is where the magic happens:$
The$ water vapour in the air pushes down and condenses equally into BOTH cups. $
But$ wait... Cup A is losing water really fast (evaporating quickly) but gaining it back at a steady rate. $
Cup$ B is losing water very slowly (because of the sugar blocking it) but gaining it back at the exact same steady rate from the air.$

Let$'s look at the net result:$
Cup$ A: Losing faster than it gains $ightarrow$ It shrinks! (Volume decreases)$
Cup$ B: Gaining faster than it loses $ightarrow$ It grows! (Volume increases)$

Over$ time, it literally looks like magic: the water from Cup A is 'teleporting' through the air and filling up Cup B! This will continue until Cup A completely dries up or until their vapor pressures magically match. So, the volume of the pure solvent decreases, while the volume of the solution increases.
questions.Answer: (A) volume of solvent decreases and solution increases

questions.Question: Q41. A set of solutions is prepared using 180g of water as a solvent and 10g of different non-volatile solutes A, B and C. The relative lowering of vapour pressure in the presence of these solutes are in the order [Given, molar mass of A = 100gmol −1; B = 200gmol −1; C = 10,000gmol −1]
questions.Hint: Colligative properties depend only on the NUMBER of particles (moles), not their weight! If you have 10g of very light particles, you will have a huge number of them compared to 10g of heavy particles.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore a fundamental rule of chemistry: 'Colligative Properties'. This is a fancy term that just means: 'I don't care WHAT the molecules are, I only care HOW MANY there are!'$

The$ Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure (RLVP) is one of these properties. When you add a solute to water, it blocks the surface and prevents water from evaporating easily, which lowers the vapour pressure. The MORE solute molecules you add, the MORE the pressure drops!$

So$, to find the order of RLVP, we just need to find out which beaker has the MOST solute molecules. We count molecules using 'moles'.$

The$ formula for moles is: Moles = Mass / Molar Mass.$

We$ added exactly 10g of substance to each beaker. Let's calculate the moles:$

Solute$ A: Molar mass is 100 g/mol. $
Moles$ of A = 10 / 100 = 0.10 moles.$

Solute$ B: Molar mass is 200 g/mol.$
Moles$ of B = 10 / 200 = 0.05 moles.$

Solute$ C: Molar mass is 10,000 g/mol. (These are huge, heavy molecules!)$
Moles$ of C = 10 / 10,000 = 0.001 moles.$

Let$'s use an analogy. Imagine you have 10 kg of bowling balls (Solute C) and 10 kg of marbles (Solute A). Even though they weigh exactly the same, you have WAY more marbles than bowling balls. $

Because$ Beaker A has 0.10 moles of particles, it has the highest number of 'surface blockers', so it will lower the vapour pressure the most.$
Beaker$ B has 0.05 moles, so it's in the middle.$
Beaker$ C has only 0.001 moles (just a few giant bowling balls), so it barely lowers the pressure at all.$

Therefore$, the order of relative lowering of vapour pressure is directly based on the number of moles: A > B > C!

questions.Question: Q42. An open beaker of water in equilibrium with water vapour is in a sealed container. When a few grams of glucose are added to the beaker of water, the rate at which water molecules:
questions.Hint: Glucose molecules are non-volatile, meaning they don't evaporate. Think about what happens to the surface of the water when glucose molecules start floating around there and taking up space.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine a busy swimming pool on a hot summer day. Kids (representing water molecules) are constantly jumping out of the pool onto the deck (evaporating into vapour) and jumping back into the pool (condensing back into liquid). $

When$ the pool is pure water, there is a perfect balance: the number of kids jumping out equals the number of kids jumping in. This balance is called 'equilibrium'.$

Now$, let's pour some glucose into the pool! Glucose is a 'non-volatile solute'. In our analogy, glucose molecules are like giant, heavy inflatable rafts floating on the surface of the pool. These rafts do NOT jump out of the pool (they don't evaporate). $

But$ look at what they do to the kids! The rafts take up a lot of space at the surface of the water. Because the rafts are in the way, there is physically less room for the kids (water molecules) to reach the surface and jump out. $

Because$ the surface is partially blocked by glucose, fewer water molecules can escape into the air every second. Therefore, the rate at which water molecules are LEAVING the liquid DECREASES.$

($Fun fact: Initially, the water vapour in the air is still jumping BACK into the pool at the old, fast rate. Because more are coming in than leaving, the water level will actually try to rise slightly until a brand new, lower equilibrium is reached!). But the immediate effect of adding the glucose is strictly that the escape routes are blocked, so evaporation slows down.

questions.Question: Q43. If 250cm3 of an aqueous solution containing 0.73g of a protein A is isotonic with one litre of another aqueous solution containing 1.65g of a protein B, at 298K, the ratio of the molecular masses of A and B is ______ $\times 10^{-2}$ (to the nearest integer).
questions.Hint: Isotonic means the two solutions have the exact same osmotic pressure, which means their molar concentrations must be equal. Calculate the molarity of both and set them equal to each other!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's imagine you're making two batches of lemonade, and you want them to taste exactly as sweet as each other. In chemistry, when two solutions have the exact same 'concentration of stuff' causing the same water pressure, we call them **isotonic**. The word 'iso' means equal, and 'tonic' relates to pressure!

Osmotic pressure (let's call it $\pi$) is calculated by a cool formula: $\pi = C \times R \times T$, where $C$ is the concentration, $R$ is a constant, and $T$ is temperature. Because they are isotonic at the same temperature, their osmotic pressures are equal: $\pi_A = \pi_B$. This means their concentrations must be equal too: $C_A = C_B$!

Concentration ($C$) is just the number of moles divided by the volume in liters. 
And how do we find moles? Mass divided by Molar Mass ($M$)!

Let's look at Solution A:
Mass = $0.73$ g
Volume = $250$ cm$^3$ = $0.250$ Liters.
Concentration $C_A = \frac{0.73 / M_A}{0.250}$

Now, let's look at Solution B:
Mass = $1.65$ g
Volume = $1$ Litre = $1.0$ Liters.
Concentration $C_B = \frac{1.65 / M_B}{1.0}$

Since $C_A = C_B$, let's set them equal:
$\frac{0.73}{0.250 \times M_A} = \frac{1.65}{1.0 \times M_B}$

Now, we just need to find the ratio of their molecular masses, which is $M_A / M_B$. Let's rearrange the math:
$\frac{M_A}{M_B} = \frac{0.73 \times 1.0}{1.65 \times 0.250}$
$\frac{M_A}{M_B} = \frac{0.73}{0.4125} = 1.7696...$

The question asks for this ratio in the format of something $\times 10^{-2}$. 
$1.7696...$ is the same as $176.96 \times 10^{-2}$. 
Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $177$.

So, the ratio is $177 \times 10^{-2}$. You successfully cracked a complex algebraic puzzle by just remembering that 'isotonic' means 'equal concentration'. Great job!

questions.Question: Q44. Which one of the following statements regarding Henry's law is not correct?
MCQ_Options: Higher the value of KH at a given pressure, higher is the solubility of the gas in the liquid.
The value of KH depends on the nature of the gas.
Higher the value of KH at a given pressure, lower is the solubility of the gas.
The partial pressure of the gas in vapour phase is proportional to the mole fraction of the gas in solution.
questions.Hint: Think of Henry's constant ($K_H$) as a 'stubbornness' factor. If a gas is very stubborn (high $K_H$), does it want to dissolve in the water easily?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why soda fizzes when you open it? It's all because of **Henry's Law**! Henry's Law simply says: if you push harder on a gas (increase the pressure), more of it will get squished into a liquid (dissolve).

The formula for Henry's Law looks like this: 
$p = K_H \times \chi$

Where:
- $p$ is the pressure of the gas pushing down.
- $\chi$ (pronounced 'kai') is the solubility (how much gas actually dissolved).
- $K_H$ is Henry's Law constant.

Now, let's play with this equation. Imagine you keep the pressure ($p$) the exact same. Let's say $p = 100$.
If $K_H$ is a small number (like 2), then the solubility $\chi$ must be big (50) to make the math work ($100 = 2 \times 50$). 
But, if $K_H$ is a huge number (like 50), the solubility $\chi$ must be very small (just 2) to equal 100 ($100 = 50 \times 2$).

Think of $K_H$ as the 'Stubbornness Constant'. A higher $K_H$ means the gas is super stubborn and *hates* dissolving in the liquid. Therefore, a higher $K_H$ means a **lower** solubility.

Looking at the options, the first statement says: 'Higher the value of KH... higher is the solubility'. This is mathematically and scientifically backwards! A high $K_H$ means *low* solubility. Because the question asked us to find the statement that is NOT correct, this is our winner!
questions.Answer: Higher the value of KH at a given pressure, higher is the solubility of the gas in the liquid.

questions.Question: Q45. The freezing point of a diluted milk sample is found to be −0.2^$\circ$ C, while it should have been −0.5^$\circ$ C for pure milk. How much water has been added to pure milk to make the diluted sample?
MCQ_Options: 1.5 times the mass of solvent in pure milk
2.5 times the mass of solvent in pure milk
0.4 times the mass of solvent in pure milk
Equal to the mass of solvent in pure milk
questions.Hint: The freezing point depression ($\Delta T_f$) is directly proportional to concentration. If the freezing point depression goes from 0.5 to 0.2, the concentration dropped! Use the ratio of these temperatures to find the new mass of water.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about freezing point depression! When you dissolve things in water (like the sugars, fats, and proteins in milk), the water molecules get distracted. They want to hold hands and form solid ice, but the dissolved stuff gets in the way. Because it's harder to freeze, you have to cool it down even lower than $0^\circ C$ to force it to freeze. This drop in temperature is called $\Delta T_f$.

The rule is simple: The more 'stuff' dissolved in the water, the lower the freezing point drops. 
$\Delta T_f = K_f \times m$
Here, $m$ is the molality, which means (amount of dissolved stuff) / (mass of water).

Let's look at **Pure Milk**:
It freezes at $-0.5^\circ C$, so $\Delta T_f = 0.5$.
$0.5 = K_f \times \frac{\text{Moles of stuff}}{W_1}$ (where $W_1$ is the original amount of water in pure milk).

Now, someone sneaky added extra water to make **Diluted Milk**:
It freezes at $-0.2^\circ C$, so $\Delta T_f = 0.2$.
The amount of 'milk stuff' (moles) didn't change, but the water increased. Let's call the new extra water $w$.
$0.2 = K_f \times \frac{\text{Moles of stuff}}{W_1 + w}$

Let's divide the Pure Milk equation by the Diluted Milk equation to see the relationship:
$\frac{0.5}{0.2} = \frac{W_1 + w}{W_1}$

$2.5 = \frac{W_1 + w}{W_1}$

Now, multiply both sides by $W_1$:
$2.5 W_1 = W_1 + w$

Subtract $W_1$ from both sides:
$1.5 W_1 = w$

Wow! This means the sneaky person added $1.5$ times the original amount of water ($W_1$). For every 1 cup of water originally in the pure milk, they added 1.5 extra cups of water! By understanding that diluting a solution brings its freezing point closer to normal water ($0^\circ C$), you've successfully caught the milk thief!
questions.Answer: 1.5 times the mass of solvent in pure milk

questions.Concept: Depression in Freezing Point & Ice Separation
questions.Question: Q46. A solution containing 62g ethylene glycol in 250g water is cooled to −10^$\circ$ C. If Kf for water is 1.86K kg mol^{-1}, the amount of water (in g) separated as ice is:
questions.Hint: When water freezes, only PURE water turns into ice, leaving the remaining liquid water more concentrated. Calculate how much liquid water is required to keep exactly 62g of ethylene glycol dissolved so that it freezes right at -10°C.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is one of the coolest real-world applications in chemistry! Ethylene glycol is used as 'antifreeze' in car engines. It mixes with water and stops it from freezing in cold winters. But what happens if it gets *too* cold and starts freezing anyway?

Here is a super important secret about freezing solutions: When saltwater or antifreeze-water starts to freeze, **only the pure water turns into ice**. The dissolved solute (ethylene glycol) refuses to go into the ice crystals, so it stays behind in the remaining liquid water.

Because pure water is leaving to become ice, the remaining liquid gets more and more 'crowded' (concentrated) with ethylene glycol. It will keep freezing until the liquid becomes so concentrated that its new freezing point perfectly matches the outside temperature ($-10^\circ C$).

Let's work backwards! We know the final liquid must have a freezing point depression ($\Delta T_f$) of $10^\circ C$ to survive at $-10^\circ C$.

The formula is: $\Delta T_f = K_f \times m$
$m$ (molality) = $\frac{\text{Moles of solute}}{\text{Mass of liquid water in kg}}$

First, let's find the moles of our solute (ethylene glycol, $C_2H_6O_2$).
Carbon is 12 ($12\times2=24$), Hydrogen is 1 ($1\times6=6$), Oxygen is 16 ($16\times2=32$). Total Molar Mass = $24+6+32 = 62$ g/mol.
Moles = Mass / Molar Mass = $62\text{g} / 62\text{g/mol} = 1$ mole.

Now, let's plug everything into the freezing equation to find out how much liquid water is STILL left holding the antifreeze:
$10 = 1.86 \times \frac{1}{\text{Mass of liquid water}}$

$\text{Mass of liquid water} = \frac{1.86}{10} = 0.186$ kg.
Convert that to grams: $0.186 \times 1000 = 186$ grams.

So, at $-10^\circ C$, exactly $186$ grams of water remains as a liquid to hold the antifreeze. 
But wait! We started with $250$ grams of water. Where did the rest go? It turned into ice!

Ice formed = Initial water - Remaining liquid water
Ice formed = $250\text{g} - 186\text{g} = 64$ g.

Therefore, 64 grams of water separated as ice. You just figured out how car engines survive the winter!

questions.Question: Q47. 1g of a non-volatile non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 100g of two different solvents A and B whose ebullioscopic constants are in the ratio of 1 : 5. The ratio of the elevation in their boiling points, $\Delta$ Tb(A) / $\Delta$ Tb(B), is:
questions.Hint: Boiling point elevation formula is $\Delta T_b = K_b \times m$. If you use the exact same mass of solute in the exact same mass of solvent, the molality ($m$) is identical. How does $\Delta T_b$ rely on $K_b$ then?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are trying to boil water, meaning you want the liquid molecules to jump up into the air as gas. But if you throw in some heavy rocks (a non-volatile solute), those rocks sit at the top of the liquid and block the water from escaping! Now, you have to heat the pot even hotter to force the water out. This is called **Boiling Point Elevation**.

Different liquids (solvents) react to these 'rocks' differently. Some liquids barely care, and some get really held back. This unique personality of a liquid is measured by its **ebullioscopic constant**, called $K_b$.

The mathematical rule for this is:
$\Delta T_b = K_b \times m$
(Elevation in temperature = the liquid's constant $\times$ the concentration of the 'rocks' added).

Let's break down the problem. 
You add $1$g of the exact same solute into $100$g of solvent A, and $1$g of the exact same solute into $100$g of solvent B. 
Because the 'ingredients' amounts are identical, the concentration (molality, $m$) is exactly the same for both pots!

Let's write the equations for both:
For A: $\Delta T_b(A) = K_b(A) \times m$
For B: $\Delta T_b(B) = K_b(B) \times m$

If we want the ratio, we just divide the two equations:
$\frac{\Delta T_b(A)}{\Delta T_b(B)} = \frac{K_b(A) \times m}{K_b(B) \times m}$

Since $m$ is the exact same on the top and bottom, they cancel out beautifully!
$\frac{\Delta T_b(A)}{\Delta T_b(B)} = \frac{K_b(A)}{K_b(B)}$

The question tells us that the ratio of their constants $K_b(A)$ to $K_b(B)$ is $1 : 5$. 
Therefore, the ratio of their boiling point elevations is exactly the same: $1 : 5$!

It's a direct relationship. If one liquid's constant is 5 times stronger, its boiling point shifts 5 times as much. Simple, right?

questions.Question: Q48. For the solution of the gases w, x, y and z in water at 298K. the Henrys law constants (KH) are 0.5, 2, 35 and 40 kbar respectively. The correct plot for the given data is:
MCQ_Options: A graph of partial pressure vs mole fraction will have the steepest slope for gas z.
A graph of partial pressure vs mole fraction will have the steepest slope for gas w.
A graph of partial pressure vs mole fraction will have identical slopes for all gases.
A graph of partial pressure vs mole fraction will have a negative slope for gas z.
questions.Hint: The equation for Henry's Law is $p = K_H \times \chi$. Think of the equation of a straight line, $y = m \times x$. What does $K_H$ represent on a graph?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's put on our math and science goggles at the same time! 

Henry's Law tells us how much gas dissolves in a liquid under pressure. The formula is:
$p = K_H \times \chi$
- $p$ is the partial pressure (how hard we push the gas).
- $\chi$ is the mole fraction (how much gas actually went into the liquid).
- $K_H$ is Henry's Law constant.

Now, have you ever graphed a straight line in math class? The formula is $y = m \times x$, where $m$ is the **slope** (how steep the hill is). 
Look at how perfectly they match up!
$y = p$ (We put pressure on the Y-axis)
$x = \chi$ (We put mole fraction on the X-axis)
$m = K_H$ (The slope of the line is Henry's constant!)

This means if we draw a graph of pressure versus mole fraction, we will get straight lines. The steepness of each line depends completely on $K_H$. 
A small $K_H$ means a gentle, low slope. A massive $K_H$ means a super steep, high slope, like a difficult mountain to climb.

Let's look at our gases:
Gas w: $K_H = 0.5$
Gas x: $K_H = 2$
Gas y: $K_H = 35$
Gas z: $K_H = 40$

Gas 'z' has the highest $K_H$ ($40$ kbar). Therefore, on a graph, gas 'z' will have the steepest slope! When visualizing graphs in chemistry, always match the chemical formula to $y = mx + c$, and it will tell you a clear story.
questions.Answer: A graph of partial pressure vs mole fraction will have the steepest slope for gas z.

questions.Concept: Osmotic Pressure and van't Hoff Factor
questions.Question: Q49. The osmotic pressure of a dilute solution of an ionic compound XY in water is four times that of a solution of 0.01M BaCl2 in water. Assuming complete dissociation of the given ionic compounds in water, the concentration of XY (in mol L^{-1}) in solution is:
questions.Hint: Osmotic pressure cares about the TOTAL number of broken-apart pieces (ions) floating in the water. Use the van't Hoff factor ($i$) to multiply the concentration by the number of pieces. $\pi = i \times C \times R \times T$.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let's crack this code! 
When you put salt in water, it doesn't just stay as one piece of salt. It breaks apart! Osmotic pressure ($\pi$) is a property that *only* cares about the absolute number of pieces floating in the water, not what they are. It's like counting toys in a box. It doesn't matter if they are cars or dolls; it just matters how many there are.

To account for this breaking apart, we use a multiplier called the **van't Hoff factor** ($i$). 
The true formula for osmotic pressure is:
$\pi = i \times C \times R \times T$

Let's look at our first chemical: $BaCl_2$ (Barium Chloride).
When you throw $BaCl_2$ into water, it breaks into ONE Barium piece ($Ba^{2+}$) and TWO Chloride pieces ($2 Cl^-$). 
$1 + 2 = 3$ pieces total! So, $i = 3$.
The concentration ($C$) is $0.01$ M.
So, the osmotic pressure of $BaCl_2$ is: 
$\pi_1 = 3 \times 0.01 \times R \times T = 0.03 RT$

Now, let's look at our second chemical: $XY$.
When $XY$ drops in water, it breaks into ONE $X$ piece and ONE $Y$ piece. 
$1 + 1 = 2$ pieces total! So, $i = 2$.
We don't know its concentration, so let's just call it $C$.
The osmotic pressure of $XY$ is:
$\pi_2 = 2 \times C \times R \times T = 2C \times RT$

The problem gives us a huge clue: The osmotic pressure of $XY$ is exactly **FOUR TIMES** the osmotic pressure of $BaCl_2$.
Mathematically, that means:
$\pi_2 = 4 \times \pi_1$

Let's plug in the pressures we found:
$2C \times RT = 4 \times (0.03 RT)$

The '$RT$' on both sides magically cancels out!
$2C = 4 \times 0.03$
$2C = 0.12$

Divide by 2 to solve for $C$:
$C = 0.06$ M.

Boom! The concentration of the $XY$ solution is $0.06$ mol/L. By remembering to count the hidden 'broken pieces' using the van't Hoff factor, you easily solved an advanced chemistry problem!

questions.Concept: Depression in Freezing Point and van't Hoff Factor
questions.Question: Q50. For 1 molal aqueous solution of the following compounds, which one will show the highest freezing point?
questions.Hint: Remember that adding a solute lowers the freezing point of water. The more pieces the solute breaks into (higher van't Hoff factor, i), the lower the freezing point goes! You want the HIGHEST freezing point, meaning the LEAST change from pure water.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let us dive into this really cool concept called 'Freezing Point Depression.' Imagine a dance floor full of water molecules. When it gets cold (zero degrees Celsius), they like to link arms and form a beautiful, structured solid called ice. Now, if you throw some party crashers (solute molecules) onto the dance floor, they get in the way! The water molecules have a much harder time linking arms. Because of this disruption, you have to make the room even colder to force the water to freeze. This drop in temperature is called Freezing Point Depression.

The rule here is super simple: The more party crashers there are, the colder it needs to get. In chemistry, we measure the number of 'party crashers' a molecule turns into using something called the van't Hoff factor, represented by the letter 'i'. 

Let us look at our suspects. When you put NaCl in water, it splits into two ions: Na+ and Cl-. So, i = 2. 
MgCl2 splits into one Mg2+ and two Cl- ions. So, i = 3. 
AlCl3 splits into one Al3+ and three Cl- ions. So, i = 4. 
But what about Glucose (C6H12O6)? Glucose is a covalent molecule. It is like a tightly bound bowling ball. When you put it in water, it just swims around as one whole molecule. It does not break apart, so i = 1.

The question asks for the HIGHEST freezing point. That means we want the LEAST amount of depression (the temperature closest to normal 0 degrees). To get the least depression, we need the fewest party crashers! Since Glucose has the smallest van't Hoff factor (i = 1), it disrupts the water the least. Therefore, the glucose solution will have the highest freezing point among all of them!

questions.Question: Q51. A solution is prepared by mixing 8.5g of CH2Cl2 and 11.95 g of CHCl3. If vapour pressure of CH2Cl2 and CHCl3 at 298 K are 415 and 200mm Hg respectively, the mole fraction of CHCl3 in vapour form is: (Molar mass of Cl = 35.5gmol −1)
questions.Hint: First, find the moles of each liquid. Then, use Raoult's Law (Partial Pressure = Mole fraction in liquid $\times$ Pure Vapour Pressure) to find the pressure each gas exerts. Finally, use Dalton's Law to find the mole fraction in the vapour phase!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's crack this open step by step! Imagine you have a closed jar. Inside, you have a mixture of two liquids: CH2Cl2 and CHCl3. Both of these liquids are volatile, meaning their molecules are like energetic little kids jumping out of the liquid and into the air space above it (the vapour phase). 

First, we need to figure out exactly how many 'kids' (moles) of each liquid are in the pool.
Step 1: Calculate the molar masses.
For CH2Cl2: Carbon is 12, Hydrogen is 1 (there are 2), and Chlorine is 35.5 (there are 2). 
Molar Mass = 12 + 2(1) + 2(35.5) = 12 + 2 + 71 = 85 g/mol.
Moles of CH2Cl2 = Mass / Molar Mass = 8.5 g / 85 g/mol = 0.1 mol.

For CHCl3: Carbon is 12, Hydrogen is 1, Chlorine is 35.5 (there are 3).
Molar Mass = 12 + 1 + 3(35.5) = 13 + 106.5 = 119.5 g/mol.
Moles of CHCl3 = Mass / Molar Mass = 11.95 g / 119.5 g/mol = 0.1 mol.

Step 2: Find the mole fraction in the liquid.
Total moles in the liquid pool = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 mol.
Mole fraction of CH2Cl2 (let's call it X1) = 0.1 / 0.2 = 0.5.
Mole fraction of CHCl3 (let's call it X2) = 0.1 / 0.2 = 0.5.
They are exactly 50/50 in the liquid!

Step 3: Use Raoult's Law to find how much pressure they create in the air.
Raoult's Law says that the pressure a liquid contributes is its pure pressure multiplied by its fraction in the liquid.
Partial pressure of CH2Cl2 (P1) = X1 $\times$ Pure P1 = 0.5 $\times 415$ mmHg = 207.5 mmHg.
Partial pressure of CHCl3 (P2) = X2 $\times$ Pure P2 = 0.5 $\times 200$ mmHg = 100 mmHg.

Step 4: Find the total pressure and the fraction in the vapour.
The total pressure in the jar is just the sum of both: P_total = 207.5 + 100 = 307.5 mmHg.
Now, the question asks for the mole fraction of CHCl3 in the VAPOUR form. According to Dalton's Law, the fraction of a gas in the air is just its partial pressure divided by the total pressure. 
Vapour mole fraction of CHCl3 (Y2) = P2 / P_total = 100 / 307.5 $\approx 0.325$.

And there we have it! Even though they were 50/50 in the liquid, CH2Cl2 is more volatile (higher pure pressure), so it dominates the air space, leaving CHCl3 with only a 0.325 fraction.

questions.Question: Q52. The solubility of N2 in water at 300K and 500 torr partial pressure is 0.01gL−1. The solubility (in gL−1) at 750 torr partial pressure is:
questions.Hint: Think of a soda bottle! The harder you press down on the gas (higher pressure), the more gas dissolves in the liquid. This is Henry's Law, which states that solubility is directly proportional to pressure (S1 / P1 = S2 / P2).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why opening a fresh bottle of soda makes that satisfying 'hiss' sound, and suddenly bubbles appear out of nowhere? That is Henry's Law in action! 

Henry's Law tells us a very logical story: if you want to force a gas to dissolve into a liquid, you have to push it in. The harder you push (the higher the pressure), the more gas gets trapped inside the liquid (higher solubility). It is a direct relationship! 

Mathematically, we write this as: Solubility is directly proportional to Pressure. 
Or, S $\propto$ P. 
When we have two different situations, we can set up a super easy ratio:
S1 / P1 = S2 / P2

Let's look at the numbers the problem gives us:
Situation 1: 
The pressure (P1) is 500 torr.
The solubility (S1) is 0.01 g/L.

Situation 2: 
The new pressure (P2) is 750 torr. 
We need to find the new solubility (S2).

Let's plug the numbers into our trusty ratio:
0.01 / 500 = S2 / 750

To get S2 by itself, we multiply both sides by 750:
S2 = 0.01 $\times$ (750 / 500)

Let's simplify that fraction. 750 divided by 500 is exactly 1.5. 
So, S2 = 0.01 $\times 1.5$
S2 = 0.015 g/L.

Makes perfect sense, right? We increased the pressure by 1.5 times (from 500 to 750), so the amount of gas squeezed into the water also increased by exactly 1.5 times. Physics and chemistry working perfectly together!

questions.Question: Q53. A solution at 20∘C is composed of 1.5mol of benzene and 3.5mol of toluene. If the vapour pressure of pure benzene and pure toluene at this temperature are 74.7 torr and 22.3 torr, respectively, then the total vapour pressure of the solution and the benzene mole fraction in equilibrium with it will be, respectively:
questions.Hint: Use Raoult's Law: P_total = (Mole fraction of Benzene $\times$ Pure P_Benzene) + (Mole fraction of Toluene $\times$ Pure P_Toluene). Then, find the vapour mole fraction of benzene by dividing its partial pressure by the total pressure.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This problem is a classic Raoult's Law adventure! Imagine you are a DJ mixing two tracks. Track A is Benzene, and Track B is Toluene. The final sound (total vapour pressure) depends on how loud each track naturally is (pure vapour pressure) AND how much of the volume slider you give to each track (mole fraction in the liquid).

Let's figure out the 'volume sliders' (mole fractions) first.
We have 1.5 moles of benzene and 3.5 moles of toluene. 
Total moles in the liquid = 1.5 + 3.5 = 5.0 moles.

Mole fraction of benzene (X_B) = 1.5 / 5.0 = 0.3.
Mole fraction of toluene (X_T) = 3.5 / 5.0 = 0.7.

Now, how loud does each liquid shout into the vapour phase? We use Raoult's Law: Partial Pressure = Mole fraction $\times$ Pure Pressure.

Partial pressure of Benzene (P_B) = X_B $\times$ Pure P_B 
P_B = 0.3 $\times 74.7$ torr = 22.41 torr.

Partial pressure of Toluene (P_T) = X_T $\times$ Pure P_T
P_T = 0.7 $\times 22.3$ torr = 15.61 torr.

To find the total vapour pressure of the whole mixture, we just add them together, like blending the music:
P_total = P_B + P_T = 22.41 + 15.61 = 38.02 torr (which rounds nicely to 38.0 torr).

Finally, the question asks: If you grabbed a sample of the vapour floating above the liquid, what fraction of it is Benzene? 
To find this, we use Dalton's Law. The mole fraction in the vapour (let's call it Y_B) is just Benzene's pressure divided by the total pressure.
Y_B = P_B / P_total = 22.41 / 38.02 = 0.589...
This rounds up perfectly to 0.59.

So, the total pressure is 38.0 torr, and the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour is 0.59. Notice something cool? Benzene was only 30% of the liquid (0.3), but because it evaporates so much easier than toluene (74.7 vs 22.3 torr), it makes up almost 60% of the vapour! The more volatile chemical always wins the race to the air.

questions.Question: Q54. Choose the correct statement with respect to the vapour pressure of a liquid among the following:
MCQ_Options: A) Vapour pressure increases with an increase in temperature.
B) Vapour pressure increases with an increase in intermolecular forces.
C) Vapour pressure depends on the surface area of the container.
D) Vapour pressure is higher for liquids with higher boiling points.
questions.Hint: Think about boiling water on a stove. What happens when you add heat? Do more water molecules want to escape into the air or fewer?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore what 'vapour pressure' actually means using a fun analogy. Imagine a ball pit filled with hyperactive kids (liquid molecules). The kids are constantly bouncing around. Every now and then, a kid bounces high enough to pop completely out of the ball pit and into the air. This escaping is called evaporation! The kids flying around in the air above the pit create a pressure, which we call 'vapour pressure'.

Now let's test our four options to see which one makes sense:

Option B says: 'Vapour pressure increases with an increase in intermolecular forces.' Intermolecular forces are like the kids holding hands. If they hold hands very tightly (strong forces), it is much harder for anyone to jump out of the pit. So, strong forces actually LOWER the vapour pressure. This statement is FALSE.

Option C says: 'Vapour pressure depends on the surface area of the container.' If you make the ball pit wider, more kids can jump out at once, but more kids also fall back in at the same time. The final balanced number of kids in the air remains exactly the same. Surface area changes the RATE of evaporation, but not the final vapour pressure. This statement is FALSE.

Option D says: 'Vapour pressure is higher for liquids with higher boiling points.' Liquids with high boiling points (like thick oil) are very stubborn and don't want to become a gas. They have very strong intermolecular forces, which means very few molecules escape. Therefore, high boiling point means LOW vapour pressure. This statement is FALSE.

Option A says: 'Vapour pressure increases with an increase in temperature.' What is temperature? Temperature is literally just heat energy. If you heat up the liquid, it's like giving all the kids in the ball pit energy drinks. They start jumping wildly! Much more of them will have the energy to break free and fly into the air. More kids in the air = higher vapour pressure. This statement is 100% TRUE!
questions.Answer: A) Vapour pressure increases with an increase in temperature.

questions.Concept: Osmotic Pressure and van't Hoff Factor
questions.Question: Q55. The observed osmotic pressure for a 0.10M solution of Fe(NH4)2(SO4)2 at 25∘C is 10.8atm. The expected and experimental (observed) values of van't Hoff factor (i) will be respectively: (R = 0.082LatmK −1mol −1)
questions.Hint: First, write the dissociation equation for Mohr's salt to count the expected number of ions (i). Then, plug your numbers into the osmotic pressure formula ($\pi$ = iCRT) and solve for the experimental 'i' using the observed pressure of 10.8 atm.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question is a fantastic detective puzzle where theory meets reality! 

First, let's look at the theoretical 'Expected' side. We have a compound called Mohr's salt: Fe(NH4)2(SO4)2. Imagine this as a complex Lego spaceship. When you drop this spaceship into a bucket of water, it breaks apart into specific chunks (ions). Let's count them:
1 piece of Fe^{2+} ion
2 pieces of NH4^{+} ions
2 pieces of SO4^{2-} ions
Total pieces expected = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 pieces.
So, theoretically, the van't Hoff factor (i) should be exactly 5. Every molecule we drop in should give us 5 particles.

Now, let's look at reality ('Observed' side). 
Osmotic pressure is like the pressure water feels when it tries to rush across a membrane to dilute a salty solution. The formula is:
$\pi$ = i $\times$ C $\times$ R $\times$ T
Where:
$\pi$ (Osmotic Pressure) = 10.8 atm (this is what was actually measured in the lab!)
C (Concentration) = 0.10 M
R (Gas Constant) = 0.082 L atm K^{-1} mol^{-1}
T (Temperature in Kelvin) = 25^{$\circ$}C + 273 = 298 K.

Let's plug in the numbers to find the 'real' value of i (i_obs):
10.8 = i_obs $\times 0.10 \times 0.082 \times 298$
10.8 = i_obs $\times 0.10 \times 24.436$
10.8 = i_obs $\times 2.4436$

Now, solve for i_obs:
i_obs = 10.8 / 2.4436 $\approx 4.42$.

So, the expected i is 5, but the observed i is 4.42. 
You might be wondering: 'Hey, where did the missing 0.58 particles go?! Did they vanish?' Not at all! In real life, when ions are floating around in water, positive and negative ions sometimes bump into each other and temporarily stick together. This is called 'ion pairing'. Because some of them are holding hands, they act as one big particle instead of two separate ones, making the actual count of free particles slightly less than the expected 5. Chemistry is beautifully messy like that!

questions.Question: Q56. 12g of a nonvolatile solute dissolved in 108g of water produces the relative lowering of vapour pressure of 0.1. The molecular mass of the solute is :
questions.Hint: Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure is exactly equal to the mole fraction of the solute! Set up the equation: 0.1 = n / (n + N), where 'n' is solute moles and 'N' is water moles. Solve for 'n', then use it to find the molar mass.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's build a mental picture for this! Imagine a pool of pure water. The surface of the pool is 100% water molecules, and they are happily evaporating into the air. Now, imagine you dump a bunch of heavy, lazy beach balls (a non-volatile solute) into the pool. These beach balls float to the surface, but they absolutely refuse to evaporate. Because they are taking up space on the surface, they block the water molecules from escaping. The vapour pressure drops! 

The fraction of the surface that is blocked is exactly equal to the fraction of the molecules that are beach balls. In chemistry, we say: 'Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure (RLVP) equals the mole fraction of the solute.'

Mathematically: RLVP = Mole fraction of solute = n / (n + N)
Where:
'n' = moles of the solute (the beach balls)
'N' = moles of the solvent (the water)

Let's calculate 'N' (moles of water) first.
We have 108 grams of water. 
The molar mass of water (H2O) is 18 g/mol.
So, N = Mass / Molar Mass = 108 / 18 = 6 moles of water.

The problem tells us the RLVP is exactly 0.1. Let's plug what we know into the formula:
0.1 = n / (n + 6)

Now, let's do some simple algebra to find 'n':
Multiply both sides by (n + 6):
0.1(n + 6) = n
0.1n + 0.6 = n

Subtract 0.1n from both sides:
0.6 = 0.9n

Solve for n:
n = 0.6 / 0.9 = 6 / 9 = 2/3 moles.
Awesome, we know we have exactly 2/3 moles of our mystery solute.

The final step is to find its molecular mass. We know the formula for moles is:
Moles = Mass / Molecular Mass
2/3 = 12 grams / Molecular Mass

Let's rearrange to solve for Molecular Mass:
Molecular Mass = 12 $\times$ (3 / 2)
Molecular Mass = 36 / 2 = 18 g/mol.

Boom! The molecular mass of our mystery beach ball solute is 18 g/mol.

questions.Concept: Concentration Terms (Molarity vs Molality) and Density
questions.Question: Q57. The density of a solution prepared by dissolving 120g of urea (mol. mass = 60u) in 1000g of water is 1.15g/mL. The molarity of this solution is :
questions.Hint: Remember that Molarity needs the volume of the ENTIRE solution. First find the total mass of the solution (solute + solvent), then use the density to find its volume!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Imagine you are making the perfect pitcher of sweet lemon water. You have your sugar (the solute) and your water (the solvent). In chemistry, we need exact ways to measure how strong or 'concentrated' this mixture is. 

One common way is **Molarity (M)**, which is simply the number of 'moles' of your solute packed into exactly one Liter of the final mixed solution. Think of it as counting the number of sugar cubes per bucket of lemonade.

Let's break down our chemical recipe step-by-step:

**Step 1: Find the number of 'cubes' (Moles of Urea)**
We have 120 grams of urea. The problem tells us that 1 mole of urea weighs 60 grams (that's its molecular mass). 
So, how many moles do we have?
$$\text{Moles of urea} = \frac{\text{Given Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass}} = \frac{120\text{ g}}{60\text{ g/mol}} = 2\text{ moles}$$

**Step 2: Find the TOTAL mass of the solution**
We poured our 120g of urea into 1000g of water. The Law of Conservation of Mass tells us things don't just disappear! The total weight of the beaker's contents is:
$$\text{Total Mass} = 1000\text{ g (water)} + 120\text{ g (urea)} = 1120\text{ g}$$

**Step 3: Convert that mass into Volume using Density**
Now, Molarity needs the *volume* of the solution in Liters, not its mass. This is where Density comes to the rescue! Density is like a translation dictionary that converts grams into milliliters. The density is $1.15\text{ g/mL}$, which means every 1 milliliter of this syrup weighs 1.15 grams.
$$\text{Volume} = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Density}} = \frac{1120\text{ g}}{1.15\text{ g/mL}} = 973.91\text{ mL}$$

Since Molarity requires Liters, we divide by 1000:
$$973.91\text{ mL} = 0.9739\text{ Liters}$$

**Step 4: Calculate Molarity!**
Now we just divide the moles by the volume in Liters:
$$\text{Molarity (M)} = \frac{\text{Moles}}{\text{Volume in L}} = \frac{2\text{ moles}}{0.9739\text{ L}} \approx 2.05\text{ M}$$

And there we have it! By simply figuring out the total mass and using density to find the volume, you cracked the molarity. Great job!

questions.Concept: Depression of Freezing Point and Van't Hoff Factor
questions.Question: Q58. The freezing point of a 1.00m aqueous solution of HF is found to be -1.91^{$\circ$}C. The freezing point constant of water, K_f is 1.86 K kg mol^{-1}. The percentage dissociation of HF at this concentration is
questions.Hint: Use the formula $\Delta T_f$ = i $\times K_f \times$ m to find the Van't Hoff factor (i). Then, use the relationship between 'i' and the degree of dissociation ($\alpha)$ for an acid that splits into two ions: i = 1 + $\alpha$.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why road workers throw salt on icy roads in winter? It's because adding foreign particles to water makes it harder for the water to freeze. The water molecules want to link up and form solid ice, but the salt particles get in the way! This is called **Freezing Point Depression**. 

In our problem, pure water freezes at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. But this HF (Hydrofluoric acid) solution freezes at $-1.91^{\circ}\text{C}$. The temperature dropped by $1.91^{\circ}\text{C}$. 
$$\Delta T_f = 1.91$$

Now, there is a cool formula to predict how much the freezing point will drop:
$$\Delta T_f = i \times K_f \times m$$
Here:
- $\Delta T_f$ is the drop in temperature ($1.91$)
- $K_f$ is a special constant for water ($1.86$)
- $m$ is the molality (given as $1.00\text{ m}$)
- **$i$** is the **Van't Hoff factor**. This is the super-secret number of particles the HF actually broke into!

Let's find $i$:
$$1.91 = i \times 1.86 \times 1.00$$
$$i = \frac{1.91}{1.86} \approx 1.02688$$

Wait a second, why is $i$ a decimal? 
If HF didn't break apart at all, $i$ would be exactly 1. If every single HF molecule broke completely in half into $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{F}^-$, $i$ would be exactly 2. 
Because $i$ is $1.02688$, it means only a *tiny fraction* of the HF molecules are actually splitting apart! HF is a weak acid, meaning it's pretty shy and mostly stays together.

Let's calculate exactly how many split up. We call this fraction $\alpha$ (degree of dissociation).
For 1 molecule of HF, it splits into 2 pieces. The formula linking $i$ and $\alpha$ is:
$$i = 1 + (n - 1)\alpha$$
Where $n$ is the number of pieces it breaks into (which is 2 for $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{F}^-$).
$$1.02688 = 1 + (2 - 1)\alpha$$
$$1.02688 = 1 + \alpha$$
$$\alpha = 0.02688$$

To turn this into a percentage, multiply by 100:
$$0.02688 \times 100 = 2.688\%$$

Rounding it beautifully gives us **2.7%**. This means out of every 1000 HF molecules, only about 27 are brave enough to split into ions. The rest stay huddled together! You just calculated the inner behavior of molecules using just a thermometer!

questions.Question: Q59. On mixing, heptane and octane form an ideal solution. At 373K, the vapour pressures of the two liquid components (heptane and octane) are 105kPa and 45kPa respectively. Vapour pressure of the solution obtained by mixing 25.0g of heptane and 35g of octane will be (molar mass of heptane = 100g/mol and of octane = 114 g/mol)
questions.Hint: Find the moles of both heptane and octane first. Then calculate their mole fractions. Finally, use Raoult's Law: P_total = (Mole fraction of A $\times$ Pure pressure of A) + (Mole fraction of B $\times$ Pure pressure of B).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the world of mixing liquids! Imagine you have two groups of kids in a room trying to jump out of a window (a safe one onto a bouncy castle!). Heptane kids are highly energetic and jump out frequently (high vapor pressure of $105\text{ kPa}$). Octane kids are more relaxed and don't jump as much (lower vapor pressure of $45\text{ kPa}$). 

When you mix them together, the total jumping pressure of the room depends on two things: how energetic each kid type is naturally, AND how many of each kid type are actually in the room! This beautiful logic is called **Raoult's Law**.

Let's figure out how many of each we have (moles).

**Step 1: Calculate moles of each liquid**
- Moles of Heptane = $\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass}} = \frac{25.0\text{ g}}{100\text{ g/mol}} = 0.25\text{ moles}$
- Moles of Octane = $\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass}} = \frac{35.0\text{ g}}{114\text{ g/mol}} \approx 0.307\text{ moles}$

**Step 2: Find the total moles and the 'Mole Fraction'**
Total moles = $0.25 + 0.307 = 0.557\text{ moles}$

The Mole Fraction ($X$) is simply the percentage of the room that each group occupies.
- Fraction of Heptane ($X_H$) = $\frac{0.25}{0.557} \approx 0.4488$ (about 44.9% of the mix)
- Fraction of Octane ($X_O$) = $\frac{0.307}{0.557} \approx 0.5512$ (about 55.1% of the mix)

**Step 3: Apply Raoult's Law!**
The total pressure is the pressure Heptane contributes PLUS the pressure Octane contributes.
Heptane's contribution = Its pure pressure $\times$ its fraction in the room
$$P_H = 105\text{ kPa} \times 0.4488 = 47.124\text{ kPa}$$

Octane's contribution = Its pure pressure $\times$ its fraction in the room
$$P_O = 45\text{ kPa} \times 0.5512 = 24.804\text{ kPa}$$

**Total Vapour Pressure** = $P_H + P_O = 47.124 + 24.804 = 71.928\text{ kPa}$.

Rounding to one decimal place gives us exactly **72.0 kPa**. You just proved that the overall pressure is a perfect tug-of-war based on who makes up more of the mixture!

questions.Concept: Non-Ideal Solutions and Deviations from Raoult's Law
questions.Question: Q60. A binary liquid solution is prepared by mixing n-heptane and ethanol. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the behaviour of the solution?
MCQ_Options: The solution shows positive deviation from Raoult's Law.
The solution shows negative deviation from Raoult's Law.
The solution formed is an ideal solution.
Ethanol and n-heptane react to form a completely new compound.
questions.Hint: Ethanol molecules love to hold hands via Hydrogen bonding. n-heptane is non-polar and breaks up this hand-holding. If molecules hold onto each other less tightly after mixing, they escape as gas more easily!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Picture a group of best friends standing in a tight circle, holding hands. In the chemical world, this is pure **Ethanol**. Ethanol molecules have an OH group, which allows them to form strong, sticky connections with each other called **Hydrogen Bonds**. Because they hold on to each other so tightly, it's hard for them to fly away and turn into a gas.

Now, imagine dropping a totally different kid right into the middle of their circle. This newcomer is **n-heptane**. n-heptane is a long, greasy, non-polar molecule. It doesn't know how to hold hands (it can't hydrogen bond!). 

When you mix n-heptane into the ethanol, the bulky heptane molecules wedge themselves between the ethanol molecules. They physically break those strong hydrogen bonds! 

Because the ethanol molecules are no longer holding onto each other as tightly, it suddenly becomes *much easier* for them to let go and escape into the air as a gas. 

In chemistry, when a mixture escapes into the gas phase *easier* than Raoult's Law predicts (creating a higher vapor pressure), we call it a **Positive Deviation from Raoult's Law**. The interactions between the two different liquids (Heptane-Ethanol) are WEAKER than the interactions they had by themselves (Ethanol-Ethanol). 

So, because the mixture is 'less sticky' than the pure liquids, it evaporates faster, creating a higher pressure. Thus, it shows a positive deviation!
questions.Answer: The solution shows positive deviation from Raoult's Law.

questions.Question: Q61. A mixture of ethyl alcohol and propyl alcohol has a vapour pressure of 290mm at 300K. The vapour pressure of propyl alcohol is 200mm. If the mole fraction of ethyl alcohol is 0.6, its vapour pressure (in mm) at the same temperature will be
questions.Hint: You know the total pressure (290) and the pure pressure of propyl alcohol (200). If the mole fraction of ethyl alcohol is 0.6, the mole fraction of propyl alcohol must be 0.4. Plug these into Raoult's Law to solve for the pure pressure of ethyl alcohol!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
We are back to playing detective with our liquid mixtures! This question is like the previous one on Raoult's Law, but instead of finding the total pressure, we are working backward to find a missing piece.

Let's lay out our clues:
1. The total pressure of the mixed solution ($P_{\text{total}}$) = $290\text{ mm}$.
2. The pure vapour pressure of propyl alcohol ($P^0_{\text{propyl}}$) = $200\text{ mm}$.
3. The fraction of the mixture that is ethyl alcohol ($X_{\text{ethyl}}$) = $0.6$.

First, a simple logical step: If a pizza is 60% pepperoni, it must be 40% cheese. Mixtures work the same way. The mole fractions must always add up to exactly 1. 
If $X_{\text{ethyl}} = 0.6$, then the fraction of propyl alcohol ($X_{\text{propyl}}$) must be $1 - 0.6 = 0.4$.

Now, let's write out **Raoult's Law**:
Total Pressure = (Pressure from Ethyl) + (Pressure from Propyl)
$$P_{\text{total}} = (X_{\text{ethyl}} \times P^0_{\text{ethyl}}) + (X_{\text{propyl}} \times P^0_{\text{propyl}})$$

Let's plug in the numbers we know:
$$290 = (0.6 \times P^0_{\text{ethyl}}) + (0.4 \times 200)$$

Now, we just do some simple algebra to solve the mystery of the missing pressure ($P^0_{\text{ethyl}}$)!
First, calculate the propyl part:
$$0.4 \times 200 = 80$$

So our equation becomes:
$$290 = (0.6 \times P^0_{\text{ethyl}}) + 80$$

Subtract 80 from both sides:
$$210 = 0.6 \times P^0_{\text{ethyl}}$$

Divide by 0.6:
$$P^0_{\text{ethyl}} = \frac{210}{0.6} = 350\text{ mm}$$

Boom! Case closed. The pure vapour pressure of ethyl alcohol before it was mixed was **350 mm**. By knowing how the team performed overall and knowing how good one player was, we calculated the exact skill level of the second player!

questions.Question: Q62. Among the following mixtures, dipole-dipole as the major interaction, is present in
questions.Hint: Look for two molecules that are BOTH 'polar' (they have permanent slightly positive and slightly negative ends) but CANNOT form hydrogen bonds. Dipole-dipole interactions happen between two polar molecules.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine tiny magnets floating around in space. Each magnet has a North pole and a South pole. If you put two of them near each other, the North end of one will stick to the South end of the other. 

In chemistry, some molecules behave exactly like little magnets! They have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end. We call these 'polar' molecules, and they possess a 'dipole'. When two polar molecules stick together, we call it a **dipole-dipole interaction**.

Let's look at our options to find the pair of magnets:

1. **Benzene and Carbon Tetrachloride**: Both of these are perfectly symmetrical and completely non-polar. They have no positive or negative ends. They are like wooden blocks, not magnets. The only force here is weak 'London dispersion' forces.

2. **KCl and Water**: KCl is an ionic salt (made of full positive K+ and full negative Cl- ions), and water is polar. This forms an 'ion-dipole' force. It's super strong, stronger than normal dipole-dipole.

3. **Benzene and Ethanol**: Benzene is a non-polar wooden block. Ethanol is polar and can do hydrogen bonding. They don't match up well. 

4. **Acetonitrile and Acetone**: Let's look at these two! 
- Acetonitrile (CH3CN) has a nitrogen atom pulling electrons towards itself, making it polar (it's a magnet!).
- Acetone (CH3COCH3 - nail polish remover) has an oxygen atom pulling electrons towards itself, making it polar too (another magnet!). 
Neither of them has an H attached directly to an N, O, or F, so they can't form super-strong Hydrogen bonds. 

Therefore, when you mix acetonitrile and acetone, their slightly positive and slightly negative ends line up and attract each other perfectly. This is the definition of **dipole-dipole interaction**! It's just two little molecular magnets sticking together.

questions.Question: Q63. For which of the following parameters, the structural isomers C2H5OH and CH3OCH3 would be expected to have the same values?(Assume ideal behaviour).
MCQ_Options: Gaseous densities at the same temperature and pressure
Vapour pressure at the same temperature
questions.Hint: Structural isomers have the exact same chemical formula, meaning they have the exact same molar mass. How does molar mass relate to the density of an ideal gas?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Lego time! Imagine you have a tiny box of Lego bricks: 2 grey carbon bricks, 6 white hydrogen bricks, and 1 red oxygen brick.

You can snap these exact same bricks together in two totally different shapes:
1. **Ethanol (C2H5OH)**: The oxygen is on the edge holding a hydrogen. 
2. **Dimethyl Ether (CH3OCH3)**: The oxygen is perfectly trapped in the middle between the carbons.

Because they are built from the exact same bricks, they weigh the exact same amount. Their **molar mass** is completely identical ($46\text{ g/mol}$). They are called 'structural isomers'.

Now, how do they behave?
In liquid form, shape matters A LOT. Ethanol has the oxygen holding a hydrogen (O-H), which allows it to form super-sticky Hydrogen Bonds with its neighbors. Dimethyl ether's oxygen is trapped in the middle and cannot hydrogen bond. 
Because ethanol is stickier, it's harder to boil. So, their **boiling points, vapour pressures, and heat of vaporization** will be totally different!

But what happens if we boil them both completely into an **Ideal Gas**?
An 'ideal gas' is a wonderful physics fantasy where molecules are flying around so fast and so far apart that they completely ignore each other. They don't stick. They don't care about their shapes. They just act like flying bouncy balls.

The formula for the density of an ideal gas is:
$$d = \frac{P \times M}{R \times T}$$
Where:
- $P$ is Pressure
- $T$ is Temperature
- $R$ is the gas constant
- **$M$ is Molar Mass**

Since they are at the *same* pressure, the *same* temperature, and have the *exact same* Molar Mass (same Lego bricks!), their **Gaseous Densities** must be mathematically identical. Once they are floating in the air far apart, their shape doesn't matter anymore, only their weight does!
questions.Answer: Gaseous densities at the same temperature and pressure

questions.Question: Q64. Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
MCQ_Options: Adding a non-volatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent.
The boiling point of a solution is always lower than that of the pure solvent.
Freezing point depression depends on the total number of solute particles.
Osmotic pressure is considered a colligative property.
questions.Hint: Think about what happens when you add salt to a pot of water to cook pasta. Does it make the water boil at a cooler temperature or a hotter temperature?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! Let's talk about what happens when you mix something into pure water. Imagine a swimming pool full of pure water molecules. These water molecules love to jump out into the air (which creates something called 'vapor pressure'), and they lock together to freeze when it gets cold.

Now, imagine you throw a bunch of heavy beach balls (this represents our 'solute', like salt or sugar) into the pool. These beach balls get in the way! They physically block the water molecules from jumping into the air. Because it is harder for the water molecules to escape, the overall vapor pressure drops. This means the first option is a true statement.

Since the water molecules are struggling to escape into the air, you have to heat the water even MORE to give them the energy they need to break free and boil. So, adding a solute actually makes the boiling point go UP! 

This means the statement 'The boiling point of a solution is always lower than that of the pure solvent' is completely backwards. It is actually always higher! This concept is known in chemistry as **Elevation in Boiling Point**.

The other options represent actual chemistry rules and are completely true: adding stuff lowers vapor pressure, lowers the freezing point (which is why salt melts ice!), and generates osmotic pressure. All of these effects are called 'Colligative Properties', which is just a fancy way of saying 'properties that change based on HOW MANY particles you add, not what they are'.
questions.Answer: The boiling point of a solution is always lower than that of the pure solvent.

questions.Concept: Depression in Freezing Point & Van't Hoff Factor
questions.Question: Q65. In a 0.2 molal aqueous solution of a weak acid HX, the degree of ionization is 0.3. Taking Kf for water as 1.85, the freezing point of the solution will be nearest to
questions.Hint: First, figure out how many total pieces the acid breaks into by calculating the Van't Hoff factor (i). Then, multiply 'i' by the freezing point constant (Kf) and the molality (m) to find out how much the temperature drops!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Have you ever wondered why we sprinkle salt on icy roads in the winter? It's because adding 'stuff' (like salt or acid) to water makes its freezing point drop! Instead of freezing at $0^\circ \text{C}$, the salty water needs to be much colder to freeze. This superpower is called **Freezing Point Depression**, and it happens anytime you dissolve something in a liquid.

Here is how we figure out exactly how cold it needs to get. There is a super handy formula:

$\Delta T_f = i \times K_f \times m$

Let's break down what these letters mean:
- **$\Delta T_f$** is the change in temperature (how much the freezing point drops).
- **$m$** is the molality (how concentrated our solution is). The question tells us $m = 0.2$.
- **$K_f$** is a special constant number just for water, given to us as $1.85$.
- **$i$** is the **Van't Hoff factor**. This is a cool chemistry term for 'how many pieces the molecule breaks into when it hits the water'.

Let's find out what '$i$' is! We have a weak acid called HX. When you put HX in water, it wants to snap into two pieces: an $H^+$ piece and an $X^-$ piece. But because it is a *weak* acid, it doesn't break apart completely. Some of it stays glued together.

The question tells us the 'degree of ionization is 0.3'. This means out of 1 whole HX molecule, only 0.3 of it snaps apart. 
So, what's left floating in our water pool?
1. The unbroken HX left over: $1 - 0.3 = 0.7$
2. The $H^+$ pieces created: $0.3$
3. The $X^-$ pieces created: $0.3$

If we add up all these floating pieces, we get: $0.7 + 0.3 + 0.3 = 1.3$. So, our Van't Hoff factor is $i = 1.3$!

Now, let's plug everything into our magic formula:
$\Delta T_f = 1.3 \times 1.85 \times 0.2$
First, let's multiply $1.85 \times 0.2 = 0.37$.
Next, $1.3 \times 0.37 = 0.481$.

This means the freezing point *drops* by $0.481^\circ \text{C}$. Since pure water usually freezes at a crisp $0^\circ \text{C}$, our new freezing point is $0 - 0.481 = -0.481^\circ \text{C}$. You totally nailed this!

questions.Question: Q1. A solution of aluminium chloride is electrolysed for 30 minutes using a current of 2 A. The amount of the aluminium deposited at the cathode is __________. [Given : molar mass of aluminium and chlorine are 27 g mol−1 and 35.5 g mol−1 respectively. Faraday constant = 96500 C mol−1]
questions.Hint: First, find out the total electrical charge passed through the solution. Then, think about how many 'electron tickets' it costs to win one Aluminum atom from AlCl3!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's dive into this problem together. Imagine you are at an arcade, and you want to win a specific prize: a shiny atom of solid Aluminum. To win this prize, you need to pay with 'electron tickets'. 

First, let's look at the chemical compound we have: Aluminium chloride, or AlCl3. In a solution, this breaks apart into Al^{3+} ions and Cl^{-} ions. Notice the 3+ charge on the Aluminum? That means each Aluminum ion is missing 3 electrons. So, to turn it back into a solid, neutral Aluminum atom, you must give it exactly 3 electrons. The reaction looks like this: 

Al^{3+} + 3e^{-} $\rightarrow$ Al

This tells us that 1 mole of Aluminum atoms 'costs' 3 moles of electrons.

Now, how many electrons did we actually pump into our 'arcade machine' (the solution)? We can find out using the formula for electrical charge: 
Charge (Q) = Current (I) $\times$ Time (t).

Here, the current is 2 Amperes, and the time is 30 minutes. But wait! In physics and chemistry, we always use seconds for time. Let's convert 30 minutes to seconds:
30 minutes $\times 60$ seconds/minute = 1800 seconds.

Now, let's calculate the total charge:
Q = 2 A $\times 1800$ s = 3600 Coulombs (C).

Okay, so we have 3600 C of electrical charge. But how many moles of electrons is that? That's where Mr. Michael Faraday steps in! The Faraday constant (F = 96500 C mol^{-1}) tells us that 1 whole mole of electrons carries exactly 96,500 Coulombs of charge. 

Let's find our moles of electrons:
Moles of electrons = Total Charge / Faraday's Constant
Moles of electrons = 3600 / 96500 = 0.0373 moles of electrons.

Remember our arcade rule? It takes 3 moles of electrons to get 1 mole of Aluminum. So, let's divide our total electrons by 3 to see how much Aluminum we won:
Moles of Al = 0.0373 / 3 = 0.012435 moles of Aluminum.

Finally, the problem gives us the molar mass of Aluminum: 27 g/mol. This means 1 mole weighs 27 grams. To find the mass of the Aluminum we deposited, we just multiply:
Mass = Moles $\times$ Molar Mass
Mass = 0.012435 moles $\times 27 g$/mol = 0.3357 grams.

Rounding to three decimal places, we get 0.336 g. You did it! You successfully calculated the exact weight of metal pulled out of thin water using electricity. How cool is that?

questions.Question: Q2. Given below are two statements : Statement (I) : Corrosion is an electrochemical phenomenon in which pure metal acts as an anode and impure metal as a cathode. Statement (II) : The rate of corrosion is more in alkaline medium than in acidic medium.
MCQ_Options: Statement I is True and Statement II is False
Both Statement I and Statement II are True
Statement I is False and Statement II is True
Both Statement I and Statement II are False
questions.Hint: Think of an anode as a piece of metal melting away, while the cathode is a safe landing pad for electrons. Also, consider what kind of liquid (acidic like lemon juice, or alkaline like soapy water) eats away at metal faster!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! Let's unravel the mystery of why metals rust and decay, which chemists call 'corrosion'. 

Let's start with Statement (I). Have you ever noticed that a highly pure piece of metal doesn't rust as easily as a cheap, impure alloy? Here's the fascinating reason why. When a drop of water sits on a piece of iron, it essentially creates a tiny microscopic battery! For a battery to work, you need two different stations: an Anode and a Cathode.

The pure parts of the iron want to dissolve. They give up their electrons and break apart into the water as iron ions (Fe^{2+}). Because this is where oxidation (loss of electrons) happens, the pure metal surface acts as the Anode. It is literally melting away into rust! 
But where do those lost electrons go? They travel through the metal to spots that have little impurities, cracks, or dirt. These impure spots act as the Cathode. The electrons sit there and help the oxygen from the air mix with the water to create hydroxide ions. So, the pure metal acts as the anode (where the damage happens) and the impure parts act as the cathode (the helper). Thus, Statement (I) conceptually is True!

Now let's look at Statement (II). It claims that corrosion is faster in alkaline (basic) mediums compared to acidic mediums. Let's think about this. Acidic liquids, like vinegar or acid rain, are famous for eating away at metals. Why? Because acids are packed with H^{+} ions. In our tiny rust battery, the cathode needs those H^{+} ions to react with oxygen and electrons to make water. If you pour acid on the metal, you are giving the cathode an endless supply of exactly what it needs to run faster! This means an acidic medium drastically SPEEDS UP the rate of corrosion. Conversely, an alkaline medium (which lacks H^{+} ions) slows it down. 

Because of this, Statement (II) is completely backwards. It is False. 

By understanding these two concepts, you now know why car manufacturers use super-pure metals, and why we have to wash the acidic winter salt off cars to prevent them from rusting away!
questions.Answer: Statement I is True and Statement II is False

questions.Concept: Standard Cell Potential and Gibbs Free Energy
questions.Question: Q3. For the given cell Fe2+(aq) + Ag+(aq) → Fe3+(aq) + Ag(s). The standard cell potential of the above reaction is Given: Ag+ + e- → Ag Eθ = xV; Fe2+ + 2e- → Fe Eθ = yV; Fe3+ + 3e- → Fe Eθ = zV
questions.Hint: You can't add standard potentials (Voltages) directly if the number of electrons doesn't match! You must convert them to Gibbs Free Energy ($\Delta$ G = -nFE), add or subtract the equations to get your desired half-reaction, and then convert back to Voltage.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a brilliant puzzle! We need to find the total 'Voltage' (Standard Cell Potential, E^$\theta)$ of a specific battery reaction. 

The reaction is: Fe^{2+} + Ag^{+} $\rightarrow$ Fe^{3+} + Ag. 
To find the total voltage, we split it into two halves:
1. Reduction (gaining electrons): Ag^{+} + e^{-} $\rightarrow$ Ag. (We know this is x Volts).
2. Oxidation (losing electrons): Fe^{2+} $\rightarrow$ Fe^{3+} + e^{-}. (We don't know the voltage for this yet!)

We are given two puzzle pieces to find that missing Fe^{2+} oxidation voltage:
Equation A: Fe^{2+} + 2e^{-} $\rightarrow$ Fe (Voltage = y)
Equation B: Fe^{3+} + 3e^{-} $\rightarrow$ Fe (Voltage = z)

Here is a massive secret in chemistry: You CANNOT just add or subtract voltages directly! Voltage is an 'intensive' property, like temperature. If you mix two cups of water at 50 degrees, you don't get water at 100 degrees! Instead, we use 'Gibbs Free Energy' ($\Delta$ G), which is like total heat or total money. You can always add or subtract $\Delta$ G. 

The magic formula connecting them is: $\Delta$ G = -nFE^$\theta$
(where n = number of electrons, F is Faraday's constant, E^$\theta$ is the voltage).

Let's convert our given equations to $\Delta$ G:
For Eq A (2 electrons): $\Delta G_A$ = -2Fy
For Eq B (3 electrons): $\Delta G_B$ = -3Fz

We want the equation: Fe^{2+} $\rightarrow$ Fe^{3+} + e^{-}. 
How do we build this from A and B? 
Notice that we want Fe^{2+} on the left, and Fe^{3+} on the right. 
If we take Equation A (Fe^{2+} on left) and SUBTRACT Equation B (Fe^{3+} on left, which flips it to the right), let's see what happens:
(Fe^{2+} + 2e^{-} $\rightarrow$ Fe) minus (Fe^{3+} + 3e^{-} $\rightarrow$ Fe)
The 'Fe' solids cancel out! We are left with:
Fe^{2+} - Fe^{3+} - e^{-} $\rightarrow 0$, which rearranges beautifully to:
Fe^{2+} $\rightarrow$ Fe^{3+} + e^{-}. 

Perfect! So, the $\Delta$ G for our desired oxidation is simply $\Delta G_A - \Delta G_B$.
$\Delta G_{oxidation} = (-2$Fy) - (-3Fz) = 3Fz - 2Fy.

Now, let's turn this back into a Voltage. Since this new reaction involves 1 electron (n=1), its $\Delta$ G is -1 $\cdot$ F $\cdot E_{oxidation}^\theta$.
So, -F $\cdot E_{oxidation}^\theta$ = F(3z - 2y).
Divide both sides by -F, and we get:
E_{oxidation}^$\theta = 2$y - 3z.

Now, returning to our main battery, the total cell potential is simply the voltage of the reduction half PLUS the voltage of the oxidation half:
Total E^$\theta$ = E_{reduction} + E_{oxidation}
Total E^$\theta$ = x + (2y - 3z) = x + 2y - 3z.

And there we have it! By converting to energy, doing our math, and converting back to voltage, we solved the puzzle flawlessly.

questions.Question: Q4. The molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte when plotted against the square root of its concentration, which of the following is expected to be observed?
MCQ_Options: A steep curve that approaches the y-axis asymptotically without intersecting it.
A straight line with a negative slope.
A straight line with a positive slope.
A curve that passes through the origin.
questions.Hint: Weak electrolytes are like shy kids. When there are too many of them around (high concentration), they huddle up and don't conduct well. But if you dilute them with lots of water (low concentration towards zero), they suddenly break apart and their conductivity shoots up incredibly fast!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine an electrolyte as a group of kids at a roller rink. Their job is to carry 'energy batons' (electricity) from one side of the rink to the other. The ability to carry these batons effectively is what we call 'Molar Conductivity'.

We have two types of electrolytes: Strong and Weak.
Strong electrolytes (like NaCl salt) are bold and completely break apart into ions the moment they hit the water. If you graph their conductivity against concentration, they just form a slightly tilted straight line. They are predictable.

But our question is about a WEAK electrolyte, like acetic acid (vinegar). Weak electrolytes are very shy. When you have a high concentration of them in water, they prefer to hold hands tightly as a complete molecule. Because they don't break apart into charged ions, there are hardly any 'kids' available to carry the energy batons. So, at high concentrations (further to the right on our graph), their conductivity is very low.

Now, here is where the magic happens. What if we start diluting the mixture by adding tons of water? As the concentration drops (moving left towards the y-axis on the graph, where concentration approaches zero), the water molecules surround the shy weak electrolyte molecules. The extra space makes them feel comfortable, and they suddenly start breaking apart into separate, moving ions! This is called an increase in their 'degree of dissociation'. 

As we get closer and closer to zero concentration, almost all of the weak electrolyte molecules suddenly snap apart into ions. Because of this sudden rush of available ions, the molar conductivity shoots upward incredibly fast. 

On a graph, this doesn't look like a boring straight line. Instead, it looks like a steep rocket taking off! It curves sharply upwards as it gets closer to the y-axis. However, because you can't have a solution with literally zero concentration (then it would just be pure water!), the curve approaches the y-axis asymptotically—meaning it gets infinitely close but never actually crosses it.

So, if you ever see a graph with a steep, shooting curve that never quite touches the y-axis, you instantly know you are looking at the shy but explosive nature of a weak electrolyte!
questions.Answer: A steep curve that approaches the y-axis asymptotically without intersecting it.

questions.Question: Q5. Match List - I with List - II :
MCQ_Options: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 (Assuming standard electrochemical matches like Kohlrausch's Law to its formula)
questions.Hint: While the exact lists got lost in the chemistry lab archives, in matching questions like this, always pair famous scientists with their legendary equations: Nernst with cell potential, Kohlrausch with infinite dilution, and Faraday with mass and charge!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! You might notice something funny about this question—the lists are completely invisible! In our original database chunk, the actual items for List I and List II got accidentally chopped off. But as a legendary chemistry mentor, I won't let that stop us from learning. 

In the spirit of the JEE exams, 'Match the Column' questions in Electrochemistry almost always test your ability to connect a famous law or term (List I) with its mathematical formula or unit (List II). 

If we were to create the ultimate Electrochemistry matching game, it would look like this:

List-I:
A. Kohlrausch's Law
B. Faraday's First Law
C. Nernst Equation
D. Cell Constant

List-II:
1. E = E^$\theta - ($RT/nF) $\times$ ln(Q) 
2. m = ZIt
3. $\Lambda_m^\infty = \lambda_$+^$\infty + \lambda_-^\infty$
4. l/A

Let's logically solve this hypothetical matching game to build your brainpower:

For A (Kohlrausch's Law): Kohlrausch figured out that at infinite dilution, the total conductivity of a compound is just the sum of its individual ions. So, A matches perfectly with equation 3!

For B (Faraday's First Law): Faraday said that the mass (m) of metal deposited by electricity depends directly on the Current (I) and Time (t). That is mathematically m = ZIt. So B matches with 2!

For C (Nernst Equation): This is the most famous equation in electrochemistry! It tells us how the voltage of a battery changes as its chemicals get used up. That is equation 1. So C matches with 1!

For D (Cell Constant): If you look inside a battery, the 'Cell Constant' just measures the physical shape of the electrodes—specifically the distance between them (l) divided by their area (A). So D matches with 4!

Even without the original data, mastering these four connections means you are fully prepared for whatever list the actual exam throws at you. You're developing a chemist's intuition!
questions.Answer: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 (Assuming standard electrochemical matches like Kohlrausch's Law to its formula)
