Step 2: Next, we add NaNO2 and HCl. When these two mix, they form Nitrous acid (HNO2). If we do this reaction in a very cold ice bath (0 to 5 degrees Celsius), something magical happens. The -NH2 group on Aniline reacts with the nitrous acid and turns into a Diazonium group (-N2+ Cl-). This creates Benzene Diazonium Chloride. So, molecule B is Benzene Diazonium Chloride! 

Why is this special? Think of the N2+ group as a loaded spring. Nitrogen absolutely loves being free nitrogen gas (N2 in the air). It is desperate to pop off the benzene ring and float away.

Step 3: In our final step, we introduce Copper(I) Cyanide (CuCN). Because that diazonium group is so desperate to leave, the moment the Cyanide ion (-CN) approaches, the N2 gas pops off the ring and bubbles away into the air! The Cyanide group snaps right into the empty spot left on the benzene ring. This specific swap is known as the Sandmeyer Reaction.

Our final product, molecule C, is a benzene ring attached to a cyanide group. We call this Benzonitrile (C6H5CN). You successfully built it step-by-step!

questions.Chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles & Techniques (GOC)
questions.Question: In the following compound, NH2-C(=NH)-NH2 the favourable site/s for protonation is/are:
questions.Hint: Look for the spot that, after taking the proton (H+), allows the molecule to share the new positive charge equally among ALL three nitrogens. Teamwork (resonance) equals stability!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello future chemist! To solve this, we need to talk about 'protonation'. Protonation just means adding a Hydrogen ion (H+). Because H+ is positive (it lost its only electron), it acts like a tiny magnet desperately searching for a pair of electrons to hold onto.

The molecule we are looking at is called Guanidine. It has a central carbon surrounded by three nitrogens: two single-bonded (-NH2) and one double-bonded (=NH). Every single one of these nitrogens has a hidden 'lone pair' of electrons. So, the H+ has three possible places it could attach to. Which one will it choose?

Molecules are fundamentally lazy; they want to be in the most relaxed, stable state possible. If a molecule gets stuck with a positive charge, it feels stressed out. However, if the molecule can shift its electrons around to share the burden of that positive charge across multiple atoms, the stress drops drastically. We call this 'juggling' of charge 'Resonance'.

Imagine what happens if the H+ attaches to one of the single-bonded -NH2 groups. That nitrogen takes the full positive charge, and it's quite hard to juggle it well. 

But, imagine what happens if the H+ attaches to the double-bonded =NH group! It turns into =NH2+. Now, look at the structure: the central carbon is bonded to three identical -NH2 groups! The molecule becomes perfectly symmetrical. The lone pairs from the other two nitrogens can fold in to create a double bond, pushing the positive charge from one nitrogen to the next, to the next. All three nitrogens work together to share the positive charge equally! 

Because this 'Guanidinium ion' has incredible resonance stabilization (teamwork!), the double-bonded nitrogen (=NH) is the most favorable and welcoming site for the H+ magnet to stick to.

questions.Concept: Protection and Deprotection in Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
questions.Question: The major product obtained in the following reaction is: C6H5NH2 (i) (CH3CO)2O $\rightarrow$ (ii) Br2, Fe $\rightarrow$ (iii) H3O+ $\rightarrow$ ?
questions.Hint: Aniline is normally highly reactive and will add three bromines at once. Step (i) puts a 'mask' on aniline to calm it down so it only adds one bromine. Step (iii) washes the mask off!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore a brilliant trick organic chemists use called 'Protection and Deprotection'!

We start with Aniline (C6H5NH2), which is a benzene ring with an amino group (-NH2). This -NH2 group is like a hyperactive cheerleader. It pumps so much electron energy into the benzene ring that the ring goes crazy! If you just pour Bromine (Br2) directly onto aniline, the ring is so hyperactive that it immediately grabs THREE bromine atoms, giving you a compound called 2,4,6-Tribromoaniline. But what if we only want ONE bromine attached? We have to calm the cheerleader down.

Step 1: We react Aniline with Acetic Anhydride ((CH3CO)2O). This acts like putting a 'mask' or a 'straightjacket' on the hyperactive -NH2 group, turning it into an amide group (-NHCOCH3). The molecule is now called Acetanilide. The heavy oxygen on the mask pulls some of the electron energy away from the ring. The ring is now calm and relaxed.

Step 2: Now we add Bromine (Br2) with an Iron (Fe) catalyst. Because the ring is calm, it only has the energy to accept ONE bromine atom. But where does the bromine go? The bulky mask on the nitrogen takes up a lot of space, making it really hard for bromine to attach right next to it (the 'ortho' position). So, the bromine naturally goes to the opposite end of the ring, where there is plenty of room. This is called the 'para' position. We've now made p-Bromoacetanilide.

Step 3: We have our one bromine attached exactly where we want it, but our molecule is still wearing that annoying mask! So, we use acidic water (H3O+) to 'wash' the mask off. This process, called hydrolysis, breaks the amide bond, perfectly restoring our original -NH2 group.

The final result? A beautiful molecule of Aniline with just one Bromine atom sitting exactly opposite to it. We call this p-Bromoaniline! You just controlled a chemical reaction like a true master.

questions.Concept: Reactivity of Carbonyl Compounds towards Nucleophilic Attack
questions.Question: The increasing order of the reactivity of the following with LiAlH4 is : CH3COCl, CH3COOC2H5, CH3COOCH3, CH3CONH2
questions.Hint: Look at the group attached to the carbonyl carbon. If the group pulls electrons away (like Chlorine), the carbon gets 'hungry' and highly reactive. If the group pushes electrons toward the carbon (like Nitrogen), the carbon feels 'full' and becomes unreactive.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's figure out how to arrange these molecules from the laziest (least reactive) to the most aggressive (most reactive) when facing LiAlH4.

All four of these molecules are 'carbonyl compounds', meaning they all have a central Carbon double-bonded to an Oxygen (C=O). Oxygen is incredibly greedy (electronegative) and constantly pulls the shared electrons towards itself, leaving the central Carbon slightly positive, or 'electron-hungry'.

When we use LiAlH4, we are throwing tiny, negatively charged Hydride ions (H-) at the molecule. The H- is looking for a positive Carbon to attack! The more positive (hungry) the Carbon is, the faster the reaction happens.

So, what controls how hungry the Carbon is? The 'neighbor' attached to it!

1. Acid Chloride (CH3COCl): The neighbor is Chlorine. Chlorine is super greedy and actively pulls even MORE electrons away from the Carbon. The Carbon is starving and incredibly positive. Thus, CH3COCl is the most reactive!

2. Amide (CH3CONH2): The neighbor is Nitrogen. Nitrogen has a lone pair of electrons and acts like a sweet grandmother. Instead of pulling electrons away, it actively shares its lone pair with the Carbon through 'resonance'. The Carbon feels totally full and satisfied. Thus, CH3CONH2 is extremely lazy and the least reactive.

3. The Esters (CH3COOCH3 and CH3COOC2H5): Oxygen is in between Chlorine and Nitrogen. It shares some electrons, but not as well as Nitrogen. So esters are in the middle! But between the methyl ester (-OCH3) and the ethyl ester (-OC2H5), which is more reactive? The ethyl group is slightly larger and pushes a tiny bit more electron density toward the oxygen (making it slightly less reactive), plus its larger size physically blocks incoming attacks (steric hindrance). Therefore, the methyl ester (CH3COOCH3) is slightly more reactive than the ethyl ester (CH3COOC2H5).

Putting it all together from least reactive to most reactive: Amide < Ethyl Ester < Methyl Ester < Acid Chloride.
Or in symbols: CH3CONH2 < CH3COOC2H5 < CH3COOCH3 < CH3COCl.

questions.Question: The compounds A and B in the following reaction are, respectively: C6H5CH2Cl (i) KCN $\rightarrow$ A (i) H2, Ni $\rightarrow$ B
questions.Hint: Step one is a simple trade: replace the Chlorine with a Cyanide group to make molecule A. Step two breaks open the Cyanide's triple bond and attaches hydrogen atoms to make molecule B.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play with some molecular building blocks to find out what A and B are!

Our starting molecule is Benzyl chloride (C6H5CH2Cl). It consists of a benzene ring attached to a CH2 group, which is attached to a Chlorine atom. 

Step 1: We introduce KCN (Potassium Cyanide). This step is a classic 'Nucleophilic Substitution'. Think of it as a simple trade. The Potassium (K+) and the Chlorine (Cl-) are desperately in love, so they run off together to form KCl salt. That leaves the Cyanide ion (-CN) to take the exact spot where the Chlorine used to be. 
So, we replace the -Cl with -CN. Our new molecule A is C6H5CH2CN (Benzyl cyanide or 2-phenylacetonitrile). Notice how we just made our carbon chain slightly longer! We added a new carbon.

Step 2: Now we take molecule A and react it with Hydrogen gas (H2) and a Nickel (Ni) catalyst. 
Remember that the Cyanide group (-CN) actually contains a Carbon-Nitrogen triple bond (C$\equivN)$. It's tightly wound up. The Nickel catalyst acts like a hot frying pan, cracking open the hydrogen gas molecules. When the tight triple bond of the cyanide touches the pan, it springs open like an umbrella, and the hydrogen atoms attach themselves to it. 
We need to fully 'reduce' this bond, so we break the triple bond all the way down to a single bond. The Carbon takes two hydrogens, and the Nitrogen takes two hydrogens. 
The -C$\equivN$ group magically transforms into an amine tail: -CH2NH2. 

Let's look at our final molecule B. We have our benzene ring (C6H5-), attached to the original CH2 group (-CH2-), which is now attached to the newly transformed CH2NH2 group. 
Putting it together, B is C6H5CH2CH2NH2 (2-Phenylethanamine). You just successfully lengthened a carbon chain and created an amine!

questions.Question: Q50. Ethylamine (C2H5NH2) can be obtained from N ethyl phthalimide on treatment with: NH2NH2, CaH2, NaBH4, H2O
questions.Hint: Think about how we can free the amine from the large phthalimide ring. We need a 'chemical bolt cutter' that acts as a strong nucleophile to rip the protective cage open.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Hello my young chemist friend! Today we are looking at a beautiful reaction known in chemistry as the Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis. Imagine you want to build a very specific toy, a primary amine called Ethylamine $(C_2H_5NH_2)$. The problem with building primary amines normally is that nitrogen is very greedy; if you feed it carbon atoms, it won't stop at just one! It will keep reacting to form secondary and tertiary amines, creating a messy soup of products. So, how do we force it to only take one carbon group? We put it in a protective cage! That cage is called a 'phthalimide' group. In our question, the nitrogen is trapped inside this large, bulky cage, and it already has our desired ethyl group attached to it (N-ethyl phthalimide). Now, the final step is to break the cage and set our pure ethylamine free. How do we do that? We need a chemical 'bolt cutter'. That is exactly what Hydrazine $(NH_2NH_2)$ is! Hydrazine has two highly reactive nitrogen atoms. These nitrogen atoms are incredible 'nucleophiles'—meaning they love to attack areas with a positive charge. The cage has two carbonyl groups $(C=O)$, which are perfectly positive targets. The hydrazine attacks these spots, literally ripping the cage apart to form a very stable byproduct called phthalhydrazide. In doing so, it completely ejects our pure, perfect Ethylamine! While water $(H_2O)$ could technically break the cage through a process called hydrolysis, it is extremely slow and requires harsh heating under pressure. Hydrazine does the job cleanly, quickly, and beautifully at much milder conditions. So, to free your amine from the phthalimide cage, always reach for your chemical bolt cutters: $NH_2NH_2$!

questions.Question: Q51. The major product 'Y' in the following reaction is: C6H5NH2 (i) NaNO2, HCl $\rightarrow$ (ii) H3PO2 $\rightarrow$ X (i) CH3COCl, AlCl3 $\rightarrow$ Y
questions.Hint: Step 1 converts aniline to a diazonium salt, and Step 2 replaces that salt with a hydrogen atom (leaving a plain benzene ring). What happens when plain benzene reacts with an acid chloride and AlCl3?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's break down this wonderful three-step molecular magic trick! Imagine we are chemical architects, and our goal is to completely transform Aniline into something totally new. Let's look at Step 1: We start with Aniline, which is a benzene ring wearing an $NH_2$ hat. We treat it with $NaNO_2$ and $HCl$. When these chemicals mix, they create a highly reactive 'wizard' called nitrous acid, which transforms that boring $NH_2$ hat into a super-charged, highly unstable group called a diazonium salt $(N_2^+Cl^-)$. This new hat is desperately trying to pop off as nitrogen gas $(N_2)$. Step 2: Now we bring in $H_3PO_2$, which is hypophosphorous acid. Think of $H_3PO_2$ as a magical eraser. It is a chemical reducing agent. When it sees that unstable diazonium hat, it gently hands over a hydrogen atom, popping the nitrogen gas completely off the ring! Poof! The hat is gone, and we are left with a plain, naked Benzene ring. This plain Benzene is our intermediate compound 'X'. Step 3: Now we have a blank canvas. We introduce $CH_3COCl$ (acetyl chloride) and $AlCl_3$. This is a classic Friedel-Crafts Acylation reaction! $AlCl_3$ is severely hungry for electrons (a Lewis acid). It rips the chlorine right off the acetyl chloride. This leaves behind a positively charged, super-reactive fragment called an acyl cation $(CH_3C=O^+)$. Our naked Benzene ring sees this positive charge, gets very excited, and attacks it! The acyl group attaches directly to the benzene ring, creating a brand new ketone. A benzene ring directly attached to a $CH_3C=O$ group is famously called Acetophenone. So, by changing hats, erasing the hat entirely, and then gluing on a brand new piece, we successfully turned Aniline into Acetophenone!

questions.Question: Q52. In the following compounds, the decreasing order of basic strength will be: C2H5NH2, NH3, (C2H5)2NH
questions.Hint: Alkyl groups push electrons toward the nitrogen atom. The more electron density nitrogen has, the better it can grab a proton (acting as a base).
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's explore what it actually means to be a 'base' in chemistry. When we call a molecule a base, we mean it acts like a sponge for protons ($H^+$ ions). Nitrogen atoms have a 'lone pair' of electrons—two extra electrons just sitting on top of the atom, not participating in any bonds. This lone pair is the perfect sticky spot for a wandering proton to attach to! The stickier and more available that lone pair is, the stronger the base. So, how do we make a lone pair stickier? We need to pump more negative charge (electron density) into the nitrogen atom. Imagine the nitrogen atom is a basketball player holding the ball (the lone pair). The alkyl groups, like the ethyl group $(C_2H_5)$, act like energetic cheerleaders. Through a phenomenon called the '+I (Inductive) effect', these carbon chains physically push their own electron clouds toward the nitrogen, pumping it up and making its lone pair super attractive to protons. Ammonia $(NH_3)$ has zero carbon chains attached. It has no cheerleaders. It's an okay base, but not the best. Ethylamine $(C_2H_5NH_2)$ has ONE ethyl group attached. That's one cheerleader pumping electrons into nitrogen. So, it's a stronger base than ammonia. Diethylamine $((C_2H_5)_2NH)$ is a secondary amine. It has TWO ethyl groups attached! That means two cheerleaders pumping negative charge into the nitrogen from both sides. The nitrogen becomes incredibly rich in electrons, making its lone pair hyper-available to grab a proton. Therefore, the base with the most cheerleaders wins! The decreasing order of basic strength is Diethylamine first, then Ethylamine, and Ammonia comes in last.

questions.Question: Q53. The major products A and B for the following reactions are, respectively: C6H5NH2 (i) NaNO2, HCl $\rightarrow$ A (i) KI $\rightarrow$ B
MCQ_Options: A = Benzene diazonium chloride, B = Iodobenzene
A = Benzene diazonium chloride, B = Phenol
questions.Hint: Aniline reacts with cold NaNO2 and HCl to form a highly reactive, unstable salt. Adding Potassium Iodide (KI) knocks nitrogen off the ring, replacing it with Iodine.
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Welcome to the fascinating world of Diazonium chemistry! This problem is a classic two-step reaction sequence that shows us exactly how to replace a stubborn amine group with a heavy halogen like Iodine. Let's start with Step 1. We have Aniline, which is a benzene ring attached to an $NH_2$ group. We mix it with Sodium Nitrite $(NaNO_2)$ and Hydrochloric acid $(HCl)$. This reaction absolutely MUST be kept super cold, right around 0 to 5 degrees Celsius (the exact temperature of an ice water bath). Why? Because this mixture forms a 'Diazonium Salt' (specifically Benzene Diazonium Chloride, which is Product A). In this salt, the nitrogen is bonded to another nitrogen with a triple bond, carrying a positive charge $(N_2^+)$. This $N_2^+$ group is incredibly unstable. If the room gets even a little bit warm, it acts like a tiny explosive and shoots off the molecule as Nitrogen gas $(N_2)$. By keeping the beaker freezing cold, we gently trap it on the benzene ring temporarily. Now for Step 2. We introduce Potassium Iodide $(KI)$ to our trapped diazonium salt. The Iodide ion $(I^-)$ is a big, soft, electron-rich atom. It sees that the $N_2^+$ group is desperately wanting to leave. The Iodide ion casually bumps into the benzene ring, and POP! The nitrogen gas explodes off the ring and floats away into the atmosphere as harmless bubbles. The Iodide atom simply takes the empty parking spot left behind on the benzene ring. This beautiful, smooth replacement reaction leaves us with Iodobenzene, which is Product B. It is one of the easiest and most elegant ways to attach Iodine to a benzene ring in all of organic chemistry! So, Product A is the unstable Benzene Diazonium Chloride, and Product B is the stable Iodobenzene.
questions.Answer: A = Benzene diazonium chloride, B = Iodobenzene

questions.Question: Q54. Aniline dissolved in dilute HCl is reacted with sodium nitrate at 0$^\circ$C. This solution was added dropwise to a solution containing equimolar mixture of aniline and phenol in dil. HCl. The structure of the major product is:
MCQ_Options: A mixture of both in equal amounts
questions.Hint: Both aniline and phenol can undergo coupling, but pay very close attention to the pH! The mixture is in dilute HCl (acidic medium). Which of the two rings is more activated in acidic conditions?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: This is an incredible question about making brilliant, beautiful colors! Did you know that chemical reactions exactly like this one are used to manufacture the bright yellow, red, and orange dyes in your clothes? This type of reaction is called 'Azo Coupling'. Let's break it down! First, we react Aniline with Sodium Nitrite $(NaNO_2)$—the text accidentally says nitrate, but nitrite is the true chemical here—and cold dilute $HCl$. As you might know by now, this magically converts Aniline's $NH_2$ group into a diazonium salt $(N_2^+)$. Think of this diazonium ion as a chemical plug looking for an electrical outlet. It's positively charged (an electrophile), so it desperately wants to connect with a molecule that is packed full of negative electrons. Now, we take our diazonium 'plug' and drop it into a solution that contains BOTH Phenol and Aniline. It has a choice to make! But here is the massive clue that solves the puzzle: the solution is in DILUTE HCl! This means the environment is acidic. In an acidic environment, Phenol (which has an -OH group) is just a decent electron source. Phenol actually strongly prefers to couple in BASIC environments, where it loses a proton to turn into a super-charged, highly negative 'phenoxide' ion. Since we are stuck in acid, Phenol’s 'outlet' is essentially turned off and sluggish. On the other hand, the free Aniline molecules floating in the acidic solution are highly activated for this exact condition. The diazonium plug easily bypasses the phenol, finds the free Aniline molecules, and attaches itself to the exact opposite side of the ring (the 'para' position) to avoid bumping into the bulky amine group. The two rings snap tightly together with a brilliant nitrogen-nitrogen double bond (an azo bridge) connecting them. The resulting massive molecule is called p-Aminoazobenzene! It's a gorgeous yellow dye. The secret to the puzzle was recognizing that the acidic pH forces the diazonium ion to completely ignore the Phenol and couple exclusively with Aniline.

questions.Question: Q55. The increasing order of diazotisation of the following compounds is:
questions.Hint: Diazotization starts when the nitrogen lone pair attacks the nitrosonium ion (NO+). Electron-withdrawing groups pull electrons away, slowing it down. Electron-donating groups push electrons in, speeding it up!
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Let's imagine we are racing cars, but instead of cars, we are racing chemical reactions! The 'diazotisation' reaction is how we turn a standard amine (like Aniline) into a diazonium salt. To start the race, the nitrogen atom on the amine must use its two spare electrons (its lone pair) to attack a starting flag called a nitrosonium ion $(NO^+)$. If the nitrogen has a full, heavy 'wallet' of electrons, it is super eager and attacks incredibly fast! But if its wallet is empty, it reacts very, very slowly. So, the speed of diazotisation depends entirely on how electron-rich the nitrogen is. Even though the original text cut off the exact compounds, let's use the most famous classic examples to explain the core chemical rule: p-Nitroaniline, Aniline, and p-Toluidine. Let's inspect our racers. In p-Nitroaniline, we have a Nitro group $(NO_2)$. This group acts exactly like an industrial vacuum cleaner! It aggressively sucks electron density away from the entire benzene ring and the nitrogen atom through something called the electron-withdrawing effect. Nitrogen's wallet is completely empty, making this the slowest reaction. Next is plain Aniline. It has no vacuum cleaners and no helpers attached. It's just perfectly average, giving us a medium speed. Finally, we have p-Toluidine, which has a Methyl group $(CH_3)$ attached to the ring. Methyl groups are like generous, wealthy friends; they constantly donate extra electrons into the ring! Because of this 'electron-donating effect', nitrogen's wallet is overflowing with negative charge, allowing it to blast off and attack the $NO^+$ ion lightning fast! So, to find the increasing order of diazotisation, just look at the groups attached to the ring. Electron-withdrawing groups (vacuums) make it slow, while electron-donating groups (helpers) make it fast. The order is: vacuum-attached (p-Nitroaniline) < neutral (Aniline) < helper-attached (p-Toluidine)!

questions.Concept: Comparison of Basic Strength (Aliphatic, Aromatic, Heterocyclic)
questions.Question: Q56. Among the following compounds, the increasing order of their basic strength is: (I) C6H5NH2, (II) C4H4NH (pyrrole), (III) (C2H5)2NH, (IV) C6H5NHCH3
questions.Hint: A base needs its lone pair to catch a proton. If the lone pair is busy participating in an aromatic ring (like in Pyrrole), it refuses to act as a base!
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Welcome to the ultimate base-strength showdown! Remember, a base is a molecule that is eager to use its lone pair of electrons to catch a passing proton $(H^+)$. The more available and prominent that lone pair is, the stronger the base. Let's look at our four contestants and see who shares their electrons the best! Contestant III is Diethylamine $((C_2H_5)_2NH)$. This is an 'aliphatic' amine, meaning no flat benzene rings are involved. It has two bulky ethyl chains that constantly pump extra electrons onto the nitrogen. The lone pair is sitting right on top of the nitrogen, perfectly localized, and super eager to grab a proton. This is our strongest base! Contestant IV is N-Methylaniline $(C_6H_5NHCH_3)$. It has a benzene ring, which acts a bit like a bully. The ring actually pulls nitrogen's lone pair inside it to surf around the carbon atoms—a process called resonance. Because the lone pair is distracted playing inside the ring, it's harder for a proton from the outside to catch it. However, the extra methyl group gives a tiny helpful push of electrons to compensate. Contestant I is plain Aniline $(C_6H_5NH_2)$. It also has a benzene ring pulling the lone pair into resonance, but it has ZERO methyl helpers to push back. So, it's weaker than IV. Finally, we have Contestant II: Pyrrole $(C_4H_4NH)$. Pyrrole is a 5-membered ring with a nitrogen in it. But here is the massive twist: Pyrrole is an 'aromatic' molecule. To maintain its magical, ultra-stable aromatic status, it absolutely MUST use nitrogen's lone pair as part of the ring's continuous 6-electron cycle. If Pyrrole shares its lone pair with an outside proton, the cycle breaks, and it loses its special aromatic stability! Therefore, Pyrrole protects its lone pair with its life. It practically refuses to act as a base. It is the weakest by far. The increasing order is: Pyrrole (II) < Aniline (I) < N-Methylaniline (IV) < Diethylamine (III)!

questions.Question: The test to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines is: Sandmeyer's reaction; Carbylamine reaction; Mustard oil test; C6H5SO2Cl
questions.Hint: Think about a special chemical 'detective' that checks how many hydrogen atoms are directly attached to the nitrogen atom.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine the nitrogen atom in an amine as a tiny person with exactly three 'hands' (bonding sites). In a primary (1°) amine, nitrogen holds one carbon chain and has two free hands holding lightweight hydrogen atoms. In a secondary (2°) amine, it holds two carbon chains and only one hydrogen. In a tertiary (3°) amine, it holds three bulky carbon chains and zero hydrogens! 

To figure out who is who, chemists use a brilliant detective chemical called benzenesulfonyl chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}$), famously known as Hinsberg's reagent. 

Here is how the test works: 
1. When Hinsberg's reagent meets a primary amine, the amine uses one of its hydrogen 'hands' to react, forming a new compound. Because the primary amine still has one acidic hydrogen left, this new compound easily dissolves when we add a base (like NaOH). So, if it reacts and dissolves in base, it is a primary amine! 
2. When Hinsberg's reagent meets a secondary amine, the amine uses its only hydrogen to react. The new compound formed has NO acidic hydrogens left. Therefore, it absolutely refuses to dissolve in a base. It just sits there as a solid. If it reacts but won't dissolve in base, it's a secondary amine! 
3. What about the tertiary amine? Since it has zero hydrogen atoms attached to nitrogen, it simply cannot react with Hinsberg's reagent at all! 

By observing these three completely different reactions, we can perfectly distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary amines. The other options are incorrect for this specific job: Sandmeyer's reaction is for making haloarenes, Carbylamine only tests for primary amines (it ignores the rest), and the Mustard oil test is also primarily for primary amines.

questions.Concept: Sequential Reactions of Aromatic Nitrogen Compounds
questions.Question: In the reaction C6H5NO2 (i) Sn/HCl $\rightarrow$ A (i) NaNO2, HCl $\rightarrow$ B (i) CuCN $\rightarrow$ C (i) H2O $\rightarrow$ D (i) H2, Ni $\rightarrow$ E the product E is :
questions.Hint: Think of this as a chemical relay race. Trace the functional group changes step-by-step: Nitro $\rightarrow$ Amine $\rightarrow$ Diazonium $\rightarrow$ Nitrile $\rightarrow$ Amide $\rightarrow$ Primary Amine.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's break down this chemical relay race step by step! Organic chemistry is just like snapping different Lego blocks onto a baseplate. Here, our baseplate is the benzene ring ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$). 

Step 1: We start with Nitrobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$). We treat it with Tin (Sn) and Hydrochloric acid (HCl). This is a classic reduction reaction. The oxygen atoms are stripped away and replaced by hydrogen atoms. This turns the nitro group into an amine group. So, Compound A is Aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$). 

Step 2: Next, we add Sodium Nitrite ($\text{NaNO}_2$) and HCl. This mixture creates nitrous acid right in the flask, which reacts with aniline at ice-cold temperatures to form a highly reactive, unstable molecule called a diazonium salt. Compound B is Benzene Diazonium Chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$). Think of the diazonium group as a loaded spring, ready to pop off. 

Step 3: We bring in Copper(I) Cyanide ($\text{CuCN}$). The cyanide group ($\text{-CN}$) swoops in, pops the diazonium group right off the ring (releasing nitrogen gas), and takes its place. This is the Sandmeyer reaction. Compound C is Benzonitrile ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN}$). 

Step 4: Now we add water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$). This causes partial hydrolysis of the nitrile group. The triple bond between carbon and nitrogen breaks open to grab oxygen and hydrogen from water, turning the $\text{-CN}$ group into an amide group ($\text{-CONH}_2$). Compound D is Benzamide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$). 

Step 5: Finally, we hit Benzamide with Hydrogen gas ($\text{H}_2$) and a Nickel (Ni) catalyst. This is another reduction! The catalyst forces hydrogen atoms onto the carbon and nitrogen, stripping away the oxygen. The $\text{-CONH}_2$ group turns into a $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ group. Therefore, our final champion, Compound E, is Benzylamine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$).

questions.Concept: Basic Strength of Amines in Aqueous Solution
questions.Question: Considering the basic strength of amines in aqueous solution, which one has the smallest pKb value? (CH3)2NH, CH3NH2, (CH3)3N, C6H5NH2
questions.Hint: A smaller pKb means a STRONGER base. Look for the 'Goldilocks' molecule: it needs enough methyl groups to push electrons, but not so many that it blocks water from helping out!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
First, we need to decode the question: what does 'smallest pKb value' mean? In chemistry, the strength of a base is measured by Kb. A larger Kb means a stronger base. However, chemists like to use 'pKb' (which is the negative math logarithm of Kb). Because of that negative sign, a SMALLER pKb means a STRONGER base! So, the question is simply asking: Which of these is the strongest base? 

A base is a chemical that loves to donate its non-bonding pair of electrons (lone pair) to a passing hydrogen ion (proton). Nitrogen has one of these lone pairs. 

Let's look at aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$). The benzene ring is an electron sponge. Through a process called resonance, it sucks nitrogen's lone pair into the ring. Since the lone pair is busy playing inside the ring, it's not available to catch protons. Aniline is a very weak base. 

Now, look at the methylamines. Methyl groups ($\text{-CH}_3$) do the opposite of benzene—they push electrons TOWARD the nitrogen, making the lone pair even more attractive to protons (this is called the +I or inductive effect). Based on this alone, you would think the tertiary amine, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{N}$, with three pushing groups, would be the strongest. 

But wait! We are in an AQUEOUS (water) solution. When the amine catches a proton, it becomes positively charged and needs water molecules to surround and stabilize it (solvation effect). The tertiary amine is so crowded with bulky methyl groups that water can't get in to help. It suffers from 'steric hindrance'. 

The secondary amine, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{NH}$, is the Goldilocks molecule. It has two methyl groups pushing electrons (great +I effect), but it still has enough open space for water to rush in and stabilize it perfectly. Because it strikes the perfect balance, the secondary amine is the strongest base in water, meaning it has the smallest pKb!

questions.Question: Complete reduction of benzene-diazonium chloride with Zn/HCl gives: Aniline; Phenylhydrazine; Azobenzene; Hydrazobenzene
questions.Hint: Zn/HCl is an incredibly aggressive reducing agent. Think of it like heavy-duty scissors that completely snip the N-N bond, rather than just adding hydrogens to it.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Benzene-diazonium chloride ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$) has two nitrogen atoms triple-bonded to each other. When we want to reduce this molecule (which means forcing hydrogen atoms onto it), the product we get entirely depends on the 'strength' of the reducing agent we use. 

Imagine you want to cut a piece of paper. If you use dull safety scissors, you might just dent or fold the paper. If you use sharp, heavy-duty shears, you cut right through it. Chemistry works the same way! 

If we use a MILD reducing agent, like Tin(II) chloride ($\text{SnCl}_2$) with HCl, or Sodium sulfite, it gently adds hydrogen atoms to the nitrogens without breaking the bond between them. This mild reduction gives us Phenylhydrazine ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH-NH}_2$). 

However, the question specifies Zinc dust with Hydrochloric acid ($\text{Zn/HCl}$) and asks for COMPLETE reduction. $\text{Zn/HCl}$ is incredibly strong—it acts like the heavy-duty shears. It forcefully jams so many hydrogen atoms into the molecule that the bond connecting the two nitrogen atoms completely shatters. 

One nitrogen atom stays attached to the benzene ring and gets two hydrogens, turning into Aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$). The other nitrogen atom gets kicked out completely, grabbing three hydrogens to become Ammonia gas ($\text{NH}_3$). Therefore, the complete reduction yields Aniline!

questions.Concept: Acylation of Amines (Determining the number of amino groups)
questions.Question: A compound with molecular mass 180 is acylated with CH3COCl to get a compound with molecular mass 390. The number of amino groups present per molecule of the former compound is: 2; 5; 4; 6
questions.Hint: Whenever an amino group reacts with CH3COCl, it swaps out a tiny Hydrogen atom (mass = 1) for a bulky Acetyl group (mass = 43). What is the net weight gained per group? Divide the total weight gained by this number!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This problem is actually a fun mathematical puzzle dressed up as chemistry! 

Let's visualize what happens during an 'acylation' reaction. You have a compound that contains amino groups ($\text{-NH}_2$). You react it with acetyl chloride ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$). The amino group is going to swap 'hats'. It takes off its lightweight hydrogen atom hat, and replaces it with a heavier acetyl group ($\text{-COCH}_3$) hat. 

Let's calculate the exact change in weight (molecular mass) for just ONE amino group making this swap: 
1. Mass of the Hydrogen atom we remove = 1 unit. 
2. Mass of the Acetyl group ($\text{-COCH}_3$) we add = (12 for C) + (16 for O) + (12 for C) + (3 for three H's) = 43 units. 
3. Net gain in mass per amino group = We added 43 but lost 1, so the net gain is exactly 42 atomic mass units. 

Now, let's look at the whole molecule. 
The original molecular mass was 180. 
After the reaction, the new molecular mass is 390. 
Total mass gained by the molecule = 390 - 180 = 210 units. 

If the whole molecule gained 210 units of mass, and every single amino group that reacted contributed exactly 42 units of mass gain, how many amino groups must there be? 
We simply divide the total mass gained by the mass gained per group: 
Number of amino groups = 210 / 42 = 5. 

So, there are exactly 5 amino groups in the original molecule!

questions.Question: The order of basicity of the compounds C6H5NH2 (I), C6H5NHCH3 (II), (C6H5)2NH (III), C6H5N(CH3)2 (IV) is IV > I > III > II; I > III > II > IV; III > II > IV > II; II > I > III > IV
questions.Hint: Aromatic basicity depends on electron availability. Methyl groups push electrons (+I effect) making the nitrogen more basic. Benzene rings pull electrons (resonance) making it less basic. Who has the most pushing groups, and who has the most pulling rings?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To solve this, we must remember what makes a nitrogen atom a 'good base'. A good base is eager and willing to share its non-bonding lone pair of electrons with a proton (H+). If the lone pair is easily available, it's a strong base. If the lone pair is hidden or distracted, it's a weak base. 

Let's analyze our four players: 

I. Aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$): The nitrogen is attached to one benzene ring. Benzene rings are like giant electron vacuums. Through a process called 'resonance', the nitrogen's lone pair gets sucked into the ring and dances around the carbon atoms. Because the lone pair is distracted, aniline is a weak base. 

II. N-Methylaniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NHCH}_3$): Here, we replaced a hydrogen with a methyl group ($\text{-CH}_3$). Methyl groups are 'electron-donating'. They push electron density toward the nitrogen (+I effect), kind of fighting back against the benzene vacuum. This extra electron push makes the lone pair more available than in regular aniline. So, II is a stronger base than I. 

III. Diphenylamine ($\text{(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)}_2\text{NH}$): Oh no! This poor nitrogen is attached to TWO benzene rings! Both rings are violently tugging at the lone pair. The lone pair is constantly lost in resonance between two giant rings and is practically invisible to passing protons. This makes III the weakest base of the bunch. 

IV. N,N-Dimethylaniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N(CH}_3\text{)}_2$): Here, nitrogen is attached to one benzene ring but has TWO methyl groups pushing electrons toward it. That double +I effect greatly enriches the electron density on nitrogen. (Fun fact: the two bulky methyl groups also twist the nitrogen slightly out of alignment with the benzene ring, which physically stops the lone pair from being sucked into the ring as easily!). Because of these two factors, IV is the strongest base. 

Putting it all together from strongest to weakest: IV > II > I > III. 
*(Note: The options provided in the raw database text contained typos, but the core conceptual ranking is definitively IV > II > I > III).*

questions.Question: In the chemical reactions, C6H5NH2 (i) NaNO2, HCl $\rightarrow$ A (i) HBF4 $\rightarrow$ B the compounds 'A' and 'B' respectively are nitrobenzene and fluorobenzene; phenol and benzene; benzene diazonium chloride and fluorobenzene; nitrobenzene and chlorobenzene
questions.Hint: Step one creates a very unstable intermediate (a 'loaded spring' of nitrogen gas). Step two uses a special boron-fluorine compound to snap a tricky halogen onto the benzene ring.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's perform some synthetic organic chemistry! We want to transform Aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$) into something new in two distinct steps. 

Step 1: The Diazotization Reaction. 
We start with Aniline and mix it with sodium nitrite ($\text{NaNO}_2$) and hydrochloric acid ($\text{HCl}$) in an ice bath (between 0 to 5°C). Why so cold? Because the reaction creates a highly unstable molecule! The primary amine group ($\text{-NH}_2$) gets converted into a diazonium group ($\text{-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$). 
Think of the diazonium group as a compressed, loaded spring. The two nitrogen atoms desperately want to break off and float away as stable nitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$). Therefore, Compound 'A' is Benzene Diazonium Chloride. 

Step 2: The Balz-Schiemann Reaction. 
Directly attaching a fluorine atom to a benzene ring is notoriously difficult because fluorine gas is aggressively explosive. Chemists use a clever trick instead. We take our loaded spring (Benzene Diazonium Chloride) and treat it with fluoroboric acid ($\text{HBF}_4$). 
First, it forms a diazonium fluoroborate salt. When we gently heat this salt, the 'spring' releases! The nitrogen gas violently bubbles away (leaving the molecule), boron trifluoride ($\text{BF}_3$) escapes as a gas, and a single Fluorine atom is left perfectly attached to the benzene ring. 
So, Compound 'B' is Fluorobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{F}$). 

Therefore, the correct pair of compounds is benzene diazonium chloride and fluorobenzene.

questions.Question: Q64. The most basic compound among the following is Acetanilide; Benzylamine; p -Nitro aniline; Aniline
questions.Hint: Think of basicity as how 'generous' a molecule is with its lone pair of electrons. Look for the option where the nitrogen's lone pair is isolated and protected from being pulled away by a benzene ring.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let us dive into the fascinating world of organic chemistry bases. In chemistry, a 'base' in this context (a Lewis base) is a molecule that has a lone pair of electrons—think of it as a free slice of pizza—that it is highly willing to share with a hungry proton (an H^{+} ion). Nitrogen naturally has one of these lone pairs. The rule is simple: the more available and localized that lone pair is on the nitrogen, the stronger the base! 

Now, let us look at the 'enemies' of basicity. If nitrogen is attached to a structure that pulls those electrons away, the nitrogen becomes less generous, and thus, less basic. This pulling effect happens heavily through a phenomenon called 'resonance,' where electrons smeared out over a molecule. 

Let us evaluate our four options:

1. Aniline: Here, the nitrogen is attached directly to a benzene ring. The benzene ring is like a sponge. Through resonance, the lone pair on nitrogen is pulled down into the ring, making it busy and much less available to share with a proton. So, aniline is a weak base.

2. Acetanilide: This molecule has the nitrogen attached to a benzene ring AND a carbonyl group (a carbon double-bonded to an oxygen, C=O). Oxygen is extremely electronegative (very greedy for electrons). It acts like a powerful vacuum cleaner, sucking the nitrogen's lone pair away even more strongly than the benzene ring alone. This is an incredibly weak base.

3. p-Nitro aniline: This is aniline, but with a nitro group (-NO_2) attached to the opposite end of the benzene ring. The nitro group is one of the strongest 'electron-withdrawing groups' in chemistry. It pulls electron density away from the entire ring, completely starving the nitrogen of its lone pair. This is less basic than regular aniline.

4. Benzylamine: Let us look closely at this one. The structure is a benzene ring attached to a -CH_2- group, which is THEN attached to the nitrogen (-NH_2). That little -CH_2- group is a game-changer! It acts as a physical wall or buffer that completely breaks the resonance connection between the nitrogen and the benzene ring. Because there is no resonance pulling the lone pair away, the nitrogen gets to keep its electron pizza all to itself. 

Because the lone pair on Benzylamine is entirely free and available, it is the most generous, and therefore, the most basic compound among the choices! Understanding this 'buffer' concept is a huge superpower in predicting chemical behavior.

questions.Question: Q65. The reaction of chloroform with alcoholic KOH and p-toluidine forms
questions.Hint: This specific combination of reagents (Chloroform + KOH) mixed with a primary amine is a famous qualitative test in organic chemistry. It creates a molecule with a famously terrible, foul smell!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are a detective in a chemistry lab, and you have a mystery clear liquid. You suspect it might be a 'primary amine' (a molecule where nitrogen is attached to only ONE carbon and TWO hydrogens, written as R-NH_2). How do you prove it? You use the Carbylamine Reaction!

This reaction is like a secret chemical handshake that only primary amines know. In this question, our primary amine is 'p-toluidine' (a benzene ring with a methyl group on one end and our primary amine -NH_2 group on the other). 

The magical reagents we add are Chloroform (CHCl_3) and alcoholic Potassium Hydroxide (KOH). Let us break down the drama of this reaction step-by-step:

Step 1: The Birth of the 'Hungry' Molecule. KOH is a strong base. It attacks the chloroform (CHCl_3), aggressively ripping away its hydrogen and one of its chlorine atoms. What is left behind is a highly reactive, unstable, and electron-hungry intermediate called 'Dichlorocarbene' (:CCl_2). 

Step 2: The Attack! This dichlorocarbene desperately needs electrons. Fortunately, the nitrogen on our primary amine (p-toluidine) has a generous lone pair of electrons. The nitrogen donates its electrons to the carbene, bonding them together.

Step 3: Building the Bridge. Now, the nitrogen and the carbon are attached, but they want to be stronger. The nitrogen still has two hydrogens attached to it, and the carbon still has two chlorines. The KOH in the solution acts like a molecular cleanup crew. It removes the two hydrogens and the two chlorines (forming water and KCl as byproducts), allowing the nitrogen and carbon to form a very strong TRIPLE BOND.

So, the nitrogen group (-NH_2) turns into a (-N $\equiv$ C) group. 

In chemistry, a carbon triple-bonded to a nitrogen (where nitrogen connects to the main molecule) is called an 'Isocyanide' or 'Carbylamine'. Because we started with p-toluidine, the final product is named 'p-Tolyl isocyanide'. 

Here is the coolest (and grossest) part: Isocyanides have incredibly strong, foul, putrid odors. Chemists actually use this exact reaction as a 'smell test'. If you mix your mystery compound with chloroform and KOH, and the lab suddenly smells terrible, congratulations—you just proved you have a primary amine!

questions.Concept: Classification of Polymers based on Intermolecular Forces
questions.Question:
Q1. Match List I with List II List I: (A) Neoprene; (B) Polyester; (C) Polystyrene; (D) Urea-Formaldhyde Resin List II: (I) Fibre; (II) Elastomer; (III) Thermoplastic; (IV) Thermosetting polymer 
Q2. Choose the correct answer from the options given below: (I) Synthetic rubber; (II) Fibre; (III) Thermoplastic; (IV) Thermosetting
questions.Hint: Think about everyday objects! What does a rubber wet-suit feel like? What happens when you melt a plastic spoon versus trying to melt an electrical switch?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! To solve this, let us imagine you are a scientist organizing materials based on how their molecules 'hold hands' with each other. This is all about intermolecular forces!

First, let us look at the four big categories in List II:
1. **Elastomers (II)**: Think of the word 'elastic'. These polymers act like rubber bands! Their molecules are coiled up like springs and have very weak forces between them, allowing you to stretch them out. When you let go, they bounce right back! 
2. **Fibres (I)**: These are the exact opposite! Think of strong ropes or the threads in your t-shirt. Their molecules are packed tightly together with super strong invisible 'magnets' (like hydrogen bonds), making them tough and perfect for weaving into fabrics.
3. **Thermoplastics (III)**: 'Thermo' means heat, and 'plastic' means moldable. If you heat these up, they melt into a gooey liquid. You can pour them into a mold, let them cool, and they harden. Think of Lego bricks or plastic water bottles! Their molecules are just lying over each other like dry spaghetti.
4. **Thermosetting polymers (IV)**: These are the stubborn ones! Once you heat them and shape them for the first time, their molecules form strong 3D web-like connections (cross-links). If you try to heat them again, they won't melt; they will just burn and turn black! Think of the hard plastic of an electrical switch or a frying pan handle.

Now, let us match them with List I!
(A) **Neoprene**: This is a synthetic rubber used to make scuba diving wet-suits. Because it stretches, it is an **Elastomer (II)**.
(B) **Polyester**: Have you ever looked at the tag on your clothes? It probably says '100% Polyester'. We use this to make threads and fabrics, so it is a **Fibre (I)**.
(C) **Polystyrene**: This is what thermocol and those white foam coffee cups are made of. If you put hot oil or acetone on it, it melts! It can be reshaped with heat, making it a **Thermoplastic (III)**.
(D) **Urea-Formaldehyde Resin**: This is an ultra-hard, unbreakable material used for electrical switches and unbreakable plates. It does not melt once formed, making it a **Thermosetting polymer (IV)**.

So, the perfect matching order is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV). Chemistry is literally all around us!

questions.Question: Q3. Polymer used in orlon is: Polyacrylonitrile; Polyethene; Polycarbonate; Polyamide
questions.Hint: Orlon is an artificial substitute for natural wool. It is made from a monomer that contains a 'cyanide' or 'nitrile' group attached to an ethene molecule.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you live somewhere freezing cold, and you really want a thick, warm wool sweater. But wait! Natural wool comes from sheep, and it can be expensive, it shrinks in the wash, and tiny moths love to eat it. 

What if scientists could create 'fake wool' in a laboratory that is just as warm, super lightweight, does not shrink, and bugs hate eating it? Well, they actually did! They created a synthetic fiber and gave it the cool commercial trade name **Orlon** (sometimes also called Acrilan).

But what is the actual chemical name for Orlon? It is **Polyacrylonitrile** (often just called PAN). Let us break down how it is made:

1. **The Building Block (Monomer)**: It starts with a tiny molecule called **Acrylonitrile**. Imagine an ethene molecule ($CH_2=CH_2$), but one of the hydrogen atoms is replaced by a cyanide group ($-C \equiv N$). So, acrylonitrile looks like this: $CH_2=CH-CN$.
2. **The Magic Reaction (Polymerization)**: We take thousands of these little acrylonitrile molecules and trigger an 'addition polymerization' reaction using a peroxide catalyst. The double bond ($C=C$) in each molecule breaks open, allowing them to reach out and hold hands in a massive, infinitely long chain!

This creates the giant polymer $-(CH_2-CH(CN))_n-$, which is **Polyacrylonitrile**. Once spun into threads, this plastic-like material becomes incredibly soft and fluffy, mimicking sheep's wool. 

Let us quickly look at the wrong options so you know why they are incorrect:
- **Polyethene**: This makes standard plastic shopping bags.
- **Polycarbonate**: This is super tough, clear plastic used to make bulletproof glass and CD/DVDs.
- **Polyamide**: This is the chemical family for Nylon (like the strings on a tennis racket or fishing line).

So, whenever you see 'Orlon' or artificial wool, immediately think of Polyacrylonitrile!

questions.Question: Q4. Match list I with List II List I: (A) Nylon-2-Nylon-6; (B) PVC; (C) Buna-N; (D) Bakelite List II: (I) Thermoplastic polymer; (II) Biodegradable polymer; (III) Elastomer; (IV) Thermosetting polymer
questions.Hint: Look for the special biodegradable polymer! Most plastics never break down, but Nylon-2-Nylon-6 was specially designed to be eaten by bacteria.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's put on our detective hats and figure out the identities of these four famous polymers!

**1. Nylon-2-Nylon-6 (A)**:
You've probably heard that plastic pollution is a huge problem because plastics take thousands of years to rot. Nature simply doesn't know how to 'eat' them. However, scientists ingeniously designed a few special polymers that bacteria *can* digest! **Nylon-2-Nylon-6** is one of these rare, environmentally friendly plastics. It naturally rots away over time. Therefore, it is a **Biodegradable polymer (II)**.

**2. PVC (B)**:
PVC stands for Polyvinyl Chloride. If you look at the thick, grey or white water pipes under your kitchen sink or the ones outside your house, those are PVC! It is tough, but if you heat it up with a blowtorch, it gets soft and bends easily. Because it softens upon heating and can be remolded, it is a **Thermoplastic polymer (I)**.

**3. Buna-N (C)**:
The word 'Buna' is a massive clue in chemistry. It stands for rubber! Buna-N is a synthetic rubber that is highly resistant to oil and petrol. That's why it is used to make the rubber seals and hoses inside car engines. Since it's a rubber that stretches and bounces back, it belongs to the stretchy family known as an **Elastomer (III)**.

**4. Bakelite (D)**:
Imagine taking a time machine back to the 1950s. The big, heavy, black rotary telephones? The shiny black handles on your grandmother's frying pans? Those are made of Bakelite! Bakelite is famous for being incredibly hard and heat-resistant. When it is manufactured, it forms a massive, tangled 3D web of molecules that lock permanently into place. If you put it in a fire, it will never melt; it will just char and turn to black powder. This makes it a **Thermosetting polymer (IV)**.

So, matching them up logically:
(A) Nylon-2-Nylon-6 matches (II) Biodegradable
(B) PVC matches (I) Thermoplastic
(C) Buna-N matches (III) Elastomer
(D) Bakelite matches (IV) Thermosetting

The correct sequence is (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

questions.Question: Q5. The polymer X-consists of linear molecules and is closely packed. It prepared in the presence of triethylaluminium and titranium tetrachloride under low pressure. The polymer X is- Polyacrylonitrile; Polytetrafluoroethane; High density polythene; Low density polythene
questions.Hint: Triethylaluminium and titanium tetrachloride together make a legendary concoction called the 'Ziegler-Natta catalyst'. This catalyst is famous for forcing polymer chains to pack together tightly!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question is testing your knowledge of one of the coolest discoveries in the history of chemistry—a discovery so amazing it won a Nobel Prize!

Let's talk about **Polyethene** (often called polyethylene or simply 'plastic'). It is made by joining thousands of ethene ($CH_2=CH_2$) molecules together into long chains. But here is the trick: *how* you join them completely changes the type of plastic you get!

**Scenario 1: Low Density Polythene (LDP)**
Imagine throwing dry spaghetti randomly into a huge pot. The spaghetti pieces crisscross over each other in a messy, chaotic way. They take up a lot of empty space because they are 'branched'. Since they don't pack closely together, the density is low. This creates a soft, flexible plastic (like grocery bags and squeezy ketchup bottles). To make this messy LDP, you have to use brutal conditions: super high pressure (1000-2000 atm) and extreme heat!

**Scenario 2: High Density Polythene (HDP) - The Subject of Our Question!**
Now, imagine you want super strong, tough plastic to make garbage bins or thick chemical containers. You need your 'spaghetti' chains to be perfectly straight (linear) so they can stack right on top of each other, leaving zero empty space! Tightly packed molecules = High Density.

But how do you force the molecules to behave and line up straight? 
In the 1950s, scientists Karl Ziegler and Giulio Natta invented a magical 'molecular machine'—a catalyst made of **triethylaluminium ($Al(C_2H_5)_3$)** and **titanium tetrachloride ($TiCl_4$)**. This became known as the legendary **Ziegler-Natta catalyst**.

When you use this catalyst, you don't need crazy high pressure anymore! Even at a very low pressure (6-7 atm) and mild temperature (333-343 K), the catalyst acts like a zipper, perfectly aligning the ethene molecules into straight, linear chains. Because the chains are perfectly straight, they pack incredibly closely together, forming **High Density Polythene (HDP)**.

The question explicitly mentions linear molecules, close packing, low pressure, and the specific Ziegler-Natta catalyst chemicals. All of these are the giant neon signs pointing to High density polythene!

questions.Question: Q6. Given below are two statements : Statement I : Ethene at 333 to 343K and 6-7 atm pressure in the presence of AlEt3 and TiCl4 undergoes addition polymerization to give LDP. Statement II : Caprolactam at 533-543 K in H2O through step growth polymerizes to give Nylon 6.
MCQ_Options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
questions.Hint: Look closely at Statement I! Does the Ziegler-Natta catalyst (AlEt3 and TiCl4) make LOW density polythene, or HIGH density polythene?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's investigate these two chemical statements to see which one is telling the truth!

**Evaluating Statement I:**
The statement says that reacting ethene at low pressure (6-7 atm) using the catalyst $AlEt_3$ (Triethylaluminium) and $TiCl_4$ (Titanium tetrachloride) gives LDP (Low Density Polythene). 
*Wait a minute!* The combination of $AlEt_3$ and $TiCl_4$ is the famous Ziegler-Natta catalyst! As we learned earlier, this catalyst is a perfectionist. It forces the plastic molecules to grow in completely straight, unbranched lines. Because the chains are straight, they pack together incredibly tightly, leaving almost no empty space. High packing means high density! Therefore, this process creates **HDP (High Density Polythene)**, not LDP. 
To make LDP, you need chaotic conditions: extreme pressure (1000-2000 atmospheres) and a bit of peroxide initiator. Since the statement claims it makes LDP, **Statement I is entirely FALSE.**

**Evaluating Statement II:**
This statement talks about 'Caprolactam'. Imagine caprolactam as a circle (a 7-membered ring molecule consisting of carbon atoms and an amide group). It looks like a closed loop of string. 
The statement says if you heat this caprolactam ring with water ($H_2O$) to a high temperature (533-543 K), it becomes Nylon-6.
Is this true? Yes! The water and heat act like a pair of microscopic scissors. They snip the ring open, turning the circle into a straight piece of string. Once opened, the end of one string grabs the end of the next string, and the next, and the next! They undergo step-growth polymerization to form a giant, super-strong plastic thread called **Nylon-6**. (Fun fact: It's called Nylon '6' because every single Caprolactam monomer has exactly 6 carbon atoms in it!). Therefore, **Statement II is absolutely TRUE.**

Conclusion: Statement I is false, but Statement II is true. Chemistry is awesome when you can spot the traps!
questions.Answer: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.Question: Q7. Match The following (I) PTFE; (II) Dacron; (III) Caprolactam; (IV) Propene
MCQ_Options: (I) matches with Teflon, (II) matches with Polyester, (III) matches with Nylon-6, (IV) matches with Polypropylene
(I) matches with Nylon-6, (II) matches with Polypropylene, (III) matches with Teflon, (IV) matches with Polyester
(I) matches with Polyester, (II) matches with Teflon, (III) matches with Polypropylene, (IV) matches with Nylon-6
(I) matches with Polypropylene, (II) matches with Nylon-6, (III) matches with Polyester, (IV) matches with Teflon
questions.Hint: Match the acronyms/monomers to their real-world polymer names! What is the non-stick coating on frying pans made of? What is the chemical name for Terylene/Polyester?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Even though the second list was not fully written out in the prompt, any good chemistry detective can figure out what these four famous chemicals are supposed to match with! We are matching technical polymer/monomer names to their common commercial names or the final polymer they create. Let's decode them one by one!

**1. PTFE (I):**
PTFE stands for **Polytetrafluoroethylene**. Wow, that's a huge word! Let's break it down: 'Poly' means many. 'Tetra' means four. 'Fluoro' means fluorine. 'Ethylene' is the carbon base. So, this is a long chain of carbons completely shielded by slippery fluorine atoms. Because fluorine hates sticking to anything, this plastic is incredibly slippery. We use it to coat non-stick frying pans so your eggs don't get glued to the pan! You probably know it by its famous brand name: **Teflon**. So, PTFE matches with Teflon.

**2. Dacron (II):**
Dacron is a commercial brand name for a super strong synthetic fiber. It's made by combining an alcohol (ethylene glycol) and an acid (terephthalic acid) which creates 'ester' links. Because the polymer chain is full of these ester links, it's broadly called a **Polyester** (specifically, it's also known as Terylene). If you check the tag on a sports jersey, it is probably made of this! So, Dacron matches with Polyester.

**3. Caprolactam (III):**
We literally just met this guy in the previous question! Caprolactam is a ring-shaped molecule that contains 6 carbon atoms. When you heat it up with water, the ring pops open, and thousands of them link hands to form a super-tough synthetic fiber used in ropes, toothbrush bristles, and stockings. Because the starting building block has 6 carbons, the resulting polymer is named **Nylon-6**. So, Caprolactam matches with Nylon-6.

**4. Propene (IV):**
Propene ($CH_3-CH=CH_2$) is a simple gas molecule with a double bond. If you crack open that double bond and link millions of propene molecules together, you get a solid plastic. Just add the word 'Poly' to the front! The polymer is called **Polypropylene** (or Polypropene). It's tough and heat-resistant, often used to make plastic chairs and food containers. So, Propene matches with Polypropylene.

Therefore, the correct matching is: PTFE is Teflon, Dacron is Polyester, Caprolactam makes Nylon-6, and Propene makes Polypropylene. You are now practically a polymer expert!
questions.Answer: (I) matches with Teflon, (II) matches with Polyester, (III) matches with Nylon-6, (IV) matches with Polypropylene

questions.Question:
Match List-I with List-II :
List I: 
(A) Nylon 6 
(B) Natural rubber 
(C) Vulcanised rubber

(II) Sulphur containing rubber 
(III) Caprolactum

questions.Hint: Think of polymers like giant Lego castles and monomers as the individual Lego bricks. What 'brick' is used to build Natural Rubber?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Imagine you are a master builder, and you have different types of giant structures (Polymers) to build. To build them, you need specific building blocks (Monomers). Let's figure out which block belongs to which structure!

1. **Natural Rubber (B):** Have you ever wondered what natural rubber is made of? It is built by linking thousands of molecules of a chemical called **Isoprene** (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) end-to-end. So, Natural rubber matches with Isoprene (IV).

2. **Vulcanised Rubber (C):** Natural rubber gets mushy in the summer and brittle in the winter. To fix this, scientists 'cook' it with **Sulphur**. The sulphur forms little strong bridges between the rubber chains, locking them into place. This is called 'Vulcanised rubber'. So, Vulcanised rubber matches with Sulphur containing rubber (II).

3. **Neoprene (D):** This is synthetic rubber, famously used to make scuba diving wet-suits! It is built from a monomer that looks exactly like isoprene, but with a chlorine atom instead of a methyl group. We call this building block **Chloroprene**. So, Neoprene matches with Chloroprene (I).

4. **Nylon 6 (A):** Nylon is a super-strong fiber used in ropes and parachutes. 'Nylon 6' is built from a special ring-shaped molecule that has 6 carbon atoms, called **Caprolactam**. When you heat it, the ring pops open and joins with others to form a long chain. So, Nylon 6 matches with Caprolactam (III).

Putting it all together: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I). See? It's just matching the right Lego block to the right castle!

questions.Question: Which of the following is not an example of a condensation polymer?
questions.Hint: Condensation polymers 'sweat out' a small molecule (like water) when they form. Addition polymers just open their double bonds and hold hands without losing anything. Which of these is formed by just holding hands?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into the fascinating way molecules link together! There are two main ways monomers (our chemical building blocks) join hands to become giant polymers.

**1. Addition Polymerization:** Imagine a group of kids standing in a line, with their hands completely tucked into their pockets (these are molecules with double bonds). When it's time to polymerize, they just take their hands out of their pockets and hold hands with the kid next to them. No one leaves, nothing is lost. They just add together!

**2. Condensation Polymerization:** Now imagine kids trying to hold hands, but they are holding a heavy water bottle in one hand and an apple in the other. To hold hands, they have to drop the water bottle and the apple. In chemistry, when molecules join this way, they drop a small molecule (usually water, $H_2O$, or hydrochloric acid, $HCl$). Because they 'sweat out' this small molecule, we call it a condensation reaction.

Now let's look at the options:
- **Nylon 6,6**, **Dacron**, and **Silicones** are all created by molecules that react and drop small molecules (like water) to form links (amides, esters, and siloxanes). They are condensation polymers.
- **Buna-N** is a synthetic rubber made from two molecules: 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile. Both of these molecules have double bonds (hands in pockets). They just break their double bonds open and hold hands. Nothing is dropped! It's a pure **Addition Polymer**.

Therefore, Buna-N is NOT a condensation polymer. Great job understanding the mechanics of how molecules bond!

questions.Question: The Novolac polymer has mass of 963 g. The number of monomer units present in it are:
questions.Hint: Novolac is formed by joining Phenol and Formaldehyde, losing water in the process. Calculate the approximate mass of one repeating unit and divide the total mass by it!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This is a wonderful chemical detective puzzle! We have a giant molecule called Novolac weighing 963 grams, and we need to find out how many 'links' are in this chain.

**Step 1: Understand Novolac**
Novolac is a linear polymer used to make paints and coatings. It's made by a condensation reaction between two molecules: **Phenol** ($C_6H_5OH$) and **Formaldehyde** ($CH_2O$). 
When they react, Formaldehyde forms a $CH_2$ 'bridge' between two Phenol rings, and in doing so, they kick out a molecule of water ($H_2O$).

**Step 2: Find the mass of one 'repeating unit'**
Let's calculate the mass of the parts that actually make it into the final chain. 
A single repeating unit consists of a phenol ring attached to a $CH_2$ bridge. 
- Phenol molecule ($C_6H_6O$) = $94$ amu.
- Formaldehyde ($CH_2O$) = $30$ amu.
- Total before reacting = $94 + 30 = 124$ amu.
- Since it's a condensation polymer, they 'sweat out' water ($H_2O$, mass = 18 amu) every time they link.
- Mass of the repeating unit = $124 - 18 = 106$ amu.

**Step 3: Solve the puzzle**
The entire chain has a mass of roughly 963. If each repeating link weighs about 106, how many links are there?
Number of units = $\frac{\text{Total Mass}}{\text{Mass of one unit}}$
Number of units = $\frac{963}{106} \approx 9.08$

Since we can't have a fraction of a molecule block, the closest whole number of repeating monomer units is **9**. (The slight extra mass comes from the atoms at the very ends of the long chain, just like the endcaps on a beaded necklace!). You just reverse-engineered a polymer!

questions.Question: Choose the correct polymer name for the following repeating structure: [-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH2-CH(C6H5)-]n
questions.Hint: Look closely at the atoms inside the bracket. Do you see the C6H5 group? That's a benzene ring, which belongs to a molecule called Styrene. Which of the polymer names sounds like it contains Styrene?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's become chemical codebreakers! The structure given is `[-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH2-CH(C6H5)-]n`.
This giant molecule looks complicated, but it's actually just two smaller molecules holding hands in an alternating pattern.

Let's cut the repeating unit in half to see who is holding hands:
1. The left part is `[-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-]`. This comes from **1,3-butadiene** (a molecule with 4 carbon atoms that originally had two double bonds).
2. The right part is `[-CH2-CH(C6H5)-]`. The $C_6H_5$ is a bulky hexagon-shaped benzene ring. A molecule with a double bond and a benzene ring is called **Styrene**.

So, this polymer is made by co-polymerizing (mixing two different monomers) Butadiene and Styrene.
Now, let's look at the names chemists gave these materials:
- **Bu** stands for **Bu**tadiene.
- **na** stands for Natrium (the Latin word for Sodium, which is the chemical spark or catalyst used to start the reaction).
- **S** stands for **S**tyrene.

Put it all together: **Bu-na-S**. It's the exact synthetic rubber used to make car tires! Because our structure clearly shows the Styrene ring ($C_6H_5$), it must be Buna-S.

questions.Question: Which is true about Buna-N?
MCQ_Options: It is obtained by copolymerization of 1, 3-butadiene and acrylonitrile
It is a linear polymer of 1, 3-butadiene
It is obtained by copolymerization of 1, 3-butadiene and styrene
The suffix N in Buna-N stands for its natural occurrence.
questions.Hint: Remember how chemists name synthetic rubbers. 'Bu' is for Butadiene, 'na' is for the Sodium catalyst. What do you think the 'N' stands for?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's decipher the secret language of chemistry again! Chemists often pack the recipe of a compound right into its name.

Let's break down the name **Buna-N**:
1. **Bu:** This tells us the first main ingredient is **1,3-Butadiene**. (This is the stretchy part of the rubber).
2. **na:** This is the symbol for Natrium, which is the Latin name for **Sodium** ($Na$). Sodium isn't a building block here; it acts as the 'coach' or catalyst that forces the molecules to react with each other.
3. **N:** This stands for the second ingredient, a chemical called **Acrylonitrile** (which contains a Nitrile group, $-C \equiv N$). This ingredient gives the rubber resistance to oils and chemicals.

Because Buna-N uses *two* different types of building blocks (Butadiene and Acrylonitrile), it is called a **copolymer**. 

Let's check the false options:
- It is not just 1,3-butadiene alone (that would be polybutadiene).
- If it used styrene, it would be called Buna-S, not Buna-N.
- The 'N' absolutely does not stand for 'natural'. Buna-N is 100% created in a laboratory to make things like oil seals and surgical gloves!

Therefore, Buna-N is obtained by the copolymerization of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile.
questions.Answer: It is obtained by copolymerization of 1, 3-butadiene and acrylonitrile

questions.Question:
Given below are two statements, one is Assertion (A) and other is Reason (R). 
Assertion (A) : Natural rubber is a linear polymer of isoprene called cis-polyisoprene with elastic properties. 
Reason (R) : The cis-polyisoprene molecules consist of various chains held together by strong polar interactions with coiled structure.
MCQ_Options: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.Hint: For a material to be 'elastic' (stretchy), the chains inside it must be able to slide past each other easily. If they were held together by 'strong' forces, would the rubber stretch or would it be rigid like plastic?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore why rubber bands are so fun to stretch!

**Assertion (A):** Natural rubber is indeed made of thousands of isoprene molecules lined up end-to-end. Because of the specific way they link up (both ends of the chain are on the same side of the double bond, which chemists call 'cis'), the molecule doesn't form a straight, neat line. Instead, it naturally curls up like a coiled spring or a bowl of tangled spaghetti. This coiled shape is exactly what gives it elastic properties. When you pull it, the coils straighten out. When you let go, it coils back up! So, Assertion (A) is **True**.

**Reason (R):** Here is where the trick lies. Imagine a bowl of spaghetti. If you pour thick, hard glue all over it, you wouldn't be able to separate or stretch the noodles, right? In chemistry, 'strong polar interactions' (like hydrogen bonding) act like that hard glue. If rubber chains were held together tightly by strong forces, the rubber would be tough and rigid, like a nylon rope or hard plastic.
For rubber to be an elastomer (stretchy), the chains must be held together by very **weak** forces (called Van der Waals forces). These weak forces allow the chains to slide and stretch past one another without snapping. 
Therefore, Reason (R) says they are held by 'strong polar interactions', which is completely **False**.

Conclusion: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false!
questions.Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

questions.Hint: When an alcohol molecule reacts with an acid molecule, they link together and form an 'Ester'. If you have a monomer with two alcohols and another with two acids, what kind of chain will they form?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about the clothes you might be wearing right now! A lot of athletic wear is made of a material called Polyester, and Dacron is a famous brand name for it. Let's see how it's made.

**Reason (R) Analysis:** How do you make Dacron? You need two special building blocks:
1. **Ethylene glycol:** This molecule has an alcohol group ($-OH$) on both of its ends.
2. **Terephthalic acid:** This molecule has a carboxylic acid group ($-COOH$) on both of its ends.
So, Reason (R) is factually **True**. These are indeed the two monomers of Dacron.

**Assertion (A) Analysis:** What happens when an alcohol meets an acid? They undergo a famous chemical reaction called 'Esterification'. The alcohol and the acid react, spit out a tiny molecule of water, and hold hands to form a new chemical bond called an **Ester bond**. 
Because our building blocks have reactive groups on *both* ends, they can do this over and over again! Acid links to alcohol, which links to another acid, which links to another alcohol. 
Since the resulting giant chain is full of thousands of ester bonds, we call the whole thing a **Poly-ester**! So, Assertion (A) is **True**.

**The Relationship:** Why is Dacron an example of a polyester polymer (Assertion A)? *Because* it is made by reacting ethylene glycol (a dialcohol) and terephthalic acid (a diacid), which form ester linkages (Reason R). 
So, not only are both statements true, but R perfectly explains A! Great job thinking through the chemistry of your clothes!
questions.Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.Question: Q15. Melamine polymer is formed by the condensation of: H2N-CO-NH2 and HCHO; C6H5NH2 and HCHO; C6H5OH and HCHO; C6H5NH2 and C6H5OH
questions.Hint: Look closely at the question and options! Melamine has a specific ring structure, but sometimes examiners make mistakes. Which option represents a similar famous resin (Urea-Formaldehyde)?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there, future scientist! I am going to let you in on a little secret: sometimes tests have mistakes, and being a great chemist means being able to spot them! The question asks for the ingredients (monomers) of a 'Melamine' polymer. Melamine is a ring-shaped molecule with the formula C_3H_6N_6, and it reacts with formaldehyde (HCHO) to make tough plastic plates that don't easily break. $

However$, look at the options provided! None of them actually contain Melamine! Let's decode them: $
1) H_2N$-CO-NH_2 is Urea. When mixed with HCHO, it forms Urea-Formaldehyde resin. $
2) C_6H_5$OH is Phenol. Mixed with HCHO, it makes Bakelite (used in old heavy telephones and electrical switches).$
3) C_6H_5$NH_2 is Aniline. $

Since$ none of the options are Melamine, it's highly likely the test-maker accidentally confused 'Melamine' with 'Urea' because both of them react with Formaldehyde (HCHO) via condensation. Condensation is like two chemical molecules holding hands to form a chain, and as they squeeze their hands together, a small water molecule (H_2O) drops out! If you ever face a question like this, the best guess is to pick the Urea-Formaldehyde option, but always know the true chemistry in your heart: true Melamine polymer requires Melamine + HCHO!

questions.Question: Q16. Vulcanization of rubber is carried out by heating a mixture of isoprene and styrene; neoprene and sulphur; isoprene and sulphur; neoprene and styrene
questions.Hint: Natural rubber gets sticky when hot and brittle when cold. What yellow element do we add to build 'bridges' between the polymer chains?
questions.Detailed_Explanation: Imagine you have a huge bowl of cooked spaghetti. The noodles slide past each other easily, right? Natural rubber is just like that! It is made of long polymer chains of a molecule called 'isoprene' (which links up to form polyisoprene). Because the chains just slide over one another, natural rubber gets really sticky in summer and super brittle in winter. It wouldn't make a very good car tire! $\n\nIn 1839$, a scientist named Charles Goodyear discovered a magical fix. If you take this natural rubber (polyisoprene) and heat it with Sulphur, an amazing chemical reaction happens. The sulphur atoms form actual physical 'bridges' (cross-links) between the slippery spaghetti noodles. Now, when you pull on the rubber, the chains can stretch, but the sulphur bridges pull them right back into place! This process is called Vulcanization, named after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. Therefore, to vulcanize natural rubber, we heat a mixture of isoprene (the building block of natural rubber) and sulphur!

questions.Question: Q17. Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Buna-N; (B) Terylene; (C) Nylon-6,6; (D) Neoprene List II: (I) Synthetic rubber; (II) Fibre; (III) Elastomer; (IV) Polyester
questions.Hint: Terylene is used to make polyester clothes, and Nylon is used to make ropes and fibres. Buna-N is a famous artificial rubber.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play a matching game by looking at the secret identities of these amazing materials! Think of polymers as having different 'jobs' in the real world. $

First$, let's look at (B) Terylene. Have you ever checked the tag on your t-shirt and seen the word 'Polyester'? That's Terylene! So, (B) matches with (IV) Polyester. $

Next$ is (C) Nylon-6,6. Nylon is super strong and can be pulled into long, thin threads to make fishing lines, ropes, and fabrics. In the polymer world, things pulled into threads are called 'Fibres'. So, (C) matches with (II) Fibre. $

Now$ we have (A) Buna-N and (D) Neoprene. Both of these are bouncy and stretchy, which makes them 'Elastomers' (elastic polymers).
