However, Buna-N is specifically famed as a 'Synthetic rubber' used to make oil seals for car engines because it doesn't melt in oil. Neoprene is a classic 'Elastomer' used to make those thick, warm scuba diving suits! So, Buna-N (A) matches nicely with Synthetic rubber (I), and Neoprene (D) goes with Elastomer (III). Put it all together, and we have a perfect match!

questions.Question: Q18. Terylene polymer is obtained by condensation of : Ethane-1,2-diol and Benzene-1,3 dicarboxylic acid; Propane-1, 2-diol and Benzene-1, 4 dicarboxylic acid; Ethane-1,2-diol and Benzene-1, 4 dicarboxylic acid; Ethane-1,2-diol and Benzene-1, 2 dicarboxylic acid
questions.Hint: Look at the name 'Ter-ylene'. 'Ter' comes from Terephthalic acid (the 1,4 position), and 'ylene' comes from Ethylene glycol (2 carbons).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered how scientists name things? Often, they hide the ingredients right inside the name! Let's break down the word 'Terylene'. $

The$ 'Ter' part stands for Terephthalic acid. 'Terephthalic' is just a fancy, old-school chemical name for a benzene ring that has two carboxylic acid groups (-COOH) attached exactly on opposite sides. In IUPAC naming, opposite sides on a 6-carbon ring means positions 1 and 4. So, its modern name is Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. $

The$ 'ylene' part comes from Ethylene glycol. 'Eth' means two carbons. 'Glycol' (or diol) means it has two alcohol (-OH) groups. So its modern name is Ethane-1,2-diol. $

When$ these two mix, the -OH from the acid and the -H from the alcohol join forces, turn into a water molecule (H_2O), and leave the chat. What is left behind bonds together to form an ester link (-COO-). Because this happens over and over, thousands of times, we get a Poly-ester! So, the monomers are Ethane-1,2-diol and Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.

questions.Question: Q19. Match List I with List II List I: (A) Terylene; (B) Nylon-6,6; (C) Buna-S; (D) Neoprene List II: (I) Buta-1,3-diene and styrene; (II) Hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid; (III) Chloroprene; (IV) Ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid
questions.Hint: Look for the obvious clues in the names! 'Buna-S' has an 'S' for Styrene. 'Nylon-6,6' uses molecules that each have exactly 6 carbon atoms.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's become molecular detectives and match these giant polymer chains to their tiny building blocks (monomers)! $

($A) Terylene: We just learned about this! 'Ter' means terephthalic acid, and 'ylene' means ethylene glycol. They form polyester. So, (A) matches perfectly with (IV). $

($B) Nylon-6,6: The numbers '6,6' are a massive clue. It means both building blocks must have exactly 6 carbon atoms! Hexamethylene diamine ('Hexa' = 6) and Adipic acid (which also has a 6-carbon chain) are the ingredients. They react to make strong threads. So, (B) pairs with (II). $

($C) Buna-S: Let's decode the name! 'Bu' stands for Buta-1,3-diene. 'Na' stands for Sodium (the catalyst historically used). And 'S' stands for Styrene! It's the rubber used in your car tires. So, (C) is matched to (I). $

($D) Neoprene: This is the superhero rubber used in chemical gloves and wetsuits. It's made by linking thousands of Chloroprene molecules together. So, (D) matches with (III). $

When$ you put all the clues together, we get a beautiful map of chemistry!

questions.Question: Q20. The structure of neoprene is [CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH2-CH(CN)]n, [CH2-CH(CN)]n, [CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2]n, [CH2-C(CH3)=CH-CH2]n
questions.Hint: Neoprene is also known as poly-CHLORO-prene. Which of the options has a Chlorine (Cl) atom hiding in it?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This might look like a scary bunch of brackets and letters, but it is actually a very simple game of 'Spot the Difference'. Let's find the structure of Neoprene! $

Neoprene$'s scientific name is Polychloroprene. Think of the word 'Chloro' - that means it absolutely MUST contain a Chlorine (Cl) atom in its chemical structure. $

Now$, look closely at the choices: $
1)$ $[CH_2-CH=CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH(CN)]_n$ has a (CN) cyanide group. This is actually a piece of Buna-N. $
2)$ $[CH_2-CH(CN)]_n$ only has a (CN) group. This is Polyacrylonitrile (used to make fake wool sweaters). $
3)$ $[CH_2-C(CH_3)=CH-CH_2]_n$ has a (CH_3) methyl group. This is natural rubber, also known as Polyisoprene. $
4)$ $[CH_2-C(Cl)=CH-CH_2]_n$ has a (Cl) Chlorine atom right there in the middle! $

When$ thousands of 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene (chloroprene) molecules line up, their double bonds shift to the center, and they grab onto each other on the ends, creating this beautiful repeating chain: $[CH_2-C(Cl)=CH-CH_2]_n$. Just finding the 'Cl' solves the mystery!

questions.Question: Q21. Which statement is correct? Buna- N is a natural polymer; Buna- S is a synthetic and linear thermosetting polymer; Neoprene is an addition copolymer used in plastic bucket manufacturing; Synthesis of buna- S needs nascent oxygen.
MCQ_Options: Buna- N is a natural polymer
Buna- S is a synthetic and linear thermosetting polymer
Neoprene is an addition copolymer used in plastic bucket manufacturing
Synthesis of buna- S needs nascent oxygen
questions.Hint: Try playing 'Two Truths and a Lie' with these options. Eliminate the ones that are definitely wrong! Thermosetting plastics can't melt, and natural rubber comes from trees, not labs.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Sometimes in chemistry, finding the right answer means proving all the other answers wrong! Let's examine these statements one by one. $

Option 1$: 'Buna-N is a natural polymer.' This is FALSE! Natural rubber comes from weeping rubber trees. Buna-N is made in huge chemical factories using butadiene and acrylonitrile. It is strictly synthetic. $

Option 2$: 'Buna-S is a synthetic and linear thermosetting polymer.' FALSE! Buna-S is an elastomer (a rubber). 'Thermosetting' means once you shape it, it becomes a hard, unbreakable block that cannot be melted (like Bakelite handles on frying pans). Buna-S is not thermosetting unless it is heavily vulcanized, and 'linear thermosetting' is basically a contradiction since thermosets require heavy 3D cross-linking. $

Option 3$: 'Neoprene is an addition copolymer used in plastic bucket manufacturing.' FALSE! First, Neoprene is made only of chloroprene, meaning it's a homopolymer (one ingredient), not a copolymer (two or more). Second, buckets are usually made of cheap, tough plastics like HDPE, not expensive scuba-suit rubber. $

Option 4$: 'Synthesis of buna-S needs nascent oxygen.' TRUE! In modern chemical plants, Buna-S is made through 'emulsion polymerization'. To kick off this reaction, we need a 'free radical initiator' - a hyper-energetic molecule. Chemists often use peroxides (like hydrogen peroxide), which break apart to provide highly reactive, single oxygen atoms (nascent oxygen) to start the polymer chain reaction. Through elimination and chemical logic, this is our winner!
questions.Answer: Synthesis of buna- S needs nascent oxygen

questions.Question: Match List-I with List-II. List I: (A) Nylon-6; (B) Buna-N; (C) Neoprene; (D) PHBV List II: (i) Biodegradable polymer; (ii) Fibre; (iii) Synthetic rubber; (iv) Elastomer
questions.Hint: Think about what makes climbing ropes so strong, what material oil pipes need, and what kind of plastic bacteria would actually love to eat!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's dive into the fascinating world of polymers. Imagine a polymer like a massive chain made of thousands of tiny interlocking Lego pieces. Different combinations of these pieces give us materials with totally different superpowers! Let's break down our matches.

First up, Nylon-6. Have you ever wondered what makes climbing ropes so incredibly strong or what stockings are made of? That is Nylon-6! It is a type of 'Fibre' because its long polymer chains pack closely together with strong forces, creating super strong threads. 

Next, we have Buna-N and Neoprene. Both of these fall into the rubber family. Buna-N is a 'Synthetic rubber' that is famously resistant to oils, chemicals, and fuels, making it perfect for the hoses inside car engines! Neoprene is an 'Elastomer' (a stretchy polymer that easily bounces back to its original shape). If you have ever touched a thick, spongy scuba diving wetsuit, you have touched Neoprene!

Finally, we have PHBV. This one is like a superhero for the environment. Regular plastics sit in landfills for thousands of years because bacteria look at them and say, 'Yuck, I cannot eat that.' But PHBV is a 'Biodegradable polymer'. It is specially designed so that naturally occurring bacteria can actually digest it and break it down into safe byproducts! 

So, if we match them up logically based on their main defining characteristics in chemistry: Nylon-6 is our super-strong Fibre (ii). PHBV is our eco-friendly Biodegradable polymer (i). Neoprene is a stretchy Elastomer (iv). And Buna-N is our tough Synthetic rubber (iii). Understanding what these materials do in the real world makes remembering their chemistry a total breeze!

questions.Chapter: Hydrocarbons / Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles
questions.Question: Match List-I with List-II. List I: (A) CH3CH2CH2Cl Alc. KOH; (B) CH3CH2C≡CH H2, Pd/BaSO4; (C) C6H6 + Cl2 h\$\nu$; (D) (-CH=CH-)n Doping List II: (1) Alkanes; (2) Alkenes; (3) BHC; (4) Conducting polymer
questions.Hint: Remember that 'Alc. KOH' loves to remove things to create double bonds, and sunlight (h\$\nu)$ gives chlorine the extreme energy needed to attack a stable benzene ring!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's unravel these super cool organic chemistry reactions! Think of chemical reactions like different types of cooking recipes—each set of ingredients (reagents) has a very specific job to do.

Let's look at reaction (A): We have a molecule with a chlorine atom on it (CH3CH2CH2Cl), and we add 'Alc. KOH' (alcoholic potassium hydroxide). Alcoholic KOH is like an aggressive bouncer at a club—it doesn't just swap things out, it kicks atoms out completely! It kicks out the chlorine and a neighboring hydrogen to create a brand new double bond. This type of 'elimination' reaction turns our starting material into an Alkene (2)!

Now for reaction (B): We start with an alkyne (CH3CH2C≡CH), which has a rigid triple bond. We add Hydrogen gas (H2) and a special catalyst called Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/BaSO4). Usually, adding hydrogen would completely smash all the extra bonds and turn the triple bond into a boring single bond (alkane). But Lindlar's catalyst is intentionally 'poisoned' or slowed down. It acts like a brake pedal, stopping the reaction halfway to safely give us an Alkene (2)!

Reaction (C): We take Benzene (a very stable, happy ring of carbons) and throw in Chlorine gas (Cl2) with bright sunlight (h\$\nu)$. Normally, benzene is lazy and doesn't want to break its beautiful ring. But the intense energy from sunlight blasts the chlorine molecules into super-reactive 'free radicals'. They relentlessly attack the benzene ring, breaking all its double bonds and creating BHC (Benzene Hexachloride) (3).

Finally, reaction (D): We have polyacetylene, (-CH=CH-)n. Normally, plastics (polymers) do not conduct electricity—that is exactly why we wrap electrical wires in plastic to protect ourselves! But scientists discovered that if you 'dope' this specific polymer by adding certain chemicals, it suddenly allows electrons to flow through it freely. It magically transforms into a 'Conducting polymer' (4), which is a mind-blowing discovery that even won a Nobel Prize! 

Matching them up: A makes Alkene (2), B makes Alkene (2), C makes BHC (3), and D makes a Conducting polymer (4)!

questions.Question: Staggered and eclipsed conformers of ethane are :
questions.Hint: Think about how a propeller on an airplane spins. The molecule isn't breaking apart or forming mirrors; it's just rotating around a single axis!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are holding two umbrellas that are glued together at their handles. If you hold one umbrella perfectly still, you can easily spin the other umbrella around the handle. This is exactly what happens in the ethane molecule (CH3-CH3)! 

The 'handle' connecting the umbrellas is the single bond (a sigma bond) connecting the two carbon atoms. Because it is a single bond, the carbon atoms are free to rotate around it like a wheel spinning on an axle. As they spin, the hydrogen atoms attached to them move into different positions. These different temporary 3D shapes the molecule makes while spinning are called 'Conformers' or 'Rotamers' (which is short for rotational isomers)!

Now, let's talk about the two extreme points of this spinning motion: 'Staggered' and 'Eclipsed'. 

Imagine the hydrogens are like big, fluffy clouds of negative electrons. Because negative repels negative, these hydrogen clouds want to stay as far away from each other as possible! When you twist the molecule so that the hydrogens on the front carbon are perfectly tucked into the empty spaces between the hydrogens on the back carbon, they are completely spaced out. This is the 'Staggered' conformation. It is super relaxed, happy, and highly stable! 

But if you keep spinning it, eventually the front hydrogens line up perfectly to hide the back hydrogens (just like the moon hides the sun during a solar eclipse). This is the 'Eclipsed' conformation. The electron clouds are squished together and repel each other fiercely! This crowding creates what chemists call 'steric strain' (physical crowding) and 'torsional strain' (electron pushing). The molecule hates this position because it costs too much energy, so it will keep spinning right back to the staggered position. 

So, because these staggered and eclipsed shapes are created entirely by simple rotation around a single bond, they are officially classified as Rotamers!

questions.Question: Match List-I with List-II : List I: (a) CH3COCl H2, Pd-BaSO4; (b) CH3CN SnCl2/HCl; (c) CH3CH2OH Cu, 573K; (d) C6H5CH3 CrO2Cl2, CS2, H3O+ List II: (i) C6H5CHO; (ii) CH3CHO; (iii) C6H5CH3; (iv) CH3COOH
questions.Hint: All these famous named reactions share a secret goal: they are highly specialized chemical factories designed strictly to build Aldehydes without over-oxidizing!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Making an aldehyde is one of the trickiest jobs in organic chemistry! Think of oxidizing molecules like climbing a staircase. Alcohols are at the bottom step, Aldehydes are on the middle step, and Carboxylic Acids are at the top step. Most chemical reactions are way too powerful—they blast right past the middle step and take you straight to the top or bottom. But the four reactions in this question are 'special ops' techniques designed perfectly to stop exactly on the middle step: the Aldehyde!

Let's break them down:
(a) CH3COCl + H2, Pd-BaSO4: This is the famous 'Rosenmund Reduction'. We want to replace the chlorine with a hydrogen to make Acetaldehyde (CH3CHO). But adding Hydrogen with Palladium is usually too aggressive. So, chemists add Barium Sulfate (BaSO4) as a 'poison' to weaken the catalyst. It is like putting training wheels on a super-fast bike—it slows the reaction down so it stops perfectly at Acetaldehyde (ii).

(b) CH3CN + SnCl2/HCl: This is the 'Stephen Reaction'. We start with a nitrile (a carbon triple-bonded to a nitrogen). The tin chloride (SnCl2) and acid team up to gently break the triple bond, and after adding a splash of water, out pops Acetaldehyde (ii)!

(c) CH3CH2OH + Cu, 573K: Here we have Ethanol (an alcohol). If we pass its vapors over scorching hot Copper at 573 Kelvin, the copper acts like a polite thief. It gently steals exactly two hydrogen atoms (a process called dehydrogenation) from the alcohol, leaving behind—you guessed it—Acetaldehyde (ii)!

(d) C6H5CH3 + CrO2Cl2: This is the 'Etard Reaction'. We start with Toluene (a benzene ring with a methyl group). If we use a strong oxidizer, it would burn the methyl group all the way to a carboxylic acid. But Chromyl Chloride (CrO2Cl2) is a specialized, gentle oxidizer. It carefully tweaks the methyl group just enough to give us beautiful Benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO) (i).

So, surprisingly, reactions a, b, and c all form Acetaldehyde (ii), while reaction d forms Benzaldehyde (i)!

questions.Question: A biodegradable polyamide can be made from:
questions.Hint: You need a combination of ingredients that nature already knows how to digest. Think about the basic building blocks of the proteins inside your own body!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about a huge real-world problem: plastic waste! Traditional plastics, like standard nylon, are incredibly tough. That is great when you are using them (like in a parachute), but terrible when you throw them away. Why? Because the bacteria and fungi in soil do not have the right 'chemical scissors' (enzymes) to cut through those artificial synthetic polymer chains. So, the plastic just sits in the dirt forever.

But chemists came up with an absolutely brilliant solution: Biodegradable Polymers! The secret trick is to build a plastic using the exact same building blocks that Mother Nature already knows how to handle. 

Think about the natural proteins in your own body or in a piece of food. Your body breaks them down every single day! Proteins are naturally made of 'Amino Acids'. So, chemists realized that if they created a polymer chain out of amino acids, the bacteria in the soil would recognize it as 'food' and successfully break it down.

In this question, we are looking to make a biodegradable polyamide called 'Nylon-2-Nylon-6'. To build it, we need two specific, natural ingredients. 
The first ingredient is Glycine. Glycine is actually the simplest naturally occurring amino acid! The second ingredient is Aminocaproic acid, which is also an amino acid. 

When we chemically link Glycine (which has 2 carbon atoms) and Aminocaproic acid (which has 6 carbon atoms) together in a long, alternating chain, we get Nylon-2-Nylon-6! 
Because this plastic is held together by the exact same 'amide bonds' (also known as peptide bonds) found in natural proteins, bacteria in the environment can easily munch on it, breaking it down safely. That is why the correct pair of ingredients is Glycine and aminocaproic acid! It is literal chemistry saving the planet!

questions.Question: Bakelite is a cross-linked polymer of formaldehyde and :
questions.Hint: Think of this missing ingredient as the straight-line 'starter string' that gets completely tangled up with formaldehyde to make a tough, heat-resistant plastic!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever seen an old-school black rotary telephone, or felt the tough, heat-resistant black handle of a cooking frying pan? You were touching Bakelite! Bakelite was actually the very first fully synthetic plastic ever invented, way back in 1907 by a genius chemist named Leo Baekeland. 

But how do we make this tough, legendary material? It is a fascinating two-step process, and the answer to this question lies right in the middle of that process! 

Step 1: We start with two simple chemicals—Phenol (a benzene ring with an OH group) and Formaldehyde (HCHO). When we mix them together with a little bit of acid or base, they start holding hands to form a long, straight chain. This straight-chain polymer has a special name: 'Novolac'. Novolac is actually quite useful on its own! Because it is a simple straight chain, it can melt and easily dissolve, and it is widely used to make paints and varnishes.

Step 2: But Novolac is not Bakelite yet. To make the plastic tough enough to withstand high heat without melting, we have to lock those straight chains together. How? We take that Novolac, add a bunch more Formaldehyde, and crank up the heat! 

The extra formaldehyde acts like millions of microscopic bridges, aggressively connecting all the straight Novolac chains together in a massive, inescapable 3D web. This structural change is called 'cross-linking'. 

Once the cross-linking happens, the material officially becomes Bakelite. Because it is securely locked into this 3D web, it can never melt again, no matter how hot it gets. This makes it a 'thermosetting' plastic. 

So, Bakelite is simply the cross-linked, ultimate form of Formaldehyde and our straight-chain starter polymer, Novolac!

questions.Question: The polymer formed on heating novolac with formaldehyde is
questions.Hint: When you heat this mixture, it locks together into an unbreakable 3D web. It is the exact same tough plastic historically used to make vintage phones and hot pan handles!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question is the perfect continuation of our plastic-making journey! Let's imagine you are an inventor trying to create a material that is completely indestructible, waterproof, and won't melt even if you set a scorching hot frying pan directly on it. 

You decide to start with a chemical called Novolac. As we learned, Novolac is a linear polymer made of phenol and formaldehyde. Think of Novolac like a massive bowl of cooked spaghetti. Each noodle represents a long polymer chain. Because the noodles are just resting next to each other in the bowl, you can easily pull them apart or slide them around, which means Novolac is relatively soft and can melt easily. 

But you want something tough! So, what happens when you heat this Novolac 'spaghetti' and add a dash of a chemical called Formaldehyde? 

When things get hot, the Formaldehyde gets to work like a microscopic master welder. It starts building incredibly strong chemical bridges between the individual spaghetti noodles. It bonds the top chain to the bottom chain, the left chain to the right chain, and so on. Suddenly, instead of a bowl of loose, slippery noodles, you have one giant, unbreakable 3D block! 

This 3D bonding process is called 'cross-linking'. When Novolac is fully cross-linked by heating it with formaldehyde, it transforms into an entirely new substance: Bakelite! 

Bakelite is famously known as a 'thermosetting' polymer. The 'thermo-setting' part means that once it is heated and set into its 3D shape, those chemical bridges are permanent. You cannot melt Bakelite back down into a liquid, which is exactly why it was historically used for making electrical switches, car parts, and pot handles that get incredibly hot without deforming! 
So, heating novolac with formaldehyde yields the tough, legendary plastic known as Bakelite.

questions.Question: Q29. Monomer of novolac is 3-hydroxybutanoic acid; phenol and melamine; o-hydroxymethylphenol; 1,3-butadiene and styrene
questions.Hint: Novolac is a linear polymer used in paints. It's the first stage of making the hard plastic Bakelite, and it is made from reacting phenol with formaldehyde.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there, young scientist! Let's talk about 'Polymers'. Think of a polymer like a massive, long chain made of Lego blocks. The individual Lego blocks are called 'monomers'. 

Our question asks about 'Novolac'. You might not have heard of Novolac, but you've definitely seen it—it's often used in paints and varnishes! Novolac is made from two starting chemicals: Phenol (a benzene ring with an -OH group) and Formaldehyde (a simple carbon molecule, HCHO). 

When these two react, they don't immediately form a giant chain. First, they combine to form an intermediate 'block'. Formaldehyde attaches to the phenol ring, usually at the position right next to the -OH group. In chemistry, the position right next door is called the 'ortho' position. This creates a molecule called 'o-hydroxymethylphenol'. 

Once you have a bunch of these o-hydroxymethylphenol molecules, they start holding hands, forming a long, straight line. Because they join together in a linear chain, we get Novolac! If we let them cross-link and tangle up into a 3D web, it becomes a super hard plastic called Bakelite (used in pan handles!). 

So, the primary building block—the monomer piece that strings together to make the linear Novolac chain—is o-hydroxymethylphenol.

questions.Question: Q30. Monomer units of dacron polymer are ethylene glycol and phthalic acid; ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid; glycerol and terephthalic acid; glycerol and phthalic acid
questions.Hint: Dacron is also known as 'Terylene'. Look for the acid that starts with 'Ter' to help you remember!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are designing a cool new synthetic fabric for a sports t-shirt. You're likely wearing a polymer right now called 'Polyester'! Dacron is just a famous brand name for a specific polyester, also known in chemistry as Terylene.

To make a polyester, you need two types of Lego pieces: one piece that has 'alcohol' hooks on both ends (a diol) and another piece that has 'acid' hooks on both ends (a dicarboxylic acid). When an alcohol hook and an acid hook click together, they spit out a tiny molecule of water. This is called 'condensation'.

Let's figure out the specific pieces for Dacron:
1. The alcohol piece is 'ethylene glycol'. It's a simple chain of two carbons, with an -OH on each end.
2. The acid piece is a benzene ring with two acid groups (-COOH) directly opposite each other. When they are on opposite sides (the 'para' position), it's called 'terephthalic acid'. 

Here is a super easy memory trick for you: Dacron is also known as Terylene. Notice how 'Terylene' sounds a lot like 'Terephthalic' acid? That's your clue! If you used regular phthalic acid (where the acid groups are right next to each other), you'd get a different, much messier polymer called Glyptal, not Dacron.

Therefore, to weave this beautiful, tough synthetic fiber, your starting materials (monomers) must be ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid.

questions.Question: Q31. Preparation of Bakelite proceeds via reactions: Electrophilic addition and dehydration; Condensation and elimination; Electrophilic substitution and dehydration; Nucleophilic addition and dehydration
questions.Hint: Think about how a benzene ring reacts. The ring is rich in electrons, so it loves to be attacked by 'electron-loving' species (electrophiles) while kicking out a hydrogen atom (substitution).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Alright, let's step into the shoes of a brilliant organic chemist! We are making Bakelite, the world's first fully synthetic plastic, invented over a hundred years ago! It's so tough it's used to make billiard balls and the black handles on your kitchen pots.

Bakelite is made from Phenol (a benzene ring with an -OH) and Formaldehyde (HCHO). But how do they actually connect? Let's look at the chemistry step-by-step:

Step 1: The Benzene Ring is an 'Electron Cloud'.
The phenol ring is packed with negatively charged electrons. Formaldehyde, in the presence of an acid, gets an eager, positive charge on its carbon. We call this positively charged carbon an 'Electrophile' (which literally means 'electron-lover'). 

Step 2: The Attack (Electrophilic Substitution).
The electron-rich phenol ring sees the positively charged formaldehyde and grabs it! In doing so, the phenol has to kick out a tiny Hydrogen atom to make room. Because an electrophile came in and a hydrogen was swapped out, this is called 'Electrophilic Substitution'. 

Step 3: Building the 3D Web (Dehydration).
Now we have these modified phenol pieces, but they need to link together into a massive 3D web to become hard plastic. When they link, an -OH from one part and an -H from another join to form H2O (water), which then drips away. Removing water is called 'Dehydration'.

Putting it all together, the reaction first uses Electrophilic substitution to prepare the pieces, and then Dehydration to link them up into un-meltable Bakelite!

questions.Question: Q32. Which one of the following polymers is not obtained by condensation polymerisation? Nylon 6,6; Buna - N; Bakelite; Nylon 6
questions.Hint: Condensation polymerization usually releases a small molecule like water. Addition polymerization is like people opening their arms and holding hands without losing anything—look for the polymer made from molecules with double bonds!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to the grand dance of molecules! In the polymer world, monomers have two main ways of joining together to form huge chains: Condensation and Addition.

1. **Condensation Polymerization**: This is like making a sandwich and cutting off the crusts. When two monomers join, a tiny piece (usually a water molecule, H2O) gets squeezed out and 'condenses' away. Nylons (like Nylon 6,6 and Nylon 6) are classic condensation polymers. They spit out water when their amino and acid groups link up. We just learned Bakelite does this too (spitting out water to link its rings)!

2. **Addition Polymerization**: Imagine a bunch of people standing in a line, each with their hands firmly tucked into their own pockets. If they want to form a chain, they just pull their hands out and grab the person next to them. Nobody gets kicked out; everyone is included! In chemistry, molecules with 'double bonds' do this. The double bond pops open, and the carbons reach out to grab the neighboring molecule.

Now look at 'Buna - N'. It is a synthetic rubber. The name gives away its ingredients: 'Bu' stands for Butadiene, and 'N' stands for Acrylonitrile (Nitrile). Both Butadiene and Acrylonitrile have carbon-carbon double bonds. When they polymerize, their double bonds simply pop open and they all link hands. No water is lost! 

Therefore, Buna-N is an *addition* polymer, not a condensation polymer.

questions.Question: Q33. The correct match between Item-I and Item - II is: (I) Polymer of isoprene; (II) Polymer of 1,3-butadiene and styrene; (III) Polymer of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile; (IV) Polymer of chloroprene
questions.Hint: Look closely at the names! 'S' in Buna-S stands for Styrene. 'N' in Buna-N stands for Nitrile (acrylonitrile). And natural rubber comes from a tree as isoprene.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's become rubber experts! Rubbers are special polymers called 'elastomers' because they are elastic—you can stretch them, and they snap right back. Let's decode the secret identities of these four famous rubbers:

1. **Polymer of isoprene**: Did you know natural rubber comes from the milky sap of rubber trees? If you zoom into that sap with a microscope, you'd see millions of 'isoprene' molecules linked together. So, poly-isoprene is simply **Natural Rubber**.

2. **Polymer of 1,3-butadiene and styrene**: Let's look at the initials. We have **Bu**tadiene, **Na** (which stands for Sodium, the catalyst originally used), and **S**tyrene. Put them together: Bu-Na-S. This gives us **Buna-S**, a super tough synthetic rubber used in car tires!

3. **Polymer of 1,3-butadiene and acrylonitrile**: Similarly, we have **Bu**tadiene, **Na** (Sodium catalyst), and Acrylo**N**itrile. Put them together: Bu-Na-N. This is **Buna-N**, which is resistant to oil and used in engine seals.

4. **Polymer of chloroprene**: Chloroprene is a molecule that looks just like isoprene, but with a chlorine atom attached. When it polymerizes, it forms poly-chloroprene. Its commercial superhero name is **Neoprene**. It's thick, waterproof, and heat-resistant—exactly what scuba diving wetsuits are made of!

So the perfect matching is: I -> Natural Rubber, II -> Buna-S, III -> Buna-N, IV -> Neoprene.

questions.Question: Q34. Poly- $\beta$ -hydroxybutyrate-co- $\beta$ -hydroxy valerate (PHBV) is a copolymer of _______. 3-Hydroxybutanoic acid and 4-Hydroxypentanoic acid; 2-Hydroxybutanoic acid and 3-Hydroxypentanoic acid; 3-Hydroxybutanoic acid and 2-Hydroxypentanoic acid; 3-Hydroxybutanoic acid and 3-Hydroxypentanoic acid
questions.Hint: In old chemistry naming, the carbon right next to the acid group is 'alpha' (carbon 2), and the next one is 'beta' (carbon 3). So 'beta-hydroxy' means the OH group is on carbon number 3!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why regular plastic pollution is so bad? It's because nature's bacteria don't know how to eat it! But chemists invented **PHBV**, a special polymer that is *biodegradable*. Bacteria can eat it, making it super eco-friendly. It's used in special medical capsules that safely dissolve inside your body!

The full name of PHBV is a mouthful: Poly-$\beta$-hydroxybutyrate-co-$\beta$-hydroxyvalerate. Let's translate this from 'Chemistry' into plain English.

First, let's understand the Greek letter $\beta$ (beta). 
When naming a carbon chain that has an acid group (-COOH) at the end:
- The acid carbon itself is Carbon #1.
- The carbon directly attached to the acid group is Carbon #2 (also called the $\alpha$ / alpha carbon).
- The next carbon in the chain is Carbon #3 (also called the $\beta$ / beta carbon).

So, if a chemical says '$\beta$-hydroxy', it means there is a hydroxyl (-OH) group sitting on Carbon #3.

Now, let's break down the two parts of PHBV:
1. **$\beta$-hydroxybutyrate**: 'Butyr' implies 4 carbons total (like butane). Since the -OH is on the $\beta$ carbon (Carbon 3), its modern scientific name is **3-Hydroxybutanoic acid**.
2. **$\beta$-hydroxyvalerate**: 'Valer' is old chemistry slang for 5 carbons (like pentane). Again, the -OH is on the $\beta$ carbon (Carbon 3). So its modern name is **3-Hydroxypentanoic acid**.

Put them together, and you have 3-Hydroxybutanoic acid and 3-Hydroxypentanoic acid!

questions.Question: Q35. The polymer obtained from the following reactions is H2N-CH2-COOH + H2N-(CH2)5-COOH $\rightarrow$ ? [OC-(CH2)4-CO-NH-(CH2)6-NH]n; [NH-(CH2)5-CO-NH-CH2-CO]n; [O-(CH2)4-O-CO]n; [O-CO-(CH2)4-O]n
questions.Hint: Write down the two molecules. When they join, the -OH from the acid part (-COOH) of one molecule reacts with an -H from the amine part (-NH2) of the other, releasing H2O. What's left connects together!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's play a chemistry matching game to build a biodegradable plastic! 

We are given two molecules to mix together:
1. **H2N-CH2-COOH**: This is an amino acid called Glycine. Notice it has 2 carbon atoms in total.
2. **H2N-(CH2)5-COOH**: This is Aminocaproic acid. It has 6 carbon atoms in total (5 in the CH2 middle, plus 1 in the acid group).

Because one monomer has 2 carbons and the other has 6 carbons, the resulting polymer is famously called **Nylon-2-nylon-6**. But how exactly do they link up to form the structure in the options?

Think of these molecules like a train car with a coupling at the front and back. 
- The front coupling is the amine group (-NH2).
- The back coupling is the acid group (-COOH).

When the back of the Glycine train car (-COOH) bumps into the front of the Aminocaproic acid train car (-NH2), a reaction happens! The -OH from the acid and one -H from the amine pop off together to form water (H2O), which drops away. 

What is left? The Carbon of the acid is now glued directly to the Nitrogen of the amine! This creates a '-CO-NH-' bond (also known as an amide, or peptide bond).

Let's write out the new connected chain. 
We take the first guy (minus an H on the left and an OH on the right): 
-NH-CH2-CO- 
And we attach it to the second guy (also minus an H and an OH): 
-NH-(CH2)5-CO- 

Stick them together and put brackets around them to show they repeat 'n' times:
[-NH-CH2-CO-NH-(CH2)5-CO-]n

If you look at the options, the second option is the exact same chain, just written with the 5-carbon block first. Since it's a repeating circle, it's totally the same thing! [-NH-(CH2)5-CO-NH-CH2-CO-]n.

questions.Question: Q36. The homopolymer formed from 4 -hydroxy-butanoic acids is : [O-CO-(CH2)3-O]n; [O-CO-(CH2)2-CO]n; [O-CO-(CH2)2-CO-O]n; [CO-(CH2)3-O]n
questions.Hint: Think about how the acid group (-COOH) and the alcohol group (-OH) on the same molecule can hook together by losing a tiny drop of water.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there, young chemist! Let's build a polymer! Imagine a polymer as a super long necklace, and the individual molecules are the beads. The bead we are given is '4-hydroxy-butanoic acid'. Let's draw it in our minds: it has a chain of 4 carbon atoms. On one end, there is a carboxylic acid group (-COOH). On the other end, on the 4th carbon, there is a hydroxyl group (-OH). So, the molecule looks like this: HO-CH2-CH2-CH2-COOH.

Now, how do we link them together? This molecule undergoes 'condensation polymerization'. Think of it like two people holding hands, but to lock their hands together, they have to drop something they are holding. In chemistry, that 'dropped' thing is usually a small molecule like water (H2O).

When two of these molecules come near each other, the -OH from one molecule and the -COOH from the other react. The -OH loses an 'H', and the -COOH loses an 'OH'. Boom! A water molecule (H2O) falls out, and the two molecules link together through an ester bond (-COO-).

Let's look at the remaining piece (the repeating unit) that forms the chain:
We removed H from the left side: leaving us with -O-
We have the three middle carbons: -CH2-CH2-CH2- (which is -(CH2)3-)
We removed OH from the right side: leaving us with -CO-

So, the repeating block is: [-O-(CH2)3-CO-]. 
If we write it exactly like the options provided, we can just read it from right to left as well: [-CO-(CH2)3-O-]. This repeating unit gets stacked $n$ times to form our giant polymer chain. Therefore, the formula is [CO-(CH2)3-O]n. See how simple it is when you just track where the water leaves?

questions.Question: Q37. Major product of the following reaction is: HOOC-CH2-CH2-COOH (i) PCl5 $\rightarrow$ (ii) CH3OH $\rightarrow$ (iii) Na, ether $\rightarrow$ ? C6H5OH, C6H5OC2H5, C6H5CH2OH, C6H5OCH3
questions.Hint: Look out! The options provided in the original text are actually for a completely different aromatic reaction! But let's act like true detectives and solve the real chemical puzzle given in the question text.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! As a budding scientist, you will sometimes encounter poorly formatted tests where the questions and options get mixed up. This is a perfect example of a 'glitch in the matrix'! The options provided (which are variations of phenol and ethers) have absolutely nothing to do with our starting material, succinic acid (HOOC-CH2-CH2-COOH). But we aren't going to let that stop us. We are going to solve the actual chemistry happening here step-by-step.

Step 1: HOOC-CH2-CH2-COOH reacts with PCl5.
Think of PCl5 as a chemical 'scissor and glue' tool that loves to replace the -OH in carboxylic acids with a speedy Chlorine atom (-Cl). Since we have two -COOH groups, both get converted. 
Product 1: ClOC-CH2-CH2-COCl (Succinyl chloride).

Step 2: Reacting with CH3OH (Methanol).
Methanol is an alcohol. Alcohols love to attack acid chlorides to form esters. The -Cl drops off, and the -OCH3 takes its place. This happens on both sides.
Product 2: CH3OOC-CH2-CH2-COOCH3 (Dimethyl succinate, a diester).

Step 3: Reacting with Na in ether.
This is a legendary name reaction called the 'Acyloin Condensation'. When you throw sodium metal into a diester, the sodium acts like a generous friend throwing electrons at the ester groups. The two ends of the molecule reach around, bite their own tail, and form a ring! The carbon atoms of the ester groups bond to each other, eventually forming a cyclic compound with a ketone and an alcohol right next to each other.
Because our starting chain had 4 carbons, they form a 4-membered ring.
Final Real Product: 2-Hydroxycyclobutanone.

Even though the test options given (Phenol, Benzyl alcohol, etc.) are completely mismatched typos from another question, you now know the true, high-level organic chemistry happening behind the scenes. Always trust your chemical logic over a confusing multiple-choice list!
questions.Answer: 2-Hydroxycyclobutanone (Note: The provided MCQ options are from a different question due to a text error)

questions.Question: Q38. Which of the following is a thermosetting polymer? Bakelite; Buns-N; Nylon 6; PVC
questions.Hint: Think of the difference between melting butter and frying an egg. Which polymer acts like an egg that permanently hardens once cooked?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's talk about how plastics react to heat, using things you'd find in your kitchen! 

There are two main types of plastics (polymers) when it comes to heat: 'Thermoplastics' and 'Thermosetting' plastics.

Thermoplastics are like a stick of butter. If you heat them, they melt into a gooey liquid. If you cool them down, they harden again. You can do this over and over. PVC (polyvinyl chloride, used in pipes), Nylon, and Buna-N (a synthetic rubber) are all thermoplastics. Their polymer chains are like long, separate strands of cooked spaghetti that can slide past each other when heated.

Thermosetting polymers, on the other hand, are like a raw egg. When you heat a raw egg, it undergoes a permanent chemical change and becomes solid. You can never melt it back into a liquid! Why does this happen? In thermosetting polymers, heating causes the long molecular chains to form strong, permanent chemical bridges with each other, called 'cross-links'. It's as if all your strands of spaghetti suddenly glued themselves together into one giant, unbreakable net.

Bakelite is the classic example of a thermosetting polymer. Because it forms this heavily cross-linked 3D net, it is incredibly hard, heat-resistant, and won't ever melt. This is why it was historically used to make electrical switches, frying pan handles, and old rotary telephones. Therefore, Bakelite is our thermosetting champion!

questions.Question: Q39. Which of the following is a condensation polymer? Buna - S; Neoprene; Teflon; Nylon 6,6
questions.Hint: Look for the polymer that requires two different molecules to snap together while 'sweating' out a tiny molecule like water.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To solve this, you need to understand the two grand ways molecules hold hands to form long chains: Addition and Condensation.

Imagine an 'Addition Polymerization' like a crowded dance floor where people are holding their arms tightly to their own chests (this represents a double bond). When the music drops, everyone opens their arms and grabs the person next to them. Nobody leaves the room; they just open up and connect. Molecules with double bonds, like those in Buna-S (synthetic rubber), Neoprene (wetsuit material), and Teflon (non-stick pans), do exactly this. They just pop their double bonds open and link up. No atoms are lost!

Now, imagine 'Condensation Polymerization' as a handshake. But wait, both people are holding a small, annoying item in their hands (like a tiny water balloon). To lock their hands together permanently, they have to drop the water balloon. Every time a new person joins the chain, a small molecule (usually water) falls out. 

Nylon 6,6 is created precisely this way! It is made from two different starting materials: one with acid groups on its ends, and one with amine (nitrogen) groups on its ends. When they link up, they form a strong 'amide' bond, and in the process, they kick out a molecule of water (H2O). Because a smaller molecule is 'condensed' or eliminated during the process, Nylon 6,6 is our condensation polymer. It's the only one on the list that 'sweats' to build its chain!

questions.Question: Q40. The correct match between Item - I and Item-II is: (I) Peroxide catalyst; (II) Condensation at high T and P; (III) Ziegler-Natta catalyst; (IV) Catalysed by acid or base
questions.Hint: Remember that peroxide makes messy, branched chains (low density), while Ziegler-Natta builds perfectly neat, straight chains (high density).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
This question tests your knowledge of how we manufacture different plastics. Think of chemical catalysts as specialized 'factory machines'. Different machines produce different types of plastics!

Let's match them up logically:

(I) Peroxide Catalyst: When we use peroxides, the chemical reaction involves free radicals, which are super energetic and chaotic. They add onto molecules wildly, creating lots of branches. Because the polymer chains are heavily branched, they can't pack closely together. This gives us Low Density Polyethylene (LDPE), which is soft and flexible (like plastic grocery bags).

(III) Ziegler-Natta Catalyst: This is an amazing, highly organized catalyst (made of titanium and aluminum compounds). Instead of a chaotic reaction, it precisely lines up the molecules one by one. This creates perfectly straight polymer chains with no branches. Because they are straight, they pack tightly together, forming High Density Polyethylene (HDPE), which is tough and rigid (like thick plastic milk jugs).

(IV) Catalysed by acid or base: When we mix phenol and formaldehyde, we need an acid or a base to spark the reaction. This reaction creates a highly cross-linked, rock-hard resin known as Bakelite.

(II) Condensation at high T and P: Melamine and formaldehyde condense together under high temperature and pressure to form Melamine polymer, a tough plastic used in unbreakable dinner plates.

So the perfect match is: Peroxide goes with LDPE, Ziegler-Natta goes with HDPE, Acid/Base goes with Bakelite, and high Temp/Pressure goes with Melamine.

questions.Question: Q41. The major product of the following reaction is: HO-CH2-CH2-OH (i) HBr $\rightarrow$ (ii) Mg, ether $\rightarrow$ (iii) CO2 $\rightarrow$ (iv) H3O+ $\rightarrow$ ?
questions.Hint: Watch out for the trap! When Magnesium attaches to a carbon that is right next to a halogen-carrying carbon, it panics and undergoes a rapid elimination to form a double bond rather than acting like a normal Grignard reagent.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to one of the most famous 'traps' in organic chemistry! Test makers love to see if you are paying attention, and I'm going to teach you how to outsmart them.

Let's look at the textbook assumption first (the TRAP):
1) You see HO-CH2-CH2-OH (ethylene glycol) reacting with HBr. You might think, 'Ah! The OH gets replaced by Br to form Br-CH2-CH2-Br.'
2) Then you add Mg. 'Cool, it forms a di-Grignard reagent: BrMg-CH2-CH2-MgBr.'
3) Then you add CO2 and acid. 'Awesome, Grignard attacks CO2 to make a carboxylic acid. I'll get HOOC-CH2-CH2-COOH (Succinic acid)!'
BEEP! WRONG! But don't worry, here is the incredibly cool real-world chemistry that happens instead.

Let's look at the REAL reaction:
Step 1: The HBr (assuming excess) indeed replaces the -OH groups, giving us 1,2-dibromoethane (Br-CH2-CH2-Br).

Step 2: You add Magnesium (Mg). The Mg inserts itself between a Carbon and a Bromine to make a Grignard reagent: Br-CH2-CH2-MgBr. 
But here is the secret: Magnesium is a chaotic metal that loves electrons. The Carbon bonded to Mg becomes highly negative. Right next door, there is a Carbon attached to a Bromine, and Bromine is pulling electrons away, leaving that carbon positive. 
The negative carbon instantly says, 'Why wait to attack CO2 later when I can attack my neighbor right now?' 
The electrons from the C-Mg bond swing in to form a double bond between the two carbons, and the neighboring Bromine is kicked out. 

This is called an 'anti-elimination'. The molecule breaks apart, dropping MgBr2, and leaves behind Ethene (CH2=CH2), a gas!

Step 3 & 4: Since Ethene gas bubbles out of the flask, adding CO2 and acid does absolutely nothing. Ethene is completely ignoring the CO2. 

The final major product is simply Ethene. You just dodged a massive trap!

questions.Question: Q42. The copolymer formed by addition polymerization of styrene and acrylonitrile in the presence of peroxide is: [C6H5-C(CH3)-C(CN)H-CH2]n, [CH2-C(C6H5)H-CH2-CH(CN)]n, [CH2-C(C6H5)H-CH(CN)-CH2]n, [C(C6H5)H-CH2-CH2-C(CN)H]n
questions.Hint: Molecules have 'heads' (the bulky side with the complex groups) and 'tails' (the simple CH2 side). In a growing chain, radicals love to form on the bulky carbon, forcing the monomers to link 'head-to-tail'.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's piece together a copolymer, which is just a polymer made from two different kinds of building blocks (monomers) instead of just one.

Our two blocks are:
1. Styrene: CH2=CH(C6H5) (Let's call the CH2 the 'tail' and the CH(C6H5) the 'head' because the bulky benzene ring is there).
2. Acrylonitrile: CH2=CH(CN) (Tail is CH2, 'head' is the CH attached to the CN group).

The reaction uses peroxide, which tells us this is a 'Free Radical Polymerization'. A radical is a highly reactive, unpaired electron.
When the radical attacks a double bond, it has a choice: does it leave the new unpaired electron on the tail (CH2) or on the head (CH-group)? 

In chemistry, radicals are like VIPs—they need stability. The bulky groups (the Benzene ring C6H5, or the Nitrile group CN) are fantastic at stabilizing that lonely electron. So, the radical almost ALWAYS forms on the 'head' carbon.

Here is how the chain grows:
The growing chain has a radical on a head: ~CH2-CH*(C6H5).
It attacks the tail of the next monomer (Acrylonitrile): ~CH2-CH(C6H5) - CH2 - CH*(CN).
Notice the pattern? It is Tail-Head-Tail-Head! This is called 'head-to-tail' addition.

Let's trace our newly formed repeating block:
We have the tail of styrene: -CH2-
Then the head of styrene: -CH(C6H5)-
Then the tail of acrylonitrile: -CH2-
Then the head of acrylonitrile: -CH(CN)-

Putting it all together, our repeating unit is: [-CH2-CH(C6H5)-CH2-CH(CN)-]n.
If we look at our options, the second one matches this pattern perfectly! The bulky groups want their personal space, so they naturally alternate with the smaller CH2 groups in between them.

questions.Question: Which of the following statements is not true? Chain growth polymerisation involves homopolymerisation only; Chain growth polymerisation includes both homopolymerisation and copolymerisation; Nylon 6 is an example of step-growth polymerisation; Step growth polymerisation requires a bifunctional monomer
MCQ_Options: Chain growth polymerisation involves homopolymerisation only
Chain growth polymerisation includes both homopolymerisation and copolymerisation
Nylon 6 is an example of step-growth polymerisation
Step growth polymerisation requires a bifunctional monomer
questions.Hint: Think of addition polymerization (chain-growth) like building a long chain of Lego blocks. Do you have to use only one color of Lego block, or can you mix different colors?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's dive into the fascinating world of polymers! Imagine you are organizing a giant school dance. A polymer is just a massive molecule made by linking together thousands of tiny, repeating units, almost like a massive conga line on the dance floor. The single individuals joining the line are called 'monomers'.

There are two main ways to build this giant molecular conga line: Chain-Growth and Step-Growth.

1. Chain-Growth Polymerization: Imagine one highly energetic student grabs another, and they immediately grab the next, snapping together quickly. This is an 'addition' process where no atoms are lost. Now, if everyone in the line is wearing the exact same red shirt (meaning we are using the exact same molecule over and over), that is called 'Homopolymerization' (the prefix 'homo' means same). But what if a red-shirted student grabs a blue-shirted student, and they alternate or mix? That is called 'Copolymerization' (the prefix 'co' means together or mixed). Because chain-growth allows us to mix different types of monomers (like when scientists make Buna-S rubber for car tires by mixing two different molecules), the statement 'Chain growth polymerisation involves homopolymerisation only' is entirely false!

2. Step-Growth Polymerization: Now imagine a different dance where people must hold both hands with two different people in a very structured way. Every time two people lock hands, they drop a tiny sweat droplet (which in chemistry is usually a small molecule like water) onto the floor. Because they are condensing out a small molecule, we call this 'condensation' or 'step-growth' polymerization. Nylon 6 is a perfect example of this! Furthermore, to keep the chain growing in both directions, every molecule involved must have two reactive ends—in chemistry terms, it must be a 'bifunctional monomer' (meaning it has two functioning 'hands').

Therefore, by understanding the dance of atoms, we can clearly see that chain-growth definitely allows for mixing and matching (copolymerization), making the first option the incorrect statement in the real world of chemistry!
questions.Answer: Chain growth polymerisation involves homopolymerisation only

questions.Question: Which of the following is a biodegradable polymer? [NH-(CH2)5-CO-NH-CH2-CO]n, [NH-(CH2)5-CO]n, [NH-(CH2)6NH-CO-(CH2)4-CO]n, [NH-CH(CH3)-CO]n
questions.Hint: Look for a special copolymer designed from two naturally occurring building blocks: Glycine (2 carbons) and Aminocaproic acid (6 carbons).
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever wondered why plastic pollution is such a huge problem for our oceans and forests? It's because standard plastics (like the ones used in water bottles or grocery bags) are made of incredibly strong carbon-carbon bonds that nature simply doesn't know how to break down. Bacteria look at a plastic bag and say, 'I have no idea how to eat this!'

To solve this, brilliant chemists decided to invent 'Biodegradable Polymers'. These are special plastics engineered to look like the natural proteins found in our bodies or in plants. Since bacteria already know how to digest natural proteins, they can easily digest these special plastics too!

Let's look at the options provided:
1. The formula [NH-(CH2)5-CO]n is standard Nylon-6. It's tough and bacteria can't digest it easily.
2. The formula [NH-(CH2)6NH-CO-(CH2)4-CO]n is Nylon-6,6. It is famously used for sturdy ropes and clothing. Also not biodegradable.
3. But look closely at [NH-(CH2)5-CO-NH-CH2-CO]n. This incredible molecule is called 'Nylon-2-nylon-6'. 

Why is it called that? Because it is built by linking two different molecules together: Glycine (which has 2 carbon atoms) and Aminocaproic acid (which has 6 carbon atoms). The 'NH-CO' bonds you see holding them together are called amide bonds. In biology, we call these exact same bonds 'peptide bonds', which are the very same links holding the proteins in your muscles together! 

Because Nylon-2-nylon-6 mimics the structure of natural proteins with those peptide-like links, enzymes from bacteria can easily come along, snip the molecule apart, and digest it harmlessly back into nature. This makes it an amazing biodegradable polymer and a huge win for the environment!

questions.Question: Which of the following polymers is synthesized using a free radical polymerisation technique? Terylene; Melamine polymer; Nylon 6,6; Teflon
questions.Hint: Free radical polymerization is an 'addition' process that usually involves popping open carbon-carbon double bonds. Which of these is made from a monomer containing a simple double bond?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's explore the magical chemistry of how we turn gases or liquids into solid plastics! There are different techniques for doing this, but one of the most exciting is called 'Free Radical Polymerization'. 

Imagine a 'free radical' as a hyperactive, incredibly energetic molecule that has one unpaired electron. It's desperate to find a partner for its electron. When you introduce this hyperactive radical to a group of molecules that have carbon-carbon double bonds (let's call them the 'monomers'), the radical attacks the double bond, forces it to pop open into a single bond, and latches on. But in doing so, it passes its hyperactive unpaired electron to the other side of the monomer! Now, that monomer becomes the attacker, grabbing the next molecule, which grabs the next, creating a massive chain reaction that builds a polymer in seconds!

Let's evaluate the choices to see which one uses this chaotic, energetic method:

1. Terylene (also known as Dacron) is used in clothing fabrics. It is made by 'condensation' (step-growth) where two molecules slowly combine and drop out a water molecule. No double bonds are popped open here.
2. Melamine polymer is used in unbreakable dinner plates. It is also made via a slow condensation reaction, releasing water or formaldehyde.
3. Nylon 6,6 is the tough fiber used in ropes. Again, it is a condensation polymer formed by combining an acid and an amine, shedding water.
4. Teflon (Polytetrafluoroethylene)! Teflon is the incredibly slick material used to coat non-stick frying pans. It is made from a monomer called tetrafluoroethene (CF2=CF2). See that double bond '='? Under high pressure and with the help of a free radical catalyst, those double bonds pop open and snap together in a massive chain reaction, creating -[-CF2-CF2-]-n. 

Because Teflon is built entirely by popping open double bonds via an aggressive chain reaction, it is the classic example of a polymer synthesized using free radical addition polymerization!

questions.Question: Assertion : Rayon is a semisynthetic polymer whose properties are better than natural cotton. Reason : Mechanical and aesthetic properties of cellulose can be improved by acetylation.
MCQ_Options: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.
questions.Hint: Think about what 'semisynthetic' means. We take a natural polymer (cellulose from wood) and chemically tweak it (like adding acetyl groups) to make it shinier, softer, and stronger, essentially creating 'artificial silk'.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's put on our detective hats and solve an Assertion and Reason puzzle! 

First, let's look at the Assertion: 'Rayon is a semisynthetic polymer whose properties are better than natural cotton.' 
What does 'semisynthetic' mean? Imagine you find a cool wooden sword in nature, but you take it into your workshop and upgrade it with a metallic blade and a leather grip. It's half-natural, half-man-made. In chemistry, a semisynthetic polymer is one where we take a naturally occurring polymer and chemically upgrade it in a laboratory. 

Cotton is made of pure cellulose (a natural polymer from plants). While cotton is great, scientists wanted something that looked and felt like luxurious silk but was much cheaper. So, they took cellulose extracted from wood pulp and chemically modified it to create Rayon. Rayon has a beautiful, silky shine, drapes gracefully, and often feels superior to raw, plain cotton. So, the Assertion is undeniably TRUE.

Now let's look at the Reason: 'Mechanical and aesthetic properties of cellulose can be improved by acetylation.'
Cellulose is a long chain of sugar molecules with a bunch of hydroxyl (-OH) groups hanging off it. By reacting cellulose with chemicals like acetic anhydride, we replace those -OH groups with acetyl groups (-O-CO-CH3). This process is called 'acetylation'. Does it improve the properties? Yes! The resulting material, Cellulose Acetate (often called Acetate Rayon), is much shinier (aesthetic improvement) and has different tensile strengths (mechanical improvement). It becomes an 'artificial silk'. So, the Reason is also TRUE.

Finally, is the Reason the correct explanation for the Assertion? Yes! The very reason Rayon (specifically acetate rayon) behaves as an upgraded, semisynthetic polymer with better properties than natural cotton is exactly *because* chemical modifications like acetylation transform the plain, natural cellulose into a structurally enhanced, luxurious material. The chemical upgrade explains the better physical properties!
questions.Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.Question: Which one of the following structures represents the neoprene polymer? [C(C6H5)H-CH2]n, [CH2-C(CN)H]n, [CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2]n, [CH2-C(Cl)H]n
questions.Hint: Neoprene is a synthetic rubber derived from a molecule that has a chlorine atom attached to it. When its two double bonds open up during polymerization, they shift to form a single new double bond in the middle of the chain.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever seen someone wearing a tight, thick wetsuit while surfing or scuba diving? That wetsuit is made out of an amazing synthetic rubber called Neoprene! It keeps them incredibly warm by trapping a thin layer of water and acts as a fantastic insulator against the freezing ocean. But what does it look like on a microscopic level?

To understand the structure of Neoprene, we have to look at its building block (its monomer), which is called 'Chloroprene'. The chemical name for chloroprene is 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene. Let's break that name down:
- 'Buta' means 4 carbon atoms in a row.
- 'diene' means there are two double bonds (located at carbon 1 and carbon 3).
- '2-chloro' means there is a Chlorine (Cl) atom hanging off the second carbon.

So, the monomer looks like this: CH2=C(Cl)-CH=CH2.

Now, how does it become a long polymer? When we trigger addition polymerization (usually with free radicals), something really cool happens called '1,4-addition'. The double bonds on the outside edges pop open to grab onto neighboring molecules. But nature doesn't like to leave those middle carbons hanging! So, the electrons from the two original double bonds shift inward to form a brand new double bond right in the center, between carbon 2 and carbon 3.

If we map that out, the edges reach out to form the long chain (-CH2- ... -CH2-), and the middle gains a double bond (-C(Cl)=CH-). 

Putting it all together in brackets to show it repeats thousands of times, the structure of Neoprene perfectly becomes: [-CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2-]n.

Let's quickly check the wrong answers just to be sure:
- [C(C6H5)H-CH2]n is Polystyrene (used in styrofoam cups).
- [CH2-C(CN)H]n is Polyacrylonitrile (used in fake wool sweaters).
- [CH2-C(Cl)H]n is PVC (used in tough white plumbing pipes).

Therefore, the correct structure for our wetsuit rubber is [CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2]n!

questions.Question: Match the polymers in column - A with their main uses in column - B and choose the correct answer: (I) Making combs; (II) Tyres; (III) Making fabrics; (IV) Ropes
questions.Hint: Think about the physical properties needed for each object. Combs need a rigid, moldable plastic. Tyres need strong, heat-resistant rubber. Fabrics need soft, wrinkle-free polyester threads. Ropes need extremely high-tensile strength fibers.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Chemistry isn't just about formulas on a chalkboard; it's the science of making every single object around you! Let's play a matching game by looking at the physical jobs certain objects have to do, and finding the perfect polymer for that job.

(I) Making Combs: Have you ever accidentally dropped a plastic hair comb? Notice how it usually doesn't shatter, but it's hard enough to untangle your hair? Combs are traditionally made by molding a hard, easily shapeable plastic. The classic choice for this is 'Polystyrene' (which can be molded into hard objects, not just styrofoam) or Bakelite. Let's keep Polystyrene in mind.

(II) Tyres: Car tires take a massive beating. They spin at high speeds, endure friction, heat, and rough roads. You need a heavy-duty synthetic rubber for this. 'Buna-S' (Styrene-Butadiene Rubber) is the superstar here. It's a synthetic rubber specifically engineered to have incredible wear-resistance, which is why almost all car tires are made with it.

(III) Making fabrics: When you buy a dress or a shirt, you want a fabric that feels nice, dries quickly, and doesn't get horribly wrinkled. Natural cotton wrinkles easily. So, chemists created 'Polyester' fabrics. The most famous commercial polyester is 'Terylene' (also called Dacron). It can be spun into fine, strong threads that are perfect for weaving into clothing!

(IV) Ropes: Think about a mountain climber relying on a rope to save their life. That rope needs to have immense 'tensile strength'—meaning it won't snap when you pull on it really hard. 'Nylon 6' and 'Nylon 6,6' are synthetic fibers famous for their ridiculous strength. Because of the strong hydrogen bonds between the polymer chains, Nylon makes perfect parachutes, fishing lines, and heavy-duty ropes.

By matching the job to the material's superpower, we get: (I) Polystyrene for rigid combs, (II) Buna-S for tough tires, (III) Terylene for wrinkle-free fabrics, and (IV) Nylon 6 for unbreakable ropes. This perfectly matches our first option!

questions.Question: Which one is classified as a condensation polymer? Dacron; Neoprene; Teflon; Acrylonitrile
questions.Hint: Condensation polymers are created when two different molecules link together and 'sweat out' a tiny side molecule, usually water. Look for a polymer that requires two different functional groups (like an alcohol and an acid) to form.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To answer this, we need to quickly revisit the two main ways polymers are born: Addition vs. Condensation.

Imagine you are building a toy train. If you have a bunch of train cars that simply snap together end-to-end without any extra pieces falling off, that's called an 'Addition Polymer'. Every single atom from the original molecules stays in the final chain. 

However, 'Condensation Polymers' work a bit differently. Imagine two Lego blocks that can only snap together if you first break off a tiny little tab from each block. When these molecules chemically bond together, they have to eject a small molecule—like a tiny drop of water (H2O), hydrochloric acid (HCl), or alcohol—to make room for the new bond. They literally 'condense' something out.

Let's investigate our suspects:
1. Neoprene: As we learned earlier, this is made by popping open the double bonds of chloroprene. It's a pure snapping-together process. No atoms are lost. It is an Addition Polymer.
2. Teflon: Made by popping open the double bonds of tetrafluoroethene. Addition Polymer.
3. Acrylonitrile (which makes Polyacrylonitrile): Also has a carbon-carbon double bond that pops open to form a chain. Addition Polymer.
4. Dacron (also known as Terylene): This is the odd one out! Dacron is built by mixing an alcohol (ethylene glycol, which has -OH groups) with an acid (terephthalic acid, which has -COOH groups). When the -OH from the alcohol meets the -COOH from the acid, they undergo a chemical reaction to form an 'ester' bond. To do this, they literally squeeze out a water molecule (H2O)! 

Because water drops out during its creation, Dacron belongs to the proud family of Condensation Polymers!

questions.Question: Q50. Structure of some important polymers are given. Which one represents Buna-S? [CH2-C(CH3)=CH-CH2]n, [CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH(C6H5)H-CH2]n, [CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH(CN)H-CH2]n, [CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2]n
questions.Hint: Look at the name 'Buna-S'. 'Bu' stands for Butadiene, and 'S' stands for Styrene. Styrene is a molecule that features a large hexagonal benzene ring (C6H5). Which option has that?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Let's talk about polymers. Imagine you have a giant bucket of Legos. A 'polymer' is just a massive, long chain made by snapping thousands of tiny Lego pieces together. The individual Lego pieces are called 'monomers'. 

Sometimes, we make a chain using just one type of Lego. But sometimes, to get special properties (like making a material bouncy but also tough), we use two different types of Legos. This is called a 'copolymer'. 

Buna-S is a very famous copolymer, mostly used to make car tires! Let's decode its secret name:
1. 'Bu' stands for Butadiene. This is a 4-carbon molecule that has two double bonds.
2. 'na' stands for Natrium, which is the Latin name for Sodium. Sodium acts as the 'catalyst'—the helper that gets the reaction started.
3. 'S' stands for Styrene. Styrene is a molecule that has a big, chunky hexagonal ring of carbon atoms called a 'benzene ring', chemically written as C6H5.

When butadiene and styrene link up, they open their double bonds (like opening their arms to hold hands with each other) and form a long, alternating chain. 

Now let's look at your options like a detective:
- The first option has a CH3 (methyl) group. That's natural rubber (Polyisoprene).
- The third option has a CN (cyanide) group. That's a different rubber called Buna-N.
- The fourth option has a Cl (chlorine) atom. That's Neoprene.
- But the second option contains that big C6H5 benzene ring! That is the styrene part. 

Therefore, the second option represents the copolymer Buna-S, combining the butadiene string with the styrene ring!

questions.Concept: Classification of Polymers Based on Linkages
questions.Question: Q51. Which of the following polymer is a polyamide? Terylene; Nylon; Rubber; Vulcanised rubber
questions.Hint: Think of the word 'polyamide'. It means many 'amide' bonds. What famous synthetic material was invented to mimic silk (which is a natural polyamide) and is used to make parachutes and stockings?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Imagine you are making a necklace by tying strings of beads together. Depending on the type of 'knot' you use to tie them, the necklace gets a different name. In chemistry, polymers are exactly like these necklaces, and the chemical bonds holding the repeating units together are the 'knots'.

One very specific type of knot is called an 'amide' linkage. An amide linkage happens when a carbon atom (that is double-bonded to an oxygen atom) holds hands with a nitrogen atom. This bond is super strong. Interestingly, your body is full of polyamides! The proteins in your hair, skin, and muscles are held together by these exact same amide knots (biologists call them peptide bonds).

In the early 1900s, scientists wanted to create a synthetic artificial silk in a laboratory. They mixed certain chemicals together that specifically formed these amide knots. The result was a spectacularly strong, stretchy, and shiny material that they named 'Nylon'!

Let's check the other options to see why they are wrong:
- Terylene is tied together using 'ester' knots, so it's a polyester (like the material in lots of modern t-shirts).
- Rubber and Vulcanised Rubber are made entirely of carbon and hydrogen atoms connected by normal bonds—there is no nitrogen to be found, so they can't be amides.

Because Nylon is made of repeating amide bonds, it is our star polyamide!

questions.Question: Q52. [C6H5OH-CH2]n is the structure of
questions.Hint: The formula contains a phenol ring (C6H5OH) and a methylene bridge (-CH2-). Which tough, heat-resistant plastic is famously made by reacting phenol with formaldehyde?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's be molecular detectives again and break down this chemical formula: [C6H5OH-CH2]n.

First, we see 'C6H5OH'. If you've studied a bit of organic chemistry, you might recognize this as 'Phenol'—a hexagonal ring of carbon atoms with an -OH (hydroxyl) group attached to it. 
Next, we see '-CH2-'. This is a methylene bridge, and it usually comes from a molecule called formaldehyde (the simplest aldehyde, HCHO).

When you mix phenol and formaldehyde together and heat them up, something amazing happens. They start playing a game of chemical tag. The formaldehyde molecules act like little wooden bridges connecting the big phenol boulders together. 

Initially, they just form a straight, long chain. This linear chain is called 'Novolac', and it's actually used in making paints and varnishes! 
If you keep heating them and adding more formaldehyde, these straight chains start connecting sideways, building a massive, tough, 3D jungle gym. This incredibly dense 3D network is called 'Bakelite'. 

Bakelite is famous for being one of the first truly synthetic plastics. Because its molecules are locked together in this tight 3D web, it doesn't melt when heated. That's why Bakelite is used to make the handles of frying pans, old-school telephones, and heavy electrical switches. 

So, the repeating formula showing phenol rings linked by CH2 bridges represents the Phenol-Formaldehyde resin family, specifically starting as Novolac and curing into Bakelite!

questions.Question: Q53. The polymer used in making orlon is
questions.Hint: Orlon is a trade name for synthetic wool. Its monomer has a cyanide (-CN) group attached to an ethene molecule. The name starts with 'Polyacrylo...'
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever worn a cozy, warm sweater that felt just like wool, but the tag said it was made of 'acrylic'? You were likely wearing a relative of Orlon! 

Orlon is a clever invention by chemists to create an artificial version of sheep's wool. Natural wool is great, but it can shrink in the wash and is expensive. Chemists wanted to make something just as fluffy and warm, but cheaper and more durable. 

They started with a tiny molecule called 'Acrylonitrile'. Imagine a standard ethylene molecule (two carbon atoms double-bonded together, holding some hydrogens), but you swap out one of the hydrogen atoms for a Cyanide group (-CN). 

When you take thousands of these acrylonitrile molecules and trigger a chemical reaction, their double bonds break open, and they all grab hands in a massive chain. This creates the polymer 'Polyacrylonitrile', commonly abbreviated as PAN.

Once the PAN polymer is created, it looks like a thick liquid. Machines push this liquid through tiny holes (like a showerhead) to spin it into long, continuous, hair-like fibers. These fibers are spun into yarn to make Orlon! 

So, whenever you see 'Orlon', just remember it's the brand name for the superhero synthetic wool, scientifically known as Polyacrylonitrile.

questions.Question: Q54. Which of the following is a step-growth polymer? PVC; Nylon-6; Neoprene; Polyethylene
questions.Hint: Step-growth polymers generally form when functional groups react with each other, often dropping a tiny molecule like water in a 'condensation' process. Which of these isn't made by just unzipping double bonds?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
To understand this, you need to know the two main ways polymers are built: 'Chain-growth' (also called addition) and 'Step-growth' (also called condensation).

Think of 'Chain-growth' like a falling line of dominoes or a zombie movie. One molecule gets activated (bitten), and it immediately attacks the next molecule by breaking its double bond, which attacks the next, and the chain grows instantly, one piece at a time. Polyethylene, PVC, and Neoprene all form exactly like this. They all start as monomers with carbon-carbon double bonds. The double bond snaps open, grabs the next molecule, and repeats. Nothing is lost or left behind.

'Step-growth' is completely different. Imagine a giant dance floor full of people. First, people pair up into couples. Then, two couples join hands to make a group of four. Then groups of four join to make groups of eight! They grow in 'steps' across the whole dance floor simultaneously. Additionally, every time two functional groups link up, they usually 'sweat' out a tiny molecule, like a drop of water (H2O), leaving it behind.

Nylon-6 is classified broadly under this step-growth/condensation category. It is made from a molecule called caprolactam. When the molecules link together to form the amide bonds (the 'knots' we talked about earlier), they behave in a step-by-step manner, unlike the rapid-fire domino effect of double-bond addition polymers. Therefore, Nylon-6 stands out as the step-growth polymer here!

questions.Question: Q55. The monomer of neoprene is
questions.Hint: Neoprene is a special, chemical-resistant rubber. The prefix 'Neo' implies it's new/synthetic, and it was made by taking the structure of natural rubber and adding a Chlorine atom to it. What sounds like a mix of Chlorine and Isoprene?
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
If you've ever touched a thick wetsuit worn by scuba divers, or a soft, squishy laptop sleeve, you've touched Neoprene!

To understand Neoprene, we have to look at natural rubber first. Natural rubber comes from the sap of rubber trees, and its basic building block (monomer) is called 'Isoprene'. Isoprene is a great molecule, but natural rubber can get ruined by oil, gasoline, or extreme heat. 

Chemists wanted a tougher version of rubber. They took the basic backbone of isoprene and made one crucial substitution: they replaced a little side group with a big, tough Chlorine atom. 

This new, upgraded molecule is scientifically named '2-chloro-1,3-butadiene', but because that's a mouthful, chemists gave it a cool nickname: 'Chloroprene'.

When you link thousands of Chloroprene molecules together in a chain, you get 'Poly-chloroprene'. When this material was brought to the market, it was sold under the brand name 'Neoprene'. 

So, the secret ingredient—the monomer—that gives Neoprene its oil-resisting, tough-as-nails properties is Chloroprene!

questions.Question: Q56. The polymer which is used in the manufacture of unbreakable crockery is
questions.Hint: Think of the hard, shiny plates you might use at a picnic or in a school cafeteria that never shatter when dropped. The name of the key molecule sounds a bit like 'Melody'.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever accidentally dropped a plastic plate or bowl on a hard kitchen floor, expecting it to shatter into a million pieces, but it just bounced with a loud clatter? That 'unbreakable' plate is a marvel of chemistry!

Standard plastics, like the ones used in water bottles (Polyethylene), are made of long, single chains that can bend and melt. But if you want a plate to be stiff, heat-resistant, and virtually unbreakable, you need something stronger. You need a 'thermosetting' polymer.

To make this super-plastic, chemists mix a special chemical called 'Melamine' with our old friend 'Formaldehyde'. Melamine is a very unique molecule because it's shaped like a ring and has three separate 'arms' (amino groups) sticking out of it. 

When Melamine reacts with Formaldehyde, these three arms allow it to link up with other molecules in three different directions all at once! Instead of forming a single string of spaghetti, it builds a massive, rigid, 3D structure—like a steel jungle gym or a solid brick wall. 

Because all the molecules are tightly cross-linked and anchored together in all directions, the final material is incredibly hard and cannot be melted down again. This amazing material is the 'Melamine-formaldehyde polymer', and it is the exact reason your picnic crockery survives drops, bumps, and the dishwasher without a single scratch!

questions.Question: Q57. The monomer of bakelite is
questions.Hint: Think of the old, tough plastic used in retro black telephones and electrical switches. It is built from a benzene ring with an alcohol group and the simplest aldehyde.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hello there! Have you ever seen an antique, heavy black telephone or the hard plastic handles on your mom's cooking pans? That tough, heat-resistant material is almost always Bakelite! To understand Bakelite, let's first talk about what a polymer is. Imagine a giant Lego castle. The castle itself is the 'polymer' (the prefix 'poly' means many, and 'mer' means parts). The individual, single Lego blocks used to build that giant castle are called 'monomers'. 

Now, unlike simple everyday plastics that melt easily when heated, Bakelite is what chemists call a 'thermosetting' polymer. This means once it is molded into a shape, it stays that way forever—just like how you absolutely cannot un-bake a cake! But what are the exact Lego blocks (monomers) used to make this incredibly tough plastic? 

Bakelite requires two very special chemical building blocks: Phenol and Formaldehyde.
