Phenol is a ring-shaped aromatic molecule (a six-carbon benzene ring attached to an -OH group), and Formaldehyde is a tiny, highly reactive molecule with the chemical formula HCHO. When we mix these two together in a laboratory with a little bit of acid or base acting as a catalyst, they start holding hands. But they don't just form a single straight line; they connect in every possible direction—up, down, left, and right! This creates a massive, rigid three-dimensional web. Because all the molecules are tightly cross-linked together in this endless 3D net, the final plastic is incredibly strong and refuses to melt. So, whenever you see an old retro electrical switch, remember the tiny molecules of phenol and formaldehyde locked tightly together in a never-ending 3D handshake!

questions.Question: Q58. Which of the following is an example of natural polymer? Buna-S; Nylon-6; Cellulose; Teflon
questions.Hint: Look for the magical biological material that plants make to build their stems, leaves, and trunks.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey! Let's talk about the incredible world of materials around us. Polymers are everywhere. As you already know, a polymer is a giant chemical molecule made by chaining together thousands of smaller molecules called monomers. But did you know that long before human scientists started making plastics in laboratories, Mother Nature was already the ultimate chemist? 

We generally divide polymers into two main categories: Synthetic and Natural. Synthetic polymers are the ones humans invent and manufacture in giant chemical factories. For example, 'Buna-S' is a synthetic rubber we use for making tough car tires. 'Nylon-6' is a synthetic fiber used in sturdy ropes and athletic clothing. 'Teflon' is the incredibly slick synthetic coating used on non-stick frying pans so your eggs don't stick. 

But 'Cellulose' is entirely different! Cellulose is a brilliant natural polymer. It is the miracle material that plants naturally make to build their stems, leaves, and trunks. Think about a towering, 100-foot-tall tree standing strong against powerful hurricane winds. How does it manage to stay up? Because of cellulose! Plants take simple sugar molecules (glucose) that they generate during photosynthesis and snap them together like a massively long chain of unbreakable paperclips. Millions of these glucose chains bundle together to form thick cellulose fibers, giving wood its incredible strength. Even the soft cotton in your favorite t-shirt is almost pure cellulose! So, out of the options given to us in the question, Cellulose is the glorious natural polymer perfectly crafted by plants, while the rest are cooked up by humans in a lab.

questions.Question: Q59. The monomer of polythene is
questions.Hint: The name of the polymer is literally a massive cheat code! Just remove the 'poly' part of the name to reveal its building block.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome to one of the most brilliant and straightforward secrets in all of organic chemistry! Sometimes, scientists name things in a way that gives the entire answer away. You have definitely encountered polythene (which is also scientifically called polyethylene) in your daily life. It is literally the most common plastic in the entire world! Every time you carry groceries in a plastic bag, squeeze a plastic water bottle, or play with a flexible plastic toy, you are likely touching polythene. 

But what exactly is its 'monomer'—the single puzzle piece used to build it? Well, let's dissect the word 'Poly-thene'. The prefix 'Poly' translates to 'many' in chemistry. If we chop the word 'poly' right off the front, what are we left with? 'Ethene'! (Sometimes it is called by its older common name, Ethylene). 

Ethene is a very small, simple gas molecule made of just two carbon atoms double-bonded together ($CH_2=CH_2$). Imagine two carbon atoms facing each other and doing a high-five with both hands. In chemistry, that double hand-shake (the double bond) is packed with a ton of energy. Under the right pressure and temperature conditions in a chemical factory, one of those handshakes breaks open. Now, each carbon atom has a free hand reaching out, desperately looking for something else to grab. It perfectly grabs the carbon atom of the next ethene molecule, which grabs the next, and the next! 

Suddenly, thousands of ethene gas molecules have joined hands to form a massive, continuous long chain: $-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-$. Because these chains become so tremendously long, they tangle up like a massive bowl of cooked spaghetti, turning from an invisible, floating gas into the solid, flexible plastic we use every day. So, the monomer of polythene is simply ethene!

questions.Question: Q60. The polymer used for making synthetic rubber is
questions.Hint: Think of the stretchy, incredibly durable material that is famous for making wetsuits for scuba divers.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Let's dive into the bouncy, stretchy, and resilient world of rubber! You probably already know that natural rubber comes from the sticky, milky white sap (latex) of the rubber tree. But back during World War II, natural rubber was in incredibly short supply. Scientists had to become super-inventors and figure out a way to make artificial rubber in the laboratory to supply tires for heavy army trucks and fast airplanes. This urgent need led to the birth of 'synthetic rubbers'.

To make a synthetic rubber, chemists needed to create a polymer that acts exactly like a microscopic spring. When you pull hard on a rubber band, the tangled polymer chains uncoil and straighten out. When you let go, they instantly snap back into their messy, coiled-up shape. This unique physical property of bouncing back perfectly is called being an 'elastomer'. 

One of the most famous and successful synthetic rubbers ever invented is called Neoprene. Imagine a tiny monomer called 'chloroprene'. It looks a lot like the building blocks of natural rubber, but it has a sneaky, heavy chlorine atom attached to its side. When millions of chloroprene molecules chemically link up hand-in-hand, they form Poly-chloroprene, which we commonly call Neoprene. 

Why is Neoprene considered so awesome? The addition of that special chlorine atom makes this synthetic rubber incredibly tough. It doesn't break down or melt in heavy oil or intense sunlight the way natural rubber does. That is exactly why today, we rely on Neoprene for making high-quality scuba diving wetsuits, chemical-resistant protective gloves, and heavy-duty industrial hoses. So, when you think of synthetic rubber, immediately think of Neoprene—the tough, stretchy, lab-made cousin of natural rubber!

questions.Question: Q61. The monomer of terylene is
questions.Hint: The name 'Terylene' sounds very much like 'Terephthalic'. It is a type of polyester, which means it is created by reacting a double-alcohol with a double-acid!
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Get ready to learn about the hidden chemistry of your own clothes! If you check the tag on your favorite sports jersey, shiny jacket, or running shorts, you might see the word 'Polyester'. Terylene (which is also famously sold in the US under the brand name Dacron) is one of the most widely used and famous polyesters in the entire world. 

But how exactly do you make a polyester? Let's break the word down: 'Poly' means many, and 'ester' is a specific type of chemical connection. In organic chemistry, an ester linkage is formed whenever an alcohol (a molecule with an -OH group) reacts with a carboxylic acid (a molecule with a -COOH group). When they bump into each other in the lab, they link together to form an ester bond, and in the process, they spit out a tiny molecule of water ($H_2O$). This is beautifully called a 'condensation reaction', kind of like how water droplets condense on a cold glass on a hot summer day!

Now, to make a giant, never-ending polymer chain of esters (a true polyester), we can't just use normal everyday alcohols and acids. We need special molecules that have chemical 'hooks' on BOTH ends! Enter our two heroic monomers: 
1. Ethylene glycol: This is a di-alcohol, meaning it has an -OH group on the left side AND the right side. 
2. Terephthalic acid: This is a di-acid, meaning it has a -COOH group on BOTH ends. 

When we mix them together and heat them up, the left side of Ethylene glycol reacts with an acid, and the right side reacts with another acid. They link up, drop a molecule of water, link again, drop water again, and form an endlessly repeating giant chain. The name 'Terylene' is actually a clever mashup of its parents: 'TERephthalic acid' and 'ethYLENE glycol'. These incredibly strong polymer chains are spun into threads to make the wrinkle-free, super-strong clothing that you wear every single day!

questions.Question: Q62. The polymer used in the manufacture of laminates is
questions.Hint: It must be a thermosetting polymer that forms a tough, rigid 3D cross-linked network, often used to make shiny, hard, scratch-resistant surfaces on wooden tabletops.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Have you ever carefully looked at a beautiful, shiny tabletop, a wooden classroom desk, or the smooth countertops in your kitchen? Very often, the underlying wood is covered in a thin, incredibly hard, scratch-resistant plastic layer called a 'laminate'. You might have heard your parents or carpenters refer to it under popular brand names like Formica or Sunmica. 

To manufacture a heavy-duty laminate, we need a very special kind of plastic. If we used regular, soft plastic like polythene or PVC, it would instantly melt the second you put a hot coffee mug or a warm plate of food on it! We desperately need a 'thermosetting' polymer. A thermosetting polymer is a type of plastic that, once it is heated and molded into its final shape, locks permanently into a rigid 3D structure and can literally never melt again, no matter how much you heat it. 

One of the absolute best thermosetting polymers used globally for making these tough laminates is called 'Urea-formaldehyde resin'. The beautiful thing about chemistry is that the name tells you exactly what its 'Lego blocks' (monomers) are! The first monomer is Urea, a simple organic compound. The second is Formaldehyde, a highly reactive gas. 

When you scientifically heat urea and formaldehyde together, they don't just form a flimsy, straight line of molecules. They chemically react and form strong covalent bonds in every possible direction—creating a massively interconnected 3D web, much like a giant microscopic spiderweb made of solid titanium! This heavy 'cross-linking' is the absolute secret to its superpower. Once this 3D web is fully formed, the molecules can't slide past each other anymore. This is exactly why the laminate surface on your desk is so incredibly rigid, heat-resistant, and tough enough to gracefully withstand years of heavy homework, dropped textbooks, and spilled hot drinks!

questions.Question: Q63. The polymer used for making fibres is
questions.Hint: Think of the ultra-strong material famously used to make heavy-duty ropes, parachutes, and stretchy athletic fabrics.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Think about the incredibly tight strings on a tennis racket, the tough bristles on your morning toothbrush, or the ultra-strong ropes used by daring mountain climbers. None of these are made of metal or natural wood—they are entirely made of synthetic polymeric fibres! But what exactly makes a polymer act like a long string or a fibre instead of acting like a squishy rubber band or a hard, unbreakable block of plastic?

For a polymer to be successfully spun into a high-strength fibre, its molecular chains must be very long, perfectly straight, and fully capable of packing very closely together side-by-side. Imagine a tightly bundled package of uncooked spaghetti; because all the pasta strands are straight and packed tightly together, the whole bundle is actually very hard to break. If the polymer chains are loosely packed and messy, the final material will be weak. If they are tightly packed, the material becomes incredibly strong. 

One of the greatest, most legendary fibre-making polymers ever invented by chemists is Nylon-6,6. It playfully gets its name from its two specific monomers (Hexamethylenediamine and Adipic acid), which both happen to contain exactly 6 carbon atoms! 

When these two monomers link up to form long, straight Nylon chains, something magical happens in the microscopic world. The chains neatly line up parallel to each other and form 'hydrogen bonds' between one another. Hydrogen bonds are basically like tiny, invisible chemical magnets. These magnets tightly stick one polymer chain to the neighboring chain, strongly preventing them from slipping apart when you pull on them. Because these chains are magnetically locked together in perfect parallel alignment, Nylon-6,6 possesses extremely high 'tensile strength'—meaning it absolutely will not snap easily when stretched tightly. That’s exactly why Nylon-6,6 is considered the true superhero of polymers, perfectly suited for spinning into practically unbreakable fibres!

questions.Question: Q64. The monomer of nylon-6,6 is
questions.Hint: Nylon-6,6 has two numbers in its name. This is a big clue! It means it is made from two different starting molecules, and each of those molecules contains exactly 6 carbon atoms.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Hey there! Let's talk about how chemists make synthetic materials like nylon, which is used in everything from rock-climbing ropes to the clothes in your closet! In chemistry, a 'polymer' is a giant molecule made by linking together thousands of smaller molecules called 'monomers'. Think of a polymer like a massive freight train, and the monomers are the individual train cars.$

Now$, Nylon-6,6 is a very special type of train. The numbers '6,6' are a huge clue! They tell us that this train is built using two *different* types of train cars, and each of those cars is made of exactly 6 carbon atoms.$

The$ first monomer is called **hexamethylenediamine**. Let's break that scary name down: 'hexa' means 6, 'methylene' refers to carbon-based $	ext{CH}_2$ groups, and 'diamine' means it has two amino groups ($	ext{-NH}_2)$ acting as hooks at the ends. So, it has 6 carbon atoms in total!$

The$ second monomer is called **adipic acid** (also known as hexanedioic acid). This molecule also has exactly 6 carbon atoms, with two carboxylic acid groups ($	ext{-COOH})$ acting as hooks at its ends.$

When$ you mix these two chemicals together and heat them up, a super cool reaction happens! The amine hook ($	ext{-NH}_2)$ of the first molecule reaches out to the acid hook ($	ext{-COOH})$ of the second molecule. They lock together, but to fit perfectly, they have to kick out a tiny molecule of water ($	ext{H}_2	ext{O})$. Because they lose water to form the link, this is called a 'condensation' reaction. They keep linking up, alternating back and forth (A-B-A-B-A-B), until they form the giant, super-strong plastic chain we call Nylon-6,6. So, the two starting pieces (monomers) you need are hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid!

questions.Hint: Orlon is a synthetic material often used as a substitute for wool. Its monomer has a carbon-carbon double bond and a cyanide (-CN) group attached to it.
questions.Detailed_Explanation:
Welcome back! Let's dive into another famous polymer. Have you ever worn a really warm, fuzzy sweater that feels like wool, but the tag says it is made of 'acrylic'? That synthetic wool is often known by the brand name Orlon! Just like we saw with nylon, Orlon is a giant polymer chain made of tiny repeating units called monomers. But this one forms in a slightly different way.$

Imagine$ you have hundreds of kids standing in a room, and each kid has both hands tucked into their pockets. Right now, they are individual, unconnected units (monomers). If you tell them to take their hands out and hold hands with the kids next to them, they form a massive human chain! This process is called 'addition polymerization'.$

The$ specific 'kid' (monomer) used to make Orlon is a molecule called **acrylonitrile**. Its chemical formula is $	ext{CH}_2=	ext{CH-CN}$. Notice that equal sign in the middle? That is a carbon-carbon double bond. In our analogy, that double bond is just like having your hands in your pockets. During the chemical reaction, that double bond pops open into a single bond. The carbon atoms reach out their 'chemical arms' (which are actually electrons) and grab onto the neighboring acrylonitrile molecules.$

They$ do this over and over again, thousands of times, linking up into a huge, long chain called Polyacrylonitrile (which scientists shorten to PAN). The 'cyano' part of the name comes from that $	ext{-CN}$ group attached to the molecule. While the main carbon atoms build the long backbone of the chain, those $	ext{-CN}$ groups hang off the sides. These side groups strongly attract each other, pulling the chains tightly together. This is exactly what gives Orlon its amazing strength and its fluffy, wool-like texture that keeps you warm in the winter! So, the single building block for Orlon is acrylonitrile.
